item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees’ front office is reportedly not happy with what captain Aaron Judge said following the team’s ALDS exit against the Tampa Bay Rays. Judge, who couldn’t feature in the 2026 postseason due to a calf strain, said the Yankees need to go “all-in” so that they have the best chance to end their World Series drought since 2009.
According to New York Post’s Jon Heyman, a couple of executives in the Yankees organization were left “somewhat annoyed” by Judge’s comments. Heyman noted that the Yankees front office believes they did their best by re-signing Cody Bellinger to a five-year, $162.5 million contract last offseason.
MLB fans on X shared their opinions on the report.
“The Yankees clearly need to clean house. Top to bottom,” one fan wrote.
Here are more reactions:
After the Yankees were swept by the Rays in the ALDS, Judge called on managing partner Hal Steinbrenner and general manager Brian Cashman to address the roster’s weaknesses aggressively.
“We’re the Yankees,” Judge told reporters. “I feel like they should go all-in and do what they need to do and if we got holes, it’s finding certain players or personnel. Whatever we need, we’ve got to go out there and get it. That’s why I signed back here to play with the Yankees, is to fight for a championship every single year and go all-in. That’s what I do every off-season is to get ready to give this team and this city everything I got. So I expect them to do the same.”
Aaron Judge Names One Yankees Teammate Important to World Series Hopes
In ALDS Game 3, the Yankees were inches away from potentially tying the game with a two-run home run from Anthony Volpe. Due to fan interference, the hit was ruled an RBI double, as the Yankees remained one run behind the Rays and eventually lost 4-3.
Advertisement
After the postseason elimination, Yankees captain Aaron Judge rated Volpe highly for almost coming through in a clutch moment. Judge believes Volpe is a key player for the Yankees to reach the World Series.
“If we were gonna go win a World Series, we need Anthony Volpe on the team,” Judge said.
This is interesting because Volpe didn’t particularly have a fine regular season and was replaced by shortstop George Lombard Jr. on the active roster in the second half.
However, it appears Volpe has earned a vote of confidence from Judge after he delivered two hits, an RBI, and a run in the decisive 4-3 defeat to Tampa Bay.

item.title: [Empire Sports Media] Giancarlo Stanton no longer deserves the Yankees' DH keys
item.dc:creator: Alexander Wilson
item.description: I’d bring Giancarlo Stanton to camp without reserving the designated hitter job for him. The Yankees can give a familiar slugger a chance to earn at-bats without building another offense around the hope that his body cooperates. The Yankees already have a productive DH The cost of that hope has changed. Ben Rice now needs a substantial place in the lineup, and Aaron Judge’s availability deserves more thought than assuming he can handle the same assignment every day. Stanton isn’t competing for a
item.content:encoded:
I’d bring Giancarlo Stanton to camp without reserving the designated hitter job for him. The Yankees can give a familiar slugger a chance to earn at-bats without building another offense around the hope that his body cooperates.
The Yankees already have a productive DH
The cost of that hope has changed. Ben Rice now needs a substantial place in the lineup, and Aaron Judge’s availability deserves more thought than assuming he can handle the same assignment every day. Stanton isn’t competing for an empty spot anymore.
Rice started 95 games at designated hitter and 53 at first base this season. He hit 41 home runs with an .897 OPS. Treating DH as a job waiting for Stanton would ignore both the offense Rice supplied and how the club actually used him.
Stanton played 24 regular-season games, hitting .256/.302/.422 with three homers. Twenty-four games can’t establish what he can provide over a full year, and they certainly don’t justify putting somebody else’s productive at-bats behind his comeback.
Judge, meanwhile, appeared in 66 games. Using DH to reduce some of his outfield work is a reasonable option to examine, not a promise that it will prevent another injury. The Yankees should retain the ability to make that choice when their medical staff and the schedule call for it.
Keeping Stanton doesn’t require promising him the job
Bryan Hoch’s Friday offseason assessment left Stanton’s role unsettled. The Yankees haven’t supplied a final 2027 alignment, and there is no verified trade or release to write as though it’s already coming.
A healthy Stanton who is hitting can still make the decision difficult. The workable version would include selected starts, useful pinch-hit opportunities and more first-base work for Rice when the complete lineup supports it. Nobody should reject production just to prove a point about age or last season.
But that has to be earned through current health and current results. The Yankees shouldn’t promise the workload first and then spend the spring trying to fit Rice and Judge around it. Moving Rice to first more often also requires evaluating the defense and the other players competing for that position; it isn’t a free solution to every crowded lineup.
Stanton’s past power gives the club a reason to keep looking for a useful contribution. It doesn’t give him first choice of the assignment that could help protect Judge and keep Rice’s bat available.
For once, let the everyday plan work without a Stanton comeback. If he earns his way into it, the Yankees can make room for actual production instead of reserving room for a possibility.
More about:New York Yankees

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees will be among the most talked about teams over the offseason.
In addition to being one of the most notable sports franchises in the world, they had another letdown in the postseason.
After finishing the year with a 93-68 record in 161 games, the Yankees were swept by the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS (on their home field).
New York Yankees Paid 31-Year-Old $52.5 Million
One of their most notable players is Cody Bellinger.
The 31-year-old finished the 2026 season batting .264 with 131 hits, 17 home runs, 73 RBIs, 73 runs and 12 stolen bases in 132 games.
He is also arguably the best fielder on the team.
Cody Bellinger #35 of the New York Yankees watches his three-run home run against the Boston Red Sox during the sixth inning in game two of the American League Wild Card Series at Yankee Stadium on September 30, 2026 in the Bronx borough of New York City.
Bellinger became a free agent over the 2025 offseason.
The Yankees signed him to a massive new contract.
Based on his signing bonus, it’s worth noting that Bellinger was paid $52.5 million for the 2026 season (h/t Spotrac).
Cody Bellinger #35 of the New York Yankees celebrates his wife, Chase Carter Bellinger after winning the Ted Williams Most Valuable Player Award at the 2026 MLB All-Star Game at Citizens Bank Park on July 14, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.
While he did not have a huge year, he deserves credit for making his first All-Star Game since the 2019 season.
ESPN’s Jeff Passan wrote (on January 21): “Cody Bellinger’s deal with the Yankees is for five years and $162.5 million, sources tell ESPN. There are opt-outs after the second and third season, a $20M signing bonus and a full no-trade clause.”
Looking At Bellinger’s Other Stops
Cody Bellinger #35 of the Los Angeles Dodgers gestures after hitting a three-run home run during the fifth inning against the Houston Astros in game five of the 2017 World Series at Minute Maid Park on October 29, 2017 in Houston, Texas.
Bellinger was picked in the 4th round of the 2013 MLB Draft.
The 2019 National League MVP has also had stints with the Chicago Cubs and Los Angeles Dodgers.
He won the 2020 World Series title with Los Angeles.

item.title: [nydailynews.com] Mike Lupica: One more Knicks celebration and then it’s time to chase the elusive repeat
item.dc:creator: Mike Lupica
item.description: The Yankees have repeated as champs plenty of times, winning as many as five World Series in a row between 1949 and 1953. The Islanders won four Stanley Cups in a row in the 1980s, even though they did it a pretty long commute from the city. And the old New York Giants baseball team won twice in a row, but that was over 100 years ago. That’s it, the list of major sports teams from around here who have managed to defend their titles. Now the Knicks, starting Tuesday night, become the latest team
item.content:encoded:
The Yankees have repeated as champs plenty of times, winning as many as five World Series in a row between 1949 and 1953. The Islanders won four Stanley Cups in a row in the 1980s, even though they did it a pretty long commute from the city. And the old New York Giants baseball team won twice in a row, but that was over 100 years ago.
That’s it, the list of major sports teams from around here who have managed to defend their titles. Now the Knicks, starting Tuesday night, become the latest team with “New York” in its name to try and repeat. You’ve read a line that covers this here before, just because it’s one of my favorites, from the great old jazz trumpet player, Dizzy Gillespie:
“The professional is the one who can do it again.”
So one of the most professional teams we’ve ever had around here in anything, and one of the most appealing, now tries to do it again. Dizzy also said this one time: “As a musician you have to keep one foot back in the past, and have one foot forward into the future.”
After the banner is raised on Tuesday night — when it is Jalen Brunson and KAT, OG and Hart and Bridges on the court at the Garden against LeBron and them — the Knicks take their first giant step into their future. Four months after Game 5 against the Spurs we officially get the Knicks back on Tuesday night.
And you better believe we start to find out on Opening Night if they really can do it again.
You know what it would mean if they do? They will be doing something that Walt Frazier never did, and Capt. Willis Reed, and Dave DeBusschere and Bill Bradley. The old Knicks couldn’t repeat the first time they won an NBA title. And couldn’t repeat after they won the second title three years later, even with a dazzling talent like Earl (The Pearl) Monroe having been added to the band, not with Willis literally on his last legs and playing only 19 games before announcing his retirement.
But now, more than a half-century later, here is the chance for Brunson’s Knicks, at full speed and full strength. Start with Brunson, the star of everything, because where else are you going to start with? He gets his shot to lead his Knicks team to a title defense, something Frazier, the greatest Knick of them all, couldn’t do. They all made history as spectacular as any New York team ever made. Now they get a chance to make more. It seems as if the parade just rolled up from lower Broadway. Now it rolls all the way back into the Garden on Tuesday night. It’s like they say in that commercial, life comes at you fast.
Brunson is never going to win as many titles as Derek Jeter did, not in his sport. Everybody knows how it goes now in the NBA, eight different champs across the last eight years. This isn’t going to be Steph Curry’s Warriors. Knick fans are just looking for their team to just somehow make it two in a row.
Do it again.
If they never win again — and, hey, they might not — they have already taken their place with the most special teams the city has ever known. For one magical year and one magical run, Mike Brown’s Knicks did become Clyde and Willis and the rest of them. The Knicks Five — Brunson, KAT, OG, Hart, Bridges — became a Core Four plus one. As great as Brunson was, and as great as Karl-Anthony Towns was from the time they were down 2-1 in the Hawks series, they really were like the old Knicks in this way:
It was about all of them. Brunson was just the leader of the band the way Clyde was. After all the talk and speculation over the past few years about whether this guy or that guy was going to be the new face of the NBA with LeBron getting up there in years, the fact is that the Knicks became the face of the NBA. All of them. Running through the opposition the way they did once they figured it all out against the Hawks, running up the score almost at will, coming from behind when they had to do that. Of course there have been other memorable and even crazy runs around here in sports. The Giants got on one when they won their first Super Bowl with Tom Coughlin as coach and Eli finally throwing it to Plaxico Burress on the Sunday night when the Patriots didn’t get to 19-0.
But in your life, you never saw anything like what we saw from the Knicks last spring, when they turned the whole city into one loud basketball block party. There was never supposed to be a New York team as special as the old Knicks, as beloved a sports team as New York had ever known. That includes a miracle team like the Miracle Mets of 1969, or Namath’s Jets, or Messier’s Ranger back in 1994. The Rangers ended 54 years of waiting for the Stanley Cup. The Knicks ended 53. And as wonderful a moment as it was for the Rangers and their fans back in ‘94, what we saw in the spring of 2026 was different, it just was. It was basketball.
It was that. It was a comment like this from Josh Hart, who always seemed to put the right words, describing the sight of his ‘Nova buddy Brunson holding the O’Brien Trophy when it was over:
“We were just sitting there. … He has a trophy, and we’re sitting there like, ‘Bro, we really did this.”
They really did. This time Haliburton’s shot didn’t fall out of the rafters and through the basket. This time OG wasn’t hurt at the end of a 7-game series like that. This time the whole thing kept getting bigger and bigger, Brunson making one big shot after another and Anunoby flying in for that tip. This time they came from 29 points down in Game 4 before finishing the Spurs off in Game 5 and touching off a celebration that seemed to last all summer long.
On Tuesday night the Knicks will celebrate one last time when another championship banner is finally raised to go with the two the old Knicks won. After that, guess what? It’s no longer last season for the Knicks. They no longer have one foot in the past. This group, all of them, really does step into whatever their immediate future is going to be.
All those years after ‘73 with the Knicks when they had to wait ‘till next year. Just not like this. Not this time and not this team. Ring out the old, ring in the new.
OK FOR YANKEE FANS TO WANT MORE, GIANTS CAN STEAL THE EAST & GOTTA LOVE THE BANK OF LSU …
There is this notion that Yankee fans are holding the owner and general manager to too high a standard, measuring their work against great Yankee teams of the past.
Yeah … no.
Yankee fans aren’t looking for multiple World Series championships at this point, are you joking?
Just one.
Watching that Dodgers-Brewers series, I couldn’t help thinking that maybe $500 million doesn’t buy you nearly what it used to in baseball.
Pretty tough to root against Pat Murphy, right?
If Donald Arthur Mattingly wants to keep managing, fine with me.
Baseball is always better with him still a part of it.
Are Aaron Judge and his corporate masters going to need couples counseling?
It is going to be a little harder for baseball owners to act as if they’re facing the apocalypse without a salary cap in a World Series where the combined payroll of the two teams left standing doesn’t even come close to $300 million.
Jets against the Patriots in Foxboro is yet another chance for Aaron Glenn’s team to show that this season really can be different.
Jameis can’t throw it to Malik Nabers enough to suit me.
Man, Sean Payton looked scared to death of his quarterback on Thursday night, right?
One more thing on that one:
Do the Seahawks miss Kenneth Walker yet?
If only the Red Sox could have had a table-setter like David Hamilton.
Oh, wait.
Take another good look at the state of the NFC East and tell me again why the Giants can’t steal it.
The president obviously remains convinced that Ukraine invaded itself to start this war.
I was waiting for Katie Zacharia, who lasted five days as White House press secretary, to say that she used to describe herself as a lawyer during TV appearances because she watched a lot of “Law and Order.”
Has Lane Kiffin won the national championship yet?
You have to love the Bank of LSU, by the way.
They paid Kiffin $91 million to come to Baton Rouge not long after they paid Brian Kelly $54 million to leave.
So coaching there is kind of nice work if you can get it.
You’re probably as worried as I am that 24 playoff teams still might not be enough for the robber barons running college football.
This from Brian Windhorst’s ESPN column the other day, addressing the Knicks’ chucklehead contract standoff with Karl-Anthony Towns:
“Owners set the system up so that the players are forced into doing extensions to maximize their value and then the owners get angry when the players who have earned it want an extension,” one prominent agent said.
Man is it great news that Clyde is still doing Knicks games on television.
I’m frankly surprised no one blamed Cam Skattebo’s fumble on Aaron Boone.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees had another strong regular season where they went 93-68 in 161 games.
They finished as the second-place team in the American League East (and swept the Boston Red Sox in the Wild Card Series).
However, the Yankees had another letdown in the postseason (getting swept by the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS).
Yankees Legend Alex Rodriguez Was Right About Aaron Judge
The Yankees played most of the season without three-time MVP Aaron Judge.
He did not play in a 2026 playoff game.
During the middle of the season, Yankees legend Alex Rodriguez spoke about Judge.
Rodriguez (via WFAN on July 17): “For me, the way that Aaron Judge is such a transformational player, but what he means in that clubhouse, what he means to the fan base, ownership, and his teammates, he’s just one of one. So I think it’s very hard to win a championship without Aaron Judge.”
It’s fair to say that Rodriguez was right, as the Yankees came nowhere near winning a title in 2026.
ESPN’s Jeff Passan wrote (on October 7): “The best team in the league finishes the sweep and heads to the ALCS. A game-tying Anthony Volpe home run was overturned because of fan interference, and the Rays held their one-run lead for the final 10 outs. The Yankees haven’t won a title in 17 years.”
Looking At Judge
Aaron Judge #99 of the New York Yankees looks on from the dugout during sixth inning of the MLB game against the Arizona Diamondbacks at Chase Field on September 19, 2026 in Phoenix, Arizona.
Judge finished the 2026 season batting .241 with 57 hits, 18 home runs, 41 RBIs, 45 runs and five stolen bases in 66 games.
He has now spent 11 seasons in the MLB (all with the Yankees).
MLB.com wrote (on October 7): “Has a “moderate grade” strain of his right soleus muscle and was not active for AL Wild Card Series or Division Series.”
Aaron Judge #99 of the New York Yankees at bat in the sixth inning against the New York Mets at Yankee Stadium on September 13, 2026 in New York City.
While Judge has been one of the best three players in the MLB for a while, the Yankees have been unable to win a title.
The furthest he reached was Game 5 of the 2024 World Series when they lost to the Los Angeles Dodgers.

item.title: [Yanks Go Yard] Yankees' silence about Aaron Boone, Brian Cashman end-of-season press conferences is getting deafening
item.dc:creator: Colin Keane
item.description: The New York Yankees' 2026 season ended in familiar fashion, with the Yanks vanquishing the Boston Red Sox in the AL Wild Card Series and then getting completely dominated in the ALCS by a separate AL East rival. It was the Tampa Bay Rays this year who embarrassed Aaron Boone's club (slightly different from last year's ALDS loss to the Toronto Blue Jays), and Boone's taken plenty of flak from the fanbase and media in the days since the Yankees' season officially ended. So has GM Brian Cashman. W
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees' 2026 season ended in familiar fashion, with the Yanks vanquishing the Boston Red Sox in the AL Wild Card Series and then getting completely dominated in the ALCS by a separate AL East rival.
It was the Tampa Bay Rays this year who embarrassed Aaron Boone's club (slightly different from last year's ALDS loss to the Toronto Blue Jays), and Boone's taken plenty of flak from the fanbase and media in the days since the Yankees' season officially ended. So has GM Brian Cashman.
What's made the buzz all the more ominous is that neither Boone nor Cashman have appeared for the customary end-of-season press conference. Fans are wondering what's taking so long.
Why haven't the Yankees held or even announced an end-of-season presser?
Last season, the Yankees allowed eight days to elapse between their elimination at the hands of the Jays (on October 8) and their end-of-season presser (October 16). On an identical schedule, this would have Cashman and Boone "due" to appear before the media at any moment, seeing as the Yanks were booted out of the playoffs this time around on October 7. But we haven't heard a peep from the organization about when the presser's going to take place. All we have so far is Bob Klapisch saying "the silence will likely be broken next week". Odd.
So, for now, we'll have to bank on comments from both Boone and Cashman that were made during the final hours of the season. Speaking after Game 3, Boone described the Yankees' clubhouse as "broken" and said that conversations about his job security were "for another day" while indicating that he expects to return in 2027. Cashman, whose contract is up, called Boone a "really good manager" before Game 3.
We also heard from Yankees captain Aaron Judge shortly after his team was bounced. Judge backed Boone publicly (but does he actually feel this way?) and vaguely suggested that the front office should go all in this offseason (nothing resembling a demand that would've pleased many fans).
So, yes ... we've heard from individuals, but there hasn't been the collective presser from the Boone/Cashman brain trust that everyone's anticipating. Surely, once the press conference does happen, both men will be asked once again to explain the decision to keep Judge and his ailing calf on ice throughout the postseason.
But there are far more ominous questions swirling around the Yankees, especially concerning Boone's future. Plenty of analysts (Buster Olney among them) assume the Yankees will stick with Boone for at least one more season. This makes some sense, especially given a possible lockout. Transitioning to a new leader during a time filled with many unknowns might be an unwise move.
Are the Yankees delaying their end-of-year press conference due to Aaron Boone?
The Boone situation is a complicated one. He did a great job this regular season (perhaps his best season as Yankees manager!), considering all of the injuries the Yankees suffered, most of all Judge's missed time. But another playoff failure was simply too much for many fans and former players to swallow. There's a growing narrative that change is needed. The "Yankee Standard" has been lost and must be found. Why should Boone be tasked with finding it? On the other hand, if not Boone, who?
Stability isn't the issue here. The Yankees are incredibly consistent and have been under the Cashman/Boone regime. It's just that they are consistently good, not great. And that's not what Yankees culture is actually about, historically. It's about championships, and nothing less. The mindset of George Steinbrenner no longer rules over this franchise, and it all feels very un-Yankee-like.
Understandably, continued silence from the organization about the end-of-season presser has fans' imaginations on fire. Is Hal Steinbrenner contemplating firing Boone? And what of Cashman's fate? The longer we don't hear anything, the weirder and wilder the fan fictions and made-up explanations will become. At this point, it behooves the Yankees to just come out and make an announcement, even if it's just to say that the presser's being delayed.

item.title: [Pinstripe Alley] The top five Yankees’ pitching performances of 2026
item.dc:creator: Matt Ferenchick
item.description: While the 2026 Yankees season has come to a frustratingly early end, it’s hard to blame much of that on the starting pitching. By several measures, the Yankees had one of the best rotations in all of baseball this year, and they have the favorite for the AL Cy Young Award in Cam Schlittler. As part of our season in review, let’s take a look back at some of the rotation’s best efforts of the year. To do that, we’re going to rank them according to the Game Score statistic. Game Score takes a varie
item.content:encoded:
While the 2026 Yankees season has come to a frustratingly early end, it’s hard to blame much of that on the starting pitching. By several measures, the Yankees had one of the best rotations in all of baseball this year, and they have the favorite for the AL Cy Young Award in Cam Schlittler.
As part of our season in review, let’s take a look back at some of the rotation’s best efforts of the year. To do that, we’re going to rank them according to the Game Score statistic. Game Score takes a variety of stats from an outing and combines them to try and determine how dominant a pitcher’s outing. Fifty is generally about average, and if a pitcher nears 100, they’re probably putting up an all-time great outing. While we didn’t get any no-hitters or perfect games this year, the Yankees’ rotation still had its fair share of excellent outings, let’s look back at the best of them.
This is a post of the top five, but there was a three-way tie for fifth, so it’ll actually include two bonus games too.
One could hope that Schlittler’s Game 2 start in the ALDS against the Rays harkened back to a regular season outing he had against Tampa Bay. Facing the Rays on July 6th, Schlittler allowed one run on four hits, while striking out eight in eight innings. None of the hits he allowed were more than a single, it’s just that one of them was to the speedy Chandler Simpson, which led to him scoring on another single.
Sneaking onto the list as part of that three-way tie for fifth is, surprise, another Schlittler start. This is the only game on the list that the Yankees ended up losing, but you can hardly blame that on the Yankees’ Cy Young candidate. In his seven frames, he held Atlanta to one run on three hits while striking out 11. Thankfully the Yankees scored a run in the eighth and the loss came in extra innings, so Schlittler didn’t get dinged with a loss for that gem.
You’ll never be able to guess who the pitcher who had the other game tied for fifth is…
While it wasn’t as statistically dominant as his start against the Red Sox in the 2025 AL Wild Card Series, Schlittler’s 2026 outing was still plenty good enough to crack this list. He only went 6.1 innings this time around, but held the Red Sox to just two hits, while striking out 10. The Yankees’ lineup poured it on late on route to a win and an eventual dominant sweep of Boston. If only the rest of the postseason went that well…
Someone else has finally made an appearance on the list. Injuries limited Fried to just 112.2 innings this season, but statistically he was still very good. This performance against the Red Sox was part of that. Having been given a 3-0 lead to work with after the top of the first, Fried proceeded to go eight scoreless innings, allowing just three hits and two walks, striking out nine Boston batters.
Normal service has resumed as Schlittler matched Fried to tie for third place. However, this was another game where he ended up with a no decision thanks to the offense. In eight innings, Schlittler held the Angels to one run on two hits, striking out nine. The only issue was that one of those hits was a Vaughn Grissom homer that tied the game at one in the seventh inning. The Yankees eventually broke through with five runs in the top of the 10th inning to seal the win, although they deprived their ace of the victory.
As it turned out, there was also a tie for first and, yes, Schlittler was involved. In July, he held a potentially very powerful Phillies’ lineup to no runs in 7.1 innings, surrendering just three hits all game. He struck out 12 batters, including Trea Turner and Bryce Harper twice each.
Tying Schlittler for the top spot is a Rodón start that had people wondering what order the playoff rotation should go in. Against the Rays in late September, Rodón threw eight shutout frames, allowing just three hits in arguably his best ever start as a Yankee. He also reached a milestone in getting to the 1500 strikeout mark during the outing.
The start — and his stretch run in general — was good enough that it led to people suggesting that Rodón should get the ball for one of the AL Wild Card Series games. In the end, they went with Schlittler, Fried, and Gerrit Cole had their been a Game 3. As it worked out, Rodón didn’t end up pitching at all in the playoffs. You can debate whether that should’ve been the case, but it’s hard to blame any of the starting pitchers for their ALDS losses.
Those are the best starts of the year according to Game Score, but which ones were the most memorably good to you?

item.title: [hitc.com] Aaron Judge makes Anthony Volpe's importance clear after Yankees elimination
item.dc:creator: Aryan Chadha
item.description: Aaron Judge has made it clear that Anthony Volpe remains an important part of the New York Yankees’ plans after their latest failed attempt to win the World Series. The Yankees were eliminated in the American League Division Series, extending their wait for another championship as questions grow over the direction of the franchise. Judge missed the entire post-season through injury but still spoke about what the team needs to succeed, with Volpe receiving a strong vote of confidence from the cap
item.content:encoded:
Aaron Judge has made it clear that Anthony Volpe remains an important part of the New York Yankees’ plans after their latest failed attempt to win the World Series.
The Yankees were eliminated in the American League Division Series, extending their wait for another championship as questions grow over the direction of the franchise.
Judge missed the entire post-season through injury but still spoke about what the team needs to succeed, with Volpe receiving a strong vote of confidence from the captain.
Aaron Judge believes Anthony Volpe can help the New York Yankees win a World Series
Speaking after the Yankees’ elimination, Judge said: “If we were gonna go win a World Series, we need Anthony Volpe on the team.”
The comments will mean plenty to Volpe, who has endured a difficult spell since arriving in New York as one of baseball’s most promising shortstop prospects.
Comparisons with Derek Jeter followed Volpe early in his career, but his struggles eventually led to the Yankees sending him back to the minors this season.
He returned to the major league side and showed improvement after moving to second base, particularly while filling in for the injured Jazz Chisholm in September.
Volpe’s defensive work and improved offence appear to have impressed Judge, who believes the infielder can help the Yankees compete for a championship with their current core.
That backing could become even more significant as New York considers its infield options for next season.
Chisholm’s future is uncertain after a disappointing season, with the report suggesting the Yankees could struggle to match offers from other teams. He was also booed by fans during his final at-bat in Game 3 of the ALDS.
Volpe started ahead of Chisholm in the Yankees’ final game against the Tampa Bay Rays, further fuelling questions about the club’s plans.
Judge’s public support also comes at a time when the captain has faced criticism for previous comments about potential team additions and the organisation’s spending.
With the Yankees once again falling short of their ultimate goal, Judge’s leadership will be under scrutiny. Volpe now has an opportunity to justify the faith placed in him and establish himself as a key part of the team’s plans for 2027.

item.dc:creator: Jake Devin
item.description: The Athletic | Chris Kirschner: The Yankees are reportedly unlikely to give Jazz Chisholm Jr. a qualifying offer, and it seems like the second baseman's time in the Bronx is just about over. That leaves the question: what do the Yankees do at second base? Captain Aaron Judge seems to have his preferred choice, telling reporters after the Yankees' ALDS exit, "If we were gonna go win the World Series, we needed Anthony Volpe on the team." Volpe did look comfortable at second after losing his short
item.content:encoded:
The Athletic | Chris Kirschner: The Yankees are reportedly unlikely to give Jazz Chisholm Jr. a qualifying offer, and it seems like the second baseman's time in the Bronx is just about over. That leaves the question: what do the Yankees do at second base? Captain Aaron Judge seems to have his preferred choice, telling reporters after the Yankees' ALDS exit, "If we were gonna go win the World Series, we needed Anthony Volpe on the team." Volpe did look comfortable at second after losing his shortstop job to George Lombard Jr., but Volpe's work with the bat still leaves plenty to be desired. Luis García Jr. is an interesting option; he's played second before (albeit with terrible defensive metrics), and looked so skilled defensively at first this year that he could convince you his agility and arm strength would play elsewhere on the diamond.
New York Daily News | Peter Sblendorio: There haven't been many ex-Yankees kicking around postseason, but one former Bomber has figured prominently in Jake Bauers. Bauers played for the club in 2023 and got off to a hot start, hitting a home run in his first game and posting a .899 OPS over his first ten games with the Yankees.
Bauers couldn't keep it going that year (neither could the Yankees) and New York ended up trading him in the offseason to the Brewers in exchange for minor league outfielder Jace Avina, who is now the Yankees' No. 24 rated prospect by MLB Pipeline. On the other end, Bauers has blossomed with the Brewers, running an .874 OPS this season and taking home deserved 2026 NLCS MVP honors.
MLB.com | Bryan Hoch: Hoch delivers his offseason preview for the Yankees, running down some of the big questions. Among them is the aforementioned second base situation, as well as the matter of what to do with Giancarlo Stanton, Austin Wells' future with the Yankees, and David Bednar's fate. Unlike Chisholm, Bednar appears likely to receive a qualifying offer, which is slated to come in at about $23 million for the 2027 season.
The Athletic | Tim Britton: The upcoming MLB free agent class is among the worst in recent memory, and The Athletic looked at the last decade of free agent classes with the benefit of hindsight to get a sense of where this group may fall. The lowest-ranked class ends up as 2017, when the top hitters to sign were Yoenis Cespedes, Dexter Fowler, and Ian Desmond, while the top pitchers were Aroldis Chapman, Kenley Jansen, and Rich Hill. The saving grace for the current crop of free agents is a fairly deep group of pitching targets, headlined by Tarik Skubal but backed up by Michael King, Sonny Gray, Kevin Gausman, and Freddy Peralta. That's somewhat unfortunate news for the Yankees, who nary need an arm but have an offense that could use reinforcements.

item.title: [Yardbarker] 'Held Aaron Judge Responsible': Yankees Star’s Feud With Front Office Exposed As Analyst Delivers Blunt Take
item.dc:creator: Srijanee Chakraborty
item.description: The Tampa Bay Rays swept the New York Yankees in three games to advance from the AL Division Series. Yankees captain Aaron Judge, meanwhile, missed all five of the team’s postseason games after being sidelined with a calf injury. Yet after the team’s elimination, the captain held the front office responsible. However, his remarks backfired as an analyst demanded more accountability from Judge. “It’s about time somebody held Aaron Judge accountable,” said Sal Licata on @Honda SportsNite, per SNY
item.content:encoded:
The Tampa Bay Rays swept the New York Yankees in three games to advance from the AL Division Series. Yankees captain Aaron Judge, meanwhile, missed all five of the team’s postseason games after being sidelined with a calf injury. Yet after the team’s elimination, the captain held the front office responsible. However, his remarks backfired as an analyst demanded more accountability from Judge.
“It’s about time somebody held Aaron Judge accountable,” said Sal Licata on @Honda SportsNite, per SNY Yankees.
“I mean, this is the second straight year that Judge threw his manager under the bus. He did it at the end of last year, and obviously this year in the postseason for a ridiculous reason….And then he goes after the organization.”
The Yankees survived a major part of the regular season without Aaron Judge. The captain fractured his first right rib and missed 84 games since early June. Following his return in September, Judge again landed on the IL due to a Grade 2 calf strain.
The latter injury kept Judge off the postseason roster. The decision did not sit well with him. He butted heads with skipper Aaron Boone, publicly expressing his desire to play in the postseason. But Boone picked a healthy roster over him, sidelining Judge.
It was not a problem in the AL Wild Card Series, as the Yankees swept the Boston Red Sox. However, it was an entirely different ballgame against the Tampa Bay Rays. In Game 1, the Yankees struggled offensively and were shut out 1-0. In Game 2, Freddy Peralta dominated the Yankees lineup as New York lost 5-2. Game 3 was riddled with defensive miscues, and Anthony Volpe’s potential game-changing homer was nullified due to fan interference.
As the Yankees dismantled both defensively and offensively, Judge could only watch from the dugout. However, he could have hit a home run or two if he had been healthy and in the lineup. Judge’s health matters because during the brief 7-game return he made in September, Judge hit only .174. With Grade 2 calf strains taking 4-to-6 weeks to heal, Boone’s decision was not unfounded. Judge may not have liked it like last year, but the manager was not in the wrong.
After the Yankees exited the postseason, Aaron Judge then turned his attention to the front office. Despite having the 3rd highest payroll in MLB, the Yankees’ captain wanted the front office to go “all-in” in the offseason. “We’re the Yankees,” Judge reportedly said. “I feel like they should go all in and do what they need to do and find. If we’ve got holes, if it’s finding certain players or personnel, whatever we need, you’ve got to go out there and get it.”
Apart from disagreeing with Boone’s decision not to play him, Judge has not lost his faith in the manager. However, recent reports claim that the Yankees brass are not pleased with Judge’s observation.
Insider Jon Heyman wrote, “Sources say one or two Yankees [bigwigs] were slightly to somewhat annoyed that captain/three-time MVP Judge suggested the $320M Yankees could spend more after they were swept by the Rays in the division series. Yankees higher-ups will get over it because Judge has a great rapport with them. But they were said to be taken aback.” While Aaron Judge was concerned about the front office’s approach in the offseason, some analysts have questioned his ability to stay healthy during the regular season.
“I think health continues to haunt this team. I really do,” Joe Girardi reportedly observed. In 2026, the Yankees were missing two key players in the lineup due to injuries: Giancarlo Stanton and Judge. Calf strains hampered Stanton throughout the season. After missing most of the regular season, Stanton appeared in 2 games against the Rays and failed to make an impact.
Whereas the Yankees’ captain remained out of the lineup the entire postseason. At 34, Judge’s good years at the plate might be limited, and Licata wants the Yankees’ captain to take responsibility for the team.
More must-reads:
Get the latest news and rumors, customized to your favorite sports and teams. Emailed daily. Always free!

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are coming off another strong regular season where they had a let down in the MLB playoffs.
They got swept by the Tampa Bay Rays (on October 7) in the ALDS.
Yankees Star Aaron Judge Was Wrong
One of the biggest disappointments during the season was the play of Ryan McMahon.
The 2024 All-Star batted just .213 with 70 hits, 11 home runs, 41 RBIs, 33 runs and three stolen bases in 124 games.
Before the season, three-time MVP Aaron Judge had high hopes for McMahon.
Ryan McMahon #19 of the New York Yankees in action during the game against the St. Louis Cardinals at Yankee Stadium on August 04, 2026 in the Bronx borough of New York City.
Judge spoke about McMahon in an interview with NBA star Kevin Durant (via Boardroom) that aired on March 25.
Durant: “Who are some of the players on your team, underrated players you feel is going to have a breakout season for y’all this year?…Who do you feel is the X-factor for y’all to take that next step? I’m sure all of you guys need to step up, but who do you think is that guy that’s going to help push y’all over the top that not too many people know about?”
Judge: “I got three guys in mind… Ryan McMahon. We got him from the Rockies. I think there’s just so much more potential in there, man. He’s had a great career with Colorado, but man, this guy’s a Gold Glove defender, but I think what he’s about to do with the bat this year, he’s going to take off for us.”
Looking At McMahon
Ryan McMahon #19 of the New York Yankees looks on during batting practice prior to the game against the Chicago White Sox at Rate Field on August 28, 2025 in Chicago, Illinois.
McMahon has now been with the Yankees for part of two seasons.
He had spent the first 8.5 seasons of his career with the Colorado Rockies (and hit 20+ home runs six times).
MLB.com wrote (on July 25, 2025): “Colorado Rockies traded 3B Ryan McMahon to New York Yankees for RHP Josh Grosz and LHP Griffin Herring.”
So far, the trade has not been a good one for the Yankees.

item.content:encoded:
New York Yankees skipper Aaron Boone is facing heat after their postseason elimination.
They haven’t won a World Series since 2009, extending their dreadful drought for yet another season.
Boone has been at the helm since 2018, but fans want him out now.
While it seems unlikely to lose his job this offseason, it never hurts to ponder the what-ifs.
Who Could Take Over for Yankees’ Aaron Boone?
Hypothetically, if Boone were to get fired, here are a few of the names floating around as replacements:
Buck Showalter
Showalter served as New York’s manager from 1992 to 1995.
Following his stint with the Yankees, he managed the Arizona Diamondbacks, Texas Rangers, Baltimore Orioles and New York Mets.
Bill Madden of the New York Daily News suggested firing Boone and calling up Showalter.
“I would then place a call to Buck Showalter, a fountain of baseball knowledge and insight, and ask him to come back home to the Bronx, where it all began for him in 1992, and straighten out this ballclub and the culture,” he wrote.
His experience alone would be beneficial, but it would also raise a few eyebrows.
Nonetheless, he did play a major role in laying a solid foundation for the Yankees all those years ago.
George Lombard Sr.
An interesting managerial pitch was tossed by Stephen Parello of FanSided last week regarding a Yankees-George Lombard Sr. possibility.
“The connection to the Yankees is obvious,” he explained. “George Lombard Sr. is the father of New York’s prized 21-year-old shortstop George Lombard Jr. But his case for the job goes deeper than reverse nepotism. Lombard Sr. also worked with Cody Bellinger when Bellinger was with the Dodgers and the elder Lombard was on the coaching staff. He’s been on Team USA’s WBC coaching staff, too.”
Between the Lombard Jr. and Bellinger connection, there would be great familiarity with New York’s ballclub.
But this alone wouldn’t be enough to convince the front office to hire him; not to mention, he’s currently the Detroit Tigers‘ bench coach, which adds an additional hoop to jump through.
Alex Cora
As controversial as this move would be, given the historic Red Sox-Yankees rivalry, Jon Heyman of the New York Post recently put the subject on the table.
Cora was dismissed by Boston in April 2026, and he’s since stated that he plans to step away from managing in 2027.
But we’ve seen stranger things unfold in the major leagues.
It’s worth noting, however, that Cora’s name has also been floating in Houston Astros‘ rumors after the dismissal of Joe Espada.
Cora landing in New York seems unlikely, but again, nothing is truly impossible in baseball.
Yankees Need a Turning Point
CHICAGO, ILLINOIS – AUGUST 30: Manager Aaron Boone of the New York Yankees speaks to the media prior to the game against the Chicago White Sox at Rate Field on August 30, 2025 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Daniel Bartel/Getty Images)
Sure, New York reached the postseason. But it wasn’t a deep run, and it’s not the first time they’ve faced early elimination under Boone.
Until changes are made — whether to the staff or the roster — criticism will continue pouring in.
The Yankees have some heavy decisions to make this offseason.
How will they choose to navigate their upcoming weeks?

He wrote in the photo: “I’m looking for new up and coming clothing lines!! I’m trying to wear all merch Tag under this post and OM ME”
He wrote in the caption: “Drop names below!!!”
There were over 2,900 likes on his post in less than 24 hours.
Comments On His Post

item.title: [Pinstripe Alley] Evaluating Yankees manager Aaron Boone’s 2026 season
item.dc:creator: Dani Mohr
item.description: Some would say that 2026 was a tumultuous season for the Yankees’ skipper, and there is a lot to be said about what went right in Aaron Boone’s decision-making and what eventually backfired to catalyze disaster. There are many occasions when Boone stepped in at the right time to pull a pitcher and allowed the players to control their own destiny from the plate. He is most confident when he’s defending his guys from the dugout and isn’t afraid to get in an umpire’s face after a bad call. This has
item.content:encoded:
Some would say that 2026 was a tumultuous season for the Yankees’ skipper, and there is a lot to be said about what went right in Aaron Boone’s decision-making and what eventually backfired to catalyze disaster.
There are many occasions when Boone stepped in at the right time to pull a pitcher and allowed the players to control their own destiny from the plate. He is most confident when he’s defending his guys from the dugout and isn’t afraid to get in an umpire’s face after a bad call. This has always been Boone’s style, and he continued his fiery streak this season with five ejections during regular season games. However, as manager, he is mandated to take accountability for some of the questionable decisions that may have put the Yankees in tougher situations.
MLB insiders Jon Heyman and Joel Sherman recently invited Joe Girardi to assess Boone’s decisions, and the former Yankees manager had a lot of positive takeaways despite a disappointing end to this season. Girardi even went on to claim that this was Boone’s best year of managing in his nine years on the job.
To give him credit, Boone had to navigate through several injuries this season and consistently found ways to keep the Yankees fighting for a playoff spot when all seemed lost, especially without Aaron Judge. Along with the Yankees captain, several star players had lengthy stints on the injured list, including Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, Carlos Rodón, Ryan Weathers, and Giancarlo Stanton. Expected 2026 contributors Cody Bellinger, Austin Wells, Trent Grisham, and Jazz Chisholm Jr. all missed a few weeks, too. Despite all the setbacks, Boone still found a way to propel the Yankees to their third conseuctive season of at least 93 wins, and he could’ve matched the 94 from both 2024 and 2025 had a rainout not nixed Game 162.
Contrast this to 2023, when Judge also missed a bunch of time and the Yankees struggled to 82 wins, their worst year in over two decades. Although the personnel may have just been better this time around, Boone did help keep the season from falling apart and rendering September irrelevant (let alone October). Credit Boone and pitching coach Matt Blake for helping the bullpen beat preseason expectations as well; others might not have had the confidence in unheralded names like Brent Headrick and Paul Blackburn, but they had strong seasons setting up for closer David Bednar.
The Yankees skipper also deserves some praise for refusing to put Judge in a spot where he could put his future career at risk. After being sidelined for the final stretch of the regular season with a moderate grade right calf strain, Judge was eager to get back into the lineup as the Yankees prepared for the postseason. Boone and general manager Brian Cashman ultimately decided to leave him off the roster for the Wild Card Series against Boston, which didn’t end up being an issue as the Yankees scored a combined 18 runs in the two-game dusting.
The Division Series was an entirely different scenario. On the advice of the Yankees’ medical staff, Judge was again absent from the series, in which the first two games were played on the turf at Tropicana Field. Judge, much like the rest of the Yankees’ offense, struggled to put up big numbers in Tampa Bay and went a combined 2-for-10 with a home run, four RBIs, and four strikeouts this season. He appeared disgruntled at Boone’s decision to keep him off the field for the series, but it may have been the best choice to allow him more time to recover from the calf injury and not put his career at risk — after all, severe Achilles injuries have been linked to the soleus muscle, which is where his calf was strained.
On the other hand, one of Boone’s most glaringly disappointing choices was putting Grisham in a leadoff spot in an elimination game when the Yankees were at risk of getting swept by the Rays on their own turf. Grisham, who barely saw any action in September, was the last of the batters left to keep the fight alive down 4-3 in the bottom of the ninth. With the hottest hitter of the postseason on deck in Ben Rice—who had been batting leadoff—Grisham ended up striking out in four pitches from Bryan Baker, allowing Tampa Bay to celebrate advancing to the ALCS from the Bronx clubhouse once again. With Grisham putting the cherry on top of an embarrassing postseason performance, the Yankees also continued their postseason losing streak and remain winless on the road since the 2024 ALCS against the Guardians.
It looks like Boone is here to stay for at least another year, as his contract runs through the end of 2027. Hopefully the Yankees can make enough clever moves during this expectedly elongated offseason to put them in a better spot for next season.
VOTE: Grade Aaron Boone's 2026 season
The Yankees' skipper had a lot of ups and downs this season, and some are calling for his job while others are giving him praise for navigating through several injuries to his star players.
What grade would you give Aaron Boone this season? Does he deserve to stick around another year, or is it time for him to go?

First the financials: For the first time that I can remember, the Yankees don’t have any dead money# on the
item.content:encoded:
State of the 2027 team at the beginning of the offseason
Given the state of labor negotiations and respective demands, perhaps it is foolhardy to anticipate what the free agent and trade markets will look like and thus how the Yankees will be able to improve. Still I’m more interested in this than in who wins the World Series so let’s see what we are starting with going into the offseason.
First the financials:
For the first time that I can remember, the Yankees don’t have any dead money# on the books!
7 guaranteed contracts: $210
2027 CBT of guaranteed contracts: $212M
MLB trade rumors estimate of 9 arbitration eligible players: $37M
Pre-arbitration 40-man: $15M
Remaining: $58M*
*If the Yankees do nothing to cut payroll, they have about $58M to the $322 they spent salaries for CBT purposes and some amount needs to be saved to spend at the deadline.
The roster (graded elite, strong, average, weak, bad, or uncertain if no particular case is likely):
32 on current 40-man roster plus depth already at AAA
The starting rotation and depth
Cam Schlittler (elite with age and stuff upsides)
Max Fried (elite with age and injury downsides)
Gerrit Cole (strong with age and injury downsides and previous ability and results upsides)
Carlos Rodon (strong with age and injury downsides and previous results and stuff upsides)
Ryan Weathers (strong with injury downside)
Will Warren (average with age upside)
Clarke Schmidt (uncertain with age upside and injury questions)
Elmer Rodriguez (uncertain with age and stuff upsides and weak MLB results)
Brandon Beck (weak)
Luis Gil (weak, may not be tendered a contract, previous results and age upsides, injury and recent performance downsides)
This is the best position the Yankees starting rotation has been in the last 4 decades and the best collection of talent and depth in the both leagues. It’s possible that some of these players are dealt to fill other needs or used in the bullpen so they can impact the major league team and maintain depth.
The bullpen and depth
Brent Headrick (good with lack of track record and heavy use downsides and recent performance upside)
Kervin Castro (weak, finished the year injured)
Angel Chivilli (weak with age and stuff upsides)
Fernando Cruz (uncertain, possible, even probably non-tender or agree to a minor league deal if TJS is needed)
Yerry De Los Santos (weak with high ground ball rate upside)
Bradley Hanner (bad, probably waived when a 40-man spot is needed)
Carlos Lagrange (uncertain, age and stuff upsides, control and injury downsides)
Alexander Cornielle (bad)
Kyle Carr (bad, rule 5 draft eligible, currently MLB NYY org #12)
Almost the opposite of the rotation. No depth and little quality.
Catcher
Austin Wells (average with age upside)
Ali Sanchez (bad)
JC Escarra (bad)
Given the criticism he gets here, a few words about Austin Wells. Wells has earned 8.1 fWar and 3.8 bWar over the last three seasons. By fwar that’s 8th over that time (if anyone knows how the sort the baseball reference leaderboard for multiple seasons let me know). The staff loves him. Wells performed in the playoffs (even his horrific baserunning blunder followed breaking up a no-hitter). He hits the ball harder than the average major league player and swings out of the zone less than the average. It should surprise no one to see Wells put together a good and even fringe All-Star season next year even if average is most likely.
First Base & Designated Hitter
Ben Rice (good with age, results, and batted ball upsides)
Luis Garcia (average with age and first half break out upsides)
Giancarlo Stanton (uncertain, with high age and injury downsides)
Heliot Ramos (weak, age upside, possibly good if just playing against lefties)
# Ok fine, it’s reasonable to say that the Stanton money is dead money. With the Garcia and Ramos trades it seems like the Yankees have already covered themselves from the predictable Stanton injury.
Second, Short, & Third
George Lombard (average, age and talent upsides)
Anthony Volpe (weak, age and defensive upsides)
Jose Caballero (weak, defensive and flexibility upsides)
Ryan McMahon (bad)
Max Schuemann (bad)
It is hard to get excited about this group. I mean at least it has age and athleticism going for it. But I'm not confident anyone here will hit. Which is why I lean towards offering Chisholm the qualifying offer.
Outfield
Aaron Judge (elite, age and injury downsides)
Cody Bellinger (good, age and injury downsides)
Spencer Jones (weak, age and athleticism upsides, swing & miss downside)
Jasson Dominguez (bad, age upside)
Only one center fielder here and his defense is pretty bad.
Tiering our 2027 players:
The core of the team:
Judge, Bellinger, Rice, Schlittler, Fried, Cole, and Rodon. Not only are these players good to great, but most have no-trade clauses. There’s some injury risk, and this top 7 is among the best in baseball. However, none of these 7 play up the middle. Not ideal.
Their salary is coming back even if they aren’t:
McMahon and Stanton - possible that they could save a little in salary dump trades, but these are our two negative value contracts
Definitely coming back and hopefully becomes a foundation piece:
Lombard
May be traded to fit other needs, but otherwise will have a substantial role:
Weathers, Warren, Schmidt, Rodriguez, Headrick, Garcia
Probably coming back, and the team is looking for upgrades:
Volpe, Caballero, Ramos, Jones, Chivilli, Castro, De Los Santos,
First prospect to make an impact:
Lagrange
Trade block and/or non-tendered:
Dominguez, McMahon, Gil, Cruz
40-man filler unlikely to stick all offseason:
Schuemann, Sanchez, Escarra, Hanner
Possible Scranton shuttle candidates:
Beck, Carr, Cornielle,
Sign in to reply to ConorGallogly

item.title: [pinstripealley.com] New York Yankees Important 2026-2027 Offseason Dates
item.dc:creator: Dani Mohr

item.content:encoded:
We are quickly approaching the start of the official MLB offseason, and there are several dates that will reveal information you won’t want to miss.
With the lockout becoming more likely to begin in December, expect to witness a lot of cancellations, alterations, or postponements of important events such as the Winter Meetings, owner meetings, and the draft lottery. If the MLBPA and the owners’ dispute lasts deep into 2027, there’s at least a chance we may not see any baseball at all in the majors in 2027. The best-case may be something like what happened last time around, when an agreement was reached in early March and no games were ultimately lost outside of spring training; the 2022 campaign just began and ended a week later than originally planned.
Regardless, the list below tracks all the important dates that you’ll need to keep track of as we make our way through the offseason, with modifications to be anticipated from the impending lockout.
Day after the World Series ends: Free agents will automatically file at 9 a.m. EST. They won’t be allowed to sign for five days.
November 1: Gold Glove Award winners will be announced at 9 p.m. EST on ESPN. Cody Bellinger, Austin Wells, and José Caballero were all named finalists this season.
November 2: The Hall of Fame eight-person Contemporary Baseball Era ballot for post-1980 managers, executives, and umpires will be released. Silver Slugger Award finalists will be announced at 2 p.m. EST, followed by the BBWAA Award finalists on MLB Network from 6 - 8 p.m. EST.
Five days after the World Series ends: Free agents are now free to sign with any team and will need to make a decision by the time night falls. This also marks the last day to reinstate players from the 60-day injured list and issue qualifying offers to free agents who are eligible. Jazz Chisholm Jr. and David Bednar are among the Yankees who could potentially receive the QO, which has been set at $23.15 million.
November 6: Hear & Hustle Awards will be announced, and the Platinum Glove Award winners will be revealed at the Gold Glove Awards dinner in New York City.
November 9: Rookie of the Year will be announced at 7 p.m. EST on MLB Network.
November 9-12: The GM Meetings will begin on November 9th and continue through the 13th.
November 10: Manager of the Year will be announced at 7 p.m. EST on MLB Network.
November 11: The Cy Young Awards and the new BBWAA Relievers of the Year honors will be announced at 7 p.m. EST on MLB Network. Yankees’ ace Cam Schlittler is a frontrunner for the Cy Young after a stellar second season in pinstripes; he would be New York’s first winner since his teammate Gerrit Cole in 2023.
The MLB Awards Show, premiering on MLB Network at 9 p.m. EST, will reveal the All-MLB first and second teams, the Hank Aaron Award winners, Comeback Players of the Year, Mariano Rivera & Trevor Hoffman Relievers of the Year, and the Edgar Martinez Designated Hitter Award winner.
November 12: This year’s MVP Award winners will be announced at 7 p.m. EST on MLB Network.
November 16: The 2027 Hall of Fame ballot will be released at 12 p.m. EST. Andy Pettitte and Alex Rodriguez are among the candidates from last year’s cycle who earned enough votes to carry over into 2027. Retirees from 2021 will be under consideration, with Giants great Buster Posey leading a group that also includes career Yankee Brett Gardner.
November 17-19: The owners meetings will take place in New York City.
November 17: The Silver Slugger Awards will be announced.
This date also marks the Rule 5 protection deadline, which means that teams have to add any eligible players to their 40-man roster in order to make sure that they aren’t available for the draft.
The deadline for players to accept qualifying offers will also be at 4 p.m. EST.
November 20: This marks the deadline for decisions on tendering or non-tendering contracts for eligible players.
December 1: The Collective Bargaining Agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. EST, and barring a surprise in the current negotiations, the lockout will officially begin. As a reminder, minor-league players who are not already on a team’s 40-man roster have their own separate CBA that ends in December 2027, and no matter how long the MLB lockout lasts, the minor-league season will begin on time.
December 6: The Hall of Fame announces the Contemporary Baseball Era inductees. As mentioned in the November 2nd note, only managers, executives, and umpires are under consideration by that commitee for 2027. The more familiar BBWAA results come later on.
December 7-9: The Winter Meetings are scheduled be held in San Diego, but the major-league parts of it will likely be cancelled due to the lockout.
December 8: The Draft Lottery will take place, but will likely be postponed due to the lockout.
December 9: The Rule 5 Draft is scheduled take place, but will likely be affected in some way due to the lockout. The MLBPA did propose moving it up to late November so that there isn’t a repeat of what happened during the 2021 lockout, when the major-league portion of the Rule 5 was cancelled and only the minor-league phase was held. (There have not been any updates on the proposal’s acceptance.)
January 8: This is the official deadline for arbitration numbers to be exchanged between players and teams, but it will likely be postponed due to the lockout.
January 15: International Free Agent market for 2027 opens.
January 19: The results of the 2026 BBWAA Hall of Fame ballot and the 2027 inductees will be revealed, and we’ll find out who will be cementing their names in Cooperstown.
February 19: Yankees spring training opener, on the road in Dunedin against the Blue Jays (subject to change due to the lockout).
March 25: Yankees Opening Day, at home against the Blue Jays (subject to change due to the lockout).

item.title: [pinstripealley.com] The three biggest surprises of the 2026 Yankees season
item.dc:creator: Jeremy Nielsen
item.description: A wise man once said you can’t predict baseball. That doesn’t stop us from trying. Ahead of every season, just about every baseball-related publication tries to glimpse the future and predict the outcome of the year ahead. And at the end of the year, we realize again and again how futile the exercise can truly be.
