item.content:encoded:
A wise man once said you can’t predict baseball. That doesn’t stop us from trying. Ahead of every season, just about every baseball-related publication tries to glimpse the future and predict the outcome of the year ahead. And at the end of the year, we realize again and again how futile the exercise can truly be. Even for a season that develops according to expectations, there will always be contours to the road that you didn’t have mapped out.
The 2026 Yankees washed out to an AL East rival in the Division Series for the second straight year; not an unforeseen fate for a team that was largely running it back with a nearly identical roster. As such, as we mark off the biggest surprises of the season, that end result isn’t all you’ll find similar with the last time we did this exercise.
So, let’s get started. Who could’ve predicted…
…that Cam Schlittler would be this good, this quickly?
We all saw glimpses of the ace starter Cam Schlittler could be when he carved up the Red Sox in the winner-take-all Game 3 of last season’s Wild Card Series, but I don’t imagine anyone anticipated the 25-year old would become the top pitcher in the American League the following year. Cam’s 14 start-run in 2025 showed a pitcher with tantalizing talent but plenty of room for refinement—namely a 10.2 percent walk rate which is the calling card of volatile and inconsistent pitchers from sea to shining sea.
That makes it all the more incredible that Cam was not only incredibly dominant, but consistently so. Schlittler didn’t really have his first bad start until June, and lest you thought that would be the moment the other shoe dropped, he didn’t let his ERA climb above 2.26 from midsummer onward. The 1.95 mark he finished with was good for a bronze medal in all-time Yankee lore. And the command troubles he flashed as a rookie vanished—he struck out 239 batters and walked only 49, a nearly 5-to-1 ratio. As of this writing, Schlittler has not yet been given the Cy Young award, but it’s a foregone conclusion. Even my most bullish preseason prediction for him probably would not have ended with him accepting that hallowed honor, but he electrified everyone and surpassed every test in 2026.
…that the Yankees would not grab a catcher at the deadline?
The vibes around this team were going sour with the June rib injury to Aaron Judge—which kept him out until September, when a quad strain would sideline him for the all-too-short remainder of the season. Brian Cashman had to act to shore up a roster which was suddenly emitting about seven distress signals. He added more offense where he could, bringing aboard Luis Garcia Jr. and Heliot Ramos while calling up reinforcements from the minors—more on them later.
Not included on his shopping receipt, however, was a catcher, which was seen as the Yankees’ biggest need. That, of course, was because of the abysmal year Austin Wells had been enduring to that point. Wells had managed just a .504 OPS through the first half—unplayably bad even if it accompanied his generally solid defense. But the task of adding a new backstop was quickly complicated by their own closest rivals, who added two of the best catchers on the market. The Red Sox made a splash by trading for Adley Rutschman from the Orioles, and the Rays dealt with the Marlins for Liam Hicks.
As the hours toward the deadline ticked down, the Yankees were stuck with a bunch of poor options. The Twins’ Ryan Jeffers was coming off a recent injury and would be expensive; so would Colorado’s Hunter Goodman. The other remaining names were lateral moves at best. So, the Yankee braintrust ultimately chose to stick with Wells.
Thankfully, this was a problem that ultimately sorted itself out, as Wells found his swing at long last in the second half. He actually became one of the more consistent bats for the Yankees in the final two months and played to a second-half .787 OPS, more than doubling his home run and RBI total in the process. Unfortunately, Wells’ season would conclude with one more surprise, and a deeply unpleasant one: getting thrown out at third trying to leg out a triple in ALDS Game 1.
…that calling up the rookies actually worked?
If you told me that Spencer Jones and George Lombard Jr. would be key planks in the Yankees’ second half lineup, I would have assumed their season had completely gone down the tubes. Jones, the powerful but whiff-prone outfielder, had not made waves in his first little Major League stint, hitting .167 in May before being sent back down to Triple-A. Lombard, the precocious shortstop, was a known commodity in the field, but a mystery at the plate—and awfully young to be thrown into the most pressure-packed spot in the league: the little patch of dirt between second and third in the Bronx.
The aforementioned injury to Judge—and later an injury to Trent Grisham—quickly brought Jones back into the fold, and the lefty picked up three hits in his first game back in the Show. Jones raised his level in June, hitting to an .808 OPS before a second brief demotion; then Cody Bellinger got hurt and he came back again, this time for good. He didn’t set the world on fire at any point in his rookie year, but Jones proved he could be a productive Major Leaguer, for at least the few months they needed him to be one. Another surprise with Jones was the somewhat ridiculous reverse splits he put up: a 1.107 OPS against lefties as opposed to just .647 off righties.
Lombard received the call to the Majors directly after the Trade Deadline, as the Yankees searched for more talent to ignite their slumbering offense. In a memorable MLB debut, Lombard made a handful of stellar plays at short, then homered in his second Major League at-bat—the same night his brother Jacob went yard in the low minors. Lombard turned a great first game into a great first week, showing composure beyond his years and an advanced approach at the plate.
The 21-year old’s offensive numbers soon dipped to pedestrian levels, and he had his defensive hiccups as well. But he never relinquished the starting shortstop position, even when Anthony Volpe—whom the Yankees had surprisingly optioned to make room from Lombard—returned to the roster. He acquitted himself well in the playoffs as well, going 6-for-18 overall. While neither he nor Jones are looking like perennial All-Stars, they may yet become mainstays on a roster in need of retooling this offseason.

item.title: [pinstripealley.com] What to do with the Yankees’ free agents
item.dc:creator: Joshua Diemert
item.description: Ten of the 26 men on the Yankees’ roster will be free agents after the World Series, and as a team that has a tremendous amount of money already locked up in various players — $177.8 million already allocated to Cody Bellinger, Aaron Judge, Gerrit Cole, Max Fried and Carlos Rodón — while caring a little bit about CBT thresholds, the money does matter to the club even if it doesn’t to me. Labor strife on the horizon also weighs in on all these conversations, while most people around baseball thin
item.content:encoded:
Ten of the 26 men on the Yankees’ roster will be free agents after the World Series, and as a team that has a tremendous amount of money already locked up in various players — $177.8 million already allocated to Cody Bellinger, Aaron Judge, Gerrit Cole, Max Fried and Carlos Rodón — while caring a little bit about CBT thresholds, the money does matter to the club even if it doesn’t to me. Labor strife on the horizon also weighs in on all these conversations, while most people around baseball think some games will be played in 2027, a possible abbreviated Spring Training or otherwise shortened season means you need players that can ramp up quickly.
Here’s our list of 10 men:
The first question is who gets the Qualifying Offer, a one-year deal at just over $23 million. Trent Grisham got the QO last year and is therefore ineligible this time around, and frankly should be allowed to walk. Backward steps offensively and defensively, along with his inability to be QO’d, makes that an easy decision for me. Contrary to perhaps popular sentiment, Jazz Chisholm Jr. should be given the Qualifying Offer, even if it seems the Yankees are unwilling to extend it.
Jazz can be an incredibly frustrating experience as a fan, but he still put up three and a half wins in what was a down year offensively. Among primary second baseman, that was good enough to be the second best at the position in the American League, and with the Yankees his 10.1 fWAR builds out to a 4.8 win season projected over 600 plate appearances. He’s frustrating to watch, and he’s also a good player!
You have to bake in some IL time and you have to square the circle of second base, where the Yankees seem willing to platoon Anthony Volpe, and there’s no sense in paying a platoon player $23 million. If you QO Jazz, he needs to be your primary option at the keystone.
David Bednar is the other guy that seems worth QO’ing, but committing high dollar amounts to relievers always worries me. The Yankees spent $26.637 million on their bullpen this year, the second-best unit in the game by ERA. In 2019, they spent just a hair over $50 million. Again, I don’t care about their budget, but the team does, and spending $23 million on a guy pitching one inning makes me a little wary of the team’s ability to make moves in-season, even more so when we consider potential changes to the way players are compensated.
At the same time I don’t love the idea of locking Bednar up for the next four or five years. His K-BB rate, my personal favorite single pitching stat, fell six and a half points this year. His four-seam velo dropped almost a full mile per hour, and you don’t really recover velocity at age 32. He’s been very good since coming to the Bronx, and seems to have the mentality to handle pitching in New York, but boy I don’t want to see what he looks like at 36.
The rest of this group is hard to parse. I don’t mind Paul Goldschmidt as a strict platoon bat in theory, but I don’t trust the org to not overplay him, and in two straight seasons we’ve seen serious dropoffs in the second half — going from a 124 wRC+ to an 83 this year, and a 114 to a 76 last year. I think the game has passed the future Hall of Famer by.
Ryan Yarbrough and especially Paul Blackburn should have some offers from multiple teams, and both should garner interest from the Yankees. Yarbrough’s flexibility in going multiple innings and Blackburn’s emergence as a true high-leverage arm both make them good candidates for something like the two-year, $20 million deal Luke Weaver signed a couple years ago, massive upgrades from their current deals.
The rest of the crop I can take or leave.
So, assuming a non-catastrophic resolution to the CBA troubles, we’ve got two, perhaps up to four, of the Yankees’ free agents returning, adding about $65 million to payroll if all four guys come back. I don’t care about the budget but the team does, and that makes me a little worried about them making any other moves.

item.title: [pinstripealley.com] Evaluating Brian Cashman’s 2026 season
item.dc:creator: Andrés Chávez
item.description: The 2026 Yankees won 93 games in a year in which superstar Aaron Judge played just 66 games. That’s not a bad total, but it feels like it could, and should, have been more. General manager and Senior VP Brian Cashman routinely builds contending teams, and he should get credit for that, but he and his staff should be aiming higher and doing more to bring the title back to the Bronx. A Wild Card Series win against the Boston Red Sox was a nice way to start the postseason, but the sweep at the hand
item.content:encoded:
The 2026 Yankees won 93 games in a year in which superstar Aaron Judge played just 66 games. That’s not a bad total, but it feels like it could, and should, have been more. General manager and Senior VP Brian Cashman routinely builds contending teams, and he should get credit for that, but he and his staff should be aiming higher and doing more to bring the title back to the Bronx.
A Wild Card Series win against the Boston Red Sox was a nice way to start the postseason, but the sweep at the hands of the Tampa Bay Rays exposed many harsh realities that are directly tied to Cashman and his decisions.
For the Yankees, 93 wins is not enough. They need to be the best team in the division, because that would bring them additional benefits in postseason play, such as home-field advantage and a ticket straight to the AL Division Series. Everybody in the organization is responsible for how the season plays out, but the spotlight will always point to the head of baseball operations.
Offseason moves and decisions
Cashman didn’t have a particularly bad offseason, but there were some notable holes when the season started. He didn’t find proper replacements for the rehabbing Anthony Volpe and the underwhelming Ryan McMahon: the former ended up being demoted in early August when the organization promoted George Lombard Jr., and the latter posted a 78 wRC+ and just 0.5 fWAR in 124 games. Volpe eventually returned and played an important role in the stretch run and during the postseason.
Extending Trent Grisham a qualifying offer was seen as a moderate risk when it happened, but it was a reasonable one since the outfielder had hit a career-high 34 homers in 2025. The outfielder declined this year, particularly on defense, but at least it wasn’t a long-term commitment.
The trade for Ryan Weathers was universally acclaimed, and it was a good piece of business on Cashman’s part. He ended up posting career-bests in ERA (3.60), fWAR (2.5), and innings pitched (137.1). The executive also brought back Paul Blackburn, Ryan Yarbrough, Amed Rosario, Paul Goldschmidt, and Cody Bellinger.
Some of them were nice additions, particularly the 2019 NL MVP, but Cashman left the roster exposed to injuries and underperformance in many spots, and that’s on him, too. The bullpen was a bit thin, as some of his past trade experiments, such as Jake Bird, Ángel Chivilli, and Camilo Doval, just didn’t work. The same can be said about Rule 5 pick Cade Winquest. We are more than willing to give Cashman a pass in the bullpen, since the unit finished with the second-best ERA in MLB, though.
Trade Deadline activity (or lack thereof)
The Bombers entered the deadline with a few notable needs, which Cashman was very much aware of. They could have used a catcher given Austin Wells’ season-long slump up to that date, a reliever or two, a starter, and a right-handed outfielder.
They flirted with several backstops, but ended up empty-handed on that front to the frustration of fans. They did bring in Luis García Jr., who had been enjoying an amazing year in Washington with 23 homers and a 133 wRC+.
Heliot Ramos’ arrival was met with mixed reviews, and he posted a disappointing 93 wRC+ in pinstripes. He did have a 184 wRC+ vs. lefties during his time in the Bronx, which was one of the main reasons behind his acquisition. Giving up left-handed pitching prospect Henry Lalane to get him hurt, though. Speaking of…
Prospects and young core
Yes, you could say that the Yankees’ deadline was a disappointment, although some might disagree. However, they managed to keep most of their top prospects, including Lombard, Dax Kilby, Carlos Lagrange, Elmer Rodríguez, and Ben Hess. The promising Lalane was the lone exception.
They represent, together with Cam Schlittler, Ben Rice, Spencer Jones, Weathers, and Will Warren, the next wave of young talent that will, theoretically at least, keep the team highly competitive for the next 3-7 years. Keeping them all, particularly Lombard when half the league was asking for him in trade conversations, was a win for Cashman.
The rest of the farm, however, needs work. A lot of work. The Yankees will need to draft well and be active in the international market in the next couple of years to revamp their depleted system. At least Cashman took a step towards solving the situation, dismissing longtime international scouting director Donny Rowland and replacing him with Mario Garza in January.
Player development wins and losses
As every general manager, Cashman had some player development wins and losses when looking at the final picture of the 2026 campaign. He and his staff managed to turn Blackburn into a very useful reliever with his 1.59 ERA in 85 innings, and he got a nice season from Weathers, too.
Schlittler took a step forward into stardom, and Brent Headrick and Warren also improved in 2026. On the other hand, they couldn’t fix Doval, Luis Gil, McMahon, or Volpe, and Jasson Domínguez remains a fringe player. Grisham and Wells were also subpar for their standard.
The offense, generally speaking, had a mediocre year with a 101 wRC+ that ranked 14th in MLB. Yes, injuries to Judge, Giancarlo Stanton, and other key hitters certainly hurt, but the feeling is that Cashman could have done better, or more.
We have said it multiple times in this space: the Yankees need new voices. They need to listen to more prepared people. They can’t keep doing the same things in personnel decisions, player analysis, research and development, and scouting and expect different results. Unless the ownership decides to part ways with their longtime executive, it will be on Cashman to push that change within the organization: does he have that in him, though? It’s at least a fair question.

item.title: [Heavy.com] MLB Insider Makes Statement About Anthony Volpe’s New York Yankees Future
item.dc:creator: Ben Stinar
item.description: The New York Yankees are currently home for the offseason after getting swept by the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS. item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are currently home for the offseason after getting swept by the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS.
While they lost 4-3 in Game 3, one of the big bright spots was the play of Anthony Volpe.
He had an up-and-down season that saw him in Triple-A twice.
That said, Volpe had two hits, one RBI and one run in the elimination game.
ESPN’s Jeff Passan wrote (on October 7): “The best team in the league finishes the sweep and heads to the ALCS. A game-tying Anthony Volpe home run was overturned because of fan interference, and the Rays held their one-run lead for the final 10 outs. The Yankees haven’t won a title in 17 years.”
Insider Makes Statement About Volpe
During his second stint with New York this year (after returning from Triple-A), he played second base due to the fact that George Lombard Jr. took over at shortstop.
This week, Joel Sherman of The New York Post (via Schein Time) spoke about Volpe.
Sherman: “So there’s got to be a lot of positions that you start to try to fill not making a lot of money, and because of that I think Volpe will be the second baseman. I think he was a better version of himself at that position. I think it’s the right position for him. I don’t think he has the arm for shortstop. I think it takes some pressure off of him. I don’t know. Will he ever be a consistent offensive guy? Will he ever get to a profile? Whoever in the Yankee organization convinced a 5-foot-8 guy that he should be a lift-and-launch guy, instead of what he was as an amateur, how he got drafted in the first round, which was a use-the-whole-field guy. I think that guy was fired. He should be fired twice. But I think that there is a Caleb Durbin-like player in Anthony Volpe who’s a good everyday player who, for not a lot of money, could solve second base for a while standing next to Lombard Jr. at shortstop.”
Volpe finished the year batting .245 with 54 hits, two home runs, 28 RBIs, 24 runs and 12 stolen bases in 70 games.

item.title: [Yanks Go Yard] Yankees 'bosses' getting upset with Aaron Judge demand is latest sign of dysfunction
item.dc:creator: Adam Weinrib
item.description: Let's call it like it is: Aaron Judge repeatedly insisting that he was in better shape than Aaron Boone was portraying all postseason long was weird. It got weirder when Brian Cashman went on record that using Judge in the ALDS "wasn't a choice," as he was too compromised to participate; Judge pushed back on that notion as well. item.content:encoded:
Let's call it like it is: Aaron Judge repeatedly insisting that he was in better shape than Aaron Boone was portraying all postseason long was weird. It got weirder when Brian Cashman went on record that using Judge in the ALDS "wasn't a choice," as he was too compromised to participate; Judge pushed back on that notion as well.
And yes, no matter what they say, it was also odd that he didn't appear in pregame intros before the Yankees' Wild Card battle with the Red Sox. "I think he was getting treatment stuff," Boone explained in the aftermath.
After the Yankees' elimination, Judge provided mostly platitudes amid the injury pushback. When pressed about his desire to go "all in" and whether the Yankees have fulfilled it, he did hesitate a bit, but then dropped a fairly non-controversial semi-banger.
“It’s tough to say,” Judge responded. “I want to trade for everybody, sign everybody every single year, but I know that’s not realistic. So they give us a winning team every single year, but that’s not good enough here in New York. We’re the Yankees. You’ve got to go out there and chase championships and go all in every year. So I’m excited to see what they do.”
The Yankees' brass didn't find it as "non-controversial" as we did, though. According to Jon Heyman, "Yankee bosses" weren't thrilled by Judge's characterization of the Yankees' spending around him. Those "bosses" believed that they'd done Judge's bidding by bringing Cody Bellinger home at the price he cost.
Aaron Judge's war of words with Yankees executives is now back in his court
It was Judge who said, "I hope we can run them back" regarding both Bellinger and Trent Grisham after the Yankees' elimination in 2025, and the Bellinger cold war seemed like it would be inevitably resolved in large part because of Judge's presence and preferences (he was also the right fit, and the Yankees' outfield would've been barren without him).
But Judge's comments this time around weren't heightened much above the generic "We're the Yankees, and we have to win" level. If team executives were frustrated by his insinuation that what we just saw wasn't good enough, then we have a problem here.
Then again, certain Yankees perceived as Judge favorites over the years either overstayed their welcomes or were given outsized roles past the point of expiration (Alex Verdugo).
Regardless, the ball is now in Judge's court as this bizarre battle of leaks continues into an offseason where the Yankees can ill afford in-fighting, especially with a lockout threatening to close off primary sources of communication.

item.title: [Cubbies Crib] Yankees' expected David Bednar decision could complicate Cubs' bullpen plans
item.dc:creator: Jordan Campbell
item.description: The Chicago Cubs have needs across the entire pitching staff this offseason, but it would seem there will be an added focus on the bullpen. item.content:encoded:
The Chicago Cubs have needs across the entire pitching staff this offseason, but it would seem there will be an added focus on the bullpen. The Cubs' bullpen was patched together last season, and if all goes well this offseason, they will have another high-leverage option added to the mix. One of those options could be David Bednar, but the New York Yankees' plans may complicate the process.
Running through the list of qualifying offer decisions, the New York Post's Jon Heyman reports the Yankees are expected to extend the offer to Bednar. That would put the Cubs in risk of giving up draft-pick compensation and potentially international bonus pool money if they were to be the team that signs Bednar.
Bednar is someone the Cubs have loosely been connected to over the years. For years, he was the lock-down closer at the back of the Pittsburgh Pirates' bullpen, but when he struggled in 2024, there was some thought of the Cubs making a buy-low trade with their division rival.
Instead, he rebounded with the Pirates in 2025, posting an ERA of 2.37 before being traded to the New York Yankees at the deadline. Upon his arrival in New York, he's been excellent. This season, he posted an ERA of 2.47 with 35 saves. His fastball sat in the middle 90s, and he struck out over 27% of the hitters he faced this year.
David Bednar's potential qualifying offer creates a new headache for Cubs
In his current form, Bednar is the type of pitcher the Cubs lacked in their bullpen for most of last season. Targeting him would give the Cubs a defined closer, pushing the likes of Daniel Palencia, Ryan Zeferjahn, and Jacob Webb down a peg in the bullpen order. Ultimately, that may be the best outcome for the Cubs' bullpen plans this season, considering how often Craig Counsell had to go to the drawing board late in games in 2026.
As for whether or not the qualifying offer would deter the Cubs from pursuing Bednar, it's possible it doesn't. The Cubs are expected to extend their qualifying offer to Seiya Suzuki, and assuming he declines, they would be in line for a draft pick after the fourth round of the 2027 MLB Draft. That could put the front office at ease with the idea of losing a draft pick if they were to sign Bednar this offseason.

item.title: [New York Post] Solving the Yankees’ third base fiasco won’t be easy – or cheap
item.dc:creator: Joel Sherman

item.content:encoded:
In Part 5 of our continuing series breaking down how the Yankees should navigate the offseason position by position, we look at third base.
The Yankees had among the majors’ worst slash lines at third – .215/.271/.358. That is more tolerable if they were getting elite defense at the position. The Rays, for example, live annually with Taylor Walls’ feeble bat because his shortstop defense is special. The Brewers just won the NL title with the same paradigm with Joey Ortiz, initially at short and now at third.

Don’t miss Greg Joyce’s text messages from The Bronx and beyond — he’s giving Sports+ subscribers the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Sign Up Now
That was Ryan McMahon for the Yankees last year after his trade-deadline acquisition provided a strong glove, which was particularly valuable, say, when lefty contact-oriented Max Fried started. But McMahon’s defense regressed and so his poor offense became more problematic. Meanwhile, the Yankees were willing to accept Amed Rosario’s lesser glove at third in exchange for him hitting lefties well. Except for the first time in his career, he didn’t.
The overall result was unacceptable, so this position must improve for next season. McMahon’s $16 million due for 2027 complicates matters. The Yankees have gotten in the habit of eating that range of contract after releasing Aaron Hicks and DJ LeMahieu. But the first route will be to try to trade McMahon by either eating a good deal of what he is owed, taking on a bad contract as a counterbalance or perhaps including him with more desirable pieces in a bigger trade.

item.title: [Empire Sports Media] NY Yankees could regret trading their most flexible infielder
item.dc:creator: Alexander Wilson
item.description: Jose Caballero can be useful enough to keep without being good enough to settle the Yankees‘ entire infield. item.content:encoded:
Jose Caballero can be useful enough to keep without being good enough to settle the Yankees‘ entire infield. Those two ideas shouldn’t be difficult to hold together after his latest recognition.
The American League utility Gold Glove finalists include Caballero, giving New York a timely reminder of what it would lose by treating him as an easy offseason trade piece. The nomination arrived Wednesday. It doesn’t make him a star, but his ability to cover several positions is worth protecting on a team that still has decisions to make.
I would keep him in a real utility role, with enough starts to make that job meaningful. Parking him on the bench for a week and then asking him to fix whichever position is suddenly exposed isn’t much of a plan.
Caballero gives the Yankees room to make better choices
Caballero appeared in 70 games at shortstop, 37 at third base and 23 at second this season. He also played all three outfield positions. Those appearances overlap, so they aren’t separate games to add together, but they describe a player who can cover more than one absence.
His value is especially useful while the Yankees decide which infield jobs require outside help. Keeping Caballero doesn’t require declaring him the answer at any one of them. It lets New York pursue the better hitter or defender available rather than buy a replacement for every possible assignment at once.
Matthew Schmidt included him among the Yankees’ offseason trade candidates Thursday for Roundtable Sports. There is a reasonable argument there: versatility can appeal to another club, and a useful player might help obtain a more important upgrade. A columnist’s trade idea, however, isn’t evidence that the Yankees are shopping him or have received an offer.
The bat still sets a limit
Caballero hit .231/.290/.365 in 136 games. A .290 on-base percentage is a real restriction, regardless of how many gloves fit in his locker. New York would be asking for trouble if it used an award nomination to explain away a full-time offensive weakness.
He stole 34 bases and was caught 11 times. The speed helps once he’s aboard, but it doesn’t supply the missing trips to first base. His best fit is a flexible assignment shaped by the opponent and the rest of the lineup, rather than a promise of everyday plate appearances at one position.
There is a price at which trading him would make sense. If New York can obtain a meaningful upgrade and already has comparable defensive coverage, keeping Caballero merely because he is familiar would be silly. The nomination also isn’t a complete defensive evaluation, and it doesn’t tell us what another team would pay.
Until that offer exists, the Yankees would be giving up a useful option to solve a problem they haven’t defined. I’d rather see them improve the weakest everyday spot and use Caballero to keep that improvement from creating two new holes elsewhere.

item.title: [New York Post] Matt Blake and the ‘pitching group’ have become indispensable to Yankees success
item.dc:creator: Greg Joyce
item.description: As the Yankees world awaits word on Aaron Boone, who still has a year left on his contract, almost as consequential is the fate of a pending free agent on his staff. Matt Blake is much less divisive than his boss, but arguably just as important, especially coming off a year in which he and the Yankees’ pitching group got the most out of a staff that was missing its highest-paid arms for considerable amounts of time and had a largely no-name bullpen — and still managed to lead the majors in ERA (
item.content:encoded:
As the Yankees world awaits word on Aaron Boone, who still has a year left on his contract, almost as consequential is the fate of a pending free agent on his staff.
Matt Blake is much less divisive than his boss, but arguably just as important, especially coming off a year in which he and the Yankees’ pitching group got the most out of a staff that was missing its highest-paid arms for considerable amounts of time and had a largely no-name bullpen — and still managed to lead the majors in ERA (3.23).
“I think he’s pretty damn good at his job,” Will Warren said as the regular season was winding down.
The expectation is that Blake will be back for a third contract, barring a surprise such as the Yankees firing Boone and a new manager wanting to bring in his own staff. Because for as many issues as the Yankees have had in recent years that have led to repeated October disappointments, their pitching mostly has been the exception.

item.content:encoded:
Joe Girardi says quiet part out loud about Giancarlo Stanton and Aaron Judge originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The New York Yankees' inability to stay healthy over the past couple of seasons has certainly contributed to the team not winning a World Series.
For the Yankees, there are two prime candidates who just haven't been able to stay healthy at all times, and it's arguably the two best players on their roster in Aaron Judge and Giancarlo Stanton.
Guys like Ben Rice have stepped up over the past year, but before Rice did what he has over the past two seasons, there was no debate that Stanton and Judge were the two most important players on this roster.
Once again this postseason, Judge and Stanton weren't able to be on the field much. Stanton got an at-bat and looked absolutely foolish against the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS in Game 3. Judge didn't play in either the Wild Card Series or the ALDS.
Former Yankees skipper Joe Girardi had a lot to say about that, adding that he's not sure these guys are completely healthy and that, while the talent was there, injuries eventually did them in.
"I think health continues to haunt this team. I really do," Girardi said, H/T Heavy.
"Look, you're playing without Aaron Judge for four and a half months. Don't have him in the playoffs. You don't have Stanton for five months, he's out. You lose guys during the course of the year… and they come back after 10 days, I'm not sure they're completely healed. I believe the talent was there. I expected them to go further. But without Aaron Judge, it changes the whole complexion of the lineup.
"And even if he was somewhat not the typical Aaron Judge because he missed so much time, he still changes the lineup. They're still careful, it's one swing always from being a two-run or three-run home run… and I just don't think they ever had their full lineup that they felt good about."
As Girardi noted, even if Judge returned, it's not crazy to say he wouldn't be the same player we're used to seeing.
That's one of the unfortunate realities the Yankees had to face this postseason, and it may have been part of why they decided to keep him out.

item.dc:creator: Andrew Wright

One of those decisions is deciding who and who not to extend the $23.15 million qualifying offer to. It appears that the Yankees have made that decision on two players and the decision is not the same for both. item.content:encoded:
After another season ended without a World Series Championship, the New York Yankees have several important decisions to make as they prepare for the offseason.
One of those decisions is deciding who and who not to extend the $23.15 million qualifying offer to. It appears that the Yankees have made that decision on two players and the decision is not the same for both.
According to MLB insider Jon Heyman, New York is expected to extend a qualifying offer to closer David Bednar, but not to second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr.
Bednar had an excellent season, collecting 35 saves while posting a 2.47 ERA with 76 strikeouts across 64 appearances and 69 1/3 innings pitched.
Chisholm, on the other hand, had an extremely disappointing season. In 137 games, he hit just .231 with 19 home runs and struck out a career high 157 times.
David Bednar was NAILS for the Yankees in 2026… should he return?
What would you offer Bednar?
2.47 ERA | 35 SV | 28.1% K% | .202 AVG pic.twitter.com/YddiwoeECn
— Yankees Worldwide (@NYYWorldwide) October 11, 2026
"I love it as a Yankee. I grew up as a Yankee fan... Who doesn't want to stay with a team you've had such great times with? To see it maybe end here sucks."
- Jazz Chisholm Jr. following New York's ALDS loss pic.twitter.com/imxKtEY6nE
— FOX Sports: MLB (@MLBONFOX) October 8, 2026
Ever since being acquired from the Pittsburgh Pirates ahead of the 2025 trade deadline, Bednar has been stellar in a Yankees uniform. Overall, he's posted a 2.39 ERA with 45 saves and 111 strikeouts in 86 appearances and 94 innings pitched.
He's claimed his role as a dominant closer in the New York bullpen, and it appears that the front office hopes to keep him around for a good amount of time.
Everyone knows that Chisholm brings a certain swag and energy to the ballpark on a daily basis. Ahead of the 2026 season, he said he was aiming to finish the year with 50 home runs and 50 stolen bases, something that clearly showed his self-confidence.
The production on the field didn't match that, though, and it is unclear as to what kind of payday he would command on the open market. It's also unclear as to what suitors Chisholm would have due to his lack of production in previous seasons.

item.title: [sbsun.com] Dodgers’ Shohei Ohtani returns to leadoff spot for must-win Game 4

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES — Desperate times call for … unexpected measures.
Two days after admitting he had a conversation with Shohei Ohtani about taking him out of the lineup for Game 3 of the National League Championship Series and one day after dropping him to sixth in the order for that game, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts moved Ohtani back to the top of the lineup.
Ohtani was in the leadoff spot for Game 4 against the Milwaukee Brewers on Thursday. It was his first time batting leadoff this postseason.
“Just seeing the work the last couple days, I like where his head is at,” Roberts said. “I liked the at-bats yesterday, and I felt that trying to shake it up a little bit – obviously we haven’t performed the way that we’re capable of, so to kind of shake it up a little bit but something that’s of somewhat normalcy that our guys are used to.”
Ohtani is just 4 for 22 (.182) in the postseason, but that hardly stands out in the unproductive lineup. Through the first three games of the NLCS, the Dodgers were hitting .165 (15 for 91) as a team with just two extra-base hits and no home runs. Only Mookie Betts (3 for 12) had more than two hits.
“I think getting back to what we’ve done all year and how it’s been going recently as far as on the offense, I think it warranted just a little bit of a shakeup,” said Roberts, who also started Miguel Rojas and Kiké Hernandez against Brewers left-hander Shane Drohan.
PHILLY CONNECTION
Before re-signing Don Mattingly to a contract extension as manager, the Philadelphia Phillies reached out to two members of the Dodgers’ front office with Philly connections – Chase Utley and Raul Ibañez.
Neither would confirm the contact, but neither interviewed for the job. Both have teen-aged children and Utley acknowledged family takes priority over pursuing a managerial career at this point.
Ibañez, currently the Dodgers’ vice president of baseball development and special projects, has been approached about managing on other occasions but declined. Utley is a special assistant to Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman.
AWARDS SEASON
Despite his injuries and a prolonged slump, Ohtani is one of the National League finalists for the Hank Aaron Award given to the top offensive performer in MLB during the regular season. Ohtani finished the season with a .275 average, 30 home runs and an .889 OPS. Ohtani has won it the past three seasons (twice in the NL and once with the Angels in the American League).
The other finalists are CJ Abrams (Washington Nationals), Jake Bauers (Milwaukee Brewers), Pete Crow-Armstrong (Chicago Cubs), Elly De La Cruz and Sal Stewart (Cincinnati Reds), Matt Olson (Atlanta Braves), Kyle Schwarber (Philadelphia Phillies), Fernando Tatis Jr. (San Diego Padres) and Jordan Walker (St. Louis Cardinals).
Ohtani is also one of three finalists for the Players’ Choice Outstanding Player Award along with Crow-Armstrong and Schwarber.
Max Muncy and Andy Pages have been named finalists for Gold Glove awards at their positions. Muncy is a finalist at third base along with Alex Bregman (Cubs) and Javier Sanoja (Miami Marlins). Pages is a finalist in center field along with Crow-Armstrong and Michael Harris II (Braves).
The Gold Glove winners will be announced on ESPN on Nov. 1.
UP NEXT
NLCS Game 5 (if necessary): Brewers (RHP Jacob Misiorowski, 16-5, 1.80 ERA) at Dodgers (LHP Tarik Skubal, 12-7, 2.72 ERA), Friday, 6 p.m. FS1, 570 AM

item.title: [thereporteronline.com] Phillies bring back Don Mattingly, hire Carlos Mendoza in staff changes
item.dc:creator: Associated Press

item.content:encoded:
By Dan Gelston
PHILADELPHIA — Dave Dombrowski believed in Don Mattingly so much that he told the interim manager following the Phillies’ elimination that he was the leading candidate to get the full-time job in 2027.
Still, the team’s president of baseball operations wanted to poke around other options, just in case.
After checking in on other potential candidates — including getting rebuffed for a second time this year by former Boston Red Sox manager Alex Cora — Dombrowski had some good news over the weekend for Mattingly: He was the manager.
“The first time the job was offered to anybody was Saturday, when I offered it to Don,” Dombrowski said Thursday.
The Phillies on Wednesday gave Mattingly a two-year deal even after a late-season collapse nearly cost the team a playoff spot. The Phillies almost blew a four-game lead for a wild card in the final week of the regular season, then lost in three games to the Atlanta Braves in the NL Wild Card Series.
Mattingly went 79-55 and earned the respect of a veteran team that largely pushed to have him return following his promotion from bench coach after Rob Thomson was fired in April
The Phillies’ core of Bryce Harper, Kyle Schwarber, J.T. Realmuto, Zack Wheeler and Aaron Nola have made five straight playoff appearances and averaged 91 wins per year during that stretch.
They just haven’t won the World Series.
There are plenty of changes ahead, and Dombrowski touched on many during a 60-minute season-ending news conference. But one constant will be in the dugout.
“Last year really wasn’t my team,” Mattingly said on a video call. “It was Thomps’ team. I took over from that point and just kind of just drove the car from there.”
He added: “I think there are things that I want to do differently.”
Just how much can Dombrowski and Mattingly do to lead the Phillies — who had a $284.7 million opening day payroll — and their aging cast of stars to their first World Series title since 2008, especially with a work stoppage almost certain in December?
Phillies expect more from Turner
Trea Turner hit .242 with a .675 OPS with a league-worst 21 errors at shortstop in his fourth season with the Phillies. He went 1 for 10 in the playoffs and still has seven years left on his $300 million, 11-year deal, all but making him immovable in the trade market.
Dombrowski told Turner during a Tuesday meeting at Citizens Bank Park that he needs to show in spring training he can play at shortstop or else the veteran could potentially move to the outfield.
“He needs to fix some things with his swing,” Dombrowski said. “From a defensive perspective we were very clear. He knows he has to be better at shortstop. I told him it’s really mandatory that it’s like that.”
Turner took the blame after the Phillies were eliminated by the Braves and noted “I’ve got a lot of work to do” to regain the form he had in 2025, when he led the NL in hitting and made only eight errors.
“He’s determined to show us he can play it,” Dombrowski said. “I said, you have to show it. You cannot play shortstop like you did defensively in ‘26 going to ’27.”
Remaking the coaching staff
The Phillies fired hitting coach Kevin Long and infield coach Bobby Dickerson.
They hired former New York Mets manager Carlos Mendoza as their new infield coach and third base coach. Mendoza was fired by the Mets in June. He had spent 15 seasons working for the New York Yankees, the last four as bench coach, before the Mets hired him to replace Buck Showalter after the 2023 season.
Anthony Contreras, who was elevated from Triple-A Lehigh Valley to coach third base when Dusty Wathan replaced Mattingly as bench coach, will stay on the major league staff in a new role.
Phillies sign Mayza
Left-handed reliever Tim Mayza and the Phillies agreed to a $2.75 million, one-year contract. He had a 3.48 ERA in 67 1/3 innings in his first season with the Phillies. The Upper Perkiomen grad even started six games as an opener.
Several Phillies face uncertain futures
Third baseman Alec Bohm is eligible for free agency, as is second baseman Luis Arraez. Bohm ended the season on a hot streak and finished with 88 RBIs and a .698 OPS. He won Game 2 against Atlanta with a two-out homer in the 10th inning. Arraez, acquired at the trade deadline, missed the playoffs with a sprained left ankle.
The Phillies have prized infielder prospect Aidan Miller cleared to play and ready to compete for a spot on the roster after he missed most of 2026 with a back injury.
Dombrowski intends to stick around
The 70-year-old Dombrowski enters the final year of his contract in 2027 but expects to stick around beyond that with the Phillies.
“I enjoy it, (I’m) healthy, have quality people around me,” Dombrowski said.

The New York Post's Jon Heyman reported Thursday the Yankees are expected to extend a qualifying offer to closer David Bednar but are "unlikely" to make the same offer to Chisholm. item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees could reportedly be considering allowing second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. to hit free agency this offseason.
The New York Post's Jon Heyman reported Thursday the Yankees are expected to extend a qualifying offer to closer David Bednar but are "unlikely" to make the same offer to Chisholm.
The Post's Joel Sherman previously reported the qualifying offer for the 2027 season will be $23.15 million.
TOP NEWS
Latest Free Agent Rumors 🐝
Buzz: Jeter's Warning to Jazz 🗣️
Early MLB Offseason Predictions on Free Agency and Trades 🔮
Bednar, 32, recorded a 2.47 ERA and 1.038 WHIP through 69.1 innings across 64 relief appearances this season. Chisholm, 28, batted .231 with 19 home runs, 55 RBI and 41 stolen bases in 137 games.
Chisholm is one year removed from becoming the third player in Yankees history to record 30 home runs and 30 stolen bases in a single season.
The following campaign ended with a postseason marred by defensive errors that led to Chisholm getting pulled from the starting lineup for Games 1 and 3 of the ALDS.
He expressed discontentment with Yankees manager Aaron Boone for not informing Chisholm ahead of time he would be replaced by Anthony Volpe in the Game 3 starting lineup.
When asked about his future with the Yankees after the Tampa Bay Rays completed their series sweep in Game 3, Chisholm still indicated he was interested in returning to the Bronx.
Bednar made three appearances during the postseason, allowing a hit and a walk but no runs in his three innings on the mound.
Keeping him in the Bronx would mark the first time in years the Yankees have committed significant money to their bullpen.
The Yankees haven't had a reliever make more than Bednar's 2026 season of $9 million since Aroldis Chapman and Zack Britton in 2022, per Spotrac.
Eight other Yankees players are heading into the offseason as pending free agents. The list most notably also includes Trent Grisham, who signed a qualifying offer to stay with the Yankees last season, alongside Paul Blackburn and Paul Goldschmidt.
Any qualifying offers to eligible players must be issued by the fifth day after the World Series. The Yankees could receive draft compensation should any players receive qualifying offers but sign with other teams.

item.content:encoded:
The Texas Rangers should strongly consider trading Josh Jung this offseason. Not because he's a bad player, but because top infield prospect Sebastian Walcott is nearing his MLB debut. Still, Texas shouldn't move Jung just to move him, as he posted a strong .827 OPS in 104 games this year.
If possible, the Rangers should deal Jung to the New York Yankees in exchange for first baseman Luis García Jr. The New York Post's Joel Sherman suggested that the Yankees could trade García this offseason.
García is coming off a 30-home-run, 90-RBI season. The Rangers' offense clearly needs a power boost, and moving Jung for García should do that. Texas ranked 21st in slugging percentage (.396) and 25th in runs (673) in 2026.
Rangers should acquire Luis García Jr. from the Yankees if Texas plans to compete in 2027
The Rangers should only make that trade if they plan to go all-in next year. García has just one year of team control, while Jung won't be a free agent until the end of the 2028 season. If Texas plans to compete in 2027 instead of undergoing a mini rebuild, adding García would be a smart move by president of baseball operations Chris Young.
García, 26, doesn't hit left-handers particularly well, so he and Jake Burger could be platoon partners. Acquiring García would also help offset the likely loss of designated hitter Joc Pederson, who is set to be a free agent this offseason.
García slashed .277/.309/.521 over 147 games this year. The New York Yankees acquired him from the Washington Nationals at the trade deadline. He is a solid defensive first baseman, posting +2 Defensive Runs Saved and +3 Outs Above Average over 985 2/3 innings this season. He also played second base and shortstop in the past, but defensive metrics suggest he should stick at first base.
García made his MLB debut with Washington in 2020. He took time to develop, but at 26, that makes sense. After four straight seasons as a below-average hitter early in his career, García posted a solid .282/.318/.444 slash line with 18 home runs and 70 RBI in 2024. He regressed in 2025, hitting just .252/.289/.412 with 16 homers and 66 RBI, before having the best year of his career in 2026. García has been worth 5.7 fWAR throughout his career, and he accounted for nearly half (2.6) of that total this year.
If Texas offered up Jung for Garcia Jr., they'd have a good chance at landing the slugging first baseman. The Yankees are desperately trying to upgrade over Ryan McMahon at the hot corner, whom they are expected to move on from after a year and a half of disastrous offensive performance.
The Rangers could also consider extending García after trading for him. When Chris Young mentioned getting younger and more dynamic, this is exactly the type of player he should be envisioning. He is still young and could be a major part of Texas' lineup for years to come.

item.content:encoded:
The best time for the New York Yankees and St. Louis Cardinals to talk about a trade involving a third baseman was probably last season when Nolan Arenado was available. The second-best time is right now, when the Cardinals are purportedly looking to fill the Arenado gap wiith a short-term solution.
The Yankees have just the thing.
While Arenado wouldn't have been a perfect ballpark fit in the Bronx last year or the summer prior, he almost certainly would've had a better tenure with the Yankees than McMahon, who was acquired in the summer of 2025 with 2.5 years left on his hefty contract. The goal was for McMahon to play exceptional defense, occasionally hook one into the short porch with his 20+ homer pop, and excel with the glove to make up for his offensive shortcomings (while batting ninth).
He was an adult in the room in '25 and ended the Red Sox in the Wild Card with a spectacular flipping catch, but didn't perform with the bat. The Yankees hoped for a bit more in 2026, and unfortunately received a bit less. He popped 11 homers with a 78 wRC+, well below league-average, while regressing defensively in the form of both decreased metrics and in-your-face blunders (we all watched Game 2). Losing range is one thing. Becoming genuinely unsteady is another. McMahon, though he seems mature and was always capable of putting up competent and productive at-bats under duress, could never be counted on to deliver actual hits instead of productive outs, and his glove hit its nadir this year.
He ... he might work in St. Louis, though, where the Cardinals are open to a short-term option at third to fill their eternal void (Nolan Gorman on line one). If the Yankees pay down his contract, as Joel Sherman has insinuated they'll try to (and they'll have to), this could be a match made in Baseball Heaven.
Yankees must move on from Ryan McMahon, even without a clear third base solution
What can the Yankees obtain for McMahon? Unfortunately, not all that much - the Cardinals have a number of young, hungry, OBP-heavy hitters, but even one of their overflow catchers feels too ambitious here. Maybe righty backup Pedro Pages. Maybe.
The most likely outcome is that the Yankees eat half or more of McMahon's contract in exchange for a bullpen piece, or they eat less than that and receive a lottery ticket prospect before heading back to the drawing board to fill third base externally.
The bottom line is that a defensive specialist whose defense has disappeared isn't a viable reason to sacrifice offense at a cornerstone position. The Yankees need a thumper at third and, failing that, need an exceptional glove. McMahon is an expensive version of neither.

item.dc:creator: Jon Heyman
item.description: The Yankees are expected to extend the $23.15M qualifying offer to free-agent closer David Bednar, who had a terrific year, sources say. item.content:encoded:
The Yankees are expected to extend the $23.15M qualifying offer to free-agent closer David Bednar, who had a terrific year, sources say.
Meantime, it’s believed the Yankees are unlikely to extend the same offer to second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr., which would represent a shocking turn off his 30-30 2025 season.
Chisholm kindly said he’d like to be back after the Yankees’ sudden playoff exit, but word is Yankees higher-ups believe it’s time to move on following his rough season. (They may also believe he might accept considering he said he wants to stay.)
The Mariners’ Randy Arozarena, Cubs’ Seiya Suzuki, Pirates Brandon Lowe and Rangers’ Trevor Rogers are also expected to receive the qualifying offer.

item.content:encoded:
- MLB. El mayor problema de Shohei Ohtani está claro: el entrenador de bateo de los Dodgers ya ha revelado por qué está teniendo tantas dificultades
- Playoffs. ¿Alguna vez un equipo de la MLB ha remontado una desventaja de 3-0 en una serie? Los Dodgers se enfrentan a una eliminación inminente en la NLCS
La eliminación de los New York Yankees en los Playoffs de MLB sigue generando repercusiones. Días después de la eliminación del equipo, comenzaron a surgir reportes sobre el ambiente interno de la organización y algunas decisiones que podrían definir el futuro de la franquicia.
Uno de los temas que más atención ha generado son las declaraciones de la superestrella Aaron Judge. El toletero, quien pasó gran parte de la temporada fuera por lesión, dejó claro que los Yankees necesitan invertir más dinero para construir un roster capaz de competir por un título de la Serie Mundial.
De acuerdo con el insider de MLB, Jon Heyman, los comentarios de Judge no fueron bien recibidos por todos dentro de la organización.
“Fuentes aseguran que uno o dos altos directivos de los Yankees se sintieron ligeramente o moderadamente molestos porque el capitán y tres veces MVP, Aaron Judge, sugirió que los Yankees, con una nómina de 320 millones de dólares, podrían gastar más después de ser barridos por los Rays en la Serie Divisional. Los altos mandos lo superarán porque Judge tiene una excelente relación con ellos, pero aseguran que quedaron sorprendidos”.
Las declaraciones reavivaron el debate entre los aficionados: ¿Judge tiene razón al pedir una mayor inversión o fue demasiado lejos al hacerlo públicamente?
Los comentarios de Aaron Judge incomodaron a la directiva de los Yankees
Las palabras del tres veces MVP habrían generado molestia dentro de la organización, especialmente porque llegaron de parte del líder del vestidor y la cara principal de la franquicia.
Judge no pudo disputar los Playoffs debido a una lesión, una ausencia que muchos consideran que tuvo un peso importante en la eliminación de Nueva York. Aun así, el jardinero cuenta con un contrato de nueve años y 360 millones de dólares, uno de los acuerdos más importantes en la historia de los Yankees.
El capitán parece considerar que el problema no es únicamente gastar más dinero, sino invertirlo en las posiciones correctas. Sin embargo, la directiva también realizó movimientos importantes antes del inicio de la temporada. Trent Grisham recibió 20 millones de dólares en 2026, mientras que Cody Bellinger firmó una millonaria extensión.
Además, salvo jóvenes como Cam Schlittler y Ben Rice, la mayoría de los jugadores del roster cuentan con contratos elevados.
El periodista de Bleacher Report, Timothy Rapp, también se refirió a la polémica:
“Los New York Yankees presuntamente no apreciaron los comentarios públicos de Aaron Judge, quien esperaba que la directiva apostara con todo durante esta temporada baja después de que el equipo nuevamente fracasara en ganar una Serie Mundial”.
La polémica volvió a abrir el debate sobre la influencia que tiene Judge dentro de la organización. Para muchos, su voz va mucho más allá del terreno de juego y sus opiniones tienen un peso importante en las decisiones que toma la franquicia.

item.title: [MARCA] Aaron Judge sparks Yankees fury with shocking post-elimination comments

Dodgers staring NLCS elimination right in the face The New York Yankees’ elimination from the MLB Playoffs continues to have major repercussions. One issue drawing the most attention is the com
item.content:encoded:
- MLB. Did Carlos Mendoza betray the Mets by signing with one of their rivals?
- MLB. Has an MLB team ever come back from 3-0 series deficit? Dodgers staring NLCS elimination right in the face
The New York Yankees’ elimination from the MLB Playoffs continues to have major repercussions. Days after the team’s exit, reports began to surface about the atmosphere within the organization and some of the decisions that could shape the franchise’s future.
One issue drawing the most attention is the comments made by superstar Aaron Judge. The slugger, who spent much of the season sidelined by injury, suggested that the Yankees should spend more money to build a roster capable of competing for a World Series title.
According to MLB insider Jon Heyman, Judge’s remarks were not well received by everyone within the organization.
“Sources say one or two Yankees [bigwigs] were slightly-to-somewhat annoyed that captain/three-time MVP Judge suggested the $320M Yankees could spend more after they were swept by the Rays in the division series. Yankees higher-ups will get over it because Judge has a great rapport with them. But they were said to be taken aback.”
The comments reignited the debate among fans: Is Judge right to call for greater investment, or did he go too far by making those remarks publicly?
Aaron Judge’s comments rubbed Yankees executives the wrong way
The three-time MVP’s remarks appear to have struck a nerve within the organization, especially because they came from the clubhouse leader and the face of the franchise.
Judge was unable to play in the Playoffs because of injury, an absence many believe played a significant role in New York’s elimination. Even so, the outfielder is in the middle of a nine-year, $360 million contract, one of the richest deals in franchise history.
Judge seems to believe the issue is not simply spending more, but spending wisely in the right areas. Still, the front office made significant investments before the season. Trent Grisham earned $20 million in 2026, Cody Bellinger signed a lucrative contract extension, and aside from young players such as Cam Schlittler and Ben Rice, most of the roster is already on sizable contracts.
Bleacher Report journalist Timothy Rapp also weighed in on the controversy.
“The New York Yankees reportedly didn’t appreciate Aaron Judge’s public comments expecting the front office to go ‘all in’ this offseason after the team yet again failed to win a World Series title.”
The controversy has reopened the discussion about Judge’s influence within the organization. For many, his voice carries far beyond the field, and his opinions play a major role in shaping the franchise’s direction.

item.title: [3wv.com] Brewers stun Dodgers with back-to-back homers in 7th inning and ride 6-2 win to 3-0 lead in NLCS | WWWV 97.5

item.content:encoded:
By BETH HARRIS AP Sports Writer
LOS ANGELES (AP) — The Milwaukee Brewers hit the second-fewest home runs in baseball during the regular season, even as they topped the majors with 103 wins.
Maybe they were saving their biggest swings for the Los Angeles Dodgers.
Jake Bauers and Garrett Mitchell launched back-to-back homers off Blake Snell in the seventh inning, and the Brewers beat the Dodgers 6-2 on Wednesday to build a 3-0 cushion in the National League Championship Series.
Jackson Chourio also went deep on the first pitch of the game to help the Brewers close within one win of their first NL pennant. Milwaukee was in the American League when the franchise reached its only World Series, a seven-game loss to the St. Louis Cardinals in 1982.
“Job’s not finished yet,” Mitchell said.
Game 4 is Thursday at Dodger Stadium, where the Brewers can become the first major league club to complete a postseason sweep after getting swept by that same opponent in the previous postseason.
Los Angeles took all four games against Milwaukee in the NLCS last year.
The Dodgers had just gone ahead 2-1 in the sixth inning before getting stunned by the Brewers in their three-run seventh. The loss pushed the two-time defending World Series champions to the brink of elimination.
“All three games we’ve played so far, and hopefully that continues, where just every time they score, we come back and score,” Milwaukee manager Pat Murphy said. “That’s not easy to do in baseball.”
It was the fifth comeback victory in seven postseason games for the Brewers, who have never beaten Los Angeles in three previous playoff series.
The only other time the Dodgers trailed 3-0 in a best-of-seven postseason series, they were swept by the Baltimore Orioles in the 1966 World Series.
The lone team in big league history to come back from a 3-0 deficit to win a best-of-seven postseason series was the Boston Red Sox in the 2004 AL Championship Series against the New York Yankees.
“We’ve won four in a row a number of times this year,” Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. “We’ve got to win tomorrow. That’s our only focus.”
Coming into the seventh, Snell had retired 14 batters in a row. But the first pitch of the game thrown by the two-time Cy Young Award winner was hit for a home run by Chourio, and his last pitch was Mitchell’s solo shot.
Andrew Vaughn drew a seven-pitch walk to open the seventh and was replaced by pinch-runner Christian Yelich. Bauers followed with a 412-foot drive to right field on the 11th pitch of his at-bat for a 3-2 lead as most of the players in Milwaukee’s dugout came onto the field to celebrate.
“I was looking for a fastball, and I didn’t want to miss it,” said Bauers, who had a team-leading 26 of Milwaukee’s 154 regular-season homers.
It was his latest relentless plate appearance, too, after Bauers drew a 12-pitch walk from Yoshinobu Yamamoto that helped the Brewers go ahead early in Game 2.
“I think what changed for me this year was I stopped caring about results,” Bauers said. “I started caring about competing. I started caring about being in the moment and getting out of my own way.”
Watching Bauers work over Snell was “super sick,” Mitchell said.
And then it was his turn.
Mitchell’s drive traveled 428 feet to right-center. That chased Snell, who hadn’t given up a home run in 46 1/3 innings this year entering the game. It was the first time in his career he served up back-to-back homers to left-handed hitters and only the second time he gave up multiple longballs to left-handed batters in one game.
Bauers and Mitchell became just the third pair of left-handed hitters with consecutive postseason home runs off the same left-handed pitcher. Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper did it for Philadelphia against Atlanta reliever Dylan Lee in an NL Wild Card Series this year, and Babe Ruth and Lou Gehrig connected for the New York Yankees off Bill Sherdel of the St. Louis Cardinals in the 1928 World Series.
Milwaukee has five homers in the NLCS and eight this postseason.
Snell gave up four runs and four hits in six-plus innings. He struck out nine and walked two.
The Brewers extended their lead to 5-2 in the eighth on Justin Wrobleski’s wild pitch that scored Brice Turang, who reached on an infield single and advanced to third on William Contreras’ single. They added another run on Joey Ortiz’s two-strike RBI single in the ninth.
The offensively starved Dodgers took a 2-1 lead on Will Smith’s two-run double off reliever Abner Uribe in the sixth.
After rookie starter Robert Gasser pitched five shutout innings, Uribe entered and loaded the bases on walks to Teoscar Hernández, Kyle Tucker and Shohei Ohtani. Smith, who was 1 for 25 in the playoffs, doubled off the left-center fence with one out for his first hit of the NLCS.
DL Hall took over from Uribe and stranded runners at second and third by striking out pinch-hitter Kiké Hernández and Tommy Edman.
Hall allowed one hit in 2 1/3 scoreless innings to improve to 3-0 in these playoffs. Trevor Megill got four outs for his second save of the series and fourth this postseason.
The Dodgers played from behind again after the 22-year-old Chourio connected for his third career leadoff homer in the postseason as fans were still heading to their seats.
After that, Mitchell walked and Cooper Pratt singled in the second before Snell retired 14 in a row — six on strikeouts — before getting hammered in the seventh.
The Dodgers had runners on base in all but three innings, but couldn’t get enough across. They have yet to homer in the NLCS and are 3 for 32 with runners in scoring position this postseason.
Ohtani was 1 for 2 with a walk while hitting sixth in the order, the lowest he’s batted since joining the Dodgers three years ago.
___

item.title: [Yahoo] Jazz Chisholm Jr. reveals Aaron Judge’s message after Yankees’ playoff exit
item.dc:creator: Andy Mailhot
item.description: Image Press Agency/Depositphotos Jazz Chisholm Jr. discusses Judge's message New York Yankees second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. discussed Aaron Judge's leadership after the Tampa Bay Rays completed a three-game American League Division Series sweep on October 7, 2026, at Yankee Stadium in the Bronx. New York lost the deciding Game 3 by a 4-3 score. Chisholm said the captain addressed teammates following elimination, offering encouragement to a clubhouse whose postseason ended after five games aga
item.content:encoded:
Image Press Agency/Depositphotos
Jazz Chisholm Jr. discusses Judge's message
New York Yankees second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. discussed Aaron Judge's leadership after the Tampa Bay Rays completed a three-game American League Division Series sweep on October 7, 2026, at Yankee Stadium in the Bronx.
New York lost the deciding Game 3 by a 4-3 score. Chisholm said the captain addressed teammates following elimination, offering encouragement to a clubhouse whose postseason ended after five games against Boston and Tampa Bay.
Conor P. Fitzgerald/Shutterstock.com
Aaron Judge keeps teammates focused
Jazz Chisholm Jr. described Aaron Judge as a captain who speaks to teammates regularly, not only when the Yankees lose. He said those conversations helped players maintain a positive outlook during challenging moments throughout 2026.
Chisholm emphasized that Judge encouraged the group to stay focused on the right path. The second baseman's comments described an established clubhouse role rather than a new strategy introduced after Tampa Bay's October playoff series.
JHVEPhoto/Depositphotos
Aaron Judge misses the entire postseason
Aaron Judge missed all five New York Yankees postseason games in 2026, including both September Wild Card Series contests against Boston. The captain remained unavailable for October's Division Series because of a right calf strain.
Judge last appeared on September 16 and went on the injured list three days later. Manager Aaron Boone said the outfielder needed additional running drills and greater endurance before he could return to game action.
Conor P. Fitzgerald/Shutterstock.com
Aaron Judge records 18 homers in 2026
Aaron Judge appeared in just 66 regular-season games for New York in 2026, batting .241 with 18 home runs and 41 RBIs. A fractured rib and subsequent calf strain limited his time in the lineup.
Judge also posted a .360 on-base percentage and a .511 slugging percentage across his limited schedule. The rib injury kept him sidelined for more than three months before his eventual return in early September 2026.
Conor P. Fitzgerald/Shutterstock.com
Jazz Chisholm Jr. questions home boos
Jazz Chisholm Jr. heard boos from home fans at Yankee Stadium after fouling out as a seventh-inning pinch hitter in Wednesday's Game 3. The reaction came during New York's attempt to keep its postseason alive.
Chisholm said the reaction confused him because teammates were competing to win the deciding game. He added that the criticism did not hurt him and questioned why supporters would discourage players during a playoff contest.
andykazie/Depositphotos
Anthony Rizzo disputes Chisholm's remarks
Former Yankees first baseman Anthony Rizzo challenged Jazz Chisholm Jr.'s response to the home crowd's boos. On the Ross and Rizzo Unfiltered podcast, he questioned why a player familiar with New York would express surprise.
Rizzo noted that Aaron Judge, Anthony Volpe, and Giancarlo Stanton had also faced unfavorable reactions from home crowds. He viewed that history as evidence that players should better understand the city's particularly demanding baseball culture.
lev radin/Shutterstock.com
Aaron Boone makes a late lineup change
Yankees manager Aaron Boone benched Jazz Chisholm Jr. for Game 3 and started Anthony Volpe at second base. Chisholm said he discovered the change when he saw the lineup card rather than through a conversation.
Before the September Wild Card Series opener against Boston, Boone had sent Chisholm an encouraging text about his role. After Wednesday's Rays game, the infielder said direct advance notice of benching would have been preferable.
Dariozg/Depositphotos
Jazz Chisholm Jr. finishes with 41 steals
Jazz Chisholm Jr. finished the 2026 regular season with a .231 batting average, 19 home runs, 55 RBIs, and 41 stolen bases in 137 games. His final totals fell short of his previously stated ambitions.
Chisholm had targeted 50 home runs and 50 steals. Against Tampa Bay in the Division Series, he went hitless in eight at-bats, drew one walk, and recorded two stolen bases across all three postseason games.
sfStudio/Depositphotos
Drew Rasmussen limits Yankees to one hit
Tampa Bay starter Drew Rasmussen held the Yankees to one hit across eight scoreless innings on October 3. He recorded 10 strikeouts and earned a 1-0 victory in the Division Series opener at Tropicana Field.
New York catcher Austin Wells broke up Rasmussen's no-hit attempt with a double in the eighth inning but was retired trying for third base. That lone hit established a franchise postseason low for Yankees batters.
AlexanderMils/Depositphotos
Yankees commit four errors in Game 2
The visiting Yankees committed four fielding errors in their 5-2 Game 2 loss to Tampa Bay on October 5. Three defensive mistakes came in the first inning, when the Rays scored once at Tropicana Field.
Jazz Chisholm Jr.'s throw went wide of first base during a fielder's choice, allowing Yandy Díaz to score. Ben Rice delivered both New York runs with two solo home runs, but Tampa Bay ultimately prevailed.
Fun fact: Before becoming Yankees teammates, Aaron Judge and Jazz Chisholm Jr. shared an unusual distinction: both appeared on MLB The Show video game covers, five years apart.
Keeton Gale/Shutterstock.com
Victor Mesa Jr. delivers decisive home run
Victor Mesa Jr. gave Tampa Bay a 4-2 lead with a two-run home run in the sixth inning of Game 3. The rookie connected against Yankees left-hander Max Fried at Yankee Stadium on October 7.
Fried allowed four runs and seven hits through 5 2/3 innings while recording seven strikeouts. Tampa Bay closer Bryan Baker secured the final out when he struck out Trent Grisham with Chisholm stranded on second.
ags1973/Depositphotos
Anthony Volpe loses homer after review
Anthony Volpe appeared to tie Game 3 with a two-run home run in the sixth inning, but officials overturned the call following a replay review. A spectator reached over the wall from the left-field seats.
Officials determined the ball would neither clear the fence nor be caught without interference. Volpe received an RBI double, allowing George Lombard Jr. to score and narrowing Tampa Bay's advantage to 4-3 in Game 3.
Want to know more about the MLB announcer's comments and why fans are discussing them? Explore the full story and see what sparked the conversation.
Conor P. Fitzgerald/Shutterstock.com
Aaron Judge urges Yankees to improve roster
Aaron Judge urged Yankees leadership to strengthen the roster following the team's postseason exit. The captain called on managing general partner Hal Steinbrenner and general manager Brian Cashman to consider changes before the 2027 season.
Chisholm said he wanted to remain with New York as free agency approached. The Yankees recorded 93 regular-season victories in 2026 but have not won a World Series title since 2009.
Is it time for some MLB teams to move into new ballparks? Explore which five teams may need new stadiums and what could shape their future plans.
Do you think Aaron Judge's leadership was what the Yankees needed after their playoff exit, or should roster changes be the priority? Please share your thoughts in the comments below!

item.content:encoded:
Yankees have troubling Ben Rice problem despite 41 home runs originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
Ben Rice had an amazing season for the New York Yankees.
Plus, he continued to rake in the postseason, hitting four home runs between the Wild Card Series and the ALDS.
Rice finished the regular season with 41 homers and a .897 OPS. Once again, he will be a key member of New York's lineup next season.
However, the Yankees need Rice to improve his defense at first base. It could cost them a game or two, and he's probably too young to be a full-time DH.
"Despite how good Rice has proved to be as a hitter (41 home runs, .897 OPS), he was bad defensively at first last season," The Athletic's Brendan Kuty wrote.
"Of the 43 players who played 300 innings at the position, Rice ranked second to last in DRS at minus-8. Only the Seattle Mariners' Josh Naylor was worse at minus-9," Kuty added.
The Yankees had Paul Goldschmidt, a four-time Gold Glove Award winner, sharing time with Rice at first base.
Still, Goldschmidt's presence and tutelage didn't seem to pay off much.
Rice also needs to play first base if the Yankees want Luis Garcia Jr. and Aaron Judge to spend more time at DH.
Garcia began his career at second base with the Washington Nationals but was one of the worst defenders in the sport at the middle infield spot.
A defensive improvement at first base from Rice could really help the Yankees' lineup and would make general roster construction a lot easier.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Yankees would be wasting Cody Bellinger at first base
item.dc:creator: Alexander Wilson
item.description: Seventeen home runs aren't enough to make everyone happy with a $162.5 million contract. item.content:encoded:
Seventeen home runs aren't enough to make everyone happy with a $162.5 million contract. Cody Bellinger's glove deserves a much fairer hearing than his power total, though, especially when the Yankees start moving names around their 2027 lineup.
I'd keep him in left field. Making Bellinger part of a first-base reshuffle might solve a daily playing-time headache, but it would also remove him from the position where he provided his clearest advantage this season.
Bellinger gave the Yankees real value in left
Wednesday's Gold Glove finalist announcement supplies a timely reminder. Bellinger led left fielders with 21 Defensive Runs Saved and finished with six Outs Above Average. Those measures use different methods and shouldn't be added together. Both, however, describe a useful defender rather than an expensive bat the club needs to hide.
The actual assignments matter. Bellinger started 112 games in left and logged 1,008 2/3 innings there. He made one start at first base. Moving him across the diamond would be a meaningful change to how the Yankees used him, not a harmless continuation of the same role.
New York can still want more offense. Bellinger hit .264/.338/.429 with 17 homers and 73 RBI in 132 games. A .767 OPS doesn't settle whether the five-year investment was wise, and a defensive award nomination certainly doesn't settle it either.
There isn't an obvious platoon problem to solve
His season wasn't built on one comfortable matchup. Bellinger had a .755 OPS against left-handed pitching and .775 against right-handers. Neither number makes him indispensable, but they don't suggest a player who needs to be pulled out of the lineup whenever the opposing starter throws with the wrong hand.
0What do you think?Post a comment.
Moving him would create another assignment
First-base flexibility has uses. On a day when Bellinger needs less running, or when another outfielder offers a clear matchup advantage, the occasional move can help. Committing him there for long stretches would be a different decision, because somebody else would have to handle those left-field innings.
I'd want the Yankees to compare the entire defensive arrangement before making that call. How much better is the new first baseman than the existing option? How much weaker does left field become? A more convenient lineup card can still produce a worse team if those costs are ignored.
There are limits to this argument. Defensive estimates vary, Bellinger's future health can't be assumed, and a genuinely superior outfield addition could change the calculation. The Yankees should remain open to those possibilities instead of treating one position as permanently reserved.
For now, the evidence favors leaving his main job alone. Bellinger can improve at the plate without the Yankees sacrificing what he already does well. Their offseason should be about adding strengths, not moving one of the existing ones to a position where it matters less.
