Moreover, the Dodgers' front office didn't tie themselves into long-term contracts that could potentially be anchors down the road. Diaz has two years left o
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are off to another NLCS as they'll meet the Milwaukee Brewers for the second straight year. Nonetheless, the Dodgers' focus is on the playoffs, but this offseason, could the Dodgers land a recognizable name in free agency?
Last offseason, Los Angeles landed two of the big free agent names: Kyle Tucker and Edwin Diaz. Moreover, the Dodgers' front office didn't tie themselves into long-term contracts that could potentially be anchors down the road.
Diaz has two years left on his contract after this season, and Tucker has three more years left on his deal, but he has player opt-out clauses after both the second and third years.
As a result, could the Dodgers once again make a move like this? Jake Elman of FanSided believes Los Angeles can, which is why he has them as one of the top five landing spots for Jazz Chisholm Jr., who is now a free agent after the New York Yankees fell in the ALDS to the Tampa Bay Rays.
"You can't make a list like this and leave out the Dodgers, regardless of their 2027 payroll," Elman wrote in an Oct. 8 article. "We always expect them to pursue any and all free agents, outside of those best suited to be an everyday designated hitter. Shohei Ohtani isn't moving back to the outfield, and we're not even sure whether he'll return to the rotation next year."
Dodgers Can Handle Jazz Chisholm Jr.'s Personality
Moreover, another reason that Elman believes that the Dodgers make sense for Chisholm is that manager Dave Roberts and, for the most part, the team's clubhouse can handle the player's personality.
"Dave Roberts has spent the last decade proving he can handle every personality imaginable, so Chisholm's chains and bat flips won't be a significant mark against him," Elman added in his article.
"That said, the two-time All-Star might not have the job security he did in New York, especially if he settles for a shorter contract."
It was a challenging 2026 campaign for Chisholm as he hit .230 with 111 hits, 19 homers, 55 RBIs, and 71 runs scored in 141 games in the 2026 regular season and playoffs, per StatMuse.
Rangers Urged to Consider Trading for Andy Pages
Speaking of the Dodgers and potential offseason moves, recently, Matt Postins of the Texas Rangers on SI floated Dodgers outfielder Andy Pages as a potential name the AL West team should consider after falling short of the playoffs this season.
"The Los Angeles Dodgers center fielder is coming off his first All-Star Game appearance and slashed .343/.468/.811 with 23 home runs and 85 RBI," Postins wrote in an Oct. 4 article. "Unlike [Evan] Carter, Pages has stayed healthy in all three of his MLB seasons.
"He's just about to enter his arbitration seasons so his cost can be controlled to some degree. He's about to turn 26 years old which means he's hitting his prime."
During the regular season, Pages hit .274 with 140 hits, 23 home runs, 85 RBIs, and 75 runs scored in 134 games for the Dodgers, per StatMuse. As a result, the best of Pages may still be to come.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Dodgers Get Clear Message on Yankees' Free Agent Jazz Chisholm Jr. appeared first on HEAVY.

item.title: [Newsday] Don't expect Yankees to part ways with Aaron Boone, Brian Cashman
item.dc:creator: Erik Boland
item.description: A Yankees team entering the playoffs with the highest of expectations saw their season end with a 4-3 loss to an American League East rival in the ALDS at Yankee Stadium. Their manager, Aaron Boone, emotions still raw from making the rounds in a disconsolate clubhouse, met with the media shortly after midnight to sort through it all. “We'll continue to work at getting to that point where we're as complete in every department as we can be, offensively, pitching, defense,” Boone said. “They just o
item.content:encoded:
A Yankees team entering the playoffs with the highest of expectations saw their season end with a 4-3 loss to an American League East rival in the ALDS at Yankee Stadium.
Their manager, Aaron Boone, emotions still raw from making the rounds in a disconsolate clubhouse, met with the media shortly after midnight to sort through it all.
“We'll continue to work at getting to that point where we're as complete in every department as we can be, offensively, pitching, defense,” Boone said. “They just outplayed us a little bit.”
Later, Boone would say: “In the end, you don’t move on usually when you can’t get enough big hits in a series.”
One can be forgiven if thinking this came out of Boone’s mouth after the Yankees fell to Tampa Bay Wednesday night in Game 3 of the ALDS, the franchise again failing to win its first World Series since 2009.
The above comments did indeed come out of Boone’s mouth…in early October of 2018 after a loss to the Red Sox in Game 4 of that year’s ALDS.
The remarks read familiar because here is some of what Boone did say, nearly eight years later to the date, after Wednesday night’s 4-3 loss to the Rays:
“We gotta be more complete offensively, defensively, pitching…they were a little bit better than us… ultimately didn’t swing the bats enough and put enough runs on the board to move on or to extend the series.”
If there has been a hallmark of Boone’s nine-year tenure, it has been taking clubs into the postseason seemingly with the pieces capable of an extended October run, only to come up short.
Often, as was the case this season – as well as in 2018, 2020, 2021 and 2025 – woefully so as those clubs failed to make even the ALCS (the 2023 Yankees missed the postseason entirely, Boone’s one playoff-less year).
This is not to focus solely on Boone, to whom the fan base has never truly warmed and whose unpopularity with it has steadily increased by the year.
Spoiler alert: there are no indications that owner Hal Steinbrenner has soured on Boone, who has one year remaining on his contract, or on Brian Cashman, the GM since 1998 whose contract expires at the end of this month, for that matter.
“Yeah, of course,” Boone said after Wednesday’s loss, asked if he expected to be back.
Though that could be read as an expression of the arrogance and condescension that occasionally creep into Boone press conferences, it should be read more as a reflection of working for owner Hal Steinbrenner. The Yankees' owner is generally loath to get rid of people with time and money left on their contracts, whether it be players, coaches or executives.
And, again, that isn’t to say if Boone’s contract was up at season’s end, Steinbrenner, consistently among Boone’s staunchest supporters over the years, would have any interest in pulling the trigger on a new manager search.
It is not anticipated Cashman will be going anywhere, either (though, separately, one does wonder if the 59-year-old executive, with the organization since his intern days of 1986 and in his current position for nearly 30 years, might at some point tire of the constant slings and arrows that come with the job and call it a day on his own).
No, the kind of changes in team hierarchy fans are clamoring for, and were clamoring for well before this most recent October flameout, remain highly unlikely.
Steinbrenner oversees an immensely successful baseball enterprise – success defined as annual playoff appearances, consistently high ratings on the YES Network and fans, from the late March/early April home opener through the end of September, streaming, proverbial wallets wide open for business, through the gates at Yankee Stadium to cheer on what is always one of the highest-paid teams in the game.
Winning the World Series is the goal, of course, and Steinbrenner, unfairly criticized for not being his bombastic father, George, very much wants to add trophy No. 28 to the franchise shelf. But, like the vast majority of his brethren now in MLB ownership, Steinbrenner is most concerned with “process.”
As long as “the process” – always treated with the utmost secrecy, lest it be subject to scrutiny of any kind – is deemed good and sound and profitable, the results, when measured in the win-loss column, become almost secondary.
That trickles from ownership on down and leads to Boone, back in 2018 and then again after Wednesday night’s game, saying things like the team vanquishing his was just “a little bit better.”
The Yankees, ever sure of their “process,” again were simply victimized by inconvenient injuries, a bad bounce, unable to get that elusive “big” hit, etc.
So, no need for true organizational self-introspection. No introspection that goes beyond throwing a member or two of Boone’s coaching staff to the wolves, or concluding an additional “war room” or two is needed behind the scenes for better implementation of said “process.”
Better that than acknowledging that the 2018 Red Sox were more than “a little bit better” than that year’s Yankees.
Just as the 2026 Rays were significantly better than the 2026 Yankees – both in the regular season and the postseason.
And on it goes.

item.content:encoded:
Otra vez octubre dejó a Yankees con las manos vacías. La derrota 4-3 ante Tampa Bay, el 7 de octubre, selló una barrida en la Serie Divisional de la Liga Americana de la MLB y reabrió el debate sobre Aaron Boone. Sin embargo, al 8 de octubre de 2026, su despido no había sido anunciado.
Boone tiene contrato hasta 2027 y conserva el respaldo de Aaron Judge. Por eso, hablar de sucesores exige una condición: que la directiva decida cambiar de rumbo. Brad Ausmus, Don Mattingly y David Ross aparecen entre las alternativas planteadas por Sportsnaut, pero no conforman una lista oficial de candidatos de la franquicia.
- LEER MÁS: ¡Adiós Yankees! Los Rays los barren y avanzan a la Serie de Campeonato
- LEER MÁS: ¡Milwaukee Brewers avanzan a la Serie de Campeonato!
Brad Ausmus representa la alternativa interna. El actual coach de banca de Yankees ya dirigió a Tigers y Angels, de modo que conoce las exigencias del cargo. Su familiaridad con los jugadores y con el funcionamiento del cuerpo técnico podría facilitar una transición sin empezar de cero en el dugout.
Sus registros como mánager fueron 314-332 con Detroit y 72-90 con Angels. Esos resultados obligan a evaluar qué podría aportar en una nueva oportunidad. Por su vínculo con el equipo actual, sería una opción de continuidad; la directiva tendría que decidir si ese perfil responde al cambio que necesita después de otra eliminación.
Suscríbete al Newsletter de Unanimo y recibe gratis las últimas noticias. Dale click aquí
Don Mattingly ofrece un perfil distinto: el peso de una figura histórica de Yankees y experiencia dirigiendo a Dodgers, Marlins y Phillies. En 2026 asumió Philadelphia después de un inicio de 9-19 y llevó al equipo a un registro de 79-55 durante su gestión. Esa recuperación aporta un argumento deportivo a una candidatura que no tendría que sostenerse únicamente en la nostalgia.
Su disponibilidad, sin embargo, está lejos de darse por descontada. Mattingly mantiene contrato con Phillies hasta 2027 y la organización todavía debe decidir quién dirigirá al club la próxima temporada. NBC Sports Philadelphia lo incluye entre sus opciones. Para Yankees, considerar su llegada también implicaría resolver ese compromiso contractual y conocer la decisión de Philadelphia.
The Aaron Boone Yankees Era has been a failure https://t.co/WUS8WqmqZu
— Onyx Odds (@OnyxOdds) October 8, 2026
David Ross completa esta selección como una opción externa con experiencia en el cargo. Dirigió a Cubs de 2020 a 2023, alcanzó la postemporada en su primera campaña y cerró su última temporada con 83-79, antes de ser reemplazado por Craig Counsell. Sportsnaut lo incluye entre los nombres que Yankees podría evaluar si se produce una vacante.
Ross continúa interesado en volver a dirigir, según NBC Sports Philadelphia, pero su balance de 262-284 con Chicago y la ausencia de victorias en series de playoffs también deben entrar en el examen. Ofrecería una voz diferente con experiencia previa. La primera decisión sigue siendo de Yankees: determinar si Boone dejará el puesto que estos nombres podrían disputar.

item.title: [Awful Announcing] Alex Rodriguez completely misunderstands 'Moneyball' while praising Milwaukee Brewers
item.dc:creator: Brendon Kleen
item.description: In 2003, “Moneyball” took MLB by storm. The book, which chronicles how the 2002 Oakland Athletics won 103 games using a data-driven approach, became the template for how baseball would be played for decades to come. Many of that Athletics team’s core “sabermetrics” tenets still drive strategy in MLB today: prioritizing on-base percentage over batting average, aggressively deploying relief pitchers, and chasing extra-base hits. item.content:encoded:
In 2003, “Moneyball” took MLB by storm.
The book, which chronicles how the 2002 Oakland Athletics won 103 games using a data-driven approach, became the template for how baseball would be played for decades to come. Many of that Athletics team’s core “sabermetrics” tenets still drive strategy in MLB today: prioritizing on-base percentage over batting average, aggressively deploying relief pitchers, and chasing extra-base hits.
In fact, some recent baseball rule changes were made specifically to counter the numbers-driven tactics that took over the sport. Some of those shifts have allowed less expensive, deeper teams to dominate once again.
The Milwaukee Brewers, headed to their second straight NLCS after a chaotic series against the San Diego Padres, are one such example. Milwaukee led the league in on-base percentage, were fifth in stolen bases, had one of MLB’s best defenses, and rode a killer bullpen through the Division Series this week.
Baseball media has a fantastic story to tell about a Brewers team outplaying its payroll and showing how to win in the modern MLB. Yet after the Brewers’ dominant Game 4 road win on Wednesday night, Fox Sports studio analyst and baseball legend Alex Rodriguez told the exact opposite story.
Teed up to give the first postgame take on Milwaukee’s win, Rodriguez puzzlingly painted the Brewers as “counter-Moneyball.”
“They’ve taken a bit of a counter-Moneyball approach,” Rodriguez said. “Meaning that because they don’t hit home runs, I don’t think people out there realize, in the national audience, how great this team is, how well-managed they are, where they do all the little things that win games. It may not get the SportsCenter‘s, but they’re top in batting average, contact, running in scoring position, defense, base-running, the best ERA in baseball.”
More than 20 years later, Alex Rodriguez has no clue what “Moneyball” means ⚾️ 📺 https://t.co/8cWxq6K9A5
— Awful Announcing (@awfulannouncing) October 8, 2026
The three-time league MVP fell into a frustrating habit among commentators across all sports these days. Rodriguez used “Moneyball” as a catch-all to describe any strategy informed by analytics. NBA analysts do the same thing with the word “analytics.” In this case, the all-out pursuit of home runs that took over baseball did come from statistical analysis. However, the Brewers are perhaps baseball’s coolest antidote to that approach — by riding the original principles of “Moneyball.”
The league office also helped by shortening the basepaths and restricting defensive shifts, bringing back small ball-style baseball. Yet no team is “counter-Moneyball” anymore. And Rodriguez’s championship Yankees team in 2009 hit more home runs than any team in the league this season.
Baseball has been overtaken by numbers in a way that frustrates fans. But the top commentators paid to cover the sport should have a much better handle on how the game is played than Rodriguez did Wednesday night.

item.title: [RPCTV] MLB: Aaron Judge exige refuerzos y respalda a Aaron Boone
item.description: Aaron Judge pasó la mayor parte de las últimas dos semanas intentando convencer a los Yankees de Nueva York de que dejaran de ser tan cautelosos con respecto a su lesión en la pantorrilla derecha, una batalla constante que terminó con el capitán viendo los cinco partidos de postemporada de la MLB desde la banca. “Somos los Yankees”, dijo Judge después de la derrota de su equipo por 4-3 ante los Rays en el Juego 3 de la Serie Divisional de la Liga Americana. “Creo que deberían apostar con todo y
item.content:encoded:
Aaron Judge pasó la mayor parte de las últimas dos semanas intentando convencer a los Yankees de Nueva York de que dejaran de ser tan cautelosos con respecto a su lesión en la pantorrilla derecha, una batalla constante que terminó con el capitán viendo los cinco partidos de postemporada de la MLB desde la banca.
“Somos los Yankees”, dijo Judge después de la derrota de su equipo por 4-3 ante los Rays en el Juego 3 de la Serie Divisional de la Liga Americana. “Creo que deberían apostar con todo y hacer lo que sea necesario. Si tenemos carencias, ya sea que necesitemos ciertos jugadores o personal, lo que sea que haga falta, hay que salir a buscarlo.
Cuando le preguntaron si cree que los Yankees han apostado con todo, Judge vaciló.
“Es difícil decirlo”, expresó Judge. “Yo quisiera hacer cambios por todos los jugadores y firmar a todos los agentes libres cada año, pero sé que eso no es realista. Así que nos dan un equipo ganador todos los años, pero eso no es suficiente aquí en Nueva York. Somos los Yankees. Hay que salir a buscar campeonatos y apostar con todo cada año. Así que estoy emocionado por ver lo que hacen”.
Aaron Judge respalda a Aaron Boone
Judge aseguró que nadie en el clubhouse está satisfecho con el resultado de este año y prometió que el equipo estará listo para “dar el siguiente paso” en el 2027. Y espera que eso suceda con Boone todavía a cargo de confeccionar las alineaciones.
“Él es nuestro dirigente. Es quien lleva el timón”, dijo Judge. “Nos coloca en la mejor posición para salir al terreno y tener éxito. Especialmente en una temporada como esta, en la que estuve lesionado y me perdí 100 juegos... Que haya sabido manejar la situación como lo hizo y ponernos en la mejor posición para llegar a la postemporada y tener la oportunidad de ganar una Serie Mundial demuestra que definitivamente siempre nos ha respaldado”.

item.title: [New York Post] It’s time for the Yankees to move on from Aaron Boone
item.dc:creator: Jon Heyman
item.description: The Yankees are awash in analytics. To their credit, they know the numbers game as well as anyone. But the most obvious number is right there in front of them, yet they ignore it. Year after year, they ignore it. Aaron Boone’s managed the Yankees for nine years, and he is zero for nine now. That isn’t good, or certainly good enough. By the old Steinbrenner standards, Boone would have been gone six years ago. We do understand the Yankees’ expectations are more normal today, in the post-Boss era.
item.content:encoded:
The Yankees are awash in analytics. To their credit, they know the numbers game as well as anyone. But the most obvious number is right there in front of them, yet they ignore it. Year after year, they ignore it.
Aaron Boone’s managed the Yankees for nine years, and he is zero for nine now. That isn’t good, or certainly good enough.
By the old Steinbrenner standards, Boone would have been gone six years ago. We do understand the Yankees’ expectations are more normal today, in the post-Boss era. I get there’s room for reason. But zero for nine in championships for this marquee franchise should still be unacceptable.
Zero for nine shouldn’t suffice for a team that has Aaron Judge, a team that perennially constructs a top-two rotation in the American League, a team that has the highest payroll in its league year after year, a team that’s searching for its 28th World Series win since 2009.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Aaron Judge Calls Out Yankees' Front Office After Getting Swept
item.dc:creator: Chris Rosvoglou

The Rays completed their ALDS sweep of the Yankees with a 4-3 win in the Bronx on Wednesday night. Victor Mesa Jr. hit the go-ahead home run for the Rays in the top of the sixth inning. Even though Tampa Bay won the AL East, there were plenty of fans who expected a better fight from New York. Of course, it doesn't help t
item.content:encoded:
Aaron Judge didn't play in the American League Division Series due to injury, but he spoke to the media following the New York Yankees' series-ending loss to the Tampa Bay Rays.
The Rays completed their ALDS sweep of the Yankees with a 4-3 win in the Bronx on Wednesday night. Victor Mesa Jr. hit the go-ahead home run for the Rays in the top of the sixth inning.
Even though Tampa Bay won the AL East, there were plenty of fans who expected a better fight from New York. Of course, it doesn't help that Judge missed the whole series due to a calf strain.
Following Wednesday night's season-ending loss, Judge was asked how general manager Brian Cashman and owner Hal Steinbrenner will react to the Yankees falling short of their ultimate goal yet again.
"We're the Yankees," Judge said. "I feel like they [the front office] should go all-in and do what they need to do. If we've got holes, if it's finding certain players or personnel, whatever we need, you've got to go out there and get it."
Clearly, Judge wants the Yankees to be more aggressive when it come to building the roster.
Expect changes for the Yankees.
For starters, the Yankees are expected to move on from a few veterans like Jazz Chisholm Jr. and Trent Grisham this offseason. The Bronx Bombers may have tipped their hand by having Chisholm on the bench for a do-or-die playoff game.
The Yankees also have to consider moving on from Ryan McMahon and Giancarlo Stanton in hopes of landing more reliable hitters.
Suffice to say, this will be a pivotal offseason in the Bronx.
This story was originally published by The Spun on Oct 8, 2026, where it first appeared in the MLB section. Add The Spun as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

item.content:encoded:
Yankees' 'offseason focus' should include David Bednar, Paul Blackburn originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The New York Yankees have plenty of roster decisions to make before next season.
Whether to re-sign second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. for the foreseeable future may be the offseason's biggest question.
The Yankees don't need Chisholm, but there aren't many other options who offer more upside than him.
Concerning the pitching staff, general manager Brian Cashman has built a strong and very deep rotation. However, the bullpen may lose multiple key arms this winter.
Tim Hill, Paul Blackburn, Ryan Yarbrough, John Schreiber, Michael Fulmer, and closer David Bednar will all become unrestricted free agents.
"Not only is this New York's biggest need, but it might also be just about their entire offseason focus," Bleacher Report's Kerry Miller wrote.
Plus, who knows what Fernando Cruz's status will be. The right-hander is attempting to recover from a partially torn UCL without surgery.
Keeping Bednar at closer should be Cashman's top priority in the bullpen.
"Bednar is the biggest one by far, owner of 35 saves and a 2.47 ERA this season. Like Chisholm, he could also be headed for a qualifying offer of an estimated $23.1M, but is expected to decline it in pursuit of something closer to a four-year, $66M contract," Miller added.
His value has skyrocketed, but the Yankees should also look to re-sign Blackburn. He went through dominant scoreless streaks and allowed just 16 earned runs in 85 innings.
Blackburn, who made a modest $2 million salary in 2026, struck out just 7.3 batters per nine innings.
Reshaping the bullpen will be a massive project for New York's front office, and retaining Bednar and Blackburn should be step one.

item.title: [amNewYork] Aaron Judge almost said the quiet part out loud about the Yankees’ problems | amNewYork
item.dc:creator: Joe Pantorno; Amnewyork

Granted, this year was a little different. item.content:encoded:
BRONX, NY — Forced to sit helplessly in the Yankees’ dugout and watch the Tampa Bay Rays execute a dominant ALDS sweep, another year of Aaron Judge in Pinstripes has come and gone without a championship.
Granted, this year was a little different. The 34-year-old slugger missed 96 games with a fractured rib and strained calf — the latter of which held him out for the entire postseason, regardless of his pleas to be included on both the Wild Card and ALDS rosters.
As this series against Tampa progressed, it became increasingly clear that even a 50% Judge would have been a better option than most of what manager Aaron Boone trotted out in each of the three games. The Yankees scored just five runs in three games, and the lineup construction fell under considerable fire, especially toward the end of Game 3 when Trent Grisham, who inexplicably was put in the lead-off spot, went down swinging to end the season with slugger Ben Rice standing on the on-deck circle with his bat on his shoulder.
Now, imagine if that was Rice leading off (and playing first base) and Judge in the DH spot?
“Look, it’s Aaron Judge, the greatest player in the world,” Boone said. “And that’s a huge person to be missing. But every team tends to deal with different attrition that they gotta face every year, and unfortunately that was for us much of this year.”
Judge had made it known in recent weeks that he was unhappy with some of Boone’s phrasing regarding his moderate calf strain, even the disclosure of the extent of his injury. Yet the two-time defending AL MVP is still riding with his manager, regardless of how hot people hope his seat might be.
“Yeah, he’s our manager,” Judge said. “He’s running this ship. He puts us in the right position to go out and succeed, especially a season like this where I’m banged up and missing 100 games, you miss [Giancarlo Stanton], [Gerrit] Cole, [Carlos] Rodon… For him to manage it the way he did and put us in the best position to get into the postseason and get an opportunity to win a World Series, he’s definitely had our back.”
The problem is that the Yankees’ roster simply was not good enough to be the best — or second, third, maybe even fourth team — in baseball. Owner Hal Steinbrenner’s frugality has constructed a roster with strong pitching, but poor defense and a lineup that offers virtually no support around a healthy Judge.
Rice is a great supporting piece, but there has to be far more than Cody Bellinger or Jazz Chisholm, or Austin Wells.
When asked whether or not Steinbrenner and general manager Brian Cashman have gone all-in enough in hopes of breaking a now 17-year World Series drought, Judge came within a few feet of laying the blame on their shoulders, saying, “It’s tough to say.”
“I want to trade for everybody, sign everybody every single year,” Judge said. “But I know that’s not realistic. They give us a winning team every single year, but that’s not good enough here in New York. We’re the Yankees. You’ve got to go out there and expect championships and go all-in every year.”
The hope is that the philosophy finally changes this winter. There are not going to be any excuses after asset firm Apollo Financial provided a $2.6 billion cash infusion.
“We’re the Yankees. I feel like they should go all-in and do what they need to do,” Judge continued. “If we’ve got holes, if it’s finding certain players or personnel, whatever we need, you’ve got to go out there and get it. That’s why I signed back here to play with the Yankees, to fight for a championship every single year and to go all-in. That’s what I do every offseason: get ready to give this team and this city everything I got. I expect them to do the same.”

item.dc:creator: Justin Tasch

I feel like they should go all in and do what they need to do,” Judge, who did not play in the playoffs due to a calf strain, said after the Yankees’ 4-3 Game 3 loss to the Rays in The Bronx Wednesday night. “If we’ve got holes, if it’s finding certain players or personnel, whatever we need, you got to go out
item.content:encoded:
After the Yankees were eliminated in the ALDS by a division rival for the second straight season, Aaron Judge delivered a message to Hal Steinbrenner and Brian Cashman.
“We’re the Yankees. I feel like they should go all in and do what they need to do,” Judge, who did not play in the playoffs due to a calf strain, said after the Yankees’ 4-3 Game 3 loss to the Rays in The Bronx Wednesday night. “If we’ve got holes, if it’s finding certain players or personnel, whatever we need, you got to go out there and get it. That’s why I signed back here to play with the Yankees is to fight for a championship every single year and to go all in. That’s what I do every offseason is get ready to give this team and this city everything I’ve got, so I expect them to do the same.”




Access the Yankees beat like never before

Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
Judge, the three-time MVP who turns 35 in April, has five years left on the nine-year, $360 million contract he signed after testing free agency following his historic 62-homer season in 2022.
Asked if he feels the front office has gone all in enough, Judge turned more diplomatic.
“It’s tough to say,” Judge said. “I want to trade for everybody, sign everybody every single year, but I know that’s not realistic. They give us a winning team every single year, but that’s not good enough here in New York. We’re the Yankees. You’ve got to go out there and expect championships and go all in every year. So I’m excited to see what they do.”
The likelihood of a work stoppage, with the players and owners locked in bitter CBA negotiations, looms over MLB’s offseason, but the Yankees have major questions on some free agents and others.
Jazz Chisholm Jr., David Bednar, Trent Grisham, Paul Goldschmidt and Paul Blackburn are among the Yankees players whose contracts are up.
The Yankees will also have to decide if they’ll stomach one final year of Giancarlo Stanton, where Anthony Volpe, Spencer Jones and Jasson Dominguez fit in, and whether to move on from third baseman Ryan McMahon.

item.content:encoded:
Oct 8, 2026, 11:35 AM ET
New York Yankees impending free-agent first baseman/designated hitter Paul Goldschmidt has expressed a desire to keep playing at age 39 in 2027, according to Gary Phillips of the New York Daily News. It is unclear if the Yankees will make an effort to re-sign the former MVP and seven-time All-Star in the offseason. Goldy had a nice bounce-back campaign in 2026 in his 16th year in the big leagues after he hit just 10 homers and drove in 45 runs in 146 games in 2025 in his first year in pinstripes. In 105 regular-season games across 380 plate appearances this year, Goldschmidt hit .252/.313/.452 with a .765 OPS, 18 home runs, 52 RBI, and 44 runs scored for the Yankees. He went hitless in eight plate appearances with two walks and a run scored in four postseason games for New York this year. Goldschmidt is obviously no longer in his prime and is no longer an everyday player, but he should still attract interest across the league for his ability to hit lefties. In 183 plate appearances against southpaws in 2026, he hit .299 (47-for-157) with 11 of his 18 home runs and 24 RBI.--Keith Hernandez
Source: New York Daily News - Gary Phillips
More Recent News
Oct 8, 2026, 11:28 AM ET
Tampa Bay Rays closer Bryan Baker shut the door in his team's 4-3 win over the New York Yankees in Game 3 of the American League Division Series on Wednesday, pitching a scoreless ninth inning with two strikeouts. Baker was a key part of Tampa Bay's three-game sweep of New York, logging saves in all three games while allowing just one baserunner to reach. The 31-year-old emerged as one of the best closers in baseball during the regular season, recording a 1.44 ERA and 0.91 WHIP with 63 strikeouts and 41 saves across 62 1/3 innings (65 games). Heading into the American League Championship Series, Baker's dominance at the end of games gives Tampa Bay a significant advantage if it can get an early lead on its opponents.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Jakob Marsee Having UCL Repair With Internal Brace


Keith Hernandez




Oct 8, 2026, 11:24 AM ET
Miami Marlins outfielder Jakob Marsee (elbow) will get a UCL repair with an internal brace of his left elbow on Monday, according to Christina De Nicola of MLB.com. The estimated return-to-play timeline for Marsee is around six months. Marsee battled through elbow issues down the stretch in 2026 in his first full season in the majors with Miami. In his first taste of the big leagues in 2025, Marsee hit .292 (61-for-209) with five home runs, 33 RBI, 14 stolen bases, and 28 runs scored in 55 games and 234 plate appearances. In 155 games and 616 plate appearances this year, Marsee slashed .231/.348/.359 with a .706 OPS, 11 home runs, 41 RBI, 23 stolen bases, and 83 runs scored for the Fish. The 25-year-old former sixth-round pick by the San Diego Padres in 2022 from Central Michigan University has a very intriguing power/speed profile as an outfielder in all fantasy leagues, but his availability for Opening Day in 2027 could be in question, depending on how he fares during his rehab after going under the knife early next week.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com - Christina De Nicola
Oct 8, 2026, 11:21 AM ET
Milwaukee Brewers outfielder Garrett Mitchell had a big game in his team's 3-1, series-clinching win over the San Diego Padres in Game 4 of the National League Division Series on Wednesday. At the plate, Mitchell went two-for-four with a triple, an RBI, and a run scored. In the field, Mitchell robbed Padres third baseman Manny Machado of what would have been a game-tying two-run home run in the eighth inning. The 28-year-old Mitchell was finally able to stay mostly healthy in 2026, hitting .262/.354/.416 with 11 home runs, 65 RBI, 74 runs scored, and 14 stolen bases across 531 plate appearances in the regular season. He was productive in the NLDS as well, logging four hits, three runs scored, an RBI, and a stolen base across 15 at-bats.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Hagen Smith Opening Game 4 of ALDS on Thursday


Keith Hernandez




Oct 8, 2026, 11:15 AM ET
Chicago White Sox rookie left-hander Hagen Smith will serve as the opener in Game 4 of the American League Division Series on Thursday at home against the division-rival Cleveland Guardians, according to Scott Merkin of MLB.com. The 23-year-old former fifth overall pick in 2024 from the University of Arkansas made 18 appearances (only one start) in his major-league debut during the 2026 regular season, posting a nice 1.29 ERA (2.35 FIP) and 0.96 WHIP with 41 strikeouts and 16 walks in 28 innings pitched. The talented young southpaw has already thrown 6 1/3 innings in his first experience in the playoffs, too, allowing just one earned run on three hits while walking five and striking out six. He started Game 1 of the ALDS against Cleveland and threw 2 2/3 shutout innings with three walks and four strikeouts in the team's 3-0 victory before allowing a run with two walks and a strikeout in two-thirds of an inning in Wednesday's Game 3 loss. Smith will probably have a short leash as the White Sox try to close out the best-of-five series, with right-hander Erick Fedde potentially piggybacking Smith in Chicago. In three relief appearances against the Guardians during the regular season, Smith allowed two earned runs with six walks and eight strikeouts in 5 2/3 innings pitched.--Keith Hernandez
Source: MLB.com - Scott Merkin
Victor Mesa Jr. Homers in ALDS-Clinching Win


Will Brady




Oct 8, 2026, 11:14 AM ET
Tampa Bay Rays outfielder Victor Mesa Jr. was one of the stars of his team's 4-3 win in Game 3 of the American League Division Series over the New York Yankees, hitting a two-run home run off Yankees left-hander Max Fried. Mesa Jr.'s home run was his only hit of the night, but it gave the Rays a 4-2 lead in the sixth inning that they would ultimately never give back. Across 262 plate appearances in the regular season, Mesa Jr. hit .260/.327/.498 with 14 home runs, 34 RBI, 37 runs scored, and nine stolen bases. After starting the year in the minors, the 25-year-old has emerged as an everyday corner outfielder for Tampa Bay and provides another dynamic power/speed bat for the Rays. If Mesa Jr. can get hot, he could help power a deep postseason run.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 7, 2026, 10:01 PM ET
Los Angeles Dodgers closer Edwin Diaz picked up his second save in as many nights on Wednesday, pitching a scoreless ninth inning with a strikeout in his team's 4-1 victory over the Atlanta Braves in Game 4 of the National League Division Series. Diaz missed most of the 2026 regular season due to elbow and neck injuries. However, he's been dominant since returning from the injured list in mid-September. Diaz allowed just two baserunners while notching nine strikeouts in his final five innings pitched of the regular season, and he's now logged low-stress saves in each of his first two appearances of the playoffs. With Diaz rounding into form, Los Angeles' bullpen looks like a major strength heading into the National League Championship Series.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 7, 2026, 9:52 PM ET
Cleveland Guardians left-hander Foster Griffin was dominant in a bulk relief appearance in his team's 9-3 win over the Chicago White Sox in Game 3 of the American League Division Series on Wednesday. Griffin followed Cleveland opener Daniel Espino and allowed two hits and one earned run while striking out seven across 2 2/3 innings of work. The 31-year-old was used exclusively as a starting pitcher during the regular season, posting a 15-6 record with a 3.60 ERA, 1.21 WHIP, and 158 strikeouts across 172 2/3 innings (31 starts) split between the Guardians and the Washington Nationals. However, Griffin struggled mightily late in the year, pitching to a 5.05 ERA in the second half and a 6.87 ERA across 18 1/3 innings in September. If Griffin can rediscover his early-season form in a bullpen role, he could help Cleveland mount a comeback in the ALDS.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 7, 2026, 9:43 PM ET
Cleveland Guardians outfielder Jo Adell had a big night in his team's 9-3 victory over the Chicago White Sox in Game 3 of the American League Division Series on Wednesday, going 2-for-4 with a walk and three RBI. With the game tied 1-1 in the third inning, Adell put the Guardians ahead for good with a three-run triple off of White Sox left-hander Hagen Smith. Across 660 regular-season plate appearances split between the Guardians and the Los Angeles Angels, Adell hit .240/.298/.401 with 23 home runs, 94 RBI, 70 runs scored, and five stolen bases. He was better with Cleveland than he was with Los Angeles, posting a .740 OPS across 204 trips to the plate after the Guardians acquired him at the trade deadline. Adell has notched a couple of key hits for Cleveland in the ALDS and now has four RBI across the first three games of the series.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 7, 2026, 9:32 PM ET
Los Angeles Dodgers outfielder Andy Pages had the key hit in his team's 4-1 win over the Atlanta Braves in Game 4 of the National League Division Series on Wednesday, logging a go-ahead two-run single off Braves right-hander Robert Suarez in the seventh inning. Pages finished the game with two hits and two RBI in three at-bats. The 25-year-old was a critical piece of the Dodgers lineup during the regular season, hitting .274 with 23 home runs, 85 RBI, 75 runs scored, and 13 stolen bases. However, Pages struggled mightily during the Dodgers' run to the 2025 World Series, notching just four hits in 55 postseason plate appearances. After his big night on Wednesday, Pages has already logged four hits in just 15 plate appearances in the 2026 playoffs.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com
Oct 7, 2026, 9:19 PM ET
Cleveland Guardians right-hander Cade Smith was lights out to secure his team's 9-3 victory over the Chicago White Sox in Game 3 of the American League Division Series on Wednesday. Smith entered the game in the eighth inning and recorded the final six outs, logging five strikeouts without allowing a single baserunner. The 27-year-old was one of the best closers in baseball during the regular season, pitching to a 1.95 ERA and 0.96 WHIP with 107 strikeouts and 41 saves across 74 innings (69 games). Smith has been dominant so far in the Division Series as well, as he's yet to allow a hit or a walk in his four innings of work. If Cleveland is going to mount a comeback in the series, it will likely need Smith to continue his dominance.--Will Brady
Source: ESPN.com

item.title: [RG.org] Aaron Judge Wants Yankees to Go All-In After ALDS Sweep
item.dc:creator: Authors; Sergey-Demidov; Sergey Demidov
item.description: (Photo by Julio Aguilar/Getty Images) Aaron Judge said the New York Yankees front office “should go all-in” this offseason after the Tampa Bay Rays completed a sweep of the American League Division Series with a 4-3 win at Yankee Stadium on Wednesday night. “We’re the Yankees,” Judge said, according to ESPN. “I feel like they should go all-in and do what they need to do and if we got holes, it’s finding certain players or personnel, whatever we need, we got to go out there and get it. That’s why
item.content:encoded:
(Photo by Julio Aguilar/Getty Images)
Aaron Judge said the New York Yankees front office “should go all-in” this offseason after the Tampa Bay Rays completed a sweep of the American League Division Series with a 4-3 win at Yankee Stadium on Wednesday night.
“We’re the Yankees,” Judge said, according to ESPN. “I feel like they should go all-in and do what they need to do and if we got holes, it’s finding certain players or personnel, whatever we need, we got to go out there and get it. That’s why I signed back here to play with the Yankees, is to fight for a championship every single year and go all-in. That’s what I do every offseason is to get ready to give this team and this city everything I got. So I expect them to do the same.”
Judge’s message to the front office comes heading into an offseason with a lockout likely to begin once MLB’s collective bargaining agreement expires Dec. 1.
Asked whether the front office and ownership had gone “all-in enough” to end the drought, the team captain stopped short of a direct answer.
Judge Watched From the Dugout
Judge was not active for either of the Yankees’ postseason series. He strained his right calf Sept. 16 in his seventh game back after missing more than three months with a fractured rib, and the team left him off its ALDS roster. The three-time AL MVP played in 66 games this season, batting .241 with 18 home runs and an .871 OPS.
“It definitely hurts,” Judge said. “I want to be out there. Doing all the rehab, all the work, coming here early. ... It definitely hurts not getting a chance to be out there and battling.”
The loss extended the Yankees’ championship drought to 17 seasons, the second-longest in franchise history. Judge, who turned 34 in April, has now completed 10 full major league seasons without a title.
“Just hating every single moment of it,” Judge said. “Thinking about the whole year, thinking about missed opportunities in the season, in that series. Things that can be improved on, things I can improve on. Just hating every single moment of it so I don’t forget.”
The Yankees beat the Boston Red Sox in the wild-card round, outscoring them 18-2, before Tampa Bay won three straight. Drew Rasmussen took a no-hit bid into the eighth inning of Game 1, the Yankees committed four errors in Game 2, and a crew chief’s review in Game 3 ruled spectator interference on Anthony Volpe’s potential tying two-run home run in the sixth inning, turning it into an RBI double.
Chisholm Calls Boos ‘Confusing’
Manager Aaron Boone started Volpe over Chisholm at second base in Game 3. Chisholm, who will be a free agent this offseason, answered “no comment” multiple times when asked about the decision. He entered as a pinch hitter in the seventh inning and was loudly booed after popping out. He went 0-for-8 with a walk in the series.
Boone, who has one year left on his contract, said he would like to return. This was his eighth postseason trip in nine seasons as Yankees manager, tying Bob Melvin for the MLB record for most postseason appearances without a World Series title.
“They beat us,” Boone said. “They’ve obviously had a great season and get to continue on. But for us, there’s just no easy way. It’s a broken clubhouse.”
Readers following the Yankees’ offseason can find licensed options in RG.org’s guide to New York sports betting, along with a broader overview of online sportsbooks.

item.title: [Newsday] Paul Goldschmidt wants to keep playing and he'd like to do it with the Yankees
item.dc:creator: Roger Rubin
item.description: The Yankees offered Paul Goldschmidt a $4 million deal to play one more season in what certainly has looked like a Hall of Fame career. He accepted, even though he knew he would no longer be the every-day starter. The organization got a massive return on their investment as the first baseman hit 18 home runs and had 52 RBI in essentially a platoon role. Goldschmidt was incredibly disappointed after the Yankees lost to Tampa Bay, 4-3, in the Game 3 of their AL Division Series on Wednesday night a
item.content:encoded:
The Yankees offered Paul Goldschmidt a $4 million deal to play one more season in what certainly has looked like a Hall of Fame career. He accepted, even though he knew he would no longer be the every-day starter. The organization got a massive return on their investment as the first baseman hit 18 home runs and had 52 RBI in essentially a platoon role.
Goldschmidt was incredibly disappointed after the Yankees lost to Tampa Bay, 4-3, in the Game 3 of their AL Division Series on Wednesday night at the Stadium. But when asked about the notion of reprising the role one more time, he replied, “I'd like to continue playing, so we'll see if that opportunity happens.”
“I’ve absolutely loved my time here – I don't know if there's anyone who loved being a Yankee more than me,” Goldschmidt said. “I love the guys in this clubhouse. I love living here in New York. But you don't really know what the future holds so I think we'll just see what happens. But I can't say enough great things about this organization and my time here. We'll see what happens.”
Goldschmidt won the 2022 NL MVP Award with St. Louis and finished second in MVP voting two other times and third once while with the Diamondbacks. He has 390 home runs, an .877 OPS and four Gold Gloves for his defense.
He will be 39 next season.
Goldschmidt played in his first postseason in 2011 when he broke into the majors as Arizona lost to Milwaukee in the NL Division Series. He made the playoffs once more with the D-backs in 2017 and then three times with St. Louis from 2019 to 2021. He’s now made it twice with the Yankees but still has yet to win a World Series.
“My mindset really hasn't changed: hopefully be able to have a chance to do that again and hopefully win a championship,” he said.
Considered a good influence on the clubhouse and on the younger Yankees in particular, Goldschmidt was asked about what his message would be to the players who are beginning to form a nucleus for the years ahead.
“I think you’ve just got to keep working, but not taking this for granted either,” he said. “You don't know if you're going to get the opportunity again. You don't know what our individual careers hold. You don't know what team you'll be playing for the next year. . . . and that's what makes this so disappointing.
“But the young guys here did great. They’ve got a great head on their shoulders, very talented physically, but also mentally. They know what they're doing, and they've done a great job. Without those guys, we wouldn't be here right now. So the future is bright for them individually, and I think for this organization too.”

item.dc:creator: Boris Alexander Cruz Caballero

item.content:encoded:
Panamá/La decisión arbitral terminó siendo determinante para el desenlace del encuentro. Los Yankees de Nueva York no pudieron concretar la remontada y terminaron cayendo 4-3 ante los Rays de Tampa Bay, resultado que sentenció la barrida de Tampa Bay en la serie y dejó al conjunto neoyorquino eliminado de la postemporada.
La polémica jugada en el jardín izquierdo
Con George Lombard Jr. en circulación, Anthony Volpe conectó un elevado profundo hacia el jardín izquierdo. La pelota viajó hacia la zona de la barda mientras el jardinero de Tampa Bay, Victor Mesa Jr., retrocedía para intentar realizar la atrapada.
La esférica terminó en las gradas y, durante algunos segundos, el público del Yankee Stadium celebró lo que parecía ser un jonrón que podía acercar a los Yankees en el marcador.
Sin embargo, Mesa Jr. reclamó inmediatamente una posible interferencia de un aficionado.
Las imágenes de televisión mostraron que un espectador ubicado detrás de la barda extendió su brazo por encima de la pared hacia el terreno de juego y tuvo contacto con la pelota antes de que esta pudiera completar su trayectoria.
La acción provocó la intervención de los árbitros, quienes determinaron que el aficionado había interferido con la posibilidad del jardinero de realizar la jugada.
La revisión arbitral cambió el resultado
El jefe de la cuarteta arbitral, Dan Bellino, comunicó la decisión en medio de los abucheos y la desaprobación de los aficionados locales.
Después de la revisión de la jugada, se determinó que la pelota no podía ser considerada un cuadrangular debido a la interferencia del espectador.
La decisión modificó el resultado de la acción: George Lombard Jr. fue autorizado a anotar, mientras que Anthony Volpe fue colocado en segunda base con un doble.
La jugada significó una oportunidad importante para los Yankees, pero también mantuvo a Tampa Bay con ventaja de 4-3, diferencia que el conjunto visitante logró conservar hasta el último out.
El aficionado fue retirado del estadio
Luego de que se anunciara oficialmente la decisión, el aficionado involucrado en la jugada fue retirado de su ubicación por el personal de seguridad del Yankee Stadium y agentes de la policía del estadio.
La salida se produjo de manera discreta y no se reportaron mayores altercados en la sección donde se encontraba el espectador.
La atención, sin embargo, permaneció centrada en una jugada que terminó teniendo un peso importante en un partido de eliminación.
Un recuerdo inevitable de Jeffrey Maier
La polémica también generó comparaciones con uno de los episodios más recordados en la historia de los Yankees durante la postemporada.
En 1996, el joven aficionado Jeffrey Maier intervino en una pelota conectada por Derek Jeter durante la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Americana ante los Orioles de Baltimore.
Maier extendió su guante sobre la barda e interfirió con la trayectoria de la pelota, que terminó siendo decretada como cuadrangular.
La diferencia fundamental entre ambos episodios fue la tecnología disponible. En 1996 no existía el sistema de revisión por video que actualmente permite a los árbitros analizar este tipo de acciones antes de emitir una decisión definitiva.
Décadas después, otra intervención de un aficionado volvió a convertirse en protagonista de una eliminación de los Yankees.
Tampa Bay avanza y los Yankees quedan fuera
Con el triunfo 4-3, los Rays de Tampa Bay completaron la barrida sobre Nueva York y avanzaron a la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Americana.
Para los Yankees, la derrota puso fin a su recorrido en la postemporada en medio de una noche marcada por una de las jugadas más controversiales del encuentro.
El batazo de Anthony Volpe que inicialmente parecía representar un cuadrangular terminó convertido en doble por la interferencia, en una acción que quedó como uno de los momentos decisivos de la eliminación neoyorquina.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Spencer Jones shouldn’t have to start over with the Yankees next spring
item.dc:creator: Alexander Wilson
item.description: Spencer Jones finally gave the Yankees a productive October night Wednesday: an RBI double, two walks and a run scored. It didn't save their season, but it should keep them from treating his next spring training like a fresh audition for a player they've never seen. New York has 86 regular-season games of major league evidence on Jones now. I'd give him a real opportunity to keep an everyday outfield role in 2027, with clear offensive improvements required. One good elimination-game performance
item.content:encoded:
Spencer Jones finally gave the Yankees a productive October night Wednesday: an RBI double, two walks and a run scored. It didn't save their season, but it should keep them from treating his next spring training like a fresh audition for a player they've never seen.
New York has 86 regular-season games of major league evidence on Jones now. I'd give him a real opportunity to keep an everyday outfield role in 2027, with clear offensive improvements required. One good elimination-game performance shouldn't guarantee the job. Two bad games shouldn't erase the work that got him there.
The Yankees have enough evidence to make a plan
Jones hit .245 with a .313 on-base percentage and .429 slugging percentage in the regular season. Eleven homers and 13 doubles gave him 24 extra-base hits before counting his one triple. He also stole 10 bases. There is enough production to keep developing, even if a .742 OPS doesn't make him a finished middle-of-the-order hitter.
The problem is just as obvious. He struck out 105 times in 289 plate appearances, a 36.3 percent rate. That puts a lot of pressure on the balls he does put in play. If New York wants a more reliable offense, it can't simply ignore that number because Jones is young and has power.
His ALDS wasn't a breakout. He went 0-for-7 across the first two games, then 1-for-2 in Game 3. The full series came to one hit in nine at-bats, with four strikeouts. Wednesday's two walks were encouraging because he contributed without having to hit everything hard, but they're two walks, not proof that his plate discipline has suddenly changed.
The reasonable next step is a focused development plan, not a promise that he's untouchable. The Yankees need to identify which pitches and locations create most of his misses, work on those weaknesses and give him enough regular at-bats to see whether the changes hold against major league pitching.
0What do you think?Post a comment.
Competition can be useful without making every game a referendum
There's a legitimate argument for adding a more dependable veteran and making Jones compete for playing time. A team trying to win cannot reserve a starting spot indefinitely for potential. If his contact problems persist and a better option is available, the veteran should play.
I'd still be careful about reducing him to occasional starts and asking him to improve with irregular work. If the Yankees decide he's a regular, use him like one. If they decide he needs a different development assignment, make that decision with specific goals rather than an undefined wait for him to look ready.
Jones' double Wednesday doesn't change the offseason by itself. It does show why a blanket response to the sweep would be lazy: one of the players with the most obvious offensive flaws also supplied an RBI and reached base three times in the final game.
Next spring, I want to see whether he can keep those productive at-bats while cutting down the strikeouts. The Yankees should give him a fair stretch to answer that, with competition available if he can't.

Goldschmidt said Wednesday after the Yankees were eliminated from the postseason that he would like to continue his playing career next season, Gary Phillips of the New York Daily News reports.
An impending free agent, Goldschmidt had a solid 2026 campaign being used primarily as a short-side platoon player for the Yankees, slashing .252/.313/.452 with 18 home runs in 105 contests. That included a .967 OPS against southpaws, so Goldschmidt shouldn't have trouble finding work this winter despite the fact that he turned 39 in September.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Yankees’ Anthony Volpe Makes Honest Admission After ALDS Exit
item.dc:creator: Keith Watkins
item.description: The New York Yankees' season ended Wednesday night in a 4-3 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays. Anthony Volpe nearly changed the outcome in the sixth inning with a drive to left field that was initially ruled a game-tying two-run homer. A fan interference call overturned it to an RBI double. The play summed up a night, a series, and a career's worth of frustration for a player who has now experienced four consecutive October exits in pinstripes. Volpe Does Not Mince Words Volpe was asked about his emoti
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees' season ended Wednesday night in a 4-3 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays. Anthony Volpe nearly changed the outcome in the sixth inning with a drive to left field that was initially ruled a game-tying two-run homer. A fan interference call overturned it to an RBI double.
The play summed up a night, a series, and a career's worth of frustration for a player who has now experienced four consecutive October exits in pinstripes.
Volpe Does Not Mince Words
Volpe was asked about his emotions after the loss. His answer was unfiltered.
"This is my fourth season," Volpe said. "It's been four too many times having this taste in my mouth."
He went further, rejecting the idea that another early exit would simply serve as motivation.
"I don't even think 'motivated' is the right word," Volpe said. "I think it's just pissed off. There's too many chips added to your shoulder. Enough's enough."
The Year That Shaped Him
Volpe's path to this moment was not straightforward. He was sent down to Triple-A earlier this season after struggling at the plate. The demotion could have broken his confidence. Instead, he came back and earned a spot on the postseason roster.
Aaron Judge spoke after the game about what Volpe's resilience says about him as a player, calling him someone the Yankees would need if they were going to win a championship.
Final Word for the Yankees
Volpe has been here four times now. Four Octobers. Four early exits.
He is not looking for fuel. He already has more than enough. What he wants is a different ending.
Enough's enough. His words.

item.description: Yankees' Aaron Boone not ready to talk about contract status after ALDS exit appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here. item.content:encoded:
Yankees' Aaron Boone not ready to talk about contract status after ALDS exit appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
New York Yankees manager Aaron Boone may not want to walk around in the Big Apple in the next few days.
The Yankees suffered an embarrassing sweep against the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS, losing in Game 4 at Yankee Stadium on Wednesday. Fans immediately brought out their pitchforks and called for the axing of Boone, who has been with New York since 2018.
In the postgame conference, the 53-year-old manager sidestepped the question about his future.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
"That's for another day. Right now, it's about trying to reflect on this, trying to connect with guys right now as much as I can," said Boone in a video posted by SNY.
"I'm appreciative of a lot of things, but those conversations and things are for another day."
Aaron Boone was asked about his contract status and his future with the Yankees:
"That's for another day. Right now is about trying to reflect on this, trying to connect with guys right now as much as I can." pic.twitter.com/K827gkVSkV
— SNY Yankees (@snyyankees) October 8, 2026
Fans, however, were not appreciative of Boone, claiming that he grossly mismanaged the team against Tampa Bay.
"We need a real manager," said @JAXhomme.
"LOL, sounds like we need to have the conversations now. Season's over. No need to connect with anyone," commented @_nickswaggerr.
"If he had any class, he would just walk away and admit he's not qualified to win it all," added @chefmattg17.
"Maybe this is finally it. It feels like it's the end for Boone," wrote @JayDhaul.
"We don't want the fake sad voice. We want new leadership! Guys need someone with balls who'll keep them accountable. This is the BRONX!" stated @Coach_Stevenss.
Boone lamented their "broken clubhouse" following their disappointing exit.
He signed a two-year, $15 million contract extension in 2025. He has amassed a 790-565 record in the regular season with the Yankees, steering them to the playoffs in eight of his nine seasons, including to the World Series in 2024.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees lost 4-3 on Wednesday night in Game 3 of the ALDS against the Tampa Bay Rays at Yankee Stadium in the Bronx.
This officially eliminated them from playoff contention, as they failed to win a game against Tampa Bay and extend the best-of-five series.
Following the game, the obvious question Yankees fans continued to ask was what the future holds for manager Aaron Boone, who has now wrapped up his ninth season with the franchise.
Boone Addresses His Future as Yankees Manager
As expected, reporters didn't take long to ask Boone about his thoughts moving forward as the Yankees manager, as he has just one season remaining on his contract.
"Yeah, of course. That's for another day," Boone said when asked if he expects and wants to be back in 2027. "Right now is about trying to reflect on this. Trying to connect with guys as much as I can. Appreciative of a lot of things, but those conversations and things
Aaron Boone was asked about his contract status and his future with the Yankees:
“That’s for another day. Right now is about trying to reflect on this, trying to connect with guys right now as much as I can.” https://t.co/K827gkVSkV
— SNY Yankees (@snyyankees) October 8, 2026
Boone Says Clubhouse Is 'Broken' After ALDS Loss
The Yankees have been highly successful in terms of winning during the regular season and reaching the playoffs throughout Boone's tenure with the team.
However, outside of one World Series appearance, which they lost in 2024, they have failed to get over the hump year in and year out.
Boone noted that the clubhouse is feeling the loss and described it as "broken."
"For us, there's just no easy way. It's a broken clubhouse," Boone said. "What you go through as a team, as a family, over the last eight, nine months getting ready for this. It's the worst.
"When you pour so much into it and it's your livelihood, it's hard to describe how awful of a feeling it is to go home again."

"It's very frustrating," Chisholm
item.content:encoded:
Yankees' Jazz Chisholm Jr. reflects on harsh reality NY is facing after ALDS sweep appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The New York Yankees' season ended far sooner than anyone in the Bronx expected. After a 4-3 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 3 of the American League Division Series on Wednesday night, the Yankees were swept out of the playoffs, and Jazz Chisholm Jr. did not try to hide how much it stung.
"It's very frustrating," Chisholm told reporters after the game. "You can see on my face, you can see on everybody else's face, we're not happy. Nobody wants to go home. Have to go home and think about it for another four months before the season starts up again."
"It's very frustrating. You can see on my face, you can see on everybody else's face we're not happy. Nobody wants to go home. Have to go home and think about it for another 4 months before the season starts up again"
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
– Jazz Chisholm Jr. on the Yankees being swept in the ALDS pic.twitter.com/pA6RGicez1
— SNY Yankees (@snyyankees) October 8, 2026
Those four months will feel even longer given how the series ended. Trailing 4-2 in the sixth inning at Yankee Stadium, Anthony Volpe drove a Griffin Jax fastball toward the left-field wall for what looked like a game-tying two-run homer. Instead, a fan in the first row reached over and touched the ball as Victor Mesa Jr. leaped at the wall.
After a review, umpires ruled spectator interference. Volpe was awarded an RBI double, George Lombard Jr. scored, and the Yankees were left a run short.
Mesa had already done damage in the top half of the inning, taking Max Fried deep for a go-ahead solo homer on the left-hander's final pitch. Fried allowed four runs over 5 2/3 innings.
New York never got the tying run home. Rays closer Bryan Baker walked a batter in the ninth before striking out Trent Grisham to send Tampa Bay to the ALCS for the third time in franchise history.
The series slipped away from the Yankees quickly. Drew Rasmussen carried a no-hitter into the eighth inning of a 1-0 Game 1 win for the Rays. Tampa Bay then took Game 2 by a 5-2 score, capitalizing on four Yankees errors.
The early exit caps a frustrating year for a team that won 93 games but still finished 4 1/2 games behind the Rays in the AL East. It also extends the franchise's World Series drought to 17 seasons, dating back to its 2009 title.
For Chisholm and the rest of the clubhouse, there is nothing left to do but wait. The questions about what went wrong, and what needs to change, will hang over the Yankees all winter.

item.content:encoded:
Anthony Volpe! Welcome to October!
In the bottom of the sixth inning, New York Yankees infielder Anthony Volpe came up clutch for his team and almost hit a game-tying 2-run home run, but there was spectator interference on the play, and Volpe instead has an RBI double in the 6th off Rays’ reliever Griffin Jax.
New York still trails 4-3. Spencer Jones struck out on the next at-bat, and the game remains 4-3.
George Lombard Jr. scored on the play, and Volpe heads into second with a double.
It’s the first game that Anthony Volpe has played in the ALDS, and it’s a pulled string by manager Aaron Boone to insert Volpe instead of Jazz Chisholm Jr.
Immediately after the umpires made the call on the field, a handful of Yankees fans in left field started to throw objects onto the field, which caused a slight delay in the game.
Reactions to Anthony Volpe Incident in Rays-Yankees Game
As you can imagine, there is immediate fan reaction to the ‘spectator interference’ call by the umpires and replay officials.
Quickly Looking at the New York Yankees Current Series with the Rays
The New York Yankees must come back on Wednesday evening if they want to keep their season alive.
New York is currently down 2-0 in the series to the Rays and is on the verge of being swept.
It’s likely that Anthony Volpe will get another chance to bat in Game Three, so it will be interesting to see what he does in the later innings.
Either way, things are getting very tense in the Bronx, with each out becoming increasingly more important.

item.content:encoded:
If you’re feeling a sense of deja vu watching the Yankees in the playoffs, you’re not alone.
Anthony Volpe hit a deep fly into left field in the bottom of the sixth inning of ALDS Game 3, which was originally ruled a game-tying, two-run homer.
However, a fan in the left field seats reached over the left field wall and interfered with the ball as Rays outfielder Victor Mesa Jr. attempted to make a leaping grab.
After a lengthy review, the umpires decided the fan had interfered, and Volpe was awarded with an RBI double.
The Rays ended the inning in the lead, 4-3.
It was eerily reminiscent of the infamous Jeffrey Maier incident during the 1996 ALCS when the then-young fan aided a Derek Jeter homer.
In Game 1 of the 2024 World Series, a fan at Dodger Stadium interfered with a Gleyber Torres long fly that was ultimately ruled a double.
Two fans later in the Fall Classic that year also grabbed a foul ball out of Dodgers outfielder Mookie Betts’ glove and were removed and banned from all MLB ballparks.

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK – Stop us if you’ve heard this one before: there was fan interference on an apparent home run ball at Yankee Stadium on Wednesday night.
Anthony Volpe’s apparent game-tying two-run homer in the sixth inning of Game 3 of the American League Division Series was instead changed to a double on replay review after umpires determined a fan had interfered with the ball. However, it was also determined that left fielder Victor Mesa Jr. would not have caught the ball even without interference.
Therefore, Volpe was awarded an RBI double, cutting the Rays lead to one run, and seemingly leaving everyone on the field understanding, if not exactly happy.
With George Lombard Jr. on first base, Volpe drilled a 1-0 sinker from Griffin Jax to left field, and the ball carried and carried to the wall. Mesa Jr. leapt to attempt to make the catch but couldn’t get there, and it hit a fan in the hands.
Unfortunately for Volpe and the Yankees, his hands were over the outfield wall and in the field of play when he made the catch. The play was reviewed, and Volpe’s homer was overturned.
It was hard not to think of one of the most famous plays in postseason history, which occurred almost 30 years ago to the day. On Oct. 9, 1996, 12-year-old Jeffrey Maier deflected a ball hit by Derek Jeter, which went for a game-tying homer in Game 1 of the AL Championship Series.

item.dc:creator: Greg Joyce
item.description:
In their biggest game of the season, the Yankees put Jazz Chisholm Jr. on the bench. And if that was going to be how Chisholm’s tenure with the team ended — replaced by Anthony Volpe at second base for Game 3 of the ALDS on Wednesday night at Yankee Stadium — it sure was telling.

item.content:encoded:
In their biggest game of the season, the Yankees put Jazz Chisholm Jr. on the bench.
And if that was going to be how Chisholm’s tenure with the team ended — replaced by Anthony Volpe at second base for Game 3 of the ALDS on Wednesday night at Yankee Stadium — it sure was telling.




Access the Yankees beat like never before

Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
“Just felt like it,” manager Aaron Boone said in his office before Game 3. “I felt like I wanted to go with [Volpe] today.”
The impetus for the move was Chisholm’s poor Game 2, when he committed a throwing error in the first inning and nearly had another before George Lombard Jr. saved him, not to mention entering Wednesday 0-for-6 with a walk in the ALDS, though he had plenty of company in that regard.
Boone was not interested in fully explaining his decision or indicating whether the move had more to do with defense or offense, other than saying he thought about it on the plane ride home late Monday night and settled on a different lineup that had Volpe for Chisholm and José Caballero for Ryan McMahon.
The manager said he did not have a conversation with Chisholm about taking him out of the lineup — which he also did for Game 1 of the wild-card series against Red Sox lefty Payton Tolle, but this one came against Rays right-hander Nick Martinez.
“But we’re ready to go,” Boone said. “As I talked to these guys before the series, it’s going to take all of us. … He’s ready to go.”
Chisholm, a pending free agent who did not take the field for any pregame work, has had a maddeningly inconsistent run with the Yankees, one that is unlikely to continue beyond this year. He may have more talent and tools than almost any other player on the roster, most notably his speed, athleticism and power, but the Yankees have not been able to get that out of him regularly enough, especially this year.
The 28-year-old hit only .231 with a .711 OPS, 19 home runs and 41 steals in 137 games during the regular season. He was finally starting to get hot late in August into September before spraining his right thumb and going on the injured list, which opened the door for Volpe to be called up from Triple-A, where the former shortstop had been transitioning to second base (and even some third base mixed in).
Volpe may well have a chance to take over at second base next season, but he also got the call Wednesday with the season on the line.
“Just [hoping for a] spark again,” Boone said. “I think Anthony has played well since coming up at the end of the year. Both sides of the ball, he’s done a good job. So, yeah, felt like it made some sense to get him in there tonight, a few more righties at least in the lineup tonight, give a little more balance.”
Chisholm’s most egregious defensive miscue in Game 2 came when he tried to turn a double play on Junior Caminero in the bottom of the first, which was going to be tough to do even if he made a perfect throw. Instead, he made an off-balance, ill-advised throw to first and it went skipping by Luis García Jr., allowing a run to score and Caminero to take second.
After the game, Chisholm said he would still make the throw if he could do it all over again, though Boone tried to downplay that as a confident player just answering a question.
Shop Yankees Merch
“I don’t think he should have thrown the ball,” Boone said Wednesday. “But when you throw the ball, you can always play catch at a high level, just because it’s late. More of an issue with making the throw and then being erratic. But sometimes when you ask athletes questions and you get a lot of people around, they answer a certain way. It’s not so much literal all the time.
“Jazz is pretty much, when he’s pressed like that, going to always answer it in the moment, ‘I’d never not do anything.’ Let’s not over-literalize everything a guy answers.”

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are one loss in the American League Division Series away from elimination, and fans online are calling for the team to move on from Aaron Boone.
Since Boone took over, the Yankees have only been to one World Series and have lost the American League Championship Series twice. The Yankees spend a ton of money, and the expectation that comes with the uniform is a World Series, year in and year out. Whether that is fair or not is another story, but it does not change the fact that the Yankees have underachieved under Boone despite having great teams every season.
Before Wednesday's do-or-die game, Cody Bellinger sang praises of his manager.
"Boone is a great guy to play for," Bellinger told reporters before the game. "I've played for four really good managers, in my opinion, and my transition over here was smooth. It's all about winning here. When you put on this logo, it's all about winning. We understand what comes with the logo, what comes with the history. He helps present that."
Bellinger thinks Boone has done a great job setting the expectations for what it means to be a Yankee. However, the team has failed to meet those expectations, and fans have a right to be upset.
Boone has one more year on his deal, and he will reportedly not be fired regardless of this year's outcome. In his defense, he did manage most of this season without Aaron Judge, which certainly made a huge impact. A healthy Judge could have drastically changed the outlook of this season.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees have reached the edge of their season with a lineup change that puts Jazz Chisholm Jr. on the bench for Game 3 of the American League Division Series.
Manager Aaron Boone, looking for any spark after a flat offensive stretch against the Tampa Bay Rays, dropped Chisholm from the starting nine and handed second base to Anthony Volpe, via Underdog MLB.
New York trails the series two games to none and plays Wednesday night with elimination on the line.
The move follows a rough night in Game 2. The Yankees lost 5-2 and committed four errors, three of them in the first inning, even with right-hander Cam Schlittler on the mound.
Boone had already hinted that he might shuffle the order in search of life at the plate. Sitting Chisholm is the clearest piece of that shuffle. The infielder had started each of the Yankees’ last three playoff games and gone 2-for-9.
The rest of the card is rearranged as well.
Trent Grisham moves into the leadoff spot in center field. Ben Rice, Luis García Jr. and Cody Bellinger follow him in the order, with Rice serving as the designated hitter, García at first base and Bellinger in left. George Lombard Jr. starts at shortstop, Austin Wells catches, Spencer Jones plays right field, and José Caballero takes third base in place of Ryan McMahon and bats ninth. Max Fried gets the ball.
That order, posted ahead of the game, is a clear attempt to reset an attack that has gone quiet.
After scoring 18 runs across two games against the Boston Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, New York has managed almost nothing against Tampa Bay.
Outside of two solo home runs by Rice in Game 2, the Yankees have only five hits combined in the series. The Rays have controlled the tempo, and the defensive mistakes in the first inning of Game 2 only widened the gap.
Boone’s decision does not read as a permanent verdict on Chisholm so much as a short-series adjustment. Postseason at-bats are scarce, and a 2-for-9 stretch is enough to cost a starter a night when a team is one loss from going home. V
olpe’s return to the infield also gives Boone a different defensive look at second after the error-filled opener of the series. Caballero’s insertion at third points the same way: cleaner defense, and a different bat at the bottom of the order.
Whether any of it matters will be settled quickly. Fried has to keep the game close, and the top of the order — Grisham, Rice, García and Bellinger — has to produce the contact that has been missing.
If the Yankees fall behind early again, the benching of Chisholm will be remembered as one more adjustment that arrived too late. If they win, it becomes the first step in a series that is still theoretically alive, if only barely.
