item.content:encoded:
Anthony Rizzo spoke with Yanks Go Yard during the MLB Playoffs on behalf of PAYDAY's Low Key Legends initiative, an effort to recognize the often-overlooked contributors who help make the game possible.
With Aaron Boone discourse hitting another fever pitch as the Yankees careen towards an early playoff exit, Anthony Rizzo picked the perfect time to break down the method behind the madness a bit, and detail the way the relationship worked best behind the scenes. He also bashed the Red Sox's hidden leadership crisis this week, which ... thank you, sincerely.
It's wild we're here again - after Boone's best season in years navigating myriad injuries, and after he outmaneuvered Chad Tracy in the Wild Card Series - but we're here. And Rizzo's admiration of his manager could help explain - as well as the uncertainty of the lockout - why he's likely to stick around through the end of his contract, at the very least.
Anthony Rizzo shares a side of Aaron Boone most Yankees fans don't see
When asked what fans outside the locker room wouldn't know or understand about Boone's day-to-day, Rizzo began with a defense of the little things.
"He's very prepared. He knows an idea and understanding of what he wants to do and he executes. His in-game decisions - and I know it's so easy, especially as a Yankee fan or a baseball fan, to nitpick everything he does, but there are reasons behind every one of his moves. There's numbers to back it up. Sometimes, he goes off-script and goes off feel," Rizzo noted.
While "being prepared" is certainly the baseline expectation, it couldn't be easier to criticize from an outside perspective, as well as blame Boone for player regressions he cannot control. Knowing his comfort in going off-script helps, too (though your mileage may vary for believing he has a workable gut).
Most of all, Rizzo enjoyed the collaborative experience.
"I loved [working with him]. I loved talking to him. I loved asking questions all the time, just understanding what he was thinking," Rizzo told us. "As a player, you want to know what your manager's thinking so you're not caught off guard or talking behind ther back, and he was so open with his moves and his decisions."
The other primary leader in the dugout during Rizzo's years - Aaron Judge - is also a man he has extensive experience alongside. Rizzo told a hilarious story during the Yankees-Red Sox Wild Card broadcast about Judge snapping back, "We're losing" after Rizzo tried to take in the immensity of Fenway Park during the 2021 one-gamer (Rizzo eventually homered, though it was not enough).
So who is Judge, exactly, during moments of rising playoff tensions?
"He's the same. He's the same person at all times," Rizzo emphasized.
"For me, my role on that team, especially with Judge being the Captain and all the pressure that comes with being Player No. 1, is to make sure everyone's loose and having a good time. I was that in Chicago, and had a lot of guys that always kept me loose," Rizzo continued. "He's joking around in-game, but also very focused, he's looking at at-bats and talking situations, like, 'Hey, why do you think he threw that pitch here or did that there? Hey, look for this.' Baserunning stuff. It's all the little things that go into a game that's 95% of the talk in the dugout, but there's always moments where you've got to take it in and have a little bit of humility."
Perhaps that's what Judge really needs? A new running mate who can bust his chops while also remaining collaborative on in-game adjustments and swing decisions. If the Yankees' season ends shortly, it's far more likely that's what the Yankees are seeking, rather than a new manager.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are coming off a very poor performance in Game 2 of the ALDS against the Tampa Bay Rays.
They committed three errors in the very first inning and finished the game with four in a 5-2 loss, despite right-handed ace Cam Schlittler taking the mound.
Now, on Wednesday night, they’ll be playing for their season as they trail 0-2 in the best-of-five series.
Ahead of the matchup, Yankees manager Aaron Boone mentioned that he may make some changes to the starting lineup to try and find some life offensively. And ultimately, he did just that.
Yankees Announce Jazz Chisholm Jr. Decision
Among Boone’s moves, he removed infielder Jazz Chisholm Jr. from the lineup and replaced him with Anthony Volpe at second base.
Chisholm Jr. started each of the last three playoff games for the Yankees and went 2-for-9 across that stretch at the plate.
Other notable moves include moving outfielder Trent Grisham into the leadoff spot. While Ben Rice, Luis Garcia Jr. and Cody Bellinger will hit behind him. Jose Caballero will also replace Ryan McMahon at third base and bat ninth.
Here’s the Yankees starting lineup:

Looking at the Yankees
New York’s offense has been dead against Tampa Bay after erupting for 18 total runs in two games against the Boston Red Sox in the Wild Card Series.
Outside of two solo home runs by Ben Rice in Game 2. The Yankees have recorded just five combined hits against the Rays.

item.title: [Pinstripe Alley] ALDS Game 3 Preview: Max Fried vs. Nick Martinez
item.dc:creator: Dani Mohr
item.description: Despite the impending birth of his firstborn child, Max Fried is starting Game 3 as the Yankees look to avoid elimination from the ALDS. During his last outing against the Red Sox in Game 2 of the Wild Card Series, Fried held steadfast through six innings, striking out six and giving up a home run (a solo shot). With an offense that isn’t offering much support outside of Ben Rice, the Yankees can’t afford any mistakes from Fried tonight as they anticipate continuing their postseason run with a w
item.content:encoded:
Despite the impending birth of his firstborn child, Max Fried is starting Game 3 as the Yankees look to avoid elimination from the ALDS.
During his last outing against the Red Sox in Game 2 of the Wild Card Series, Fried held steadfast through six innings, striking out six and giving up a home run (a solo shot). With an offense that isn’t offering much support outside of Ben Rice, the Yankees can’t afford any mistakes from Fried tonight as they anticipate continuing their postseason run with a win at home. There’s no doubt that the roars from the Bronx crowd in an elimination game can be intimidating, but Fried must block out the noise to stay focused on shutting down the Rays’ offense.
It’s possible that home-field advantage could help the Yankees’ offense and hopefully fuel some fire as they fight through every at-bat. They’ll need as much ammunition as they can get to face Rays righty Nick Martinez, who has a 2.25 ERA through 12 innings in the Bronx this season with 14 hits and three earned runs allowed.
Yankees skipper Aaron Boone is expected to shuffle around the lineup heading into the do-or-die scenario, and it would be reassuring to give a few guys on the bench, including José Caballero and Anthony Volpe, a shot at making the start. Errors from Game 1 and Game 2 starters Ryan McMahon and Jazz Chisholm Jr. have frustrated fans, to say the least, and it would be reassuring to give Caballero and Volpe a shot at keeping the Yankees’ postseason run going for another day. Boone was reportedly considering starting Volpe at third over McMahon for Game 2, but was quoted as saying he wanted to “prioritize the defense.”
Volpe made his last postseason start in Game 2 of the Wild Card Series and got a hit off Red Sox rookie Payton Tolle. Caballero, on the other hand, has yet to make his postseason debut at the plate this year. He does, however, have decent numbers against righties this season, batting .233 with .295 OBP and .666 OPS.
The Yankees have their work cut out for them as they strive to stay alive against Tampa Bay, and hopefully we’ll see some changes to the starting nine that can instill some feelings of confidence.
ALDS Game 3 Info
Teams: No. 4 seed Yankees vs. No. 1 seed Rays
Series: Rays ahead 2-0
Ballpark: Yankee Stadium, Bronx, NY
Start time: 8:00 p.m.
TV: TBS/truTV

Local English radio: WFAN 660 AM / 101.9 FM
Local Spanish radio: WADO 1280 AM

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees will take their home field Wednesday night with their backs against the wall.
The Yanks are facing elimination as they trail the Tampa Bay Rays 2-0 in the American League Division Series, needing three straight wins to move on.
It goes without saying that the Yanks should like their chances to survive at least one more day, as Max Fried will toe the slab in the Bronx - unless the offense continues to have other plans.
This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.
However, rumors swirled that Fried is expecting a baby at any moment, potentially putting his start in jeopardy.
Fried, without getting "too into the personal stuff," confirmed Tuesday the news that he is having a baby "any day now." However, no matter what happens, Fried will be on the bump in the Bronx.
"I've got a really supportive family that understands that this is my job, and it's not going to affect what happens tomorrow," Fried said.
When asked if the baby "complicated" any plans, he simply answered, "No."
Fried's commitment to the Yanks came just hours before the San Diego Padres announced that star closer Mason Miller would miss one to three days after going on the paternity list for the birth of his firstborn. Miller blew a save in Game 2, but his Padres survived without him in Game 3 and trail their series with the Milwaukee Brewers, two games to one.
Fried has missed some time with injuries this season, but when he's been on the mound, he's been his typical ace-like self. He pitched to a 2.80 ERA (35 earned runs/112.2 innings) and is coming off a six-inning, one-run gem against the Boston Red Sox in the Wild Card Round.
The Yankees, however, are hitting .086 this series, and players not named Ben Rice and Austin Wells are a combined 1-for-46.
First pitch in the Bronx is shortly after 8 p.m. ET.

item.content:encoded:
Los Yankees de Nueva York saltarán al campo este miércoles por la noche con la espalda contra la pared.
Los Yankees se enfrentan a la eliminación, ya que van perdiendo por Tampa Bay Rays 2-0 en la Serie Divisional de la Liga Americana, y necesitan tres victorias seguidas para pasar de ronda.
No hace falta decir que a los Yankees les deben parecer bien sus posibilidades de aguantar al menos un día más, ya que Max Fried se subirá al montículo en el Bronx... a menos que la ofensiva siga teniendo otros planes.
Esta página puede contener enlaces de afiliados a socios de apuestas deportivas legales. Si te registras o realizas una apuesta, FOX News podría recibir una compensación. Este contenido lo ha creado un equipo que trabaja de forma independiente de la redacción de FOX News.
Sin embargo, corrían rumores de que Fried está a punto de tener un bebé en cualquier momento, lo que podría poner en peligro su participación como titular.
Fried, sin entrar «demasiado en detalles personales», confirmó el martes la noticia de que va a tener un bebé «en cualquier momento». Sin embargo, pase lo que pase, Fried estará en el montículo en el Bronx.
«Tengo una familia que me apoya muchísimo y que entiende que esto es mi trabajo, y que no va a afectar a lo que pase mañana», dijo Fried.
Cuando le preguntaron si el bebé había «complicado» algún plan, se limitó a responder: «No».
El compromiso de Fried con los Yankees se produjo apenas unas horas antes de que los Padres de San Diego anunciaran que su estrella Mason Miller se perdería entre uno y tres días tras incorporarse a la lista de paternidad por el nacimiento de su primer hijo. Miller falló un salvamento en el segundo partido, pero sus Padres se las arreglaron sin él en el tercero y ahora van perdiendo la serie contra los Brewers de Milwaukee por dos a uno.
Fried se ha perdido algunos partidos por lesiones esta temporada, pero cuando ha estado en el montículo, ha vuelto a ser el as de siempre. Ha registrado una efectividad de 2,80 (35 carreras limpias en 112,2 entradas) y viene de hacer una gran actuación de seis entradas y una sola carrera contra los Boston Red Sox en la ronda de comodines.
Los Yankees, sin embargo, tienen un promedio de bateo de 0,086 en esta serie, y los jugadores que no se llaman Ben Rice ni Austin Wells suman entre todos 1 de 46.
El primer lanzamiento en el Bronx será poco después de las 20:00 h (hora del Este).

item.title: [Yanks Go Yard] Yankees' Max Fried just helped fuel the paternity leave debate no one asked for

item.content:encoded:
There is apparently a paternity leave debate happening in Major League Baseball this postseason.
Why?
Seriously. Why are we doing this?
San Diego Padres closer Mason Miller missed Game 3 of the NLDS against the Milwaukee Brewers on Tuesday because his wife, Jordan, went into labor with their first child. The Padres placed Miller on MLB's postseason paternity list, which permits a player to be away from his team for between one and three days.
The Padres were facing elimination. Miller is their All-Star closer. His absence unquestionably mattered from a baseball standpoint. It also shouldn't have required a second of explanation.
Then, on the other side of the country, Max Fried unintentionally gave baseball's worst possible discourse more oxygen.
With the New York Yankees facing elimination in Game 3 of the ALDS against the Tampa Bay Rays, Fried confirmed Tuesday that he plans to make his scheduled start even if his girlfriend goes into labor. She is due to give birth any day, but Fried said he has a supportive family and that the situation would not affect his availability Wednesday. And that's completely fine, too.
If Fried and his partner have discussed the situation and decided that he should pitch, nobody outside their family has any business telling them otherwise. But Fried's decision cannot become some ridiculous masculinity test for Miller — or for the next player who chooses differently.
Fried pitching through the possibility of his child's birth does not make him tougher, more committed or more serious about winning than Miller. Miller stepping away from an elimination game does not mean he cares less about his teammates.
These are deeply personal decisions involving two people, one of whom is quite literally giving birth. They are not clubhouse leadership exercises, and they certainly aren't opportunities for fans to determine which player "wants it more."
Every MLB fan debating paternity leave should remember Alex Vesia
The fact that baseball is having this conversation less than a year after what happened to Los Angeles Dodgers reliever Alex Vesia makes it particularly gross.
Vesia stepped away from Los Angeles before the 2025 World Series because of what the Dodgers initially described only as a "deeply personal family matter." His wife, Kayla, had been expecting their first child.
Later, the Vesias announced that their newborn daughter, Sterling Sol, died on Oct. 26. Vesia missed the World Series because his family needed him during an unimaginable tragedy.
Months later, Vesia explained that leaving his teammates was difficult but the decision itself was easy: his family needed him. That should have ended this conversation forever.
Nobody watching from the couch knows what is happening inside a delivery room. Nobody knows whether a pregnancy that appears routine will remain that way. Nobody knows what complications could arise for the mother or child. Nobody knows what that particular couple has experienced privately before reaching that moment. And frankly, nobody needs to know.
That is exactly why Miller shouldn't have to justify leaving the Padres during an elimination game. It is why Fried shouldn't have to justify pitching for the Yankees, either. The only people whose opinions matter are the players and their partners.
Max Fried, Mason Miller prove there is no ‘right’ way to handle paternity leave
There is also something deeply backward about treating a father being present for childbirth as an optional luxury that becomes increasingly selfish depending on the importance of the baseball game happening that night.
MLB literally has a paternity list for this reason. Miller didn't abandon his teammates. He used a collectively recognized form of leave because his wife was giving birth to their child.
And despite being without their closer, the Padres survived. They beat Milwaukee 4-3, with Michael King recording a six-out save to extend their season. Funny how that works.
Baseball teams are built with 26 players. Organizations have contingency plans for injuries, illness and every other form of unexpected absence because human beings are not machines programmed exclusively around a postseason schedule. Having a baby belongs pretty comfortably in the category of "life event more important than baseball."
Meanwhile, none of this should diminish Fried's choice. The Yankees' season is on the brink, and their ace wants the baseball. Yankees fans can appreciate his willingness to pitch an elimination game while understanding that another player could make the exact opposite decision and deserve precisely the same respect.
That's the distinction this conversation keeps missing. Fried doesn't need to be criticized for pitching, and Miller doesn't need to be criticized for leaving. And after watching the baseball world rally around Vesia and his family less than a year ago, we really shouldn't need another reminder that there are moments when the scoreboard becomes spectacularly insignificant.
A player should never have to wonder whether strangers will accuse him of abandoning his team because he chose to be beside his partner while their child entered the world.
Max Fried has made his choice. Mason Miller made his. Both were theirs to make. There never needed to be a debate in the first place.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Breaking Down One Way Yankees Could Get Aaron Judge on the ALDS Roster
item.dc:creator: Joseph Randazzo; Unknown
item.description: Max Fried took the sentiment "married to the game" literally when he said he would take the bump in Game 3 of the American League Division Series, whether his girlfriend gave birth or not. The New York Yankees would never push him to make that decision. item.content:encoded:
Max Fried took the sentiment "married to the game" literally when he said he would take the bump in Game 3 of the American League Division Series, whether his girlfriend gave birth or not. The New York Yankees would never push him to make that decision. Still, they're probably secretly happy, seeing as their big-money southpaw has been one of the league's better starters for years, and they signed him after Juan Soto went to Flushing.
While it seems a bit uncouth to start thinking strategy when a man and woman are expecting a baby, the paternity list could be one way for the Yankees to get a start from Fried, and if they win Game 3 on Wednesday night, activate Aaron Judge from the IL on Thursday. Not only is this happening with Fried, but on the West Coast, the Padres saw their star closer, Mason Miller, hit the Postseason Paternity List, and in his stead is former Yankee Wandy Peralta.
As the MLB PR Account on X explained, Miller can be away from the club for a maximum of one to three days. Once he's back, he'll take Peralta's spot.
Fitting Aaron Judge onto the ALDS roster
Again, the Yankees could do this if they take Game 3 — if they feel Judge is healthy enough to play. Fried can make his start and then, if the season is still alive, hit the Paternity List for the rest of the ALDS. At that point, Games 4 and 5 would play over three days anyway, and the Yankees wouldn't need Fried.
However, if the Yankees take this route, there's no doubt it's a desperate move. Judge wasn't healthy enough to start this series, and if he comes in, he probably still isn't. With the season on the line, though, Aaron Boone would probably feel better having Judge with one good leg out there than no Judge.
If this happens, though, the Yankees would be without Luis Garcia Jr. at first base, and Ben Rice wouldn't serve as the designated hitter. The best version of the Yankees would have Judge in right field, but with a bad calf, they may want him at DH and have Rice at first. This would leave a healthy Garcia out for a hobbled Judge.
That said, the Yankees still need to win Game 3 before even considering this, but the paternity list could be one way to pull it off.
Joe Randazzo is a reference librarian who lives on Long Island. When he’s not behind a desk offering assistance to his patrons, he writes about the Yankees for Yankees On SI. Follow him as @YankeeLibrarian on X and Instagram.

item.title: [Sporting News] Yankees playoff history in Aaron Judge era: New York's poor results prove club is wasting slugger's prime | Sporting News
item.dc:creator: Daniel Mader
item.description: No matter how great one player is, it takes an entire organization to win a World Series title. From Ted Williams and Ty Cobb to Barry Bonds and Ken Griffey Jr., a long list of Hall of Famers and baseball superstars finished their careers without their team ever sitting on top of the throne. If things don't change quickly for the Yankees, Aaron Judge may be in peril of joining that list of ringless legends. Judge, now 34, hasn't been healthy enough to play in New York's 2026 postseason run. Now
item.content:encoded:
No matter how great one player is, it takes an entire organization to win a World Series title. From Ted Williams and Ty Cobb to Barry Bonds and Ken Griffey Jr., a long list of Hall of Famers and baseball superstars finished their careers without their team ever sitting on top of the throne.
If things don't change quickly for the Yankees, Aaron Judge may be in peril of joining that list of ringless legends. Judge, now 34, hasn't been healthy enough to play in New York's 2026 postseason run.
Now trailing the Rays in the ALDS, the Yankees are on the brink of another postseason exit in the Judge era — despite one World Series appearance and three ALCS berths, New York has consistently come up short.
Here's a look at the Yankees' postseason history with Judge over the past decade.
Yankees playoff results in Aaron Judge era
2017: Lost to Astros in ALCS
After missing the postseason in 2016, in Judge's rookie year, New York finished with a wild-card berth behind their young slugger's 52-homer season.
It wound up being one of the Yankees' deepest October runs of the Judge era. After beating the Twins in the AL Wild Card game and Cleveland in the ALDS, New York pushed the Astros to the limit, winning three consecutive games in the ALCS to take a 3-2 series lead.
Houston, though, rode Justin Verlander to a Game 6 win, then shut out the Yankees 4-0 in Game 7. After coming within a win of the World Series, the Yankees' season ended in the ALCS.
2018: Lost to Red Sox in ALDS
Despite winning 100 games in the regular season, the Yankees were a wild-card team in 2018, and their postseason run did not last long.
A lineup featuring six 20-homer-hitters fell to the eventual champion Red Sox in the ALDS after winning a one-game Wild Card matchup against the A's. In Aaron Boone's first season at the helm, New York had plenty of regular-season success, a potent lineup and a collection of veteran starters, but Boston won the ALDS in four games, including a 16-1 Game 3 win.
2019: Lost to Astros in ALCS
The Yankees won the AL East for the first time in the Judge era in 2019, winning 103 games to best their 2018 total. Again, they appeared set for a deep postseason run, sweeping the Twins in the ALDS to reach another ALCS against the Astros.
Again, however, the Jose Altuve-Gerrit Cole-Alex Bregman era Astros got the best of the Yankees. Houston won the series in six games, capped by Altuve's walk-off home run off Aroldis Chapman to win Game 6 and go to the World Series.
2020: Lost to Rays in ALDS
In the shortened 2020 season, the Yankees grabbed another wild-card spot after winning 33 of 60 games.
Their postseason result looked similar to prior years: a Wild Card sweep over Cleveland, but an ALDS loss to the Rays. In the decisive Game 5, Judge homered, but that was the Yankees' lone run as Chapman allowed a homer to Mike Brosseau in the eighth that ultimately won it for the Rays.
2021: Lost to Red Sox in AL Wild Card
The Yankees grabbed another Wild Card spot in 2021 after a 93-win season. This time, though, they didn't reach the ALDS.
In the one-game playoff, Nathan Eovaldi went a strong 5.1 innings for the Red Sox, while Xander Bogaerts and Kyle Schwarber both homered in a 6-2 win for Boston.
2022: Lost to Astros in ALCS
For the third time in six years, the Yankees lost to the same pesky Astros squad in the ALCS in 2022.
This time, it wasn't particularly close. New York, which won 99 games in the regular season and beat the Guardians in the ALDS, was swept by Houston. Verlander, Framber Valdez and Christian Javier silenced the Yankees' bats, while Chas McCormick and Jeremy Pena both homered twice in the series.
2024: Lost to Dodgers in World Series
The Yankees finally broke through to the Fall Classic in 2024, their first World Series appearance since winning in 2009 and first with Judge. But in a star-studded matchup, they couldn't quite get the long-awaited ring.
New York bounced back from missing the postseason in 2023 by winning 94 games and taking down the Royals in the ALDS, then Guardians in the ALCS. But the Yankees then ran into arguably the most dominant team in baseball of the era, the Dodgers.
Los Angeles quickly took a 3-0 series lead behind Shohei Ohtani, a Game 1 walk-off home run from Freddie Freeman, and strong pitching from Walker Buehler and Yoshinobu Yamamoto. By the time the Yankees won Game 4 with 11 runs, it was far too late.
The Dodgers took Game 5, 7-6, after scoring two late runs, with Ohtani winning his first World Series title.
2025: Lost to Blue Jays in ALDS
Last year, the Yankees fell to an AL East rival in the postseason for the fourth time in the Judge era.
After Judge won his third MVP in the regular season, the Yankees did take down the Red Sox in the AL Wild Card series — partially due to a dominant Game 3 start from Cam Schlittler — but they didn't find as much success against Toronto in the next round.
Vladimir Guerrero Jr. led a dominant Blue Jays lineup to a 3-1 series win in the ALDS, sending the Yankees home early. In all three of Judge's MVP seasons (2022, 2024, 2025) the Yankees couldn't get him a ring.

item.content:encoded:
Max Fried’s relationship is in the headlines in early October.
The New York Yankees‘ left-handed pitcher and his long-time companion, Reni Meyer-Whalley, are expecting their first child.
The timing could’ve been better. Fried is slated to start Game 3 of the ALDS on Wednesday night against the Tampa Bay Rays, and it’s a game that would end the Yankees season if they lose.
This is what he said in the lead-up to the game, via MLB.com’s Bryan Hoch:
“I’ve got a really supportive family that that understands that this is my job, and it’s not going to affect what happens tomorrow.”
No matter what the timing ends up being, fans are going to be paying attention to how Fried handles this situation. There definitely has to be a lot on his mind.
Is Max Fried Married?
No, Max Fried is not married.
He’s in a long-term relationship with his girlfriend, Reni Meyer-Whalley.
They became publicly official in 2024, as they took part in MLB All-Star festivities together.
Who is Reni Meyer-Whalley?
Reni Meyer-Whalley is a native of Los Angeles who played Division I volleyball.
Her career began at the University of Washington before she transferred to USC.
Meyer-Whalley was a libero and a defensive specialist, working to stop the other team from scoring — a role Fried holds on the diamond in a different way.
She had actually stepped away from volleyball in the middle of her college tenure before coming back to the court for the Trojans.
“My volleyball journey has been interesting to say the least,” Meyer-Whalley said during her time at USC. “It’s been really long. I’ve been playing since I was 8, and I also never thought that I’d make it here.”
For those volleyball fans out there looking for a few stats: Meyer-Whalley finished her final season at USC with 268 digs, including a season-high of 15 in one match. She also served 29 aces that year.
Meyer-Whalley studied communication and media studies at USC, and her collegiate bio lists her as one of nine children.
Sports Illustrated describes the start of their public-facing relationship like this:
“Exactly when Fried and Meyer-Whalley began dating isn’t publicly known, and the two haven’t offered much help filling in the blanks. Their relationship became public in July 2024, when they attended the MLB All-Star Red Carpet Show together in Arlington, Texas. They walked the carpet holding hands, marking a rare public glimpse into the pitcher’s life away from baseball.”
Now, they’re side by side as Fried navigates what it’s like to pitch in the playoffs for the Yankees, and soon they’ll be welcoming new life into the world together.

item.title: [Heavy.com] Spencer Jones Letting Yankees Down
item.dc:creator: Billy Heyen
item.description: Spencer Jones is on the verge of a postseason that he’ll want to forget. The 6-foot-7 lefty slugger was quite impressive for the New York Yankees during his rookie season after being called up for the first time to MLB. In the playoffs, though, Jones has really struggled. item.content:encoded:
Spencer Jones is on the verge of a postseason that he’ll want to forget.
The 6-foot-7 lefty slugger was quite impressive for the New York Yankees during his rookie season after being called up for the first time to MLB.
In the playoffs, though, Jones has really struggled.
There was the ball hit to the outfield earlier in the week that Jones said he misjudged and should’ve caught.
There was that swing pictured atop the article when Jones had his helmet fall off right into his face.
And really, he just hasn’t made a positive impact at all when stepping into the batter’s box.
Spencer Jones Playoff Stats
It’s a small sample size, and that’s worth acknowledging, because playoff baseball can often paint the wrong picture.
But so far, Jones is just 2-for-15 in his playoff at bats so far, entering Game 3 of the ALDS against the Rays.
Both of those two hits have been singles. He’s also walked once, stolen one base and scored three runs.
Maybe most concerning: Jones has struck out seven times in 15 at bats.
Jones was always viewed as a swing-and-miss dilemma coming through the minor leagues. Everyone knew if he made enough contact in the majors, he’d do damage, but there were huge questions about the odds of him actually doing that.
The playoff sample is small, but Jones ending nearly half his at bats in Ks isn’t great.
It’d be easier to live with if Jones’ two hits were homers, but right now he’s hitting .133 with just a pair of singles.
With Aaron Judge out, the Yankees need Jones to be good, and so far, he hasn’t been. It’s the kind of thing that would potentially even out over a longer sample, but the playoffs don’t provide that kind of runway.
Reason for Hope
The biggest reason to believe in Jones is that over the longer sample he had in the regular season, he was much better than this.
A 15-AB sample isn’t much to go on. If it hadn’t happened in his first 15 playoff at bats of his career, it might not even be noticed.
Game 3 of the ALDS is against a righty, Nick Martinez, so Jones should be in the lineup.
Martinez is crafty and has had an incredible season, but he conceptually is a matchup Jones could solve if he takes a good approach to the plate.
The Yankees, in part by default, have put their faith in Jones to be ready for the playoff stage.
They’re all running out of time, but it’s not done yet. Jones still has a chance to deliver.

item.content:encoded:
All eight teams remaining in the MLB playoffs are in action on Wednesday night, the final time this postseason that we’ll have four games to decide between in the home run market.
There have been a ton of big-time homers and hits in the ALDS and NLDS, and more players have a chance to become postseason heroes with Cleveland, New York, San Diego and Atlanta all facing elimination on Oct. 7.
While pitching in the playoffs is a lot tougher to bet against since starters usually have very short leashes, the home run market also features some better odds. So, who is worth a look on Wednesday?
I’m targeting three players to leave the yard, including a pick for Manny Machado, who has been red hot in five games this postseason.
Best MLB Home Run Prop Bet Picks for Wednesday, Oct. 7
Manny Machado to Hit a Home Run (+492)
Earlier today, I shared this prop for Machado in SI Betting’s preview of Brewers vs. Padres Game 4:
The 2026 regular season wasn’t a great one for Manny Machado, as he hit just .217 with a .711 OPS. The seven-time All-Star did hit 30 home runs, bumping his average up over .230 after the All-Star break.
He’s really come around so far in the postseason, hitting .375 with a 1.211 OPS across five games. Machado has at least one hit in four games, two multi-hit games and a home run (Game 1 of the wild card against Chicago).
Chad Patrick is the only potential Milwaukee starter that Machado even has at-bats against, but I don’t want to base this play off of matchups since both teams will likely lean on their bullpens in a must-win game for San Diego.
In the playoffs, it's important to target a hot bat when looking at home run props, and Machado has that for the Padres with six hits (three extra base hits) in five games. He’s worth a shot at nearly 5/1 against a Brewers pitching staff that isn’t nearly as dangerous when Jacob Misiorowski isn’t on the mound.
Ben Rice to Hit a Home Run (+318)
New York Yankees star Ben Rice has been dominant this postseason, hitting .467 with a 1.889 OPS and four home runs in four games.
He’s been by far the most effective hitter in baseball this postseason, and I love the matchup for him at home against Tampa Bay Rays right-hander Nick Martinez.
During the regular season, Martinez allowed 22 home runs in 31 appearances, and his expected ERA was much higher than his actual ERA. He’s also struggled against Rice in his career.
The Yankees star is 4-for-9 (.444 batting average) with three doubles, two walks and 1.323 OPS against Martinez in his career.
With the short porch at Yankee Stadium, I’ll take a shot on Rice to keep the Yankees’ season alive on Wednesday.
Freddie Freeman to Hit a Home Run (+660)
Freddie Freeman has homered in back-to-back games for the Los Angeles Dodgers, and I can't pass him up at this price against Tyler Mahle and the Atlanta Braves.
Mahle allowed 20 home runs in 27 appearances during the regular season, and he’s really struggled against Freeman in his career.
The 10-time All-Star is hitting .421 (8-for-19) with a double, a homer and a 1.132 OPS against Mahle in his career, and he’s clearly found a new gear in the postseason.
After homering just 16 times during the regular season, Freeman seems to have found some power in this series. He’s also playing in a familiar stadium after he spent the beginning of his career in Atlanta.
At +660, this matchup is too enticing to pass up on Wednesday.
Odds refresh periodically and are subject to change.

item.content:encoded:
NY Daily News | James O'Connell: The Yankees ran out the same exact lineup in Games 1 and 2 of their ALDS matchup against the Rays, but aside from Ben Rice and his pair of home runs no one else is really contributing. As the series shifts over to New York for Game 3 tonight, manager Aaron Boone was amenable to some lineup tinkering though he wouldn't get into specifics of who could find their way in and who would get sent to the bench. Some of the more likely candidates to sit include those who both haven't found their way into a hit yet and also fumbled the ball around in their atrocious Game 2 showing, such as Ryan McMahon and Jazz Chisholm Jr.
NY Post | Mark W. Sanchez: Max Fried is lined up to start tonight on the mound in Game 3, but there was the potential for that to not be the case. Fried's partner is due to give birth in the coming days and there was the possibility that Fried would have to miss this start, but the lefty confirmed that he will be there for the team adding that he's "got a really supportive family that understands that this is my job." Fried's focus is leaving it all on the line for his team as the Yankees face elimination, and hopefully that dedication pays off for him.
MLB.com | Matthew Leach: So the Yankees are down in an 0-2 hole, but is there any hope of a comeback? There's a few reasons to believe in a turnaround, namely that they largely beat themselves in Game 2 and have an elite pitching staff that could lock down opposing bats so long as the defense stops putzing the ball around. Getting out of Tropicana Field is also a big plus, and even though a potential Game 5 would see them return to that house of horrors, they've got to win the first two before worrying about that.
MLB.com | Mike Lupica: The Yankees are certainly not strangers to reverse sweeping in an ALDS, as Lupica takes us through the history of the team's ability to flip the script. Unfortunately, that history all lies in the recent past as Aaron Boone's squads have largely been unable to answer back after getting punched in the face in a series — let's see if they can change that narrative this time around.
The Big Lead | J.P. Hoornstra: Sadly, we end our notes with the passing of 'Sudden' Sam McDowell, who died on Monday. McDowell was a six-time All-Star throughout his 15-year MLB career, and he played for the Yankees at the tail end of his career for the 1973-74 seasons. From all of us here at Pinstripe Alley, we send our condolences to Sam's family and friends.

item.title: [New York Post] Rookie moments beginning to pile up for Yankees’ George Lombard Jr., Spencer Jones
item.dc:creator: Mark W Sanchez
item.description:
Momentum and narratives swing wildly in October. Against the Red Sox, George Lombard Jr. and Spencer Jones looked like the present and future of the Yankees. In two games against the Rays, they have looked like rookies.
Access the Yankees beat like never before
Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees. Try it free They have had plenty of company on a team that has neither hit n
item.content:encoded:
Momentum and narratives swing wildly in October. Against the Red Sox, George Lombard Jr. and Spencer Jones looked like the present and future of the Yankees.
In two games against the Rays, they have looked like rookies.




Access the Yankees beat like never before

Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
They have had plenty of company on a team that has neither hit nor won, but Lombard and Jones have been part of the problem for a Yankees club on the brink of elimination.
For Lombard, the largest issue was two plays in the Game 2 loss — one deemed an error (even if the error could have been assigned to Luis García Jr.) and the other generously ruled a fielder’s choice that allowed a run to score.
Jones had his own questionable play in right field Monday, but the bigger problem is the slugger going hitless in seven at-bats against Tampa Bay and now being 2-for-15 with seven strikeouts in the postseason.
“It was just one of those games where things kind of compiled and stacked up on top of each other,” Lombard said after the team combined for four errors in the 5-2 loss.
The worst moment for Lombard — who went 4-for-8 against Boston and has gone 0-for-7 against Tampa Bay, albeit with some hard-hit outs — came in Monday’s fifth inning. With one out and Junior Caminero on third and the Yankees trailing 2-1, Chandler Simpson tapped one softly to shortstop. Lombard charged, attempted to field on the backhand and rush a throw to the plate, but even as his arm was beginning his throw, the ball deflected off his glove.
Probably contributing to the play was that the 21-year-old had not played at Tropicana Field before this series.
“I wouldn’t say tough. It’s definitely different,” Lombard said of the turf. “But we went out there in practice and kind of tried to get accustomed to it. But it’s different than other fields. But that’s the same thing with every other stadium — everyone’s going to play different.”
His next mistake was less field dependent: Two batters later, Jonny DeLuca hit a three-bouncer to Lombard, who could not charge it because Simpson cut in front of him on his way to third.
He then had to rush. “I just pulled the throw a little bit,” Lombard said, with García unable to make a stretch and catch on a throw that was not that far offline.
In an inning that should have been over, Richie Palacios then knocked a two-run single that essentially put the game out of reach.
Jones’ defensive night was more debatable. The four-run fifth inning began with Jonathan Aranda smacking a line drive in front of him.
Maybe Jones had a chance at charging, diving and making a remarkable grab. Maybe an overaggressive Jones would have dove and allowed the ball to get past him.
Shop Yankees Merch
In reality, Jones did not get a great jump and then played it on a hop for a single.
“Playing it back in my head, I thought I had a good first step,” Jones said. “I just hesitated, and then that was the difference between making a play and then just trying to keep it in front of me.”
His manager did not take issue with the play.
“There are plenty of others to pick on tonight,” Aaron Boone said after the game. “That wasn’t one of them.”
Easier to pick on have been Jones’ at-bats. He looked overmatched against Drew Rasmussen (as did the rest of the lineup), swinging through high fastballs and low changeups on a night he struck out twice and went 0-for-3. Monday, he struck out once, grounded out twice and found some terrible luck with his first well-hit pitch of the series: a towering fly ball to center that bounced off one of the rings high above the field.
Alert right fielder in Victor Mesa Jr. ran over and caught the ricochet.
“I didn’t know what happened,” Jones said.
— Additional reporting by Greg Joyce

item.title: [Orange County Register] ALDS: Down 2-0 to Rays, Yankees’ World Series title drought could grow
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press

After making four errors in a dismal Game 2 defeat, New York’s players and staff arrived home about 5 a.m. on Tuesday in a 2-0 American League Division Series deficit for the second straight year, this time against the Tampa Bay Rays. T
item.content:encoded:
By RONALD BLUM AP Baseball Writer
NEW YORK — Max Fried’s words were as sharp as the break on some of his pitches.
“It’s important to have a little bit of pride and to be able to say: ‘That’s not us and we’re going to prove it,’” the New York Yankees pitcher said.
After making four errors in a dismal Game 2 defeat, New York’s players and staff arrived home about 5 a.m. on Tuesday in a 2-0 American League Division Series deficit for the second straight year, this time against the Tampa Bay Rays. The best-of-five matchup resumes Wednesday night (5 p.m. PT, TBS, truTV) in the Bronx with Fried – a former Harvard-Westlake standout – starting for the Yankees and Nick Martinez for the Rays.
With one more loss to Tampa Bay, the World Series title drought for MLB’s winningest franchise would extend to a 17th season – matching the most since Babe Ruth led New York to its first championship in 1923. New York hasn’t advanced past a higher-seeded team in a postseason series since 2020.
“This group has done a really good job all year of bouncing back through a tough game, through some tough moments in the season and handled it all very well. So that’s my expectation this time. It has to be,” said Manager Aaron Boone, who spoke with players individually rather than give a rah-rah speech.
Tampa Bay could party at Yankee Stadium for the second time in two weeks, after clinching the AL East on Sept 22.
Seeking their first World Series title, the Rays are nearing an AL Championship Series against the Chicago White Sox or Cleveland. They haven’t advanced that far since 2020, when they lost in the World Series to the Dodgers.
Martinez used to sit in the Yankee Stadium bleachers when he played college baseball from 2009-11 at Fordham University, located about 5 miles away.
“I imagine it’s going to be an electric crowd with their season on the line,” he said.
Teams taking 2-0 leads in best-of-five postseason series have won 83 of 93 times, according to MLB. The last comeback from an 0-2 deficit was the 2017 Yankees against Cleveland.
“There’s no taking games off,” Rays outfielder Jonny DeLuca said. “Obviously taking the first two has put us in a really good spot, but it’s still the same mindset going forward.”
ERROR ISSUES
Third baseman Ryan McMahon, second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr., shortstop George Lombard Jr. and catcher Austin Wells all made errors in Game 3 that led to three unearned runs in New York’s 5-2 loss.
In addition, Lombard didn’t field Chandler Simpson’s two-hopper and right fielder Spencer Jones allowed Jonathan Aranda’s liner – a ball with 65% hit probability – to fall starting the fifth, which sparked a four-run inning.
“It was just one of those things that it all kind of happened back-to-back-to back,” Lombard said.
Throwing errors by McMahon and Chisholm in the first along with a catcher’s interference call against Wells gave the Yankees their first three-error postseason inning.
“It didn’t seem like we really showed up today,” pitcher Cam Schlittler said.
Two years ago, the Yankees had two errors and a mental lapse that led to five unearned runs in a season-ending Game 5 World Series loss to the Dodgers.
Tampa Bay put 31 balls in play, two shy of the high for any team in a postseason game this year. The Rays were just behind Milwaukee for the top regular-season team batting average, .2585 to .2581, and led the American League in on-base percentage.
Simpson is 12th in sprint speed and DeLuca 16th among players with at least 150 competitive runs this year, according to MLB Statcast.
“Just very contact-oriented,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said. “Just the speed getting down the line, the urgency it forces on the infielders, really good infielders – it forces them to get out of their comfort zone and make a highlight-reel play. Those are tough to make.”
YANKEES’ VANISHING OFFENSE
New York’s players in the third through seventh spots of the batting order went 0 for 33 with 11 strikeouts in the first two games: Luis García Jr., Jones, Lombard, Chisholm and Trent Grisham.
Aaron Judge’s absence has been glaring.
New York was fourth in runs, 13th in batting average and second in OPS through May 31, its last game before the three-time AL MVP went on the injured list due to a fractured rib.
From June 1 through the end of the season, the Yankees were 24th in runs, 29th in batting average and 27th in OPS. Judge returned for seven games from Sept. 8-16, hitting .174 with three RBIs before a calf strain.
“I’m considering a couple things but haven’t settled on anything,” Boone said of possible lineup changes.
FRIED HAS BABY ON THE WAY
Fried’s longtime girlfriend, Reni Meyer-Whalley, is due to give birth any day.
“I’ve got a really supportive family that understands that this is my job, and it’s not going to affect what happens tomorrow,” he said Tuesday.

item.title: [MLB.com] Rays-Yankees ALDS Game 3 FAQ (Wed., 8 p.m. ET, TBS/HBO Max)
item.dc:creator: Adam Berry; Bryan Hoch
item.description: NEW YORK -- Two weeks ago, the Rays went wild in the visitors’ clubhouse at Yankee Stadium after clinching their first American League East championship in five years. That party started shortly after a win over the Yankees and carried late into the New York night. Could they have another celebration in store in the Bronx? It’s time for the American League Division Series to shift venues, going from the Rays’ home dome at Tropicana Field to Yankee Stadium for Game 3 on Wednesday night. But the R
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK -- Two weeks ago, the Rays went wild in the visitors’ clubhouse at Yankee Stadium after clinching their first American League East championship in five years. That party started shortly after a win over the Yankees and carried late into the New York night.
Could they have another celebration in store in the Bronx?
It’s time for the American League Division Series to shift venues, going from the Rays’ home dome at Tropicana Field to Yankee Stadium for Game 3 on Wednesday night. But the Rays are still right where they want to be, holding a commanding 2-0 lead in the series with three chances to advance to the AL Championship Series.
“It's amazing, man. It's exactly the way we wanted to start the series,” Rays closer Bryan Baker said. “To be able to play in front of these fans in this building and take a 2-0 series lead was exactly what we wanted, so it feels really good right now.”
Maybe home-field advantage is what the Yankees need after coming up empty against Rays ace Drew Rasmussen in Game 1 and kicking the ball around the infield in a mistake-filled Game 2 defeat. Or maybe it’ll help to send left-hander Max Fried to the mound, knowing how tough he’s been on Tampa Bay throughout his career.
“We've got to get over it,” Yankees manager Aaron Boone said after Game 2. “We've responded all year to difficult times, and we've got to do that again. We've got to get ourselves up off the mat.”
Tampa Bay’s pitching staff held what looked like a red-hot New York lineup to only two runs in the first 18 innings of this series. If the Rays keep that up, they could enjoy another champagne-soaked night in the city that never sleeps.
“I think it's sweet either way. Doesn't matter the clubhouse,” Rays center fielder Jonny DeLuca said. “Obviously, going over there, having the chance to do that would be pretty special.”
When is the game and how can I watch it?
First pitch for Game 3 of the Yankees-Rays Division Series is set for 8 p.m. ET on Wednesday at Yankee Stadium. The game will be broadcast on TBS, truTV and HBO Max.
The ALDS will be available in Spanish on UniMas, while Univision’s TUDN Radio will provide Spanish-language audio coverage. ESPN Radio will provide live national coverage of all 2026 MLB Postseason games.
Who are the starting pitchers?
Rays: Nick Martinez, RHP
Key stats: 7-3, 2.38 ERA in 16 road starts this season
After rolling out Rasmussen in Game 1 and Freddy Peralta in Game 2, Martinez was the logical choice for the Rays with the series moving to the Bronx. The veteran right-hander was a reliable presence on the mound for Tampa Bay all season, as he posted a 3.10 ERA over 180 innings while the club went 22-9 in his starts. He was at his best on the road, including two outings in the Bronx. The first-time All-Star held the Yankees to only three runs over 12 innings in their home ballpark.
Yankees: Max Fried, LHP
Key stats: 5-1, 1.81 ERA in 7 career GS vs. Tampa Bay
Fried is coming off a sharp outing against the Red Sox in the decisive Game 2 of the AL Wild Card Series, holding Boston to a run on three hits over six innings. Fried walked one and struck out six, his third postseason start since joining the Yankees.
This will be Fried’s third time facing the Rays this season. He last saw them on Sept. 22 in New York, taking the loss in a 6 2/3-inning effort as Tampa Bay clinched the AL East.
Fried also went up against the Rays on April 11 at Tropicana Field, taking a no-decision after permitting three runs over eight innings. For his career, Fried is 5-1 with a 1.81 ERA in seven starts vs. Tampa Bay, including 3-0 with a 0.84 ERA in three starts during the 2025 season.
What might the starting lineups look like?
Rays: It seems likely the Rays will change things up a bit against the Yankees’ left-handers, opting for the right-handed side of most platoons and leaving their lefty hitters available off the bench. Here’s one potential look for a more right-handed lineup.
Yankees: The Yankees have used the same lefty-heavy lineup three times this postseason against right-handed pitchers, including twice in the ALDS. Boone said he is considering shaking things up for Game 3. Boone said before Game 2 that he was considering starting Anthony Volpe at third base. Jose Caballero and Paul Goldschmidt could also enter the mix.
How will the bullpens line up after the starter?
Rays: The Rays really couldn’t be in much better shape thanks to their starting rotation. Rasmussen handled eight innings in Game 1, and the duo of Peralta and Ian Seymour combined to work 7 2/3 innings in Game 2. So, their traditional relievers have recorded seven of the 54 outs so far this series: six from Baker and a big one from lefty Cam Booser. They may not turn to Peralta or Seymour in Game 3, but they still have starter Griffin Jax available -- and the Yankees have yet to face setup men Tyler Wells and Kevin Kelly in this series.
Yankees: Ryan Weathers replaced infielder/outfielder Amed Rosario for this series, returning from a left flexor strain sustained in late August. David Bednar, Paul Blackburn and Brent Headrick should all be leaned upon for high-leverage outs. Will Warren is now in the bullpen after appearing in 32 games (29 starts) during the regular season. Warren made one appearance in the Wild Card Series, tossing 1 2/3 innings.
Any injuries of note?
Rays: Nothing new. Everyone who was expected to be available for this series is on the roster. The most notable injury situation to watch moving forward is that of left-hander Shane McClanahan, whose status is unclear except that he will not pitch in this series.
Yankees: Aaron Judge was left off the ALDS roster, though Boone said it was a “close” call. Judge has yet to run the bases as he recovers from a right calf strain, though he has been performing outfield running. He has also been taking numerous live at-bats while throwing. Clarke Schmidt has been ruled out for the remainder of the postseason.
Who is hot and who is not?
Rays: Aranda doesn’t get as much love as the other members of the “Big Three,” but his left-handed bat is key. He hit better than either Caminero or Díaz in September, and he had the lone big hit of the night in Game 1 before picking up two more hits in Game 2. Richie Palacios finished strong, too, posting a .981 OPS with five homers in September before delivering the biggest hit of Game 2, and the Brooklyn native likes hitting against his hometown Yankees. Tampa Bay’s entire rotation surged into the postseason, highlighted by Rasmussen and Peralta, the September AL Pitcher of the Month.
The Rays’ outfield is off to a slow start in this series, offensively, but they all showed the impact they can have by putting the ball in play in Game 2. And their defense has been consistently excellent.
Yankees: Rice has been the Yankees' most productive hitter in the postseason, and given how the ALDS has gone, it hasn't been particularly close. Rice is 7-for-15 (.467) in the playoffs, including his two-homer performance in ALDS Game 2. Rice has four homers and eight RBIs overall. Wells is 5-for-12 (.417) in the playoffs, including a couple of doubles in the ALDS. Everyone except for Rice and Wells has combined to go 1-for-46 (.022) in the ALDS so far.
Anything else fans might want to know?
• The Yankees won four of the six games these clubs played in the Bronx during the regular season, splitting a pair of games in late May, then taking three of four the final week of the season. However, the Rays have already celebrated once at Yankee Stadium, as they clinched the AL East title with a 6-1 win in the second half of a doubleheader on Sept. 22.

item.title: [Heavy.com] Yankees' Max Fried Reveals ALDS Game 3 Plans With Baby On Way
item.dc:creator: Billy Heyen
item.description: There will be those who agree wholeheartedly with Max Fried’s thinking, and there will be those who disagree entirely. That won’t change Fried’s decision, though. The New York Yankees‘ left-handed pitcher is slated to start Game 3 of the ALDS on Wednesday, and that start will come with the potential for a baby to be born to him and his girlfriend any day now. Fried’s girlfriend, the former Division I volleyball player Reni Meyer-Whalley, is just about due. It’s certainly not ideal timing, given
item.content:encoded:
There will be those who agree wholeheartedly with Max Fried’s thinking, and there will be those who disagree entirely.
That won’t change Fried’s decision, though. The New York Yankees‘ left-handed pitcher is slated to start Game 3 of the ALDS on Wednesday, and that start will come with the potential for a baby to be born to him and his girlfriend any day now.
Fried’s girlfriend, the former Division I volleyball player Reni Meyer-Whalley, is just about due.
It’s certainly not ideal timing, given that the Yankees’ season will end if they lose on Wednesday.
On the flip side, this will be the first child for Fried and his significant other.
One way or the other, Fried has to make a potentially tough call.
Max Fried Decision
Fried told reporters on Tuesday afternoon that he will be starting ALDS Game 3 and that he doesn’t expect that plan to change.
This is what he said, via MLB.com’s Bryan Hoch:
“I’ve got a really supportive family that that understands that this is my job, and it’s not going to affect what happens tomorrow.”
Ballplayers through the years have taken all kinds of different approaches to an upcoming baby’s birth, from pulling a player in the middle of a game to letting him get away in advance to be there.
The tricky part about baseball season is that games are almost every day, so if a baby is coming, it’ll likely arrive on a gameday one way or another.
MLB even has a paternity list to allow roster construction to be handled while a new father steps away from the team.
Rarely, though, does this come up in October. It’s pivotal timing, and it’s two big parts of life overlapping for Fried.
Max Fried Sets Up Jokes
Fried’s choice to not miss his start has set up a similar brand of jokes on social media.
This is what one commenter wrote:
“Another egregious error by a yankees player. Your kid being born is once-in-a-lifetime moment. The Yankees getting eliminated in the postseason in embarrassing fashion is an October tradition.”
Then there was this one:
“This man’s about to risk relationship trouble for a team that’s not gonna give him an ounce of run support.”
There’s certainly ample opportunity for Yankees haters to pile on here.
Fried could also have everything work out. There’s no guarantee his child will be born while he pitches on Wednesday night.
It’s not a call that many would like to have to make, though. Fried and the Yankees are in a tough spot, and the team can’t really make a choice of their own here. It’s gotta be up to the pitcher/father.
And right now, it looks like Fried has made up his mind.

item.title: [Yanks Go Yard] Yankees’ Heliot Ramos trade somehow looks layers more disastrous after ALDS Game 2
item.dc:creator: Matthew Swigonski
item.description: It would be perfectly understandable if that headline made you double check the box score to see if you somehow missed Heliot Ramos taking the field in the New York Yankees’ tough Game 2 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays. item.content:encoded:
It would be perfectly understandable if that headline made you double check the box score to see if you somehow missed Heliot Ramos taking the field in the New York Yankees’ tough Game 2 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays. But it's the fact that the Yankees struggle to find any real use for Ramos that makes his trade a real disaster and a complete waste of a roster spot.
The Rays trotted out two lefty relievers in Game 2 in an attempt to neutralize the Yankees’ onslaught of left-handed bats. Cam Booser came in for Rays’ starting pitcher Freddy Peralta and he walked one heck of a tightrope to narrowly escape a fifth inning jam. After facing just two batters and recording only one out, Rays manager Kevin Cash decided to bring in LHP Ian Seymour to bridge the gap to closer Bryan Baker in the ninth.
Despite giving up a solo shot to Ben Rice in the eighth inning, Seymour tossed three spectacular innings and made sure he never gave the Yankees any hope of mounting a comeback. With the lineup filled with eight left-handed batters, the Yankees seemed to play right into Cash’s master plan.
You might assume that a player like Ramos would make for the perfect option to bring into the game in place of one of those lefty hitters. If you recall back at the trade deadline, Yankees GM Brian Cashman acquired Ramos for the exact purpose of becoming another one of the team’s weapons to combat left-handed pitching.
As Ryan Garcia of Just Baseball pointed out, the Yankees traded prospects Kaeden Kent and Henry Lalane to the San Francisco Giants to add Ramos to their roster. The Yankees thought highly enough of him to surrender Lalane, a top-five prospect in their system, in hopes he would provide some much-needed pop against lefties.
But with Paul Goldschmidt hitting for Ryan McMahon in the top of the eighth inning, he became the Yankees only pinch hitter of the game. Even as Luis García Jr. and Spencer Jones struck out in their at-bats against Seymour, Ramos never left the comfort of his own spot on the bench. If he couldn’t even be brought out for an at-bat against the Rays’ southpaws, why is he even on the ALDS roster for the Yankees?
Heliot Ramos never seemed like a good fit for the Yankees
With a .297/.383/.525 slash line against LHP in 2026, Ramos can rake. We can’t pretend that he isn’t a quality player for that skillset. He even had a brief redemption arc that made fans briefly think that the Yankees won the trade. But with a .651 OPS in 303 at-bats against right-handed pitchers this season, Ramos has gradually limited himself at the plate. His strength against LHP still makes him a very strong platoon player to have on a Major League roster. Just not the Yankees’ roster.
As a poor defender, Ramos is tough to justify penciling in the lineup as an outfielder. That means that he is best suited to fill in as a DH. But with Rice now almost exclusively serving as the Yankees’ full-time DH, Ramos will never steal at-bats away from the Yankees' best offensive player in 2026.
At the same time, Ramos’ lack of defensive prowess makes him a liability to have out there in the field with a team already famous for giving their opponent extra outs to play with. That leaves his only option as a pinch hitter against LHP. Even then, Yankees manager Aaron Boone couldn’t see the value in taking the bat out of the hands of anyone else in the lineup in Game 2.
That all but puts the final nail in the coffin for Ramos’ career with the Yankees. For a rebuilding team looking to add a solid hitter, he can provide solid value at the plate. For a playoff contending team looking for a platoon player to face off against LHP as their DH, Ramos can again provide solid value. But the Yankees have neither of those needs. And their Game 2 loss against the Rays’ lefties made that obvious.

item.content:encoded:
As they say, “if it ain’t broke, don’t fix it.”
Well, the Yankees’ offense is certainly broken, and it likely requires fixing beyond what’s in their current tool bag. However, manager Aaron Boone is ready to at least try some different screws and make some changes to his Game 3 lineup with the Yankees trailing 2-0 to the Tampa Bay Rays.
“Yeah. I’m considering a couple things,” said Boone on Tuesday when asked about making lineup changes.
“But I haven’t settled on anything. I’ll kind of work through that through the day and talk to some of my coaches and make a decision, hopefully tonight on which way I want to go.”
The Bombers ran back the same exact lineup in the first two games of the five-game set and they scored a total of two runs — both solo homers in Game 2 off Ben Rice’s bat.
It’s been the definition of lifeless performances as they’re combined 5-for-51 in the ALDS.
“Obviously Rasmussen really shut us down the first night,” said Boone on their offensive struggles. “Like hit a couple of balls on the screws, but for the most part he had his way with us and kind of dominated the game.
“[Monday] I thought offensively better at-bats, like we had some opportunities, especially in the middle of the game. I thought Belly had a great at-bat with the bases loaded there. We were able to knock Peralta out. Didn’t find the hole and then just not enough. But the story is we gotta play cleaner baseball than that.”
The obvious areas for potential change are second and third base. Ryan McMahon and Jazz Chisholm Jr. are combined 0-for-9 in the two games and both were at the center of a putrid first inning on Monday, registering an error apiece.
Anthony Volpe is a top candidate to take a spot as the middle infielder had a strong performance in his lone start against the Boston Red Sox in Game 1 of the Wild Card Series, going 1-for-3, including a sacrifice bunt. Jose Caballero and Amed Rosario are the other candidates for some shakeup.
Perhaps Giancarlo Stanton could play some sort of role as the DH, although Boone did indicate that the veteran would be limited to pinch-hitting duties prior to the Wild Card series. However, desperate times call for desperate measures and the Yankees season will be on the line on Wednesday night.
The Bombers put 15 position players on the 26-man roster to play the platoon game and give them options; now it’s time to see what all of those options can provide.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees fell into an 0-2 hole Monday night after losing to the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 2 of the ALDS.
New York sent ace Cam Schlittler to the mound, and while he didn't have his best stuff, the defense behind him didn't help him one bit.
The Yankees committed three errors in the first inning and four total for the game as they lost 5-2, with both of their runs coming on solo home runs by Ben Rice. As a team, they recorded just four hits, following a one-hit performance in Game 1 that resulted in a 1-0 loss.
Stephen A. Smith Calls Out Aaron Boone
Now, with the Yankees' backs against the wall and one loss away from elimination, conversations are beginning about what manager Aaron Boone's future looks like in the Bronx.
On Tuesday, ESPN's Stephen A. Smith made it very clear that he's out on Boone after supporting him since he was hired back in 2017 by New York.
"This is a disgrace. I'm looking at Aaron Boone now. I've been a supporter of Aaron Boone for years. I can't support him any longer. You can't have a team out there looking like the bad news bears," Smith said. "It's bad enough that only Ben Rice is hitting the damn ball… but you can't have a professional baseball team in Major League Baseball looking like this. This is disgraceful.
"It ain't one person, it ain't two people, it ain't three people, five different people made errors… I couldn't believe it."
Looking at the Yankees
The ALDS will now shift to New York, where the Yankees will play Game 3 on Wednesday in the Bronx and potentially Game 4 if they can win tomorrow and extend the series.
If they lose one more game, though, the series will conclude, and the Rays will advance to the ALCS, where they'll face the winner of the Chicago White Sox and Cleveland Guardians series. The White Sox currently lead that series 2-0.
New York is expected to send left-hander Max Fried to the mound for Game 3, while left-hander Carlos Rodón would start a potential Game 4.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Stephen A. Smith Calls Out Yankees Manager Aaron Boone After ALDS Loss appeared first on HEAVY.

item.title: [Defector] The Yankees Look Meek And Flubby | Defector
item.dc:creator: Ray Ratto
item.description: You've been fighting it off as best you can, but the weight of the evidence is starting to hit your hips, knees and ankles in a series of small electric spasms. item.content:encoded:
You've been fighting it off as best you can, but the weight of the evidence is starting to hit your hips, knees and ankles in a series of small electric spasms. You've tried to explain it away as "Well, the league's weird this year," and while you're right no matter what league you're referring to, the disorientation is still there and getting worse.
The Tampa Bay Rays look like they are going to win their American League Division Series, but that's not the thing that's making you nickname your persistent migraine as though it were a mischievous nephew. It's that they're making the New York Yankees look like the Los Angeles Angels, which is not just laughing at the power of branding but making a fresh mockery of a town that already has to put up with the Mets.
The Rays gnaw at a game like hyperactive beavers, eschewing home runs (except for Junior Caminero) and embracing the annoying little things that modern baseball once disdained: speed, defense, and even the occasional bunt. The Yankees have struggled with stuff like catching the ball or throwing it in a useful direction, which have always been in fashion. That is how Game 2, a 5-2 Rays win, played out Monday night. The Yankees' four errors were spectacular, the second-most put up by the team in its 448 all-time postseason games, highlighted but by no means concluded by Jazz Chisholm Jr.'s comprehensive mangling of a double-play pivot on the Rays' third at-bat of the game. Had it not been for Ben Rice's two solo homers, the Yankees would have looked utterly Angelic in all the worst ways.
The Yankees' heel turn has been as remarkable as it has been swift. They beat Boston twice, 9-0 and 9-2, to scratch a traditional itch, but after traveling to Florida to face the ultra-modest and scrupulously mistake-averse Rays, they have reverted to a deeply dark place. They were one-hit and utterly baffled by Drew Rasmussen over eight innings in a 1-0 Game 1 loss, and farted away Game 2 in an inning; they suddenly look light years worse than a Rays team that won just five more games than them in the regular season.
By logic, this should be close. Thus far, it really hasn't been. Optically, the Yankees look like they're starting a rebuild—unfinished, unpolished, and fragrant in worrying ways. Mostly they've looked confused. Their worldview in this series can be summed up by Spencer Jones staring stupefied at the catwalk he hit with a fly ball that was caught for an out. The ball would have been an out anyway judging by the body language of center fielder Jonny DeLuca, who was waiting for the ball to come down before it introduced itself to the local infrastructure. The fact that it turned wacky because Tampa plays in a glorified ball pit doesn't change the fact that an out only became a slightly different out. The significant thing was that it amounted to nothing.
It should be said here that our well-developed sense of glorified perversity demands that we get not only an ALCS that involves Tampa and the second team in Chicago, but a potential World Series between those teams and the Milwaukee Brewers. Anything that helps undermine the owners' argument for a salary cap is objectively admirable and to be desired, so there's that. But beyond that targeted billionaire schadenfreude, the Yankees have been abject in this series, playing like a team that is either ready to go on vacation or already on one. They were dramatically less competitive in Game 2 than they were in a game in which they were nearly no-hit. Even after you caveat the small sample size, the Yankees are slashing .086/.145/.224, which is less Angelic than sub-Cherubic.
Worse still, New York had more players commit an error than players who got a hit on Monday night, the first time that has happened since Roy Halladay no-hit the Reds in 2010. You have to believe to an inordinate level in the power of history and the weight of Yankee Stadium to see a long-term escape for them, here. The Rays were better for six months, and they are better now.
That can turn in a short series, of course, but the Yankees have been placed in a position where they have to react to the Rays, rather than other way around. They may not butcher an evening's entertainment in the slapstick fashion they did last night, but if they're going to get back into the series, they'll have to do it the hardest possible way, without inherited swagger. The Rays and Brewers, optimized and seamless as they are, currently feel like the future of a game that pretends not to have one, and the first two games of this series—grounder to short, Lombard snares it, and the throw to first SAILS INTO THE SEATS, and that will score two runs—have been proof that this is so.

item.title: [The Big Lead] Jazz Chisholm Jr. has no regrets about costly error vs. Rays
item.dc:creator: Stephen Douglas
item.description: The Tampa Bay Rays beat the New York Yankees, 5-2, in Game 2 of the American League Division Series on Monday, Oct. 5. The Rays now hold a commanding 2-0 lead in the best-of-five series. Tampa Bay played error-free ball and pulled away with a four-run fifth inning and never looked back. The Yankees, meanwhile, had as many errors as hits (four) and are on the verge of elimination. New York’s first three errors of the game happened in the opening stanza. The second error was the most costly. With
item.content:encoded:
The Tampa Bay Rays beat the New York Yankees, 5-2, in Game 2 of the American League Division Series on Monday, Oct. 5. The Rays now hold a commanding 2-0 lead in the best-of-five series. Tampa Bay played error-free ball and pulled away with a four-run fifth inning and never looked back.
The Yankees, meanwhile, had as many errors as hits (four) and are on the verge of elimination. New York’s first three errors of the game happened in the opening stanza. The second error was the most costly. With runners on first and second, Jazz Chisholm Jr. took an off-target toss from shortstop George Lombard Jr. and tried to turn and throw to first in one motion. In his hurried attempt to turn a double play, his throw was not even close to first baseman Luis Garcia Jr.. The error allowed Yandy Diaz to score and immediately put the Yankees in a hole.
Chisholm was asked about the play after the game and did not second-guess his decision, per SNY Yankees on X.
Jazz Chisholm Jr. has no regrets
Jazz Chisholm Jr. was asked how he’d do-over the Junior Caminero ground ball in the first inning that led to the first run of ALDS Game 2 "I’d probably still throw it, honestly. The play that was trying to be made. I feel like I could’ve made an even better throw" https://t.co/EgQa71F3kb
— SNY Yankees (@snyyankees) October 6, 2026
“I’d probably still throw it, honestly,” Chisholm said. “The play that was trying to be made, I feel like I could’ve made an even better throw.”
Turning around and rolling the ball toward first would have constituted an “even better throw” in this case. So you can understand what Chisholm means here. Or maybe not.
The good news for Chisholm is that this error happened so early in the game and the Yankees committed so many more errors and lost by more than one and … that actually doesn’t sound like good news at all actually.
In case you missed it, here is Chisholm’s throwing error as shared by MLB on X. You will probably agreed it could have been better.
Jazz Chisholm Jr.’s Game 2 error
The Rays score first in ALDS Game 2! https://t.co/H44QiuPjq3
— MLB (@MLB) October 6, 2026
The teams have a day off Tuesday and will resume the series with the Yankees fighting for their lives at 8 p.m. ET Wednesday on TBS.

item.content:encoded:
Yankees' Ben Rice makes one-of-a-kind MLB postseason history with two HR night originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The New York Yankees lost on Monday night to the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 2 of the ALDS, dropping to a 2-0 deficit in the series, on the brink of elimination.
Through two games, the defense has been horrible, and more worrying is that their offense has been awful. That is, except for Ben Rice. He hit two home runs in Game 2 of the ALDS, the second time he's had a two-homer game this postseason.
According to Sarah Langs, Rice's pair of two-homer games for the Yankees made some never-before-seen MLB history. Not once in postseason history has a player ever had two two-HR games in the first four games of a postseason run, until now.
Ben Rice makes impressive MLB postseason history with a pair of 2-HR games
"Ben Rice is the first player in postseason history with two multi-homer games in his team's first 4 games of a single postseason," Langs shared.
This statistic from Langs is not cherry-picked, nor is it an overly specific stat that's incredibly challenging to accomplish.
Rice hitting two home runs in a single game twice through just four games in the playoffs is something no hitter has ever done before.
He had a two-homer performance against the Boston Red Sox in the series-opening game, which included a grand slam and six total RBIs for Rice in a fantastic way to begin the playoffs.
While he and the Yankees did not win this second instance, Rice still hit two home runs, this time two solo homers, to become the only player ever in postseason history to have two multi-homer games in the first four games of the postseason.
He has a long way to go if he wants to join the legendary postseason performers, but this is a good way to carve his name into MLB history, even though this record-setting feat came in a loss to go one more defeat from elimination.

item.title: [Pinstripe Alley] Yankees At-Bat of the Week: George Lombard Jr. (9/30)
item.dc:creator: Peter Brody
item.description: Welp, the Yankees forgot to bring their bats to Game 1 against the Rays and now they forgot their gloves in Game 2.
