In an attempt to cling on to a positive memory of these playoffs, I present our first At-Bat of the Week of the 2026 postseason, this edition featuring George Lomb
item.content:encoded:
Welp, the Yankees forgot to bring their bats to Game 1 against the Rays and now they forgot their gloves in Game 2. Five errors in the first five innings destroyed any advantage they might have gained from Cam Schlittler starting, their self-immolation eerily reminiscent of the fifth inning collapse in Game 5 of the 2024 World Series. In an attempt to cling on to a positive memory of these playoffs, I present our first At-Bat of the Week of the 2026 postseason, this edition featuring George Lombard Jr. in Game 2 of the AL Wild Card Series against the Red Sox.
We join Lombard with no outs in the sixth inning last Wednesday at Yankee Stadium. The Yankees blew Boston’s doors off in Game 1, 9-0, on the back of Ben Rice’s historic two home run, six-RBI performance. That game was close until the Yankees blew things open in the eighth, and this game is following a similar pattern with Max Fried and Sonny Gray largely holding both offenses in check.
And just like in Game 1, Chad Tracy came out with a quick hook for his starter, which is how we see Garrett Crochet pitching out of the bullpen to open the sixth. Crochet hadn’t thrown an MLB pitch since April, missing most of the season with a left shoulder injury, but made it back just in time to sneak onto the Wild Card roster. Spencer Jones stands on first after reaching on a leadoff strikeout wild pitch, and as we’ll soon see his hustle down the line will prove to be the turning point in the game.
I can almost guarantee that Lombard and everyone else in the stadium is expecting Crochet’s first MLB pitch in over five months to be his overpowering four-seamer. Perhaps Crochet looks to play off this expectation, because he introduces a wrinkle with a first pitch cutter trying to get a hitter sitting four-seamer to chase below the zone.
The intent is sound but the execution isn’t quite there. This pitch starts as a ball low out of Crochet’s hand and never looks like a strike. Lombard isn’t tempted to chase and spits on this cutter for ball one.
After showing Lombard a fastball that breaks glove-side, there is an opportunity for Crochet to steal a called strike inside. His four-seamer breaks in the opposite direction as the cutter, so a pitch that starts a little in off the plate and tails back to the inside edge should freeze the hitter.
It’s clear Crochet’s command is rusty given he misses his target on the opposite side of the plate. He wants to get this four-seamer in under Lombard’s hands but instead lands it low and away, just out of the zone. It still requires an impressively disciplined take from Lombard given it lands mere inches from the outside edge, made doubly difficult considering it immediately follows a cutter that breaks toward the plate from outside to in.
Lombard has worked the count leverage in his favor, 2-0. You’d expect most pitchers to come into the zone with a heater to avoid falling behind, 3-0, especially a pitcher with as blazing a fastball as Crochet’s.
Lombard completely sells out for the four-seamer and is made to look a little bit foolish on this back foot cutter. Make no mistake, this is a filthy pitch from Crochet. It looks like a strike middle-down out of the hand before the late movement zips it down and in under Lombard’s bat.
So far, the cutter appears to be coming out of Crochet’s hand a lot better than the four-seamer. After getting the chase and whiff on the previous one, he doubles up with another back foot cutter.
Crochet is able to pinpoint the bottom rail of the zone with this cutter for called strike two. Lombard is taking all the way to give Jones the opportunity to steal second . It’s a good thing he didn’t swing, because an errant throw to second from Adley Rutschman allows Jones to take the extra base, putting him 90 feet away from scoring an invaluable insurance run. Even if Jones hadn’t been running on the play, I still like this take from Lombard — this pitch had tailor-made groundball written all over it.
In the span of two pitches, Crochet has swung the count leverage in his favor, from 2-0 to 2-2. Having shown Lombard three cutters out of four pitches and with his first chance for a strikeout, Crochet attempts to gas a four-seamer by the Yankees rookie, the pitch coming in seven mph faster and with eleven inches less drop than the cutter.
What a swing by Lombard! This is a nasty heater from Crochet, 98 mph and just off the corner up and away. The situational hitting by Lombard is mature well beyond his 21 years. Living by the old adage of hitting the ball back the way it came, Lombard stays through this outside heater and shoots it to the opposite field for an RBI single. It’s such a simple approach and swing — short and compact to the pitch making sure to stay behind the baseball — the rookie not trying to do anything more than the pitch will allow him to do, knowing that solid contact the other way is almost certain to get the run in.
Here’s the full AB:
Proper credit has to be awarded to Jones as the precursor to this AB. Not giving up on the play when he struck out, the wheels to steal second and then the awareness to see the ball rolling into center and take off for third put Crochet on the ropes, and Lombard’s single opened the floodgates. To get that kind of mature contribution from a pair of your homegrown rookies in the playoffs against your age old rival is such a shot in the arm for the rest of the team. And returning to Lombard, I cannot say enough about how mature his approach was in this AB. It would be easy for any player, especially a 21-year-old rookie in his first postseason, to let the tension and stress creep in after Crochet quickly flipped the count from 2-0 to 2-2. However, he clutched up and came through with one of the finer pieces of situational hitting you are likely to see this postseason, giving his team an indispensable two-run cushion and setting the stage for the fireworks that would follow later in the frame.

item.title: [Empire Sports Media] NY Yankees can't ignore their third-base decision any longer
item.dc:creator: Alexander Wilson
item.description: Aaron Boone considered starting Anthony Volpe at third base before Monday’s game. He kept Ryan McMahon there because he didn’t want to put a player still learning the position on Tropicana Field’s artificial turf. Then the Yankees committed four errors and lost 5-2. I’d revisit that decision before Wednesday’s elimination game. Boone was already weighing the move before the defensive mess, so this goes beyond blaming McMahon for one bad hop. He has a real choice to make at third, and the series
item.content:encoded:
Aaron Boone considered starting Anthony Volpe at third base before Monday’s game. He kept Ryan McMahon there because he didn’t want to put a player still learning the position on Tropicana Field’s artificial turf. Then the Yankees committed four errors and lost 5-2.
I’d revisit that decision before Wednesday’s elimination game. Boone was already weighing the move before the defensive mess, so this goes beyond blaming McMahon for one bad hop. He has a real choice to make at third, and the series is returning to Yankee Stadium.
No change has been announced. Volpe at third is an option Boone has discussed, and my argument is that it deserves another look. It shouldn’t be sold as a guaranteed defensive upgrade when his experience at the position is still limited.
Yankees can’t fix four errors with one substitution
McMahon’s first-inning error started the trouble. Jazz Chisholm Jr.’s errant double-play throw allowed a run, and Austin Wells was charged with catcher’s interference. George Lombard Jr.’s throwing error came in the fifth, when Tampa Bay scored four times.
That distribution matters. Benching the third baseman wouldn’t have prevented a bad throw from second, interference behind the plate or a throwing error at short. The entire infield has to play cleaner, regardless of who gets the next start.
Volpe’s readiness still matters
Boone’s hesitation about Volpe was also reasonable. Third base requires different reactions and throwing angles than shortstop or second. A playoff elimination game is a lousy place to find out a player needs more work there. But Boone’s concern Monday specifically included the turf, and that part of the decision changes in the Bronx.
The move has to improve the lineup
I’d want Boone to choose Volpe because he expects the full lineup to be better, rather than because fans understandably want someone held accountable. McMahon’s error is one piece of the evaluation. Volpe’s readiness at third and the expected offensive matchup have to be part of it, too.
The Yankees are down 0-2, and they have a day to work through the alignment before Game 3. Boone doesn’t need to overhaul every position. He does need to make a fresh decision at third instead of treating Monday’s lineup as the automatic choice.

item.dc:creator: Gary Phillips
item.description: The Yankees’ defense looked abysmal while committing four errors in Game 2 of the ALDS. Their baserunning — or Austin Wells’ baserunning — may have cost them in Game 1. While the Yankees put together a lowlight reel fit for the Benny Hill theme in other facets of the game, that shouldn’t be overlooked with the team on the brink of elimination. “The Rays’ pitchers, like they have all year, they’ve done well these last couple games and executed pitches,” said Ben Rice, who supplied t
item.content:encoded:
The Yankees’ defense looked abysmal while committing four errors in Game 2 of the ALDS. Their baserunning — or Austin Wells’ baserunning — may have cost them in Game 1.
But their _l. While the Yankees put together a lowlight reel fit for the Benny Hill theme in other facets of the game, that shouldn’t be overlooked with the team on the brink of elimination.
“The Rays’ pitchers, like they have all year, they’ve done well these last couple games and executed pitches,” said Ben Rice, who supplied those aforementioned runs with a pair of solo shots in Monday’s 5-2, Game 2 defeat. “We mixed in some good swings here there that we didn’t have much to show for, but we gotta find a way to get runs across.”
One of those good swings that didn’t yield results on Monday came from Cody Bellinger, who ripped a ball 102.9 mph with the bases loaded in the fifth inning. Unfortunately for him and the Yankees, it landed in Jonny DeLuca’s glove on the warning track in center.
While Bellinger hit the ball well, he acknowledged it “ultimately wasn’t good enough.” The same can be said of an entire offense that mustered just one hit in Saturday’s 1-0 loss and four more in Monday’s.
“We’ve got to be able to score some runs and do a better job of preventing than we did tonight,” Aaron Boone said after Game 2.
With the Yankees dominated by longtime nemesis Drew Rasmussen in Game 1, Boone opted for an identical, left-heavy lineup in Game 2 despite stewing on some changes. While the Bombers were able to get Freddy Peralta out after 4.2 innings, Rice was the only one to do damage, and they only drew two walks.
The Yanks were also held to two walks in Game 1, and Rasmussen fanned them 10 times.
Even though the Yankees beat up on Boston’s bullpen in the Wild Card — not Red Sox starters, mind you — it’s not surprising to see them scuffling at the plate with Aaron Judge absent from this lineup and roster due to a calf strain. The pinstripers have struggled in the past when the three-time MVP is hurt, including earlier this season when Judge missed 99 days with a fractured rib.
The Yankees had one of the worst offenses in baseball during that IL stint, ranking last in K% (26.1%); 29th in wRC+ (90) and average (.227); 28th in wOBA (.299); 27th in OPS (.681); and 24th in runs scored (341) from June 2 through Sept. 7
But even without Judge, the Yankees’ offense should be better than this. Rice, recently named a Hank Aaron Award finalist, held up his end of the bargain while batting first on Tuesday, but the Yankees need more from those behind him, especially in the heart of the order.
So far this series, the Yankees’ starting 2-through-7 hitters are 1-for-41.
That’s not going to cut it, even if the club cleans up its play in other parts of the game.
“You just got to take it game by game, at-bat by at-bat, and keep trying to win pitches,” Rice said with Game 3 coming on Wednesday. “When you think about how it’s an uphill battle or whatever, it can seem a little daunting. That’s why we just gotta keep staying focused on the next one.”

item.content:encoded:
- martes 06 de octubre de 2026 - 11:00 AM
Los Yanquis de Nueva York están contra las cuerdas y necesitan reaccionar de inmediato si quieren mantener con vida su camino en los playoffs de las Grandes Ligas.
Nueva York cayó anoche 5-2 ante los Rays de Tampa Bay en el Tropicana Field anoche y quedó abajo 2-0 en la Serie Divisional de la Liga Americana, a punto de ser eliminados.
Ahora, los Yanquis regresan a casa con la obligación de cambiar la historia. El tercer partido de la serie se disputará mañana en el Yankee Stadium, desde las 7:00 de la noche, donde Nueva York buscará aprovechar el respaldo de su afición para iniciar la remontada.
Para este encuentro, los Yanquis enviarán al montículo al zurdo Max Fried, mientras que Tampa Bay contará con el derecho Nick Martínez.
El margen de error es mínimo para los neoyorquinos. Una derrota significa el final de la temporada.
Caballero, con poco juego
El panameño José Caballero volvió a formar parte del equipo durante el segundo encuentro, aunque su participación estuvo limitada a labores defensivas.
Caballero ingresó para jugar la tercera base, en el octavo episodio, pero no tuvo turnos oficiales al bate durante el partido.
El santeño ha sido poco utilizado por los Yanquis en esta ronda, a pesar de su velocidad y defensa.
El Yankee Stadium será ahora el escenario donde Nueva York intentará evitar la eliminación y comenzar una remontada que, hasta el momento, parece cuesta arriba.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees had their ace on the mound for Game 2 of the American League Division Series, but they did not do enough to help him out.
The Yankees made three errors in the first inning, and Schlittler exited after 4 1/3 innings of work. The extra pitches caught up to him, and he ended up allowing four runs. Only two of the runs were earned, but overall, his defense let him down.
After the game, Schlittler noted that the Yankees have a great defense, and that Monday night did not go their way. He instead said that he did not do his job and the loss starts with him.
"Obviously it starts with me," Schlittler said after the game, per YES Network. "I'll be the first one to say that I didn't do my job."
"Just didn't have my stuff today," he added. "I didn't get great results. Some timely hits there and didn't get through the fifth."
Schlittler was critical of himself, but remained confident that the Yankees could come back and win the series. Aaron Boone, however, was not as critical of Schlittler, noting that the rest of the team did not do enough to help him.
"He battled," Boone said after the game, per MLB.com's Matthew Leach. "Obviously, (he) picked us up kind of all night. It's just hard to do that time after time. Too many free outs out there or free baserunners. So I thought Cam threw the ball well. They did a good job against him of putting pressure on him and putting the ball in play and started to get some really good swings off him there that last time through.
"But Cam did his job. We didn't give him a good enough chance to really do his job."
The manager and the player have differing opinions on whether Schlittler did his part on Monday night, but ultimately the end result is a loss regardless. The Yankees have to get more out of their offense if they want any chance to win. Against a team like the Tampa Bay Rays, defense is even more important as they thrive on putting the ball in play.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are a loss away from watching their season end. The Tampa Bay Rays hold a 2-0 lead in the American League Division Series after back-to-back wins at Tropicana Field. Drew Rasmussen shut them out in Game 1. Four errors helped bury them in Game 2.
The series shifts to Yankee Stadium on Wednesday for Game 3, and the Yankees need a lifeline.
The Yankees May Have a Lifeline
Max Fried will start Game 3 on six days of rest.
The left-hander is 3-1 against Tampa Bay across five starts since signing with New York.
His most recent outing for the Yankees came in the Wild Card round, when he held the Red Sox to one run across six innings in Game 2. That performance came on the same mound he will pitch on Wednesday.
Fried posted a 2.80 ERA across 112 2/3 innings during the regular season while missing time with a left elbow bone bruise. His 104 strikeouts were modest by ace standards, but strikeouts have never been the foundation of what makes him effective.
What the Matchup Looks Like on Paper
The Rays posted the lowest strikeout rate in baseball this season at 18.8 percent. They put the ball in play constantly and create pressure with speed and situational contact.
Opposing hitters barreled just 2.4 percent of the balls they put in play against Fried this season, and his groundball numbers ranked among the best in the league. Tampa Bay's offense also performed worse against left-handed pitching throughout the regular season.
Final Word for the Yankees
The numbers suggest the matchup bodes well for Fried. That does not guarantee anything. The Yankees defense still has to hold up behind him, and the offense still has to score.
Wednesday will tell the rest.

item.title: [Yanks Go Yard] Austin Wells just admitted the Yankees' biggest flaw as scouts swarm to laugh at them
item.dc:creator: Adam Weinrib

Every single one of them seemed to say something like, "Here we go!" or "Clown show" or "How does this keep happening?" Everybody knows it. It's transcended beyond the territory of "open secret". item.content:encoded:
How many times - HOW MANY TIMES - did you scroll past a tweet on Monday night or Tuesday morning that recounted a "scout's text" to a beat writer about the Yankees, sneering and smirking?
Every single one of them seemed to say something like, "Here we go!" or "Clown show" or "How does this keep happening?" Everybody knows it. It's transcended beyond the territory of "open secret". Every scout is perfectly willing to go on record saying that the Yankees cannot handle pressure and are prone to goofs and flubs.
Maybe they know it's become so obvious to the naked eye that they gain nothing from hiding and leaking their takes. Maybe they know that the organization has proven, three-plus years running, that there will be no repercussions, so they're willing to speak freely without fear of costing anyone their job.
Or maybe they know the reckoning actually is coming, so they don't have to worry about protecting Aaron Boone's feelings any longer? Nah. Probably not that. But maybe that! No, definitely not. Oh well.
Baseball is an infuriating little game of inches that runs and ruins our lives. Maybe, just maybe, if Cody Bellinger's absurdly well-struck fly ball with the bases loaded in the fifth had been pulled a little bit instead of mashed to dead center, we'd be talking about how the Yankees overcame their own first-inning malfeasance and became the first-ever MLB team towin a playoff game while committing three or more errors.
Instead, we're talking about how they had a second unraveling left in 'em after getting whatever that was out of their system in the first inning.
And if the 2024 Dodgers barking about it wasn't enough to let the league in on these scouts' little secret, Austin Wells put the cherry on top in Monday's postgame. As Jazz Chisholm Jr. defended his baffling throw, admitting he'd do it again if given the chance, Wells all but revealed that the Rays poked at the Yankees' gaping wound and left them exposed for the entire league to feast on again next year.
“They put pressure on you. They’re fast, they bust their butt out of the box, so they make you feel like you have to do more," Wells told Bob Klapisch. And the Yankees' rebuttal? Still waiting.
The Rays, the Dodgers, the Toronto Blue Jays ... they aren't building teams to beat the Yankees in the same way the Red Sox were, piling on left-handers in an attempt to counteract the Yankees' boppers (update?). They're merely building baseball teams, and the consequence of the Yankees smashing together a bunch of mismatched, all-or-nothing parts is that baseball teams tend to beat them like drums, rather consistently.
If you can pair 97+ MPH with a changeup that tails away from lefties, field your positon, and gameplan offensively to put pressure on an ace, then congratulations. You've left the Yankees in the mud, fumbling for the ball. The Rays, hitting .203 with no pop in this series, haven't even been special yet. They've just pitched to the promise of the premise and outworked the unprepared and undercooked Yanks.
Maybe next year.

New York Yankees designated hitter Ben Rice provided the offense in the Yankees' 5-2 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 2 of the ALDS on Monday. Rice was 2-for-3 with two solo homers and a walk on his night in Tampa. The Yankees were bothered by four errors and the Rays made them pay, but Rice was the lone bright spot for New York. Rice is hitting .467 in the postseason with a .556 on-base percentage. The two homers bring his postseason total to four homers and his RBI total to eight this postseason. Rice has been powering the Yankees offense all postseason long, but the Bronx Bombers find themselves down 2-0 to Tampa Bay in the ALDS. Rice has done his part offensively but needs some help as the Yankees are trying to piece things together without an injured Aaron Judge.--Brian Buckey - RotoBaller

The 33-year-old got the scoring started with a two-run home run in the fourth inning and finished the game with two hits and an additional run scored in four at-bats. Hernandez had an up-and-down regular season in 2026, hitting .267/.334/.425 with 16 home runs, 64 RBI, 66 runs scored, and five stolen bases across 491 plate appearances. The veteran slugger posted a middling .706 OPS across 251 plate appearances before the All-Star break, but he closed the season by hitting .341 with four home runs and 18 RBI across 100 trips to the plate in September. If Hernandez can carry his recent hot streak into the postseason, he could be a major difference-maker for Los Angeles.--Will Brady

The 29-year-old allowed just one earned run on two hits and two walks while striking out seven across six innings of work. Skubal was excellent in the regular season after being acquired by the Dodgers from the Detroit Tigers at this summer's trade deadline, recording a 5-2 record with a 2.61 ERA, 1.05 WHIP, and 70 strikeouts across 62 innings (10 starts). The hard-throwing lefty also has an impressive resume in the postseason, allowing just 10 earned runs while logging 63 strikeouts across 45 2/3 career playoff innings (seven starts). Skubal's next scheduled start will be in Game 5 of the NLDS, if the series goes that far.--Will Brady

Messick will look to shut down a talented White Sox lineup that is very deep and can do damage from all thirds of the lineup. Messick will take the ball as the Guardians' ace and face an opener in Hagen Smith. The Guardians will hope to get some length from Messick to set up what is a good bullpen backed by quality closer in Cade Smith. item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Rays Neutralize Cam Schlittler, Yankees To Take 2-0 ALDS Lead
item.dc:creator: Kenneth Teape; Unknown
item.description: The Tampa Bay Rays knew they had a tall task ahead of them if they wanted to take a 2-0 lead in their ALDS matchup with the New York Yankees. item.content:encoded:
The Tampa Bay Rays knew they had a tall task ahead of them if they wanted to take a 2-0 lead in their ALDS matchup with the New York Yankees.
They would have to defeat Cam Schlittler, the favorite to win the American League Cy Young Award this season. He has dominated opponents all season long, leading the AL with a 1.95 ERA in the regular season across 193.2 innings pitched with 239 strikeouts.
In his Wild Card Round start against the Boston Red Sox, Schlittler threw 6.1 shutout innings with 10 strikeouts, allowing only two hits and one walk. He was rolling into Game 2 against the Rays, but it was Tampa Bay that was able to come out ahead.
The Rays won the game 5-2 to take a commanding 2-0 lead in the series, in large part because they neutralized the strengths of Schlittler and the Yankees. The emerging ace threw 76 pitches through 4.1 innings of work, with Tampa Bay consistently putting pressure on him and the New York defense.
Rays brand of baseball flummoxes Yankees again
He gave up six hits and issued one walk, resulting in four runs being scored against him, only two of which were earned. There have been only eight occasions in 35 starts in 2026, including the playoffs, that Schlittler has given up at least six hits; two of those times, it has been the Rays who have done it.
The other impressive feat that Tampa Bay accomplished was avoiding strikeouts. They are the best team in baseball when it comes to making contact and putting the ball in play. That skill was on full display in Game 2, with Schlittler recording only two strikeouts, the least he has had in a start this season.
Constantly putting the ball in play meant the Yankees’ defense had to step up and make plays, and it failed to do so. They committed four errors in the game, which matches the number of hits they had.
At one point that error count was up to five, but a misplay by shortstop George Lombard in the deciding bottom of the fourth inning, when he didn’t field a Chandler Simpson ground ball cleanly, was changed. He would record a real error later in the inning on an errant throw.
Richie Palacios made them pay with a two-RBI single to extend the lead to 5-1, taking full advantage of the New York miscues.
Playing clean, high-IQ and fundamental baseball is key to finding success in October, with so many high-pressure situations. It is something the Rays thrive in, amping things up to 10 against a Yankees team that crumbled once again with an ugly brand of baseball.
Tampa Bay is now one victory away from clinching a spot in the ALCS.
Kenneth Teape is an alumnus of SUNY Old Westbury and graduated in 2013 with an Honors Degree in Media Communications with a focus on print journalism. During his time at Old Westbury, he worked for the school newspaper and several online publications, such as Knicks Now, the official website of the New York Knicks, and a self-made website with fellow students, Gotham City Sports News. Kenneth has also been a site expert at Empire Writes Back, Musket Fire, and Lake Show Life within the FanSided Network. He was a contributor to HoopsHabit, with work featured on Bleacher Report and Yardbarker. Previously, he is a reporter for both NBA Analysis Network and NFL Analysis Network, as well as a writer and editor for Packers Coverage. You can follow him on X, formerly Twitter, @teapester725, or reach him via email at teapester725@gmail.com.

item.title: [Boston.com] Rays announcer, fans trolled Cam Schlittler after comments about Tropicana Field
item.dc:creator: Hayden Bird

item.content:encoded:
Add Boston.com as your preferred source on Google to see more of our stories.
Cam Schlittler is once again the focus of another fanbase: Walpole native Cam Schlittler, a Cy Young Award contender and recent annihilator of the Red Sox (for the second year in a row), enjoys being the opposing fanbase’s focus.
As MLB Network’s Lauren Shehadi noted prior to Monday’s Game 2 of the American League Division Series, the 25-year-old Yankees right-hander “wants all the smoke.”
“He watches the video clippings of the doubters and the haters, and he uses it for fuel,” Shehadi added. “He grew up in the Boston area watching No. 45, Pedro Martinez, who was the ultimate competitor.”
And having drawn the ire of Red Sox fans in the previous postseason round (before dominating Boston in his Wild Card Series win), Schlittler went above and beyond to earn the scorn of Rays fans as well.
While answering a question about the prospect of pitching on the road, Schlittler eventually offered some commentary on the Rays’ home setup at Tropicana Field.
“I wouldn’t say there’s really too much of a [home] crowd here,” Schlittler said on Saturday. “I expect there to be a lot of Yankees fans here. In some ways, you’re playing at home. The guys are excited to have that atmosphere here.”
By the numbers, Schlittler is correct that Tampa Bay ranks below most MLB teams. The Rays averaged 17,468 fans per game, according to figures via ESPN. That ranks 28th out of 30 teams.
Still, this was obviously not going to be well received from Rays fans.
On Monday, Schlittler was not as dominant as he had been in the previous series against the Red Sox, but was also hurt by poor Yankees defense. New York made four errors, with two of Schlittler’s four allowed runs being unearned in the eventual 5-2 defeat.
The crowd, which was a sellout of more than 40,000 for the second straight game, also played a conspicuous role. Any questions about whether the majority of fans were rooting for the home team were dispelled in the first inning when Schlittler had to pause because he couldn’t hear his PitchCom communication system.
He was pulled after just 4.1 innings (76 pitches in total).
And as he exited the mound, Schlittler was predictably greeted with jeers. Rays radio announcer Andy Freed also referenced the New York pitcher’s pre-series comments.
“I’m guessing this crowd is a little bit more pro-Ray than he expected.”
After the game, Schlittler took the blame for the loss, but added that he didn’t think his teammates were ready either.
“It starts with me,” he said of the defeat, dropping the Yankees to the brink of elimination in a best-of-five series. “I’d be the first one to say that I didn’t do my job. It didn’t seem like we really showed up today. That’s what happens. They played really good baseball and took advantage of those opportunities.”
Schlittler, who grew up in Walpole and pitched for Northeastern, went 14-6 with a 1.95 ERA in the regular season. He remains the odds-on favorite to win the 2026 American League Cy Young Award.
Trivia: According to Opta Stats, the Yankees had more players commit an error (four) in Monday’s Game 2 of the ALDS than get hits (three). The last team to do this in the postseason was the Reds in 2010 as they were getting no-hit in a loss. What pitcher no-hit them?
(Answer at the bottom).
Hint: He pitched 12 years for an American League East team before being traded to a National League East team (where he eventually faced the Reds in the playoffs). He’s in the Hall of Fame.
More from Boston.com:
The Patriots’ locker room: Take another satisfying spin through some Patriots’ postgame content following the dramatic win in Buffalo.
Pedro Martinez vs. Jose Alvarado: In a segment via Bleacher Report, the former Red Sox ace took the mound once again.
On this day: In 1996, the Patriots moved to 3-2 on the season after defeating the Ravens 46-38 in an entertaining matchup. Drew Bledsoe threw for four touchdowns, while Tedy Bruschi notched two sacks and returned a blocked punt for a touchdown.
Also, a 20-year-old golfer named Tiger Woods notched his first PGA Tour win at the Las Vegas Invitational.
Daily highlight: Though it came late in Monday’s game (with the score beyond doubt), this was still an absolutely sensational touchdown catch from Saints wide receiver Devaughn Vele.
Trivia answer: Roy Halladay

item.title: [Empire Sports Media] Ben Rice's historic October is being wasted by the Yankees
item.dc:creator: Alexander Wilson
item.description: Ben Rice hit two home runs Monday and still walked out of Tropicana Field with the Yankees one loss from elimination. Both were solo shots. Those were New York’s only runs in a 5-2 defeat that put Tampa Bay ahead 2-0 in the ALDS. I don’t know what more the Yankees can reasonably ask of him. item.content:encoded:
Ben Rice hit two home runs Monday and still walked out of Tropicana Field with the Yankees one loss from elimination. Both were solo shots. Those were New York’s only runs in a 5-2 defeat that put Tampa Bay ahead 2-0 in the ALDS.
I don’t know what more the Yankees can reasonably ask of him. Rice is delivering the kind of postseason that should carry a team through a series, and they’re wasting it. He can hit a ball out, but he can’t put somebody on base in front of himself.
The frustration shouldn’t obscure how good Rice has been. He became the first Yankee with two multihomer games in a single postseason. He also became the first player in MLB history to do that within his team’s first four games of an October run.
Yankees have a middle-of-the-order bat hitting first
Rice has seven hits in 15 postseason at-bats, four homers and eight RBIs. That’s a .467 average in a small sample, with plenty of damage behind it. His two-homer Wild Card opener against Boston now has a matching performance against Tampa Bay.
He led off Monday as the designated hitter. Keeping your hottest hitter at the top gets him more plate appearances, and I understand that choice. The drawback becomes obvious when the rest of the order produces so little: a home run can tie the game or cut into a deficit without changing the inning much.
I’m not arguing for a lineup shuffle just to look busy. Rice is getting good swings and the Yankees should protect that. The hitters behind him have to turn those swings into the beginning of a rally rather than the entire rally.
Two different pitchers, the same mistake
Both of Rice’s homers came on changeups, one from Freddy Peralta and the other from left-hander Ian Seymour. He punished the pitch against pitchers throwing with different hands, which makes it harder to dismiss the night as one favorable matchup.
For me, Rice’s performance is the reason to keep believing this lineup can do something Wednesday. He’s already shown he can produce against the pitching Tampa Bay is using in October. The Yankees need somebody else to have a productive night, because another two solo homers won’t automatically buy them a Game 4.
More about:New York Yankees

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Yankees’ George Lombard Jr. Addresses Costly Decision in Game 2 Loss to Rays
item.dc:creator: Keith Watkins
item.description: The New York Yankees were tied 1-1 with the Tampa Bay Rays heading into the bottom of the fifth inning of ALDS Game 2 on Monday night. Ben Rice had just tied the game with a solo homer in the fourth. Cam Schlittler was grinding through a tough outing but keeping the Yankees within striking distance. Then the fifth inning started. Tampa Bay scored four runs on the way to winning 5-2, and took a commanding 2-0 lead. Game 3 is set for Wednesday at Yankee Stadium. Lombard on the Fifth Inning With ru
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees were tied 1-1 with the Tampa Bay Rays heading into the bottom of the fifth inning of ALDS Game 2 on Monday night. Ben Rice had just tied the game with a solo homer in the fourth. Cam Schlittler was grinding through a tough outing but keeping the Yankees within striking distance.
Then the fifth inning started. Tampa Bay scored four runs on the way to winning 5-2, and took a commanding 2-0 lead. Game 3 is set for Wednesday at Yankee Stadium.
Lombard on the Fifth Inning
With runners on second and third, Chandler Simpson bounced a ground ball toward the left side. George Lombard Jr. tried to backhand the ball and throw home. He never got a clean grip on it. The ball got past him, and the runner scored to make it 3-1.
When asked afterward whether he had a play at the plate if he fielded the grounder cleanly, the rookie was honest about his assessment.
"I'm not sure," Lombard said. "It might have been one that I should have just gone to first…but yeah it was a tight one, I have to watch it back and see if I show something different."
The error extended the inning and opened the door for everything that followed.
The Play Changed the Course of the Game
Before Lombard's error, the Yankees were in a one-run game with their best pitcher still on the mound. After it, the situation spiraled. Schlittler was pulled soon after. Richie Palacios then drove both runners home with a line drive to center that blew the game open at 5-1.
Tampa Bay's bullpen locked things down from there, with three relievers combining to allow just one run over the final four innings.
Lombard also reflected on the challenge of playing on the Tropicana Field turf, calling it different from dirt infields while noting the team had practiced on it beforehand. He acknowledged both sides contributed to the outcome, crediting the Rays for being a team that does not let up.
Final Word for the Yankees
Lombard is a rookie playing in his first postseason. The turf was fast, and a split-second decision went the wrong way. That is part of growing up in October.
The Yankees need Lombard on Wednesday. How he responds will say more than what happened Monday.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Yankees' George Lombard Jr. Addresses Costly Decision in Game 2 Loss to Rays appeared first on HEAVY.

item.title: [pinstripealley.com] Yankees’ season ends after their offense stays dormant against Blue Jays
item.dc:creator: Michael Zeno
item.description: I hate Tropicana Field. I know many of you do too. If you are not a Yankees fan and are doing what I am also guilty of doing—reading the reactions of salty fans after playoff losses—grab your popcorn. item.content:encoded:
I hate Tropicana Field. I know many of you do too. If you are not a Yankees fan and are doing what I am also guilty of doing—reading the reactions of salty fans after playoff losses—grab your popcorn. This is the good stuff you’re probably looking for.
It blows my mind that baseball games in 2026 are played at places like this. It honestly blows my mind even more that this place was destroyed by an act of God two years ago, was rebuilt despite plans to replace it in the near future, and is being used for big playoff games. The roof is baseball-colored; there is statistical proof that teams other than the Rays struggle defensively here due to a lack of experience; the turf leads to weird hops that cause more errors to be committed against Tampa Bay than any other team in baseball. It’s the strangest home-field advantage in baseball, and one that the Rays ran roughshod over to take advantage of a Yankees team that was just not focused from the jump tonight—and one that, to be clear, absolutely deserved this atrocious loss, even if it was played in the baseball version of Elysian Fields.
Alright, enough of my anger-filled soapbox. The Yanks set the tone for this one with three brutal first-inning errors, played shoddy defense the rest of the night, and just got Rays’d. Any opportunity they had to use their speed or slap hitting, they used it. The Yankees were not prepared. Aside from two home runs from Ben Rice and an oh-so-close deep fly out from Cody Bellinger with the bases juiced, the offense was dead again in a 5-2 loss that puts the season on the brink.
When you get no-hit for nearly eight innings the game before, you desperately want to get the monkey off your back early the next night. The quality of contact was good in that first inning against Freddy Peralta, with a warning-track fly out from Rice and a scorched Bellinger lineout, but the Yankees went quietly in the first before the utter chaos of the bottom half.
On just Cam Schlittler’s second pitch of the game, Yandy Díaz hit a soft Trop chopper to Ryan McMahon, which he promptly booted after misreading the hop. Jonathan Aranda then lined a single up the middle for the one real hit in the inning. Needing a double play, Schlittler got Junior Caminero to spike a ball into the turf that was snared by George Lombard Jr. for a brilliant flip for a forceout. Unfortunately, Jazz Chisholm Jr. decided to throw the ball into the dugout with no chance to turn two, giving the Rays the early lead.
The defensive inning from hell continued when a three-pitch strikeout from Liam Hicks was overturned into a catcher’s interference error on Austin Wells. Awarding a batter a base for a check-swing catcher’s interference is dumb, and I will forever believe that. The speedy Chandler Simpson ripped a ball to second for what looked like a tailor-made double play, but an awful throw from Chisholm pulled Lombard off the bag. The rookie shortstop somehow managed to tap the bag after to avoid a fourth error in the inning, and Cam survived the inning from hell with only one run allowed.
We got more Trop shenanigans when Spencer Jones hit a ball a mile high off the B-ring in center field, which was caught by Victor Mesa Jr. Objectively, almost every other team drops that ball because of their lack of experience reading fly balls here, but the Rays caught it, naturally. Two more quick outs had Peralta rolling through two.
Jonny DeLuca golfed an 0-2 curveball in the dirt for a leadoff double in the second, but was stranded on a trio of groundouts surrounding a two-out walk. The bottom of the order went down quietly as well, giving Peralta a perfect game through three innings just one night after Rasmussen’s brilliance. At this point, I’m not sure the vibes could get much worse.
Schlittler continued to grind through the third, allowing singles to Caminero and Simpson, but got out of a jam after a 108.5 mph scorched grounder from DeLuca was fielded cleanly by Lombard to end the threat. Just one batter later, with the Yankees entering their 13th inning of the series with just one hit, Rice allowed everyone on the team and in the fanbase to breathe for a second, smashing a leadoff home run in the fourth to tie the game at one.
Bellinger followed with a single, but was stranded by the next three hitters. Schlittler responded to the desperate gasp for a shutdown inning, retiring the Rays in order with help from a surprisingly solid play by Trent Grisham in center field. Peralta seemed to be cruising again after retiring the first two in the fifth, but things got interesting after a bullet double by Austin Wells and a gritty walk by Ryan McMahon. The ever-aggressive Kevin Cash pulled him for Cam Booser, betting on his lefty specialist to neutralize the best hitters on the team.
He walked Rice on five pitches to bring up Bellinger with the bases loaded. This was the moment. This was where the Yankees could show who they were. For a brief second, it seemed like they would. The All-Star left fielder absolutely pummeled a bad 0-2 fastball to deep center field. 102.9 mph, 405 feet. In 12 ballparks, it’s a grand slam. In some others, it’s off the wall. Unfortunately, as has happened all too many times in the postseason in the Judge era, the big hit fell just a few inches short, landing harmlessly in the glove of DeLuca.
It’s the type of gut punch that takes the air out of a fan, and maybe it took the air out of the team. It’s not how baseball works, but maybe it is. Schlittler allowed a bullet single (that Jones maybe should’ve caught?) and a bullet double from Caminero to set up second and third with nobody out. Usually, a team’s cleanup and five-hole hitters wouldn’t be conducive to 55 and 65 mph choppers that bounce two feet in front of home plate in RBI opportunities, but these are the Rays. Both runs scored on back-to-back Baltimore chops that the Yankees had no chance of getting an out at the plate on, even if Lombard had defended the latter cleanly. That gave the Rays a 3-1 lead.
The frustration didn’t end there. After Brent Headrick entered and struck out Mesa, we got another Trop chop grounder to Lombard. Due to the bounce the ball took and the speed of DeLuca, he had to rush the throw, which forced a long stretch from Luis García Jr. If the play was made cleanly, DeLuca would’ve been out by an eyelash, which tells you how perfect they had to be, but García couldn’t squeeze the throw, and everyone was safe. Another error. One batter later, Richie Palacios hit a two-run single to effectively ice this one, making it 5-1 Rays.
We then hit a weird point in the game. Ian Seymour came in for the Rays as a lefty bulk reliever, but Aaron Boone elected to keep his righties in the dugout. As a fan who was resigned to the outcome after the Palacios single, it seems like nothing, but damn, that’s pretty rough of your manager to be so apathetic in this spot. The lineup had no pulse against him in some rough matchups.
Playing out the string, John Schreiber tossed a scoreless sixth, Ryan Weathers and Paul Blackburn combined for the seventh, and Blackburn and David Bednar combined for the ninth. For the offense, all they had left was another home run for Rice, who continues to have a postseason to remember while his teammates give him no help, like 2018 LeBron.
Bryan Baker got the save in the ninth, 1-2-3, to solidify Game 2 for the Rays. If the Yankees want to win this series and get to the ALCS, they must win three straight against a team they’ve struggled against all year and win a game at Tropicana Field on Saturday after going 2-7 there to start this season. We’re essentially right back where we were a year ago with the Yankees down 0-2 and leaving Toronto. Bleak, I know.
There will be baseball played on Wednesday. After that, it’s up to the Yankees to decide. Game 3 will be at Yankee Stadium at 8 pm EDT. It’s Max Fried (pending the birth of his child) against a pitcher to be determined, but it will likely be Nick Martinez.

Jonathan Aranda and Junior Caminero each had two hits and a run for the Rays, who are in control of the best-of-five series. Game 3 is Wednesday in New York. The Yankees did themselves no favors by committing four errors, including three in the firs
item.content:encoded:
Richie Palacios ripped a two-run single to highlight a four-run fifth inning, fueling the Tampa Bay Rays to a 5-2 victory over the New York Yankees on Monday in St. Petersburg, Fla., and a two-games-to-none edge in an American League Division Series.
Jonathan Aranda and Junior Caminero each had two hits and a run for the Rays, who are in control of the best-of-five series. Game 3 is Wednesday in New York.
The Yankees did themselves no favors by committing four errors, including three in the first inning.
New York’s lone bright spot was Ben Rice, who hit solo homers in the fourth and eighth innings. He has two multi-homer games in this postseason.
In a 1-1 game, Aranda singled to lead off the fifth inning, advanced to third base on Caminero’s single and scored on Liam Hicks’ slow grounder to second base. Caminero moved to third base on that play and scored on Chandler Simpson’s infield single.
Brent Headrick relieved Cam Schlittler (1-1) and struck out the first batter he faced before an error by shortstop George Lombard Jr. on a ball hit by Jonny DeLuca extended the inning. DeLuca then stole second. Palacios, a New York native, then drove a line-drive single to center field, plating both runners and boosting the Rays’ lead to 5-1.
Schlittler was charged for four runs (two earned) on six hits in 4 1/3 innings. He walked one and struck out two.
Cam Booser (1-0) relieved Rays starter Freddy Peralta and induced Cody Bellinger to fly out with the bases loaded to end the top of the fifth inning.
Ian Seymour struck out four batters while allowing just one hit, Rice’s second homer, in three innings. Bryan Baker tossed a 1-2-3 ninth to notch his second save in as many games of the series.
Sloppy defense by New York led to Tampa Bay opening the scoring in the first inning. Yandy Diaz reached base after third baseman Ryan McMahon failed to handle a routine grounder. Diaz advanced to second on a single by Aranda and scored after a throw by second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. in a bid to complete a double play sailed wide of first base.

item.content:encoded:
Yankees Errors Lead to Game 2 Loss to Rays, Box Score Stats, Highlights, Updated MLB Playoff Bracket
Four errors paved the way for the New York Yankees' Game 2, 5-2 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays on Monday, dropping them to 0-2 in the American League Divisional Series on the road.
With their backs against the wall and down 0-1, the Yankees entered as 1.5-point favorites over the Rays, per FanDuel Sportsbook, with Cam Schlittler starting on the mound.
Schlittler finished the regular season tied for third in MLB with 239 strikeouts, entering the postseason as one of the Yankees' biggest weapons.
He backed it up in his first playoff start, a win over the Boston Red Sox, allowing just two hits while striking out 10. But Monday was a different story, as he surrendered seven hits, managed just two strikeouts and gave up two earned runs.

Tampa Bay struck first, with its first three batters reaching base in the first inning. Yandy Díaz scored on a throwing error by second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. after Junior Caminero grounded into a fielder's choice.
Schlittler and the Yankees escaped the bottom of the first with minimal damage, allowing one run despite a disastrous start that included three errors, stranding two runners at the corners.
The Yankees answered in the bottom of the third when Ben Rice launched a 372-foot solo home run to tie the game at 1-1.
It was a busy fifth inning for the Rays.
With two runners in scoring position, Liam Hicks grounded out to second to bring home Jonathan Aranda. Chandler Simpson followed with an RBI single after another Yankees miscue, giving Tampa Bay a 3-2 lead in the bottom of the fifth and prompting the Yankees to pull Schlittler.
Building on their lead, Richie Palacios ripped a line drive for a two-run double, bringing home Trent Grisham and Simpson to stretch Tampa Bay's lead to 5-1.
Rice capped a big night with his second home run in the top of the eighth, accounting for both of the Yankees' runs. But with one final chance in the ninth and trailing 5-2, New York went down in order to fall to 0-2 in the ALDS.

item.dc:creator: Billy Heyen
item.description: No one had done this against Cam Schlittler before. The Tampa Bay Rays, though, aren’t just any team. They had the American League’s best record in the regular season, finishing with 100 wins. So when faced with the New York Yankees‘ right-handed pitching phenom in Game 2 of the ALDS, they weren’t fazed. And when the Rays knocked Schlittler out of the game, they held a 3-1 lead. item.content:encoded:
No one had done this against Cam Schlittler before.
The Tampa Bay Rays, though, aren’t just any team. They had the American League’s best record in the regular season, finishing with 100 wins. So when faced with the New York Yankees‘ right-handed pitching phenom in Game 2 of the ALDS, they weren’t fazed.
And when the Rays knocked Schlittler out of the game, they held a 3-1 lead.
Tampa Bay had already won Game 1 of the series by a 1-0 score in a one-hitter that featured the Yankees’ only hit being thrown out at third base before he could even stand there for a pitch.
Schlittler was the Yankees’ best chance to turn that around, but the Rays wouldn’t let him do it.
Rays Do Something Different
The one thing Schlittler almost always does, no matter how many outs he gets or how many runs he allows, is strike batters out.
The Rays hardly struck out at all on Monday night.
They finished with just two strikeouts against Schlittler, the lowest total he has ever allowed:
Tampa Bay Rays hitters had the lowest strikeout rate in MLB this year. And against Cam Schlittler, who’s winning the American League Cy Young, they punched out just two times — the lowest total in any of Schlittler’s 35 starts this season. Schlittler is done. Yankees trail, 3-1.
— Jeff Passan (@JeffPassan) October 6, 2026
As Passan suggests, it’s not a total surprise that the Rays did this. But having that few of strikeouts against Schlittler is unheard of.
Schlittler had struck out 10 batters in his last start, during a 6.1-inning outing against the Red Sox in the Wild Card Series.
His last outing of the regular season was just 3.0 innings against the Rays as the Yankees held up his pitch count at 70 pitches, and even in that outing, Schlittler had five Ks.
What happened on Monday night was different.
Cam Schlittler Stats
Schlittler went 4.1 innings. That means he got 13 outs.
Only two of them were strikeouts.
He also allowed seven hits and a walk, and he had four runs charged against him. Two of them were earned.
In a season when Schlittler has essentially had no bad outings, this was about as poor as it gets for him.
The Rays cashed in against reliable lefty reliever Brent Headrick when Schlittler left, too, and he was charged with a run, as well.
Tampa Bay had a 5-1 lead after five innings. That’s not something anyone saw coming when matched up with Schlittler. No one would’ve seen these two strikeouts coming, either. Schlittler always gets more, until now.

item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. (AP) — Sloppy defense cost the Yankees a first-inning run in Game 2 of their AL Division Series against the Rays on Monday night.
New York made three errors in the inning and nearly a fourth, but ace right-hander Cam Schlittler held Tampa Bay to one run.
Third baseman Ryan McMahon misplayed a bouncer by Yandy Díaz to begin the bottom of the first. After Jonathan Aranda singled, Junior Caminero hit a bouncer up the middle. Rookie shortstop George Lombard Jr. fielded the ball behind the bag and flipped to second for a forceout, but Jazz Chisholm Jr.’s ill-advised, off-balance throw to first sailed wide, allowing Díaz to score and Caminero to reach second.
Liam Hicks then struck out but reached on catcher’s interference, with an error charged to Austin Wells. The 21-year-old Lombard then saved Chisholm from another error when he extended to catch a high toss to second following a sharp grounder by Chandler Simpson. Lombard came off the bag and quickly reached back with his leg to beat Hicks and get the second out.
Schlittler, the favorite to win the AL Cy Young Award, retired Victor Mesa Jr. on a grounder to prevent more damage.
New York became the first team to commit three errors in the first inning of a playoff game since the Oakland Athletics in Game 1 of the 1975 American League Championship Series against Boston, according to Sportsnet Stats.
The Yankees infamously unraveled on defense in the fifth inning of Game 5 of the 2024 World Series against the Los Angeles Dodgers. Leading 5-0 with Gerrit Cole on the mound, New York committed two errors and a mental lapse while allowing five unearned runs to score, and the Dodgers went on to win the game and clinch the championship.
The Rays held a 1-0 lead in this best-of-five series.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. (AP) — Yankees rookie Spencer Jones hit a towering flyball off a catwalk at quirky Tropicana Field that was caught by Rays right fielder Victor Mesa Jr. for an out in the second inning of Game 2 in their AL Division Series on Monday night.
Jones kept running around the bases as the ball rattled around and fell to Mesa, who ran over to make the catch in center. Center fielder Jonny DeLuca thought he was camped under it but started pointing upward when the ball hit one of the two rings high above the field and below the roof. Mesa caught it several feet in front of DeLuca.
Umpires conferred and confirmed the out, per the stadium’s ground rules.
It was the second time a roof impacted play in this postseason.
In the ninth inning of Milwaukee’s 3-2 win over the Padres in Game 1 of their NL Division Series on Saturday night, San Diego’s Ty France hit a high drive that appeared as though it might be headed over the left-field wall for a go-ahead homer until it struck a cable on the retractable roof of American Family Field in Milwaukee.
The ball then fell into the glove of Brewers left fielder Jackson Chourio on the warning track to retire the hitter.

item.title: [Yahoo] Yankees put Cam Schlittler in early hole with 3 first-inning errors in ALDS Game 2 vs. Rays

With presumptive AL Cy Young winner Cam Schlittler on the mound, New York's defense bungled the first inning with three errors that allowed the Rays to take a 1-0 lead. In the first at-bat of the game, Schlittler induced a ground ball from Yandy Díaz that should have been a routine out. But the ball bounced off Ryan
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees were fortunate to come away from the first inning Monday having allowed only one run in Game 2 of the American League Division Series against the Tampa Bay Rays.
With presumptive AL Cy Young winner Cam Schlittler on the mound, New York's defense bungled the first inning with three errors that allowed the Rays to take a 1-0 lead.
In the first at-bat of the game, Schlittler induced a ground ball from Yandy Díaz that should have been a routine out. But the ball bounced off Ryan McMahon's glove, allowing Díaz to reach safely.
Díaz reached second on a single by Jonathan Aranda, then scored on New York's second error of the frame.
On a ground ball from Junior Caminero, Jazz Chisholm Jr. misfired on a throw to first base that could have completed a double play. Chisholm successfully got the out at second on a nice fielding play by George Lombard Jr. But his relay throw to first was well off target and bounced off the face of the Tampa Bay dugout.
That allowed Díaz to score without a play at the plate and Caminero to advance to second.
On the very next at-bat, the Yankees committed a third error, this time on catcher's interference by Austin Wells that negated a strikeout.
Liam Hicks swung and missed at a 1-2 fastball for strike three. But the Rays challenged, and replay revealed that Wells' glove made clear contact with Hicks' bat as Hicks swung.
Slow-motion replay revealed that the contact was made after the ball was in Wells' glove. Hicks was late with his swing and didn't stand a chance to make contact. But the catcher's interference ruling awarded first base to Hicks.
That put runners on first and second with one out in a situation that could have quickly unraveled for Schlittler and the Yankees.
But Schlittler's the Cy Young favorite for a reason. He induced two ground balls to get out of the inning with no further damage, and Tampa Bay's lead was limited to one run.
That said, the Yankees' mistakes cost them more than that run. Schlittler was forced to throw 19 first-inning pitches amid the chaos in a frame that could shorten his outing as the Yankees seek to avoid a 2-0 series hole.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees must decide whether to extend Jazz Chisholm Jr. a $23.1 million qualifying offer, a raise of about 126% over his $10.2 million salary, according to Spotrac‘s contract page for Chisholm.
The qualifying offer number is not yet official. MLB and the Players Association have not formally announced it, but a source told the New York Post it will climb from $22.03 million last winter to roughly $23.1 million, according to the Post‘s Joel Sherman. Teams have five days after the World Series ends to extend the qualifying offers to eligible players entering free agency.
Chisholm is a pending free agent after the one-year deal he signed Jan. 8 to avoid arbitration. The Yankees must now decide whether to make the offer available to Chisholm.
If a team extends a qualifying offer to a pending free agent who then rejects it, the team receives a compensatory draft pick if the player signs elsewhere. That makes players more difficult to sign, because the signing team loses a draft pick.
But if the player accepts the qualifying offer, the team is stuck paying him a one-year salary it may not feel the player is worth. Either way, the qualifying offer represents a gamble for both player and club.
Yankees Weigh Jazz Chisholm Jr. Qualifying Offer
Chisholm slashed .231/.312/.399 with 19 home runs, 55 RBIs and 41 stolen bases in the regular season, according to Baseball-Reference‘s player page. Those are his lowest average, slugging percentage and OPS in a full season. A right thumb sprain put him on the injured list from Sept. 9 to Sept. 22, and his 1.7 bWAR trails the 4.1 he posted in 2025, when he hit 31 homers and won a Silver Slugger.
Chisholm struck out in 29.5% of his plate appearances, according to Baseball-Reference. Heyman wrote that he was benched in Game 1 for Anthony Volpe.
MLB insider Jon Heyman doesn’t see the qualifying offer as a given for Chisholm. His down year and Chisholm’s wild-card series Game 1 benching against Red Sox left-hander Payton Tolle mean the roughly $23 million bid is no longer a lock, Heyman wrote.
Others see the Chisholm decision differently.
“A team with the Yankees’ resources should absolutely extend him the qualifying offer,” The Athletic‘s Tim Britton opined.
MLB Trade Rumors calls Chisholm a qualifying-offer candidate, but not a sure receive-and-reject case like Pittsburgh’s Brandon Lowe. Most expert opinion points toward an offer going out to the second baseman.
Jazz Chisholm Jr. Free Agent Value Estimate
Would Chisholm make more than $23.1 million next year in free agency? Britton projects multi-year interest, probably four years at $20 million to $25 million per season. He cited Trevor Story’s six-year, $140 million contract as a comparable.
Chisholm has said he believes he would command $35 million a year for seven or eight years, Heyman reported, and he aimed to become the second 50-homer, 50-steal player.
That didn’t happen. Talk of a $300 million deal is gone, but a contract comfortably above $100 million remains possible, especially if Chisholm’s October goes well, according to MLB.com‘s Mark Feinsand. But his career postseason line entering this round was .170 with a .543 OPS in 24 games.
Chisholm has said he wants to remain a Yankee. He has also asked what happens to qualifying-offer money if he accepts and a lockout wipes out the season, according to Pinstripes Nation. He added that the club told him it generally does not do extensions. The MLB Basic Agreement expires Dec. 1, 2026.

The 25-year-old righty will be making his second career ALDS start and will look
item.content:encoded:
Aaron Boone is sure Cam Schlittler is built for moments like getting the start against the Rays in the ALDS.
During his conversation with the media ahead of Game 2 on Monday, the Yankees’ skipper responded to comments about Schlittler’s confidence when the lights are brightest. The Division Series was a bit bumpier for him in 2025 than the Wild Card Series showdown with Boston, so he’ll look to put that behind him. The 25-year-old righty will be making his second career ALDS start and will look to continue his current postseason hot streak as New York faces Tampa Bay.
“You never know a result is going to be in a given game, but he’s certainly equipped to handle it,” Boone stated. “He’s got a ton of confidence and is fearless in these spots.”
During his previous postseason outing, Schlittler barred the Red Sox offense from gaining an edge in Game 1 of the Wild Card Series, throwing six and a third scoreless innings and racking up 10 strikeouts. It’s no surprise that he showed up and shelled out, following the discourse behind his rivalry with New England fans and media outlets.
The Yankees will have the opportunity to head back to the Bronx, with hopes of a split series, and have Max Fried take the mound for the Game 3 start against Tampa Bay. Boone also announced that Carlos Rodón would get the nod in a possible Game 4 at Yankee Stadium, which New York would very much like to force tonight rather than waiting until Wednesday.
You won’t want to miss a second of Schlittler’s outing as the Yankees face off against the Rays in Game 2 of the Division Series Monday at 8 p.m. EST.

The Yanks could re-sign Chisholm, but they might have needs elsewhere to focus on. If Chisholm ends up elsewhere, they’ll need a replacement. Turns out, that replacement might already be in a Yankees uniform. He’s just playing a different position. Yankees Potential Jazz Chisholm Jr. Replacement The Yankees seem to be considering the idea of Luis Garcia Jr. moving to a dif
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees could need a new second baseman in the 2027 MLB season. Jazz Chisholm Jr. is slated to be a free agent.
The Yanks could re-sign Chisholm, but they might have needs elsewhere to focus on. If Chisholm ends up elsewhere, they’ll need a replacement.
Turns out, that replacement might already be in a Yankees uniform. He’s just playing a different position.
Yankees Potential Jazz Chisholm Jr. Replacement
The Yankees seem to be considering the idea of Luis Garcia Jr. moving to a different infield position in 2027.
Garcia is currently playing first base for the Yankees.
Boone, in pregame comments before ALDS Game 2, had this to say about Garcia:
Interesting. Boone said this about Luis García Jr.:
“Obviously an infielder in his past, and feel like that could even be in play, you know, moving forward in coming years.”
Maybeee the Yankees would look at García at second base next season?
— Brendan Kuty 🧟♂️ (@BrendanKutyNJ) October 5, 2026
Garcia isn’t regarded as a great second baseman, and the Washington Nationals had already moved him off that position before the Yankees traded for him this summer.
Still, having that versatility could give the Yanks a way to move things around.
Second base isn’t a crucial defensive spot, and as long as Garcia’s bat keeps up the good work, he’d be just fine as a replacement for Chisholm there.
Another Option for Luis Garcia Jr.
Given the way Boone said it, maybe the Yankees would also consider him at a different spot: third base.
He doesn’t have the same level of experience there, but it would be another option for New York, which might want to move on from Ryan McMahon at that spot after this season.
It would be more of a risk to go into the 2027 season simply planning on Garcia playing third. There’d be no guarantee of it working. But it would be another choice.
How This Helps Yankees
Moving Garcia off first base would have a helpful trickle-down effect.
Ben Rice has been the DH with Garcia at first, but if Garcia moves elsewhere in the infield, Rice could then go to first base again.
That would open up the DH spot, whether the Yankees want to use it for Giancarlo Stanton or for one of their assortment of outfielders.
It would also create flexibility to add a bat this offseason without having so many players locked into different spots.
The Yankees have been linked to Brandon Lowe as a direct replacement at second base for Chisholm, but this would be an alternate option.

item.content:encoded:
Mason Miller's two year run of dominance has entranced the baseball world at large. New York Yankees fans aren't immune, fantasizing for a moment about what it would take to get him in pinstripes when it looked like the San Diego Padres were going to be sellers at the trade deadline.
Miller struck out 47.4% of hitters he faced this season en route to a 1.67 ERA and 1.17 FIP over 70 games and posted 38 saves. It was easy to be fascinated by how he carved up lineups with his 101 miles per hour heat and wipeout slider. However, some have gotten carried away and forgotten what the gold standard is for dominance at the closer position.
In Game 2 of the NLDS, we were all reminded that Miller is, in fact, human. Already down 1-0 in the series, the Padres decided to go to Miller for a two-inning save. After a three-up, three-down bottom of the eighth, things got dicey for San Diego's flamethrower in the bottom of the ninth.
Miller lost control of the strike zone and, with two outs in the frame, walked old friend Gary Sánchez to bring Jackson Chourio to the plate with the bases loaded and San Diego clinging to a 3-2 lead. The Brewers phenom turned a 101 MPH four-seamer into a single to center, plating both the tying and winning runs in dramatic walk-off fashion.
The exhilarating comeback made one thing clear. For as scary as Miller can be, he's got a long way to go to catch the greatest of all time and isn't close to Mariano Rivera in pressure-packed playoff situations. The meltdown reminded folks just how great Mo truly was.
As good as Yankees legend Mariano Rivera was in the regular season, he was even better in the playoffs
Rivera is MLB's all-time saves leader with a seemingly unbreakable 652. Trevor Hoffman comes in at second place with 601, and no one else in history has even reached the 500-save plateau, though Kenley Jansen is the active leader with 498. Miller is already 28 and, with just 88 career saves, likely never comes close to touching Mo.
Rivera, of course, wasn't just a compiler. He was a force to be reckoned with in the regular season, with a 2.21 career ERA over 1,283 2/3 innings and 1,173 strikeouts to his name. As amazing as all of that is, it pales in comparison to his October resume.
In the postseason, Rivera logged a mind-boggling 141 innings and allowed just 11 earned runs. That's good for a ridiculous 0.70 ERA. To put that into context, my favorite baseball stat of all time is the fact that more men (12) have walked on the moon than scored on Mariano Rivera in the playoffs. Let that sink in for a moment.
NBA personality and host of the Game Theory Podcast Sam Vecenie posted his amazement at Rivera's October achievements on Twitter/X, writing, "Watching the best closers in baseball semi-regularly get hammered in the playoffs -- even as closer stuff continues to get even more unhittable -- puts Mariano Rivera posting a 0.70 ERA in 141 postseason innings in an even more impossibly impressive light to me."
While the Rivera discourse was raging through social media, there were a handful of trolls who tried to poke holes in Rivera's impeccable postseason resume. One common, and incorrect, refrain was that Rivera didn't get called upon for two-inning saves that often. Quite the opposite, actually.
The Hammer of God was called upon for 31 saves of at least four outs, which included 14 saves of at least six outs. Rivera had 45 save opportunities in the playoffs and converted 42 of them, meaning the 14 times he went two innings represent 33% of his total postseason saves.
That's just the saves, too. Rivera made 96 total postseason appearances, so he wasn't always just reserved for save opportunities. In fact, one of his most iconic playoff performances was one where he was credited with the win. In what was one of the greatest Game 7s of all time, Mo entered the deciding matchup of the 2003 ALCS and threw three scoreless innings to set up Aaron Boone's series-clinching homer off of Tim Wakefield to vanquish the Red Sox.
The fact of the matter is, most of Rivera's regular-season saves were of the one-inning variety, but he could turn it on in the playoffs whenever it was needed. It should also be noted that Rivera did what he did at the peak of the steroid era, making his accomplishments even that much more impressive.
The last thing the haters will bring up is the 2001 World Series. Just remember, if the infield were playing at normal depth, that looper off of Luis Gonzalez's bat likely would have landed in Derek Jeter's glove. Luck just didn't happen to be on Mo's side.
But more importantly, Miller's failure reminded everyone of Mo's greatness. We likely won't ever see such a singular talent again, so it's always nice to see him get the love he deserves.

item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG – The Yankees will have to decide if they want to risk paying David Bednar and Jazz Chisholm Jr. $23.1 million next season, The Post has learned.
MLB and the Players Association have yet to officially agree on what the qualifying offer will be for this coming offseason, but a source told The Post it will rise from the $22.03 million of last season to just about $23.1 million.
The qualifying offer is calculated based on the mean salary of the 125 highest players in MLB. It can be offered to a free agent one time in their careers (so Bo Bichette had it put on him last offseason by the Blue Jays, so can’t this offseason if he opts out of his deal with the Mets).
Teams have until five days after the World Series ends to extend the qualifying offer, and players then have 10 days to accept or decline. A player who accepts, like Trent Grisham last year for the Yankees, is signed and no longer a free agent. A player who rejects becomes a free agent. Teams with players who reject receive draft pick compensation and those that sign such a player forfeit picks depending upon their luxury tax and revenue-sharing status.

item.title: [Yanks Go Yard] Aaron Boone's Yankees vs. Rays Game 2 lineup proves he's either confident or stubborn

item.content:encoded:
Aaron Boone's in a true no-win situation. He's had a largely effective year, transitioning the Yankees through injury after injury to collect 93 wins (better than most best-case projections). He defeated - no, destroyed - the Boston Red Sox in the AL Wild Card Series. But after being shut down in Game 1 by Drew Rasmussen of the Tampa Bay Rays, the boo birds are back anyway - and they won't be changing their tune unless things flip on a dime.
One specific area where Boone will never be able to win his haters over is lineup construction. For years, certainly folks have dug their heels in that if only Boone could keep his lineup consistent, his Yankees would finally be able to get in an offensive rhythm. Now, after Boone's announcement of his Game 2 lineup ahead of Yankees-Rays, the same people are almost certainly yelling, "No, not consistent like THAT, you clown!" blaming Boone for allowing the Rays' righty starter to get in a comfortable lane with the same eight lefty batters.
Yup, you heard that right. It's the same starting nine from Game 2 against Boston (massive blowout win) and Game 1 against the Rays (depressing, dispiriting loss). What's on the horizon for Boone's Yankees? Dunno. Probably one of the two.
Remember when Heliot Ramos was going to be huge for the Yankees with Aaron Judge out? Anyway...
It's on Yankees players to step up and learn changeup recognition in Game 2 vs. Rays
There's something to be said for a little bit of variance. If I made the lineups - I don't, but... - I would've started Jose Caballero, who is on record as wanting to make the Rays "suffer," and benched Trent Grisham. Seven lefties, two righties. Caballero has a two-homer game against his old team at The Trop this year. It's not much, but it's a little something.
That said, there weren't many different overly creative directions for Boone to go here - and, of course, he gets guff whether he keeps the lineup consistent (stubborn!) or switches it up (panic!). The onus is on the players, who must work the count early against Peralta, drive up his pitch count, and lay off the changeup.
Otherwise, it's going to be a true "Run it Back" scenario, where both Kevin Gausman and Trey Yesavage were able to dominate the Yankees with the exact same gameplan back-to-back nights to start off last year's ALDS in Toronto. And if Boone's players have another negligent game, he'll be blamed instead of them for doing what the fans regularly ask him to.

item.title: [heavy.com] Yankees' Cam Schlittler Has Some Ridiculous Postseason History Before ALDS Start
item.dc:creator: Zach Kaplan
item.description: We all know Cam Schlittler is good, Cy Young-level good, but ahead of Schlittler’s start versus the Rays in Game 2 of the ALDS, one stat revealed just how elite the young ace’s first three postseason starts have been. With the season effectively on the line, and the Yankees hoping to avoid falling into a 2-0 deficit against their division foe after a brutal offensive showing Saturday night, the Yankees will turn to their almost-certain Cy Young winner in Schlittler, who once again dominated the
item.content:encoded:
We all know Cam Schlittler is good, Cy Young-level good, but ahead of Schlittler’s start versus the Rays in Game 2 of the ALDS, one stat revealed just how elite the young ace’s first three postseason starts have been.
With the season effectively on the line, and the Yankees hoping to avoid falling into a 2-0 deficit against their division foe after a brutal offensive showing Saturday night, the Yankees will turn to their almost-certain Cy Young winner in Schlittler, who once again dominated the Red Sox in the Wild Card to help the Yankees get to this point.
Through his first three playoff starts, two in the Wild Card against the Red Sox and one in last year’s ALDS against the Blue Jays, Schlittler has 24 strikeouts and just one walk. According to optaSTATS, the only other pitcher to have 20+ strikeouts and no more than one walk in his first three postseason starts is Schoolboy Rowe in 1934-1935.
Cam Schlittler’s Starts Against the Rays This Season
Ahead of his start Monday, where a win could firmly turn the tide in the Yankees’ favor with the series shifting to the rowdy Bronx for two games, it’s fair to put a lot of emphasis on how important Schlittler’s start is for the Yankees, who were no-hit through seven innings by Rays ace Drew Rasmussen and only scraped together one hit over the course of the game.
This season, Schlittler has been more human against the Rays, going 1-1 with a 2.81 ERA in three starts against Tampa. Only one of those starts came at Yankee Stadium, with the division already wrapped up for the Rays and the top wild card seed clinched for the Yankees, and Schlittler was pulled after just three innings as a result.
Certainly one of the highlights of Schlittler’s season came at the very same Tropicana Field he will pitch at tonight, where the Yankees’ ace threw eight innings of one-run ball, giving up just four hits and issuing no walks while striking out eight. He only needed 101 pitches to get through eight frames, and the Yankees would surely appreciate a similarly economical start from their ace tonight.
Schlittler’s Tropicana Field Diss
Schlittler tried to rouse up some online agitation earlier this week when he claimed Tropicana Field, which usually covers its upper deck with a tarp, doesn’t present much of a home crowd, and Floridians who grew up supporting the Yankees usually come out and drown out the Rays fanbase.
That didn’t seem to be the case on Saturday, when the usually dormant Rays faithful came out in droves and filled the Trop to one of its top ever crowd sizes, and it’s fair to assume that could have played a part in the Yankees’ offense looking like of a shell of itself after an incredible Wild Card series.
With the sort of history Schlittler has shown in his first three playoff series, the Yankees could have a lot to look forward to out of their ace, who also proved more adept in his road starts this season.
