item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK (AP) — Baltimore’s Shane Baz led in pitch clock violations for the second straight season and the New York Yankees’ José Caballero topped batters while the Orioles and San Francisco Giants tied for the high among teams.
Baz’s six violations for the Orioles was the high among pitchers, the same total he had for Tampa Bay in 2025.
Miami’s Eury Pérez and Texas’ Kumar Rocker tied for second with five apiece. Anthony Nunez, Cade Cavalli, Yoendrys Gómez, Camilo Doval and George Soriano had four each.
Among batters, Caballero led with four. MLB decided his routine of waiting to acknowledge the pitcher just before the pitch clock reached eight seconds amounted to deception, prompting squabbles between Caballero and umpires.
Chase DeLauter, Jung Hoo Lee aand Luis Lara had three each.
Baltimore and San Francisco tied for the overall lead with 19 clock violations, followed by Houston and San Francisco with 18 apiece, and the Los Angeles Dodgers and Yankees with 17 each.
Philadelphia had a low of five and the Rays had six.
Violations by batters, pitchers and catchers dropped from 1,048 when the clock was instituted in 2023 to 602 the following season, 465 in 2025 and 387 this year.
Pitchers committed 290 violations this season, batters 92 and catchers five. The hitters’ total included 12 timeout violations.
There were just two defensive shift violations, against Rays second baseman Ben Williamson with Minnesota’s Ryan Jeffers at the plate on April 3 and against Orioles second baseman Jeremiah Jackson with Toronto’s Sean Keys at the plate on Sept. 23.
After 26 shift violations in the first year of the rule in 2023, there were two in 2024 and one in 2025.
___

Sabathia Makes Personal Announcement On Monday, amid al
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are set to take the field on Monday night for Game 2 of the ALDS against the Tampa Bay Rays.
Tuning into all the action as part of the NBC Sports crew, as well as being a Yankees legend, has been former right-handed pitcher CC Sabathia.
Sabathia recently had his Yankees jersey No. 52 retired during the final weekend of the regular season against the Baltimore Orioles. He spent 11 of his 19 years in MLB with the Yankees.
Sabathia Makes Personal Announcement
On Monday, amid all of his recent success, Sabathia shared some extremely positive personal news on social media, revealing that he is now 11 years sober.
“11 years sober! One of the best decisions I ever made on this day in 2015,” Sabathia posted on X. “Grateful for everyone who has supported me along the way to regain control and wake up every day a better version of myself as a father, husband, and friend. For anyone out there battling, just know you’re not alone and please speak up. There is a light at the end of the tunnel.”
11 years sober! One of the best decisions I ever made on this day in 2015. Grateful for everyone who has supported me along the way to regain control and wake up every day a better version of myself as a father, husband, and friend. For anyone out there battling, just know you’re not alone and please speak up. There is a light at the end of the tunnel 🙏🏾
— CC Sabathia (@CC_Sabathia) October 5, 2026
Congratulations Pour In for Sabathia
MLB fans gathered to congratulate Sabathia on the tremendous achievement after he shared the news.
“Congrats CC! Very happy for you and you look great. Go Yanks!” a fan said.
Someone else added, “Congrats CC, awesome to hear!!!!”
Another person wrote, “Congrats CC! Great milestone, here’s to many more.”
“Congratulations. Hated seeing you on the bump against the Sox. But this accomplishment is much bigger than baseball,” a fan shared.
One more commented, “Congrats legend!”

item.title: [Pinstripe Alley] Brian Cashman and Dave Dombrowski: A comparison on how to build a contender
item.dc:creator: Michael Zeno
item.description: The Wild Card Series came and went this year without much intrigue. The Yankees blew the Red Sox out of the water, the White Sox stuck the final stake into the dying heart of the Astros, and the Padres embarrassed the Cubs. None of those series were competitive, but there was one that at least reached a Game 3: the divisional battle between the Braves and Phillies. item.content:encoded:
The Wild Card Series came and went this year without much intrigue. The Yankees blew the Red Sox out of the water, the White Sox stuck the final stake into the dying heart of the Astros, and the Padres embarrassed the Cubs. None of those series were competitive, but there was one that at least reached a Game 3: the divisional battle between the Braves and Phillies.
For one side, it was a mental block that had to be erased. The Braves hadn’t won a playoff series since winning the World Series in 2021, and had lost to the Phillies in consecutive NLDS in 2022 and 2023 to springboard their latest contention window. It’s a win-now core, and even though they had a lot of issues, they weren’t a team that can accept a loss this early.
The other side couldn’t really accept that either: the Phillies had been eliminated earlier and earlier since a heartbreaking loss in the 2022 World Series. Their core was much older, with much less young talent to supplement it. They had stumbled into the playoffs with a disastrous final week that messed up their pitching. They had reached the point where most teams are at the end of their contention window. If you don’t show reason to believe in this core, it’s going to be dismantled.
The Braves won that grudge match in Game 3, sending the Phillies home with another disastrous season and ensuring no October baseball in the City of Brotherly Love for the first time in five years. It’s a sobering defeat for a team whose best players are past their prime, which has an interim manager, and which faces an extremely bleak outlook. Such a bleak outlook is solely because of one man and his ideas of roster construction: Dave Dombrowski.
At the same time that the Phillies and their brass were openly wondering what was next for the franchise, the Yankees were preparing to play Game 1 of the ALDS at Tropicana Field, which they lost last night in St. Petersburg. It came in the team’s 34th consecutive winning season and their ninth playoff appearance in the last 10 years.
Despite having a core of older veterans who do have a gradually closing window, like the Phillies, the Yankees found a lifeline in the development of two little-known prospects into the likely AL Cy Young and a slugging first baseman/DH who will get down-ballot MVP votes in his second full season. The much-maligned architect of this entire core, and several before it, is Brian Cashman.
Cashman and Dombrowski have spent a long time as adversaries. While he was no longer in charge, a roster full of players acquired under Dombrowski beat the dynasty Yankees in the 2003 World Series. His next team, the Tigers, beat the Yankees in the postseason in 2006, 2011, and 2012. His Red Sox took out the Yankees in 2018 en route to a World Series. You’d think the guy who has won all these head-to-head battles would be heads and shoulders above, but then you must wonder why he’s had to bounce around so much.
Here, what we really get is two entirely different executives with entirely different philosophies about how to build a contender. Neither has much experience overseeing failure, so the large part of their careers has been defined by their climb toward the top of the mountain.
With Cashman, as we’ve seen for essentially three decades, it’s an approach that is more focused on long-term sustainability. He’s been blessed with the power of working with one of the league’s deepest pockets in the biggest market in baseball, which usually allows him the bandwidth to fill crippling holes. His approach in the offseason is predicated on getting high-end talent on big deals in free agency to flex their financial muscle, but also making shrewd, under-the-radar trades to fill much of the roster.
While he’s willing to shell out for big contracts both via trade and in free agency and absorb the financial risk that he knows ownership can deal with, he’s more measured when it comes to truly taking that next step. You’ll see him balk at an additional year in a free-agent deal or hold onto a top prospect in trade discussions for a top-level talent. There are times this works, but there are also times he’s left at the altar and burned for it. Yoshinobu Yamamoto’s free agency and trade discussions for Gerrit Cole in the winter of 2017 ring a bell for that.
That restraint is based on his belief in long-term sustainability. The Yankees rarely have a great farm system, but if they can produce an era-defining superstar (hello, Aaron Judge), it makes everything drastically different for roster construction. By that note, he’ll always leave holes on the roster to allow for a cheap, homegrown player to fill them. From here, it can go two ways. You can get a Judge and some great complementary pieces on rookie contracts like Gleyber Torres and Gary Sánchez, but you can also get burned by hoarding a prospect in trade talks (Chance Adams, Clint Frazier, Deivi Garcia).
This mentality is completely different than the one you’ll see Dombrowski employ. His approach to roster building, while similarly predicated on a very generous owner with deep pockets, is more based on taking risks in both free agency and the trade market, pursuing as much proven talent as possible. This approach narrows a contention window, but it’s something he’s able to work off of. It’s a lot easier to do your job when you identify a five-year window to win and disregard anything that comes after it.
Looking at how he’s managed this throughout his tenure, he made some gigantic trades and signings to turn Detroit into a perennial AL contender, acquiring Miguel Cabrera from his old stomping grounds in Miami in 2007 and David Price in 2014, while also inking Prince Fielder to a ridiculous nine-year contract. In Boston, he made blockbuster signings in Price and J.D. Martinez while swinging a franchise-altering deal for White Sox ace Chris Sale. In Philly, he’s been more muted, but gave a massive 11-year deal to Trea Turner to solidify the shortstop position. You’re never bored in an offseason under Dombrowski.
This approach is predicated on doing whatever it takes to climb to the mountaintop, looking to increase the team’s chances of raising the Commissioner’s Trophy at least one time by enough that it offsets the losses that will come down the road. It’s risky in a sport that has so much randomness in the postseason, but if it pays off, it’s genius. Just ask the 2018 Red Sox, who proceeded to bottom out in the ensuing two seasons and only make one playoff appearance over the next six seasons, if they’d trade that title for more wins in those lost seasons.
When it doesn’t work? It leads to a lot of resentment. The Tigers won a pair of pennants in 2006 and 2012, but in an extended, decade-long run with the same core of Cabrera and Verlander at the forefront, the Tigers imploded, missing the playoffs in four consecutive years between those pennants and ultimately wound up spending over a billion and burning up the farm system for no World Series. After Dombrowski was dismissed after a terrible 2015 season, the Tigers wouldn’t make the playoffs again until 2024.
The Phillies hired him to be their President of Baseball Operations in 2020, and he did what he does best. He got Turner; he got Kyle Schwarber; he extended Zack Wheeler and Aaron Nola. In lieu of blockbusters, he elected to slowly chip away at the farm depth by making a mountain of smaller moves every winter and summer. It was, honestly, his least all-in job as an executive since he was in Miami, but it’s still leading to the same place as Detroit. He was hailed as a savior in 2022 when the Phils won the pennant, but is now on the verge of being driven out of town as they stare down an unbelievably bleak future without a title to show for it.
The strengths and weaknesses of Cashman and Dombrowski are directly opposite of each other. They show the two ways you can run a perpetual contender. Cashman’s philosophy allows him to keep his job for decades and decades, while Dombrowski often gets canned after the contention window slams shut. You might think Cashman’s job security is a byproduct of organizational complacency, but there’s a reason he’s universally revered for his work in baseball circles.
The two rarely go head-to-head for big signings or trades, but you can imagine how they would go. Dombrowski might give a guy an extra year or two in a deal that Cashman is apprehensive about doing. It could either end up like Yamamoto, where his prime wins you multiple championships, or like Turner, who’s turning into one of the worst contracts in the sport just four years in. In the trade market, Cashman might balk at the asking price for a big-time player, while Dombrowski would go for it. That could lead to a massive success like Sale, or a massive failure like what the Mets did with PCA.
If Dombrowski ran the Yankees over the last 15 years, do we see a World Series? I’m not sure. I’d imagine he’d be much more interested in that mega-deal the Braves proposed in 2014 that would’ve sent Luis Severino, Sanchez, and Judge to Atlanta for a box full of proven talent. He’d also be much more likely to pull the trigger on a Kyle Tucker trade that included Ben Rice in the winter of 2024 or a Eugenio Suarez/Merrill Kelly deal with the D-Backs that would’ve sent Cam Schlittler to the desert.
All in all, as the Phillies enter an offseason where they must consider firmly shutting their contention window, the Yankees not only still have a chance to win this year, but seem to have enough young talent left over to win down the road when Judge and Gerrit Cole hang up their cleats. It’s the latest chapter evolving in the several decades that Dombrowski and Cashman have spent as two of the league’s most famous executives, a chess match to truly decide which is the better style of building a contender.

item.title: [wfmd.com] Yankees send Cam Schlittler to the mound in Game 2 looking to even the Division Series with the Rays
item.dc:creator: Latest; Breaking News

Saturday is dominated by college football, and Sunday is dominated by NFL games. However, if you missed watching the baseball games from the Division Series, you definitely missed out. Playoff baseball is always more exciting, and we’ve seen some great games in every series so far. Tonight we have Game 2 between the Yankees and Rays. The New York Yankees made light work of the Boston Red Sox in
item.content:encoded:
I know that yesterday and weekends in October, in general, are more focused on football than anything. Saturday is dominated by college football, and Sunday is dominated by NFL games. However, if you missed watching the baseball games from the Division Series, you definitely missed out. Playoff baseball is always more exciting, and we’ve seen some great games in every series so far. Tonight we have Game 2 between the Yankees and Rays.
The New York Yankees made light work of the Boston Red Sox in the Wild Card round, but this was going to be a different task. Being at home, especially in the playoffs, is typically a bit easier. The Yankees have been a good team on the road this season, but in Game 1, they looked lost. Was it because it was their first road game in a week, or was it because the Rays pitched a gem of a game? Probably mostly the ladder, but it is still worth considering that perhaps there could be some road woes for the Yankees. The Yankees were 2-5 in Tampa this season.
The Yankees get a great chance to even up the series tonight as they send Cam Schlittler to the mound. He was fantastic in his first postseason start against the Red Sox. He went 6.1 innings and allowed just two hits and one walk. He didn’t allow a run and struck out 10 hitters. It was a bit concerning that he threw 117 pitches in the game; that was 11 more pitches than he threw in any game this season. Actually, it is the most he has thrown in any game of his career.
The Tampa Bay Rays were the best team in the American League this season, and they are looking to make that regular-season success into some postseason magic. In Game 1, the team didn’t exactly break out the bats, but they didn’t need to. Thanks to Drew Rasmussen, they didn’t need much help. Rasmussen went 7.2 innings without allowing a hit. He allowed one in the bottom of the eighth, and the runner was thrown out trying to get to third. The lone run of the game came in the third inning when Jonathan Aranda hit a homer off of Gerrit Cole.
The Rays knew they had something special going this season, which is why they went out and traded for the second-best pitcher available on the market. Freddy Peralta came over at the deadline after a miserable start with the Mets. He seems to have locked in during September with 28 innings pitched and just three earned runs allowed in the month. The Rays have won the past six Peralta starts. He did face the Yankees earlier in the year with the Mets and went five innings and allowed three earned runs. Cody Bellinger has mashed Peralta in the past, going 6-for-14 against him.
Tonight should be a great game between the two starters. I’m really not sure how you fade the Yankees with Schlittler on the mound, but the Rays are officially 30 games over .500 in home games this year after a Game 1 win. Peralta has pitched well, and the Rays seem to get the most out of their starters. Peralta is 1-3 with a 4.32 career ERA in the postseason. I lean toward the under, but I’m going to take Schlittler and the Yankees at -127 to win the game as my official play.
For more sports betting information and plays, follow David on X/Twitter: @futureprez2024

item.title: [awfulannouncing.com] Derek Jeter asks if Atlanta Braves are trying to 'play spoiler'
item.dc:creator: Brandon Contes
item.description: The Atlanta Braves might not be expected to beat the Los Angeles Dodgers, but Derek Jeter has to know they still expect to. After losing Game 1 of their National League Division Series in Los Angeles on Saturday, the Braves stole home-field advantage by winning Game 2 Sunday night. All of a sudden, the idea of Atlanta knocking off the two-time defending World Series champions just got real. So real that the Braves aren’t just thinking about playing spoiler; they’re thinking they might win the wh
item.content:encoded:
The Atlanta Braves might not be expected to beat the Los Angeles Dodgers, but Derek Jeter has to know they still expect to.
After losing Game 1 of their National League Division Series in Los Angeles on Saturday, the Braves stole home-field advantage by winning Game 2 Sunday night. All of a sudden, the idea of Atlanta knocking off the two-time defending World Series champions just got real. So real that the Braves aren’t just thinking about playing spoiler; they’re thinking they might win the whole f*cking thing.
Outfielder Michael Harris II led the Braves to their Game 2 win, hitting a triple and scoring the go-ahead run. Following the win, Harris joined the Fox Sports postgame show, where Jeter asked about his mindset entering the series.
“Your mindset, your mentality, is it you guys want to play the spoiler? Or you’re just not necessarily thinking about the Dodgers?” Derek Jeter to Michael Harris II after the Braves won Game 2 against the Dodgers. https://t.co/JR1oq6u1w1
— Awful Announcing (@awfulannouncing) October 5, 2026
“I just want to ask this question: we’re talking about mindset, coming into the series, it seems like the whole world, all they are talking about is the Los Angeles Dodgers going for a three-peat,” Jeter noted. “And you guys sort of just seem to fly under the radar. Your mindset, your mentality, is it you guys want to play the spoiler? Or you’re just not necessarily thinking about the Dodgers? You’re just out there trying to prove to the rest of the world that you have the best team in baseball?”
What a strange and clunky question. Is Jeter really asking Harris about playing spoiler two games into the NLDS? And does Jeter really think the Braves are just here to play spoiler? “Just here to play spoiler” means the Braves can’t win a championship of their own; they’re just trying to keep the Dodgers from winning their third in a row. Which is ridiculous. Of course the Braves are thinking about winning their own title, not just playing defense to prevent the Dodgers from winning.
Maybe Jeter just doesn’t know what “playing spoiler” means because he was always going for a championship with the Yankees. But you can only imagine what Jeter would have been thinking if Mike Francesa or Chris Russo asked him about playing spoiler during any of his playoff runs with the Yankees. Although it probably would have sounded similar to the Jeterian answer Harris gave.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Yankees’ Cam Schlittler becomes first pitcher in 90 years to accomplish MLB postseason feat
item.dc:creator: Matt Larter
item.description: The MLB postseason has seen New York Yankees ace Cam Schlittler accomplish a feat that has not been matched in 90 years. Cam Schlittler has 24 strikeouts and 1 walk allowed through 3 career postseason starts.The only other pitcher with 20 or more Ks and no more than 1 walk through his first 3 playoff starts all-time is Schoolboy Rowe (20 K, 0 BB) in 1934-1935. https://t.co/F3FfMIHHBg — OptaSTATS (@OptaSTATS) October 5, 2026 Schlittler has recorded 24 strikeouts and just one walk through his firs
item.content:encoded:
The MLB postseason has seen New York Yankees ace Cam Schlittler accomplish a feat that has not been matched in 90 years.
Cam Schlittler has 24 strikeouts and 1 walk allowed through 3 career postseason starts.The only other pitcher with 20 or more Ks and no more than 1 walk through his first 3 playoff starts all-time is Schoolboy Rowe (20 K, 0 BB) in 1934-1935. https://t.co/F3FfMIHHBg
— OptaSTATS (@OptaSTATS) October 5, 2026
Schlittler has recorded 24 strikeouts and just one walk through his first three career playoff starts, putting him in incredibly rare company.
The only other pitcher in MLB history to record at least 20 strikeouts while allowing no more than one walk through his first three postseason starts was Schoolboy Rowe of the Detroit Tigers, who struck out 20 and walked none between 1934 and 1935.
Schlittler dominates in postseason
Jul 29, 2026; Chicago, Illinois, USA; New York Yankees starting pitcher Cam Schlittler (31) walks back to the dugout during the sixth inning of a baseball game against the Chicago White Sox at Rate Field. Mandatory Credit: Kamil Krzaczynski-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)
Schlittler's latest performance came against the Boston Red Sox in the opening game of the American League Wild Card Series. The right-hander delivered 6.1 scoreless innings while striking out 10 batters, leading the Yankees to a commanding 9-0 victory.
New York went on to sweep Boston in two games, with Schlittler playing a major role in helping the Yankees advance.
The 25-year-old sophomore has been one of the most dominant pitchers in baseball throughout the 2026 season. During the regular season, Schlittler posted a 14-6 record with a remarkable 1.95 ERA and 0.92 WHIP across 33 appearances. He also recorded an impressive 239 strikeouts.
Those numbers have made Schlittler one of the leading candidates for the American League Cy Young Award.
Yankees turn to Schlittler again
Schlittler's dominance has carried over into October. Through his first three career postseason appearances, he now owns a 0.87 ERA and a microscopic 0.77 WHIP.
The Yankees will need another strong performance from their young ace after dropping Game 1 of the American League Division Series to the Tampa Bay Rays. New York suffered a narrow 1-0 defeat against the division-winning Rays, putting additional pressure on the Yankees heading into Game 2.
Schlittler is expected to take the mound Monday, giving New York a chance to even the series with its most reliable postseason weapon.
With his combination of strikeout ability, control and run prevention, Schlittler has already etched his name alongside a pitcher from nine decades ago. Another dominant outing could further cement his status as one of the Yankees' emerging postseason stars.

item.content:encoded:
Last week, the St. Louis Cardinals had their season come to an end.
They played their final game of the 2026 regular season against the Milwaukee Brewers (and lost by a score of 6-4).
The Cardinals missed the MLB playoffs for the fourth straight year.
Ex-Cardinals All-Star Will Be A Yankees Free Agent
With the Cardinals out of the mix, it’s worth noting that one of their former star players is currently in the 2026 MLB playoffs.
Paul Goldschmidt is currently in the ALDS with the New York Yankees (against the Tampa Bay Rays).
The 39-year-old finished the regular season batting .252 with 87 hits, 18 home runs, 52 RBIs, 44 runs and one stolen base in 105 games.
Paul Goldschmidt #48 of the New York Yankees bats against the Baltimore Orioles during their game at Yankee Stadium on September 25, 2026 in New York City.
Goldschmidt will also become a free agent this winter.
He will be available to sign with any team in the MLB.
Despite his age, Goldschmidt is still a very valuable player (and would likely have a lot of teams with interest).
Looking At Goldschmidt’s Time With The Cardinals
Paul Goldschmidt #46 of the St. Louis Cardinals is congratulated by teammates in the dugout after hitting a two-run home run against the Los Angeles Dodgers in the second inning at Busch Stadium on August 16, 2024 in St Louis, Missouri.
Goldschmidt spent six seasons with the Cardinals.
Despite joining the franchise at 31, he had an excellent run.
In 2022, Goldschmidt won the National League MVP Award (and made the All-Star Game).
He batted .317 with 35 home runs and 115 RBIs.
Paul Goldschmidt #46 of the St. Louis Cardinals rounds the bases after hitting a home run against the American League during the 92nd MLB All-Star Game presented by Mastercard at Dodger Stadium on July 19, 2022 in Los Angeles, California.
Goldschmidt left the Cardinals to sign with the Yankees (as a free agent) before the 2025 season.
Looking At Goldschmidt’s Entire Career
Paul Goldschmidt #48 of the New York Yankees celebrates in the dugout following his eighth inning solo home run against the Boston Red Sox at Yankee Stadium on August 30, 2026 in New York City.
Before the Yankees and Cardinals, Goldschmidt had spent the first eight years of his career on the Arizona Diamondbacks.
The seven-time MLB All-Star will have a chance to make the Hall of Fame.

item.dc:creator: Michael DeRosa

New York Yankees Predicted to Trade Luis Gil & Ryan Weathers to White Sox In a recent article for Bleacher Report, K
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are currently facing the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS.
The Yankees will be looking to bounce back against the Rays in Game 2 after losing Game 1. A loss in Game 2 would put the Yankees in an incredibly difficult spot.
Now, as the Yankees continue their series against the Rays, they are now being predicted to trade away two of their pitchers during the offseason.
New York Yankees Predicted to Trade Luis Gil & Ryan Weathers to White Sox
In a recent article for Bleacher Report, Kerry Miller predicted that the Yankees will trade pitchers Luis Gil and Ryan Weathers to the Chicago White Sox this offseason. Miller also predicted that the Yankees will acquire prospects Caleb Bonemer and Pierce George in the move.
“The Yankees also have four more years of Will Warren, two years left on both Luis Gil and Ryan Weathers, one more season of Clarke Schmidt and two MLB-ready 23-year-olds in Elmer Rodríguez and Carlos Lagrange,” Miller wrote. “That’s quite the stockpile of starting pitching that they could use to perhaps pluck a quality prospect from a team that needs to bolster its rotation.”
With the Yankees having plenty of pitchers, it would be understandable if they moved Gil and Weathers this offseason. They need to strengthen their roster elsewhere, while Gil and Weathers could benefit from a fresh start elsewhere.
Looking at Gil & Weathers
Gil appeared in nine games this season with the Yankees, where he had a 1-2 record, a 4.61 ERA, and 17 strikeouts. This was after he had a 4-1 record and a 3.32 ERA in 11 games for the Yankees during the 2025 season.
Gil was memorably named AL Rookie of the Year in 2024 after his strong campaign. In 29 games this regular season for New York, he posted a 15-7 record and a 3.50 ERA. With numbers like these, he could certainly generate interest from a team like the White Sox this offseason.
As for Weathers, he had a 5-8 record, a 3.60 ERA, and 143 strikeouts in 25 games this regular season. Overall, the 6-foot-1 righty had a solid first season with the Yankees. Yet, it is still fair to wonder if he could be moved due to New York’s strong pitching depth.
Bonemer & George Would Be Great Prospects for Yankees to Add
PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA – JULY 12: Caleb Bonemer #21 of the Chicago White Sox on the American League Team warms up at Citizens Bank Park on July 12, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Al Bello/Getty Images)
Bonemer would be a very intriguing prospect for the Yankees to add to their system. The 21-year-old just had a monster season in 2026. In 132 games split between High-A and Double-A, he posted 37 home runs, 92 RBI, and a .251 batting average. With numbers like these, he would give New York another exciting prospect who has plenty of power.
As for Pierce, New York would be adding a promising pitcher to their system. The 23-year-old had a 9-3 record, a 3.56 ERA, and 82 strikeouts in 51 minor league games this year.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Yankees’ Jazz Chisholm Jr. Makes Feelings Clear Ahead of Rays Game 2
item.dc:creator: Keith Watkins
item.description: The New York Yankees spent Sunday away from Tropicana Field. Some players headed to the team's player development complex in Tampa to get work in before Monday's Game 2 against the Tampa Bay Rays. Others took the day to reset after a 1-0 loss that featured a historically quiet offensive performance. Drew Rasmussen's near no-hitter left the Yankees staring at a 1-0 series deficit in the best-of-five ALDS. History says the vast majority of teams that drop the first two games of a five-game series
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees spent Sunday away from Tropicana Field. Some players headed to the team's player development complex in Tampa to get work in before Monday's Game 2 against the Tampa Bay Rays. Others took the day to reset after a 1-0 loss that featured a historically quiet offensive performance.
Drew Rasmussen's near no-hitter left the Yankees staring at a 1-0 series deficit in the best-of-five ALDS. History says the vast majority of teams that drop the first two games of a five-game series do not recover. Losing Monday would make the climb significantly steeper once the series shifts to Yankee Stadium.
When the topic of urgency came up after Saturday's game, Jazz Chisholm Jr. did not need long to answer.
Chisholm Leaves No Room for Interpretation
A reporter asked Chisholm whether Game 2 qualifies as a must-win. His response cut straight through the question.
"Every game is a must-win," Chisholm said.
For a team trailing in a short series against a division rival that owned the best home record in the American League, treating every remaining game as an elimination scenario is the only approach that makes sense. Chisholm framed it that way without hesitation.
The Matchup for Game 2
Monday's Game 2 gives the Yankees their best pitching matchup of the series.
Cam Schlittler, the likely AL Cy Young winner, faces Freddy Peralta with the Yankees needing the offense to match the arm on the mound.
Final Word for the Yankees
The series is 1-0. The margin for error is gone. Every game from here carries elimination weight whether the math technically says so or not.
The Yankees heard Rasmussen's message on Saturday.
Now they need to deliver one of their own.
This article was originally published on HEAVY

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Austin Wells could win the Yankees a playoff out with one tap
item.dc:creator: Alexander Wilson
item.description: Austin Wells finished the regular season with a 63% success rate on ABS challenges, and he's already carried that skill into October for the Yankees. Wells successfully challenged a called ball in Game 1 of
item.content:encoded:
Austin Wells finished the regular season with a 63% success rate on ABS challenges, and he's already carried that skill into October for the Yankees.
Wells won 82 of his 131 challenges as a catcher and ranked sixth among MLB catchers in overturns above expected. He also made the fourth-most challenges at the position, giving the Yankees a catcher willing to act when he thinks an umpire missed a pitch.
That paid off Tuesday against Boston. Wells successfully challenged a called ball in Game 1 of the Wild Card Series, getting it overturned to a strike. The Yankees won 9-0, so that particular correction didn't decide a nail-biter. The next one could arrive with considerably less room for error.
I wouldn't be surprised if Wells gets the Yankees out of a dangerous inning with a well-timed challenge this postseason. Across 131 attempts, he's shown both the willingness to question a call and the judgment to get it changed more often than he gets it wrong.
Yankees pitchers benefit from Wells knowing when to challenge
The sixth-place ranking concerns his results above an expected baseline, rather than his raw success percentage. Pitch location and game situation help establish that baseline, adding context to how a catcher uses his opportunities.
For the Yankees, Wells' workload is encouraging. He's made these decisions throughout a full season, with different pitchers, hitters and counts. Getting the call right requires him to judge where the ball crossed the zone and request a review immediately, while he still has a challenge available.
We've spent plenty of time on Wells' bat, including his late-season lift against Tampa Bay. His ability to correct a missed call gives him another way to help on a night when the hits aren't coming.
0What do you think?Post a comment.
A full count can turn on one decision
Each team begins with two ABS challenges and retains successful ones under MLB's challenge rules. A catcher who gets a review right can fix the count and preserve an opportunity for later in the game.
Picture a full count with two outs and the bases loaded. A pitch that clips the zone gets called ball four. A successful challenge changes that walk into a called third strike, ending the inning before the next hitter gets a chance to do damage.
Don't be surprised if Wells sends a Yankees pitcher back to the dugout this October with a challenge. When the alternative is a bases-loaded walk, I'll take that contribution every time.

For anyone who still posts that video of Judge dropping a fly ball in the World Series, this situation might give them a little more ammunition, even if the Yankees are the last team standing. item.content:encoded:
One scenario that might give the trolls some joy. What if the New York Yankees win a World Series without Aaron Judge, and Ben Rice puts up the kind of postseason numbers Judge has never been able to?
For anyone who still posts that video of Judge dropping a fly ball in the World Series, this situation might give them a little more ammunition, even if the Yankees are the last team standing.
It shouldn't matter, but at some point in the dead of winter, when baseball is months away — or if a lockout makes MLB's start date a complete unknown — a conversation about this might spark on WFAN. Shaun Morash might bring it up to Tiki Barber and Evan Roberts, and if things are going well for the Rangers and Knicks, it could be one of the few things to grumble about.
Indeed, Judge has wildly underperformed in his career when the lights are brightest, but if there's one way to think about a Judge-less championship, the Yankees carried their captain after years of him carrying them. They may not have won anything in decades, but the only reason they've had a puncher's chance at a title since Judge took off in 2017 is because of their captain.
Taking turns carrying each other
Think of that roster in 2022. Without Judge chasing down Maris, they would have missed the playoffs. That notion proved true the next year when Judge crashed into a Dodger Stadium wall, and the Yankees' postseason chances followed him to the IL.
In 2024, Judge had Juan Soto to back him up, but for a while, it did seem like their hold on the division could slip at any time. Their two sluggers pulled them out of a Summer funk and led them to the World Series. The 2025 team was a bit more balanced and had one of the best offenses in baseball, but another MVP effort helped push the Yankees over, even though they ultimately lost to the Toronto Blue Jays in the ALDS.
This year, with a healthy Judge, the Yankees might win the division, or it's closer than it was.
The fact is, it would only be fitting if the Yankees won without Judge and delivered their captain a World Series ring — his first. After years of him dragging them across the finish line, his teammates are finally doing something for him.
Judge's legacy is still that of a three-time MVP and one of the all-time great right-handers in the sport's history. Albert Pujols, Hank Aaron, Willie Mays, and Judge will be on that right-handed Mount Rushmore. Judge will find his way to the Hall of Fame, and if he's getting the loudest pops every time the Yankees are introduced, then rightfully so.
Bruce Wayne is still the one true Batman of Gotham, even though he's incapacitated for a time and Dick Grayson needs to take up the cape and cowl. In this case, Rice is the Robin.
The most important thing to remember, if this happens, is that the Yankees did win a World Series, and if they do, it's the only thing worth mentioning. No one should rain on that parade. Just look at the Atlanta Braves. They won without their star Ronald Acuña Jr., but nobody would nullify his impact on the Braves or think less of that championship.
The only reason it would be a conversation is that it's New York, and the biggest stars around here will always have a target on their back. Tyrese Haliburton is a great player, but a good portion of his allure is tied to what he did against the New York Knicks.
All that potential noise won't matter, though. At least the Yankees will have won, and it would be their first championship since 2009.
Joe Randazzo is a reference librarian who lives on Long Island. When he’s not behind a desk offering assistance to his patrons, he writes about the Yankees for Yankees On SI. Follow him as @YankeeLibrarian on X and Instagram.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] AL Division Series Game 1 Preview: New York Yankees @ Tampa Bay Rays
item.dc:creator: Estevão Maximo
item.description: Sweeping the Red Sox with two blowout wins was a joyous occasion, not to mention the tangible positive impact of setting up your rotation for the ALDS. The Yankees can begin the series against the Rays with Gerrit Cole as the Game 1 starter, which is only fitting considering Cole's regular-season campaign in 2026 began and ended against the Rays, both times with a quality start. Making his postseason debut this season, Cole will get the ball after nearly a week and a half off, his longest time b
item.content:encoded:
Sweeping the Red Sox with two blowout wins was a joyous occasion, not to mention the tangible positive impact of setting up your rotation for the ALDS. The Yankees can begin the series against the Rays with Gerrit Cole as the Game 1 starter, which is only fitting considering Cole's regular-season campaign in 2026 began and ended against the Rays, both times with a quality start.
Making his postseason debut this season, Cole will get the ball after nearly a week and a half off, his longest time between starts since returning from injury. In three appearances against the AL East champs in the regular season—the most he had against any single team—Cole averaged six innings and delivered a 2.50 ERA, enjoying success against a team not known for its home run pedigree.
Having last played a competitive meaningful game well before the end of the regular season, the Rays will set out to prove there is no rust in their game with Drew Rasmussen starting Game 1. Who better to represent what the Rays are all about than Rasmussen, acquired for the power-hitting Willy Adames as a swingman/backend starter, only to turn into one of the more dominant starters in the AL?
The postseason scenario and all that it entails could be seen as an opportunity to test the Rays' resolve when it comes to their ace. Rasmussen was already dominant last season—part of what held him back from entering the conversation with the big boys was just how carefully managed he was by the Rays, who only let him reach or surpass 90 pitches twice in 2025. This year, Rasmussen has done that 17 times, including a career-high 114 pitches in a win over the Yankees just a couple of weeks ago—one in which perhaps the Rays gave a sign of their intentions with a trial run. With this extra leeway, Rasmussen managed to pitch 22 more innings than last season despite having one fewer start (31 to 30).
Rasmussen's ability to go deeper into games than what we're accustomed to seeing not only from him but also from the Rays as a team is of great value—especially if we are to read into regular season numbers. As much as the Yankees may have a better rotation, perhaps the biggest advantage in this series is in the bullpen. While New York had the second-lowest bullpen ERA in baseball, Tampa was only number 14. The key here, particularly looking at the postseason and a matchup with the Yankees lineup, is that the 95 home runs allowed by the Rays' bullpen represented the third-highest mark in the bigs.
Then again, this is a Tampa team with the benefit of off-days between each of the first three games. One can only imagine how aggressive they might be willing to go with the likes of Bryan Baker, Cam Booser, and Kevin Kelly. While Baker is the closer, Booser gets the nod as the X-factor for the Rays in Game 1 and this series as a whole—the Yankees were 1-for-10 against him in the regular season, the one being an Austin Wells home run.
Booser's importance stems from a complete lack of southpaw options for a team whose only other left-hander who finished the season on the active roster was Steven Matz. Garrett Cleavinger was cleared to be a part of the ALDS roster, but his 2026 numbers were quite bad, with an 89 ERA+ in 41.1 innings.
Unlike the Red Sox, all the Rays' top starters are right-handers, allowing Aaron Boone to utilize his lefty-heavy lineup without fear, starting in Game 1 against Rasmussen. And if Booser can't shut them down out of the bullpen, Tampa all of a sudden has an incredibly difficult mission to contain Ben Rice, Cody Bellinger, Luis Garcia Jr., and company.

Right-hander Gerrit Cole gets the ball for the New York Yankees in Game 1 of the ALDS. He put together another solid campaign in his return to baseball in 2026 and ended the year on a particularly high note.
He allowed just two runs in each of his final two starts, posting a 2-0 record with a 3.09 ERA and a 0.86 WHIP over that stretch. The latter of those two outings came against the Tampa Bay Rays, a game in which Cole surrendered just three hits across nearly six innings.
Tampa Bay is a team that Cole has historically dominated. Over the past 12 meetings, Cole is 5-2 with a 2.31 ERA and a 1.00 WHIP.
A pitching duel could be in store, given that right-hander Drew Rasmussen takes the mound for the Rays. One of the most consistently dominant pitchers in the AL over the past few years, Rasmussen is coming off the best season of his career.
A likely AL Cy Young finalist, the right-hander finished 2026 with a 16-5 record, a 2.67 ERA and a 0.91 WHIP. His underlying metrics were equally impressive.
Entering the postseason, Rasmussen ranks in the top third of the league in xERA, xBA, barrel rate and hard-hit rate. Like Cole, Rasmussen enters this series in particularly dominant form.
The 31-year-old has allowed one or fewer runs in five of his past six starts, posting a 3-0 record with a 1.43 ERA and a 0.80 WHIP. The latest of those starts came against New York, a game in which Rasmussen allowed just one run on one hit across nearly seven innings.
There were just seven total runs scored in that game, and another low-scoring affair is likely in Game 1 of the ALDS. Not only are both starting pitchers statistically and analytically excellent, but both have also fared well in this specific matchup.
Cole's success against the Rays was already highlighted above, but Rasmussen has been even more impressive against the Yankees. In 11 career meetings, Rasmussen is 5-2 with a 1.81 ERA and a 0.85 WHIP.
In 139 combined plate appearances against Rasmussen, the current New York roster owns a mere .163 batting average, a .256 slugging percentage and a .217 wOBA.
Pick: Under 7 (-115 at DraftKings | Play to -120)

item.title: [heavy.com] Yankees Still Owe Gerrit Cole $72 Million
item.dc:creator: Billy Heyen
item.description: The New York Yankees haven’t made quite as many Yankees-of-old signings in recent years, the kind where they just blow the rest of the sport out of the water with a gigantic payday to ensure they get the player they want. Maybe the last such deal like that was with Gerrit Cole. When Cole was a free agent before the 2020 season, the Yankees handed him a record-setting contract, and he’s been in the Bronx ever since. The signing continues to loom large as crucial to the Yankees’ chances of success
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees haven’t made quite as many Yankees-of-old signings in recent years, the kind where they just blow the rest of the sport out of the water with a gigantic payday to ensure they get the player they want.
Maybe the last such deal like that was with Gerrit Cole.
When Cole was a free agent before the 2020 season, the Yankees handed him a record-setting contract, and he’s been in the Bronx ever since.
The signing continues to loom large as crucial to the Yankees’ chances of success, because Cole is starting Game 1 of the ALDS on Saturday at Tropicana Field against the Tampa Bay Rays.
For the Yanks to go on a deep October run, Cole is going to have to pitch like the guy the Yankees signed to that ginormous contract more than half a decade ago.
Gerrit Cole Contract
That contract’s value? It was for $324 million over nine years.
It pays Cole $36 million per season, and it isn’t split up in any odd way. He actually just gets $36 million per year.
That means that this year, he made $36 million — and Cole had his worst ERA (still sub-4.00) in nearly a decade.
Cole isn’t young anymore, which is always part of the risk with such a contract, particularly for a pitcher.
The big right-hander turned 36 years old in September — which means that by the end of the 2027 season, he’ll be 37, and then the following year, 38.
How Many Years Left?
Cole’s contract, after this one, has two years remaining.
The nine-year deal began in 2020 and runs through the end of the 2028 season.
That means the Yankees still have two more seasons of paying Cole $36 million per year, so in total, they’ll owe him $72 million for next season and the following one.
The hope whenever a team hands out such a contract is that a player makes the value worth it in the front half so that even if they decline in the back half, they’ve already affirmed their worth overall.
Cole mostly did that, although he did miss the entire 2025 season with Tommy John surgery — to be fair, though, that’s also expected with long-term pitcher contracts these days. There’s going to be a missed season in there somewhere due to injury.
Otherwise, Cole has been mostly healthy and mostly dominant.
Still, big contracts do start to feel particularly hefty as players start to decline just a bit.
Yankees fans sure would love to see Cole hold off Father Time a bit this October and help anchor the New York rotation on a deep playoff run.
Even if he doesn’t, though, he still has been mostly worth the price. It just has the potential to feel more expensive in the next two years if Cole really is on the downslope of his career.

item.title: [fansided.com] Four reasons the white-hot Yankees could derail a Dodgers three-peat
item.dc:creator: Jake Elman
item.description: For the second time in three years, we have a shot at seeing the New York Yankees and Los Angeles Dodgers battle it out in the World Series. Both teams continue the postseason this weekend, with the Yankees facing the Rays in the ALDS and the Dodgers welcoming the Braves for an NLDS clash. Even with Aaron Judge still on
item.content:encoded:
For the second time in three years, we have a shot at seeing the New York Yankees and Los Angeles Dodgers battle it out in the World Series. Both teams continue the postseason this weekend, with the Yankees facing the Rays in the ALDS and the Dodgers welcoming the Braves for an NLDS clash.
Only seven wins separate those four teams — and the other four still alive — from the pennant, and the Yankees looked sharp in their Wild Card Series sweep of the rival Red Sox. Even with Aaron Judge still on the mend, the 27-time World Series champions are built to capture only their third pennant since the start of 2004.
And while casual fans may think Shohei and the Dodgers are guaranteed a third consecutive title, don’t rule out the Yankees just yet.
Welcome to the Yankees’ George Lombard Jr. experience
Somewhere out there is a baseball fan feeling old because they’re watching George Lombard Sr.’s son play for the Yankees. If it’s any consolation, the 2023 first-round pick began his playoff career with four hits — three coming in Game 1 — and three runs scored against the Red Sox. Yep, he belongs, and he clearly can handle the New York spotlight.
Although Lombard’s defensive issues were a significant talking point down the stretch, he handled all seven chances without an error. He also became the youngest Yankees shortstop to start a playoff game at 21 years and 119 days old.
“It’s really cool,” Lombard said following the Wild Card Round. “There’s been a lot of countless legends that have come and played in the pinstripes so it’s really cool.”
How can you complain when you have Cam Schlittler and Max Fried?
No, we’re not forgetting Carlos Rodón or Gerrit Cole, the latter of whom is expected to start Game 1. But Schlittler showed why he’s the presumptive AL Cy Young winner by dominating the Red Sox yet again, allowing only two runs and one walk over 20.2 career postseason innings.
Elbow injuries limited Fried to 20 starts, though his 2.80 ERA and 24.0 percent strikeout rate were both in line with last year’s 2.86 ERA and 23.6 percent strikeout marks. Schlittler is expected to start Game 2, with Fried, Rodón, or Cole likely to follow in Game 3 (depending on who starts the ALDS opener).
The Jazz Chisholm and Austin Wells comeback trains are back on
Wednesday’s Game 2 showed exactly why Chisholm, who reached base three times and recorded two steals, could still command a multi-year deal this offseason. Injuries and a sharp reduction in power make it easy to forget how electrifying the two-time All-Star second baseman is, both as a player and an energetic personality. He marches to the beat of his own drum, and the Yankees need that balance of power, speed, and enthusiasm.
As for Wells, look who finally won back Yankees fans’ support. The embattled catcher quietly hit .229 with a .787 OPS in the second half, drastically up from his .155 and .504 marks over his first 66 games. Any concerns about that being a flash in the pan ended — or at least temporarily paused — after the fourth-year backstop went 3-for-6 with four RBIs in the Wild Card Series.
Imagine telling someone immediately following the trade deadline that Wells and Chisholm are among the Yankees’ most intimidating bats entering the ALDS.
We don’t talk enough about David Bednar and the Yankees’ bullpen
Not only did the Yankees bullpen’s 3.13 ERA lead baseball, but it ranked considerably above the second-place Brewers’ 3.22 mark. Bednar was fantastic in his first full Yankees season, racking up 35 saves — the most by a Yankees closer since Arolis Chapman’s 37 in 2019 — and a 2.47 ERA in 69.1 innings. He’s a pending free agent who has set himself up to cash in, and we’ll see whether the Yankees pay up.
Keep your eyes on Paul Blackburn, who pitched to a career-best 1.69 ERA — nearly three full runs fewer than his lifetime 4.46 ERA — in 85 innings. Although his 9.8 percent walk rate is concerning, he’s carved out a Luke Weaver-type role as a reliable swingman.

item.content:encoded:
Los New York Yankees están a horas de conocer si podrán contar con su capitán para la Serie Divisional de la Liga Americana. Aaron Judge continúa trabajando para recuperarse de una distensión en el sóleo de la pantorrilla derecha, pero el equipo todavía no ha tomado una decisión definitiva sobre su inclusión en el roster para enfrentar a los Tampa Bay Rays.
- LEER MÁS SOBRE: Dodgers vs Braves: revancha, poder y alto voltaje en la NLDS
- LEER MÁS SOBRE: Las claves de los cuatro Juegos 1 de las Series Divisionales de la MLB
Suscríbete al Newsletter de Unanimo y recibe gratis las últimas noticias. Dale click aquí
Judge no juega desde el 16 de septiembre, cuando sufrió la lesión durante el encuentro ante los Minnesota Twins. El problema llegó poco después de que el jardinero regresara de una fractura en la costilla derecha que lo mantuvo fuera durante buena parte de la temporada. En total, disputó apenas 66 partidos de temporada regular y bateó para .241, con 18 jonrones, 41 carreras producidas y .871 de OPS.
Sin embargo, el tres veces MVP de la Liga Americana ha acelerado su recuperación durante los últimos días. El jueves tomó turnos ante lanzadores en vivo en Yankee Stadium y este viernes volvió a realizar trabajo de bateo durante la práctica del equipo en Tampa Bay. También ha comenzado a correr sobre el terreno después de trabajar previamente en una caminadora antigravedad.
El principal interrogante está precisamente en la exigencia física que implica jugar en el jardín derecho. Judge todavía no ha corrido las bases desde que sufrió la lesión, aunque el manager Aaron Boone explicó que eso no necesariamente significa que el jugador deba completar esa prueba para ser incluido en el roster. El cuerpo médico tendrá un papel importante en la decisión.
El escenario también tiene una particularidad: el Juego 1 de la ALDS se disputará este sábado en el Tropicana Field, cuya superficie artificial es otro elemento que los Yankees deben considerar al evaluar el estado de la pantorrilla de Judge. Boone reconoció que el terreno entra en la valoración, especialmente por tratarse de una lesión muscular.
Nueva York, además, tendrá que decidir cómo utilizarlo en caso de que esté disponible. Judge ha señalado que su intención es regresar como jardinero derecho, mientras que una alternativa sería emplearlo como bateador designado o emergente. El problema es que los Yankees ya tienen competencia por el puesto de DH, con Ben Rice, Paul Goldschmidt y Luis García Jr. entre las opciones.
Ver esta publicación en Instagram
La incertidumbre llega después de que los Yankees demostraran que pueden producir sin su principal estrella. Nueva York barrió a los Boston Red Sox en la Serie de Comodines y los superó 18-2 en los dos encuentros, avanzando a una ALDS en la que enfrentará al equipo con el mejor récord de la Liga Americana durante la temporada regular.
Los Yankees deben entregar su roster de 26 jugadores antes de las 10:00 de la mañana del sábado, aproximadamente diez horas antes del primer lanzamiento. Para entonces tendrá que estar resuelta la gran pregunta que ha acompañado a Nueva York desde mediados de septiembre: si Aaron Judge estará listo para volver al terreno o tendrá que esperar una oportunidad más adelante en octubre.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Gerrit Cole set for first postseason start since Tommy John, Yankees mulling Aarond Judge decison
item.dc:creator: Abbey Mastracco; New York Daily News
item.description: ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — For all of the noise that has been made about the Yankees' use of analytics in recent years, their postseason decisions show the feel the club has for the game, something numbers can't quantify. Calling on Gerrit Cole to start Game 1 of the ALDS is one of those decisions. The Yankees may have four aces in their rotation, and the Rays have struggled against left-handers. But Cole, a right-hander, is the quintessential big-game pitcher. He's the guy who can set the tone for
item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — For all of the noise that has been made about the Yankees' use of analytics in recent years, their postseason decisions show the feel the club has for the game, something numbers can't quantify.
Calling on Gerrit Cole to start Game 1 of the ALDS is one of those decisions. The Yankees may have four aces in their rotation, and the Rays have struggled against left-handers. But Cole, a right-hander, is the quintessential big-game pitcher. He's the guy who can set the tone for his team in a meaningful way, and this start against the Tampa Bay Rays has extra meaning, being the first postseason appearance for Cole since his 2025 Tommy John surgery.
"It's incredibly special," Cole said Friday at Tropicana Field. "Coming back from surgery, I mean there's not much more I could ask for. I feel tremendously blessed. I feel that the people in the clubhouse that have contributed to the success this year deserve a lot of the credit. It's been a team effort overall, and so excited to go out and compete again."
Whether Cole competes with Aaron Judge is yet to be determined.
Judge could be active for this next round, even if he isn't ready for Game 1. The Yankees could include him on the roster to utilize him as a pinch hitter. The winner of the last three MVP Awards, Judge hit at Yankee Stadium on Thursday, and spent Friday working out nearby at GMS Field before joining the team for the workout day in St. Petersburg.
Judge took batting practice on the field, but did not run the bases. He declined to take questions from the media.
Manager Aaron Boone was non-committal on the status of his captain's strained right calf. Boone has not seen Judge run the bases, but did confirm that he has started running. The turf at the Trop could be reason enough to hold him out of action in this round, but if they can use him in New York, it might be advantageous to include him on the roster.
"[The turf] plays into it a little bit; it's just as far as him and the field, potentially," Boone said. "But we're looking at the days, so it's more, is he going to be available at some point in this series, potentially, as a player? That's what we're kind of weighing, and then seeing where he's at now these last few days having taken live BP. We'll see how today goes."
Whether the Yankees have Aaron Judge or not, Cole provides a presence.
It's been a learning experience for the 36-year-old as he progressed through rehab and through the season. The elbow injury that started with edema in 2024 and culminated in ulnar collateral ligament reconstruction in 2025 was the first major injury of a career that has spanned nearly 13 years. One of the more durable aces in the game, Cole is one of the few starters who still regularly throws 200 or more innings and makes 30 or more starts.
He edited and updated his routine this season as needed, ultimately going back to what has always worked for him in the past. Cole wanted to stay flexible and open to anything that could keep his elbow healthy, while also maintaining his effectiveness on the mound.
"Humans, we don't progress in a linear fashion, or there are times where we have to adapt," Cole said. "I spoke about just staying curious about the process earlier in the season; I thought that really carried us a long way in terms of making some of the adaptations."
Limited to 95 innings in 2024, and 127 this season, Cole is coming into the postseason with a well-rested arm. He last pitched 10 days ago against Tampa Bay in a 5 2/3-inning effort for his 10th win of the season. He knows the lineup, and he's pitching in a place he enjoys.
The Trop might be the target of ridicule from fans around the league, but if it's good enough for Cole, it can't be all that bad. He's also had success in Tampa, with a 3.32 ERA at Tropicana Field in 10 starts. The Rays have hit .218 off Cole in their home park.
Still, Cole said his arm doesn't feel any different than it usually does at this time of year, probably because he's gotten a lot of mileage out of it throughout the years, and he's coming off a 22-start season.
"I do feel just to an extent I've been pitching all year, and I feel that you know I've had opportunities to settle into the season and settle into the routine, so that there's really nothing new approaching me at this point," Cole said. "So in that regard, it's pretty much the same."
While he may have more excitement for this start given that it's his first in the postseason since the 2024 World Series, his mentality isn't any different either, because postseason starts are always special. Judge or not, Cole provides an intangible presence that can't be measured by any analytical formula.

item.title: [MLB.com] How Yankees' best hitter matches up with AL's best team
item.dc:creator: David Adler
item.description: Rice wrecked the Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, tacking two more homers onto the 41 he hit in the regular season. He showed he can carry this Yankees postseason lineup, Judge or no Judge. With that Judge uncertainty still ongoing, Rice is the most important hitter in the Bronx Bombers' lineup entering the American League Division Series against the Rays. He's one of the best hitters in the AL, facing the best team in the AL. And guess what? Rice KILLED the Rays all year. (Or did he?) The Rice
item.content:encoded:
Rice wrecked the Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, tacking two more homers onto the 41 he hit in the regular season. He showed he can carry this Yankees postseason lineup, Judge or no Judge.
With that Judge uncertainty still ongoing, Rice is the most important hitter in the Bronx Bombers' lineup entering the American League Division Series against the Rays. He's one of the best hitters in the AL, facing the best team in the AL.
And guess what? Rice KILLED the Rays all year.
(Or did he?)
The Rice vs. Rays matchup is one of the most interesting of the Division Series. Let's dive in.
What were Rice's numbers vs. Tampa Bay this season?
In 13 games against the Rays, Rice batted .356 with a .431 on-base percentage, .889 slugging percentage, 1.320 OPS and seven home runs. Facing the Rays was his Home Run Derby-away-from-the-Home Run Derby.
So he's just going to mash them in the ALDS?
Facing the Rays ace, Rice was just 1-for-10 with five strikeouts and a 50% swing-and-miss rate. Hmmm.
Rice did take Rasmussen deep once, but that's a pretty dominant pitching performance against him from a guy he could face twice in a best-of-five Division Series.
But "batter vs. pitcher" stats don't mean THAT much, right?
Right. Rice could definitely tee off against Rasmussen in the ALDS the same way he teed off against the Red Sox. But what we can take away from those regular-season at-bats is how Rasmussen attacked Rice, to get a clue what the Rays' approach might be in the playoffs.
So how did Rasmussen get Rice out?
With a steady diet of cutters and changeups -- and by mostly staying away from his four-seamer (except to go up the ladder with two strikes).
Rasmussen threw Rice cutters 41% of the time -- way higher than his typical cutter usage against left-handed hitters, which was 27% this season.
His next most-thrown pitch to Rice was the changeup at 23%, and only then did he mix in four-seamers, just 15% of the time (six of 39 total pitches to Rice).
Interesting … especially after we saw the way Rice hit against Boston. More on that in a sec.
Is Rasmussen's approach representative of how the Rays pitching staff went after Rice as a whole?
Yes. The Rays did not want to throw Rice a lot of straight fastballs. Their right-handed pitchers, led by Rasmussen but not just Rasmussen, threw him mainly changeups (25%) and cutters (21%). Their lefties threw Rice mostly changeups (24%) and sweepers (24%). You might notice that that's a lot of lefty-lefty changeups -- same-sided changeups are a rare pitch. But that doesn't bother the Rays if the changeup is the best pitch to get a certain hitter out.
Meanwhile, Tampa Bay only threw Rice 18% four-seamers. The Rays even threw him more sinkers (36 total) than they did four-seamers (33 total).
To sum up that strategy, it was basically: attack Rice with changeups, cutters/sweepers (depending on whether it was a right-handed or left-handed pitcher) and sinkers.
Why would they pitch him that way?
Rice is the single best four-seam fastball hitter in the Majors this year. Between the regular season and playoffs, he's batting .347 and slugging an MLB-best .855 against them, with 17 home runs.
Highest batting value vs. 4-seamers this season
1. Ben Rice: +25 runs created 
2. Bryce Harper: +23 runs created 
3-T. Pete Crow-Armstrong: +20 runs created 
3-T. Bryce Eldridge: +20 runs created 
5-T. Yordan Alvarez: +18 runs created 
5-T. Kazuma Okamoto: +18 runs created
So it makes a ton sense that the savvy Rays would want to throw him junkballs instead of fastballs.
Tampa Bay's sinkers to Rice outnumbering their four-seamers makes basic sense, too. Rice's run value vs. sinkers in the regular season was minus-2, so his results against them were a small net negative for the Yankees.
Is that the Rays pitching to their own strengths, or to Rice's weaknesses?
Both. The Rays pitching staff was already throwing fewer four-seamers than most MLB teams. So it's not like they changed their approach just because of the damage Rice can do against heaters.
Tampa Bay threw four-seamers just under 28% of the time this season, bottom-10 in the Majors and bottom-three in the American League (only the Red Sox and Royals threw fewer).
And the changeup -- the pitch the Rays threw to Rice the most -- is Tampa Bay's signature pitch. The Rays threw by far the most changeups of any team this season, with 21% usage. Pitchers like Rasmussen, All-Star closer Bryan Baker, Nick Martinez, Griffin Jax and Ian Seymour threw changeups by the hundreds.
Rice is not a bad changeup hitter, either. He generally hits cutters pretty well, too. He's just a really elite four-seam fastball hitter.
That's a lot of changeup specialists. But what about "Fastball Freddy" Peralta?
You might think the one chance Rice will have in the ALDS to take a bunch of rips at heaters is whenever the Rays face Freddy Peralta. He's nicknamed "Fastball Freddy" for a reason, after all -- Peralta has relied on his four-seamer for years.
But wait a minute. Since the Rays traded for Peralta at this year's Deadline … they've even got him throwing more changeups. Peralta's changeup usage vs. lefties before he got to the Rays was just under 24%. With the Rays, it's up to 34%.
Lucky for Rice, Freddy hasn't abandoned the fastball, though. He's still throwing right around 50% four-seamers to lefty sluggers in Tampa Bay.
So there's some good news for Rice after all.
Yep. And it's not just that.
While Rice might have struggled against Rasmussen and all those cutters and changeups (except the one cutter he homered against), he had plenty of success against other Rays pitchers, even ones using a similar approach.
Rice smacked around Martinez, Seymour and Peralta (when he was still on the Mets), including a homer off Peralta's changeup and Seymour's sinker, a double off Martinez's changeup and base hits off Martinez's righty-lefty cutter and Seymour's lefty-lefty sweeper.
In other words, Rice has shown he can handle the Rays' arsenals -- he just needs to actually do it against Rasmussen (and Griffin Jax to a lesser extent).
Any other good signs for Rice?
Sure. If the Rays try to go after him with sinkers over four-seamers … he just needs to keep doing what he was doing in the Wild Card Series.
Both of Rice's home runs in Game 1 against the Red Sox were off sinkers -- and upper-90s sinkers, too. He hit his first one lefty-lefty off a 97 mph sinker from Erik Miller, and his second one off another 97 mph sinker from righty Brayan Bello.
And it's not like you can throw Rice zero four-seamers in a whole series. Then, when he does get his chance, he's going to rip them -- like the 110 mph double he ripped off a 99 mph four-seamer at the top of the zone from Red Sox ace Payton Tolle.
What else?
Rice should have a much better platoon situation than he did in the Wild Card Series.
The Red Sox were a historically lefty-heavy pitching staff. The Rays have a lot more righties. (Consider this: Over 70% of Tampa Bay's pitches were thrown by right-handers this season; barely 40% of Boston's were thrown by righties.)
So Rice should start his at-bats with the advantage more often -- and he has a .970 OPS vs. righties this season, sixth-best in the Majors behind only Yordan Alvarez, Rafael Devers, Bryce Harper, Juan Soto and Nick Kurtz.
The Rays will probably try to use their changeups as the equalizer -- for a right-handed pitcher facing a lefty hitter, offspeed stuff can be the go-to choice -- but Rice is a dangerous enough hitter to overpower that.
Plus, even when he does face a lefty, Rice is a fine lefty-lefty hitter in his own right. He has an .803 OPS in lefty-lefty matchups this season after rapping three hits off good Red Sox lefties in the Wild Card round -- his homer off Miller, his double off Tolle and a single off Alec Gamboa.
Rice has become a superstar-level hitter. The Rays can't change that, no matter how smart their plan against him. Rice and the Rays have seen a lot of each other, and both teams have to know that his at-bats could swing the Division Series.

item.title: [Newsday] Was Yankees' Gerrit Cole's postseason resume the difference in deciding the ALDS Game 1 starter?
item.dc:creator: Erik Boland

Not all that much, but some. It was not a surprising announcement and one, considering Cole’s resume, that was somewhat expected. It was one thing to tell Cole, the ace of pr
item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — One measure of just how good the Yankees' rotation has been this season (and now two games into the postseason) is this oddity:
By choosing to go with Gerrit Cole in American League Division Series Game 1 against the Rays on Saturday night, the Yankees actually left themselves open to second-guessing.
Not all that much, but some.
It was not a surprising announcement and one, considering Cole’s resume, that was somewhat expected.
It was one thing to tell Cole, the ace of pretty much every rotation he’s been a part of, that Cam Schlittler would start Game 1 of the Wild Card Series against the Red Sox.
Schlittler, the presumed American League Cy Young Award winner after going 14-6 with a league-low 1.95 ERA, had one of the best seasons any Yankees pitcher has ever had.
Cole himself would have tabbed Schlittler to start Game 1 against the Red Sox (the Yankees did debate starting Max Fried in Game 1 against Boston but ultimately chose not to outthink themselves and went with the no-brainer decision to start Schlittler).
But telling Cole, who is 11-6 with a 2.77 ERA in 22 career postseason starts — including getting the nod in eight Game 1s — that he would be bypassed for this one even in favor of the red-hot-down-the-stretch Carlos Rodon, might have been dicey.
Based on late-season accomplishment, Rodon certainly belonged in the discussion. As manager Aaron Boone put it Friday before his team worked out at Tropicana Field, Rodon wasn’t merely in play for ALDS Game 1.
“Carlos has been a consideration, literally, [for] Game 1 of the Wild Card, 2 of the Wild Card, potentially Game 3, and every game moving forward,” said Boone, who added that Rodon will start either Game 3 or 4 of this series. “So it's one of those difficult decisions we have, one of those good difficult decisions we have, because we have four guys that are very high-end. So it's at least a conversation every time.”
Rodon put himself in the conversation with his work during the last month-plus. The lefthander, who had two separate stints on the injured list, went 7-3 with a 2.67 ERA in 16 starts and was particularly good late, pitching better than anyone in the rotation not named Schlittler with a 3-1 record and a 1.89 ERA in his final seven starts.
Cole, meanwhile, wasn’t nearly as good as the season drew to a close. He went 10-9 with a 3.61 ERA in 22 starts after beginning the year on the IL while recovering from Tommy John surgery, but in his last seven starts, he went 4-3 with a 4.46 ERA, allowing 11 homers in 40 1/3 innings. He allowed seven home runs in a span of 9 1⁄3 innings against the Padres and Mets and then gave up another one against the Diamondbacks, making it eight in a 13-inning span.
Looking at each pitcher’s last start of the season against the Rays also boosted Rodon’s candidacy for Game 1 of this series.
Facing the Rays on Sept. 22 in the first game of a doubleheader with the Yankees still mathematically alive for the AL East title, Rodon produced perhaps his best outing of the season in a 2-0 victory, allowing three hits in a season-high eight innings.
“One of the best-pitched games I saw all year,” one rival scout said that day.
Facing the Rays in a game without meaning a day later — Tampa Bay had clinched the division title by winning the second game of the Sept. 22 doubleheader — Cole allowed two runs and three hits, including a home run, in 5 2/3 innings of a 9-2 victory. He walked three and struck out eight.
“I thought Carlos really, really pitched well down the stretch,” Cole said on Friday.
But the Yankees weighed more than the stretch run.
The pitchers’ respective postseason resumes don’t compare, for one. Cole has been good far more often than not in his 22 starts, 12 of those with the Yankees, for whom he’s gone 5-2 with a 2.93 ERA. Rodon has been the opposite, 1-3 with a 7.53 ERA in eight games (six of those with the Yankees, going 1-2 with a 6.92 ERA).
Part of the calculus has been Cole’s relative consistency over the years against the Rays and, more significant, at Tropicana Field, where the Rays tied for MLB’s best home record at 55-26 this season.
Cole is 2-4 with a career 3.32 ERA in 10 starts at the Trop and 2-2, 3.52 in six starts as a Yankee in this quirky ballpark. Rodon hasn’t been bad in three career Tropicana Field outings, 0-1 with a 3.68 ERA, but doesn't have nearly the track record there that Cole has.
Cole didn’t throw especially well in this stadium in his one start there this season on July 8, allowing three runs and seven hits in 6 1/3 innings of a 3-0 loss.
Still, as Boone said: “I feel like he's always thrown the ball really well here. Not that that's everything.”
Though not the lone factor in swaying the Yankees, it clearly was far from an insignificant one.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees will have their toughest test yet against the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS.
The Rays, who have arguably been not only the best team in the American League for much of the campaign, but also in all of Major League Baseball, always find ways to win.
While the Yankees are much more talented than the Rays in terms of payroll, on paper, and in other ways, this is not a series the Yankees are going to just walk away with. There's a reason why Tampa Bay won the division, and it is going to show that in this series.
Keeping everybody healthy for the Yankees is a top priority, but unfortunately, that doesn't look guaranteed.
For Yankees slugger Aaron Judge, it remains uncertain whether he'll play.
There's a lot of hope that Judge might eventually be activated in this series, but the latest reports suggest it will take time, if the Yankees decide to do so.
"Judge's status for the Yankees' AL Division Series matchup against the top-seeded Tampa Bay Rays remains up in the air and is unlikely to be decided until shortly before the series begins Saturday, sources familiar with the deliberations told ESPN.
"Some in the organization want him to play. Others, wary of him further aggravating the injury and imperiling him for the remainder of the postseason, would prefer to wait another week. Further complicating matters is the likelihood that Judge could be resigned to designated hitter duties, potentially taking at-bats from Luis Garcia Jr," Jeff Passan of ESPN wrote.
There's unfortunately so much that has to happen for the Yankees over the next 24 hours for this to be a reality, and the biggest one is that even if Judge does return, there's going to be a big question about whether he's the same type of player that everybody expects him to be.
Regardless, the Yankees have to feel somewhat confident that he's going to be good to go, as Judge is the best hitter in Major League Baseball, and having him in the lineup, even if he's not fully healthy, completely changes the dynamic of this lineup.

item.description: The New York Yankees enter the offseason with nine arbitration-eligible players projected to cost a combined $36.7 million in 2027, according to MLB Trade Rumors' Matt Swartz, who creates the projections on an annual basis.
