item.content:encoded:
Well that's how you win a playoff series! The Yankees swept aside an inferior Red Sox squad, outscoring their opponents, 17-2, in two games in the Bronx. They are set for a date with the Rays in what should be a thrilling ALDS. However, before we get to that, we get to introduce our first Sequence of the Week of the postseason, Cam Schlittler setting the tone in Game 1 for the eventual sweep of Boston.
We join Schlittler in a packed house at 161st St. and River Ave., the Yankees ace set to throw the first pitch of this seventh playoff meeting between eternal foes. He is the best pitcher in the AL, the presumptive Cy Young winner after posting the third-lowest ERA (1.95) by a starter in a season in franchise history. He owns the Red Sox in his young career and is looking to author another chapter in his postseason biography after tossing eight scoreless innings and striking out a dozen to eliminate the Red Sox in Game 3 of last year's AL Wild Card Series. The Red Sox offense may have been hobbled by injury in September, but they are not a group to be trifled with, starting with leadoff hitter Roman Anthony. Anthony missed most of the season with a torn finger ligament but returned at the end of August to post a 119 wRC+ in his final 25 games.
Schlittler certainly wants to declare a statement of intent from the first batter he faces, particularly the face of the Boston franchise. Everybody in the stadium and watching the broadcast knows a heater is coming first pitch, the only question is how fast.
We have our answer. Schlittler throws one of the fastest pitches of his season, dotting this 101 mph four-seamer on the corner away and at the knees for strike one. If anyone had any doubts whether Schlittler would be amped up for this start, this pitch is a resounding yes.
With the adrenaline coursing through his veins, it looks like Schlittler has access to a couple more mph on his fastball. He looks to take advantage of this fleeting boost in velo with another four-seamer to Anthony, convinced that he can throw it by the dangerous Boston lefty.
This one comes in at *just* 100 mph. Austin Wells sets a target up and in and Schlittler doesn't miss his spot by much, tugging this pitch just a few inches inside. It starts as a ball out of his hand and never really deviates toward the zone, making for a pretty straightforward take by Anthony.
After two pitches, it appears Schlittler's release is better aligned for that outside lane than to the glove side. Anthony showed zero interest in offering at the first pitch fastball called for a strike, so Schlittler and Wells go back to that well.
Schlittler throws almost an identical copy of the first pitch of the game, dotting another 101 mph four-seamer low and away. Same pitch, same result. Anthony is clearly hunting something up and on the inner half. It wouldn't make sense for him to be guarding against the breaking ball below the zone considering Schlittler threw a fastball roughly 90-percent of the time during the regular season.
It's been a slightly different approach from Schlittler to start the game, as he generally likes to live up in the zone with all three of his fastballs. That partially helps to explain Anthony's passivity against the two in-zone four-seamers low, however that approach now has him in the hole, 1-2. There's no subtlety to the following pitch selection, Schlittler looking to bully Anthony into submission with another heater over the plate.
This is Schlittler's third four-seamer at 101, though this one catches way more plate than the other two. All the same, Anthony still can't catch up despite knowing exactly what's coming, his late swing slashing the pitch foul back to the screen.
Following that foul ball, Schlittler introduces his first wrinkle of the AB. After finally establishing his four-seamer in the zone but above the knees, Schlittler has the situation perfectly set up to get Anthony to chase a curveball in the dirt.
You might wonder why an MLB hitter would swing at a pitch that bounces in front of home plate. However, out of the hand this curveball looks exactly like the four-seamer in the zone that immediately preceded it. Because he has to stay geared up for 101, Anthony is almost forced into starting his swing before that curveball's downward break kicks in, leaving him no chance to check his swing in time. I'll admit I was shocked to see Schlittler throw a curveball this early in the game. I was expecting a diet of purely fastballs in the first inning and maybe even the whole first time through the order before using the curveball later in the game as a change of speeds and change of look.
Here's the full sequence:
This outing was vintage Schlittler against Boston, but with an extra twist that could vault the Yankees ace into truly untouchable territory this postseason. He threw a career-high 32 curveballs to the tune of a gaudy 50-percent whiff rate. It surely confounded the Red Sox game plan against him and they were helpless against the Uncle Charlie for the entirety of his outing. Even if he ups the fastball usage in subsequent starts, the curveball usage rate in this game plants the seed of doubt in the mind of anyone attempting to game plan for Schlittler. Don't be surprised to see his calling card elevated heater rack up whiffs in bunches now that hitters have to be mindful of the hook.
Though not quite as stratospherically dominant as last season's Wild Card start against the Red Sox, Schlittler still found a way to silence Boston without his A-1 fastball command. He threw a career-high 117 pitches across 6.1 scoreless, striking out ten to join Bob Gibson as the only other pitcher in MLB history with multiple scoreless starts with double-digit strikeouts against the Red Sox in the playoffs. Needless to say, we are excited to see what brilliance he cooks up next.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees have gotten off to an incredibly fast start to the 2026 MLB postseason. They made quick work of their arch rival Boston Red Sox in the best-of-three Wild Card series, outscoring them 18-2 in a 2-0 series win.
New York will next meet their division winner Tampa Bay Rays in the best-of-five ALDS. That series begins Saturday in Tampa Bay and continues there on Monday before coming back to the Bronx next Wednesday.
Once again, the Yankees will head into the division series on the heels of a lights-out performance from their ace right-hander Cam Schlittler. In Game 1 against Boston, he hurled 6 ⅓ scoreless innings while racking up 10 strikeouts.
Potential reinforcements
Following Wednesday’s series conclusion in Game 2, Schlittler spoke on currently injured outfielder Aaron Judge. Per Greg Joyce of the New York Post, the ace said that he believes Judge is the best player in baseball and that the club will only get stronger upon his return.
The 34-year-old appeared in just 66 games this season, missing a huge chunk of time through the summer before briefly returning in September. He unfortunately suffered a moderate calf strain Sept. 16 and has been on the injured list since.
When he was on the field, Judge admittedly was not quite playing like himself. Across 285 plate appearances, he slashed .241/.360/.511 (.871 OPS) with 18 home runs and 41 RBIs.
With the ALDS versus the Rays beginning Saturday, that will mark 17 days since Judge suffered the calf strain. Only time will tell whether he will be healthy enough to play, though there is some serious doubt on that.
Series outlook
For the Yankees side of things, it will be either righty Gerrit Cole or lefty Carlos Rodón on the mound for Game 1 of the ALDS. That choice from the club will come out in the next couple of days.
Schlittler will be on five days’ rest to pitch Game 2 on Monday, before lefty Max Fried gets the ball in Game 3 back in the Bronx. Beyond that, a prospective Games 4 and 5 do not have pitching probables.
Surprisingly enough, despite the two teams’ competitiveness over the last several years, they have yet to meet in the postseason following a normal 162-game season. It will be the first time each club has headed to the other’s venue for playoff baseball in their histories.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees benched Jazz Chisholm Jr. for Game 1 of the Wild Card Series on Tuesday night. Manager Aaron Boone started Anthony Volpe at second base against left-hander Payton Tolle.
Chisholm sat and watched the Yankees win 9-0 without him.
On Wednesday, he got his chance. He made sure everyone noticed.
Chisholm Delivers in Game 2 for the Yankees
Chisholm was back in the lineup for Game 2 against right-hander Sonny Gray and immediately made an impact on both sides of the ball.
In the sixth inning, he tracked down a shallow fly from Adley Rutschman, turning his back to the infield and making the grab on the run. It turned what looked like a clean single into a highlight.
“I practice that play almost every day,” Chisholm said.
At the plate, he went 2-for-3 with a single in the sixth that helped load the bases during the decisive rally. In the seventh, with the game well in hand, he walked, stole second standing up, swiped third, and scored on an Austin Wells single.
The stolen bases in a lopsided game carried a familiar echo. On August 31, Red Sox radio voice Will Flemming called Chisholm a “bush-league player” for stealing bases in a blowout win over Boston. Flemming later apologized. Chisholm has not forgotten.
“I just wanted to keep things going,” Chisholm said. “No lead is safe in baseball and I’m just here to win. If he wants to hate, he can hate.”
What the Benching Meant
Chisholm said Wednesday that the outcome mattered more than the lineup card.
“I didn’t care if I played or not today, as long as we win,” Chisholm said. “Boone’s done a great job. I always think my manager has done a great job, especially when we’re winning.”
Why Chisholm Matters Going Forward
The Yankees head to Tampa Bay for the ALDS starting Saturday. The second base decision between Chisholm and Volpe will be one of Boone’s most important lineup calls throughout the series.
Boone acknowledged the balancing act.
“I feel like Jazz is an important part of this, especially moving forward,” Boone said. “We’re going to need both guys to win big.”
Chisholm sounded like a player who believes the best version of this team includes him in the lineup.
“When everyone’s working in sync like that, especially the talent we have on this team,” Chisholm said, “I feel like we’re unbeatable.”
Final Word for the Yankees
Jazz Chisholm Jr. sat for Game 1. He answered in Game 2 with two hits, a highlight catch, two stolen bases, and a message for anyone who questioned his approach.
Jazz has heard the criticism. He has heard the doubts about his maturity. And then he responded the way he always does.
“Every time we beat Boston, it’s amazing for me,” he said.
The ALDS is next. Chisholm is ready for it.

item.content:encoded:
There obviously are plenty of Yankees fans who aren’t enamored with Aaron Boone’s managerial body of work, but let’s give the man some flowers here for his and his team’s performance in their wild-card series blowout of the Red Sox.
Boone, still looking for his first World Series title in nine seasons on the job, managed circles around Boston’s Chad Tracy in the two-game sweep in The Bronx. That is indisputable.
Tracy’s hiring after Alex Cora was canned in April following a 10-17 start was largely credited with the Red Sox’s 32-5 run that vaulted them back into playoff position this summer. But he looked like a panicked manager in quick-hooking starters Payton Tolle and Sonny Gray with matching 1-0 deficits in the fifth inning of each game — only to watch the Yankees hammer his bullpen for an 18-2 aggregate drubbing in their two wins.
Boone certainly benefitted from starters Cam Schlittler and Max Fried pitching to a 0.73 ERA with one run allowed over a combined 12 ⅓ innings.

item.content:encoded:
Por Nelson de la Rosa
Prensa CBPC
SANTO DOMINGO, RD – El 1 de octubre de 1961, Roger Maris llegó al último partido de la temporada con 60 cuadrangulares, exactamente la misma cantidad que Babe Ruth había conectado en 1927. Pero le faltaba uno.
En la cuarta entrada, frente al derecho Tracy Stallard, de los Boston Red Sox, Maris envió la pelota por encima de la verja del jardín derecho del Yankee Stadium. Era su jonrón 61 y con él establecía una nueva marca de Grandes Ligas para una temporada.
La persecución del récord había acompañado a Maris durante buena parte de aquel verano. Su compañero Mickey Mantle también estuvo en carrera y terminó la campaña con 54 cuadrangulares, pero fue Maris quien llegó hasta el último día con la posibilidad de superar una de las cifras más famosas del béisbol.
Maris terminó 1961 con 61 jonrones y 141 carreras impulsadas y conquistó por segundo año consecutivo el premio al Jugador Más Valioso de la Liga Americana. Su récord sobrevivió durante 37 años, hasta que Mark McGwire conectó 70 en 1998.
Precisamente aquella carrera de 1998 tuvo como uno de sus grandes protagonistas a un pelotero del Caribe. El dominicano Sammy Sosa conectó 66 cuadrangulares con los Chicago Cubs y, aunque terminó detrás de McGwire, protagonizó una de las temporadas ofensivas más extraordinarias de la historia.
Sosa volvería a superar la barrera de los 60 en dos ocasiones: conectó 63 en 1999 y 64 en 2001. De esa manera se convirtió en el único jugador en la historia de las Grandes Ligas con tres temporadas de 60 o más jonrones.
El paso del tiempo fue colocando también a otros bateadores caribeños cerca de cifras que alguna vez parecieron inalcanzables. David Ortiz, también dominicano, llegó a 54 jonrones con Boston en 2006, mientras el curazoleño Andruw Jones disparó 51 con Atlanta en 2005.
El venezolano Eugenio Suárez alcanzó 49 en 2019, superando los 47 que Andrés Galarraga había conseguido en 1996. Ese mismo año, el cubano Jorge Soler terminó con 48 cuadrangulares, la mayor cantidad conseguida en una temporada por un jugador nacido en Cuba, dejando atrás los 47 de Rafael Palmeiro.
Entre los nacidos en México, Vinny Castilla tiene como tope los 46 jonrones que conectó con Colorado en 1998, mientras Carlos Delgado alcanzó 44 con Toronto en 1999, una de las mayores demostraciones de poder para un bateador nacido en Puerto Rico.
Son números que ayudan a dimensionar lo ocurrido aquel 1 de octubre de 1961. Cuando Roger Maris conectó el 61, estaba entrando en un territorio que ningún bateador había alcanzado antes en una temporada de Grandes Ligas.
Han pasado 65 años de aquel batazo. El récord cambió de dueño, aparecieron nuevas generaciones de grandes jonroneros y el Caribe terminó escribiendo también algunos de los capítulos más poderosos de una historia que tuvo en aquel jonrón 61 de Roger Maris uno de sus momentos inolvidables.

item.content:encoded:
The goal of Major League Baseball is to score more runs than your opponent, piling on as many as possible to ease the job of your pitchers. In the postseason, the value of each individual run rises tenfold. That is to say if Jazz Chisholm Jr. was smart enough to steal second and third base with a six-run lead in a regular-season Yankees-Red Sox rivalry game, he was certainly keen enough to do it again in the postseason.
When Chisholm Jr. sprinted around the bags in the four-game series finale back in August, Red Sox radio announcer Will Flemming called him "bush league" and implored the lefty reliever on the mound to both drill Austin Wells and go punch Chisholm. With an 8-2 lead on Wednesday in the seventh inning of Game 2, Chisholm Jr. saw the exact same opportunity - and did the exact same thing.
Did Flemming ever return from his nebulous "planned absence," which conveniently came as soon as the Sox returned home from that controversial series? If so, would love to hear his thoughts on this!
Jazz Chisholm Jr. responded to Aaron Boone's plea by tying a bow on Yankees-Red Sox
Chisholm Jr. had a ton of fun on the field Wednesday night, but he's on record that he doesn't enjoy platooning, especially in Game 1 of a heated playoff series. Knowing he planned to keep him off his feet against a lefty in Payton Tolle, Aaron Boone texted him ahead of time, demanding his attention and asking him to rise to the challenge.
"Hey, you might be the most important person in the building tonight. We need you to be ready to go for the biggest spot, potentially," Boone texted Chisholm Jr. prior to Game 1, per Chris Kirschner of The Athletic.
He wasn't needed in the 9-0 victory, but you could certainly read that as Boone making sure that Chisholm Jr.'s antenna was up from the jump, and that he planned to be himself when called upon. We knew it wouldn't, but the ugliness in Flemming's voice at the end of the Yankees and Red Sox's final regular season matchup did not deter Chisholm Jr. from continuing to play through the whistle. That's what the postseason is all about. Hell, that's what every opportunity to take the field is all about.
If Flemming didn't learn that lesson in his first 47 years on earth, or back in August, he certainly should've learned it on Wednesday. If he was still watching at that point. After all, he's on record that a six-run lead is apparently game over in his book.

item.title: [yanksgoyard.com] Cody Bellinger takes Chad Tracy's gift, ends Red Sox season in Yankees legacy moment
item.dc:creator: Adam Weinrib
item.description: Though Cody Bellinger didn't spend much of his childhood in the new Yankee Stadium, that should've been all the more motivation for him to join the Yankees and make this place sound like the old one as often as he possibly could. On Wednesday night, with a chance to end the Red Sox season in Game 2 of the Wild Card Series, and with his champion dad Clay in the building (first pitch duties), he responded directly to Sox manager Chad Tracy opening the door with a pair of punishing blows. Payton To
item.content:encoded:
Though Cody Bellinger didn't spend much of his childhood in the new Yankee Stadium, that should've been all the more motivation for him to join the Yankees and make this place sound like the old one as often as he possibly could. On Wednesday night, with a chance to end the Red Sox season in Game 2 of the Wild Card Series, and with his champion dad Clay in the building (first pitch duties), he responded directly to Sox manager Chad Tracy opening the door with a pair of punishing blows.
Payton Tolle getting the 83-pitch early hook in Game 1 was somewhat defensible. He was losing grip. He's past a career high in innings. They have the horses. Removing Sonny Gray from this do-or-die game before the end of the fifth inning, midway through a masterpiece, was one of the silliest bits of overmanaging you'll see. Bringing in Erik Miller, who was victimized with two outs in the fifth in Game 1 to get victimized again was even sillier.
Bellinger smoked a two-out RBI single off Miller to add a second run to the Yankees' lead. The next time he strode to the plate, he made a much larger impact.
Cody Bellinger cements Yankees' ownership of the Boston Red Sox
Gone. Very gone. In a snap, the Yankees turned two productive outs and a three-run mash into an 8-1 ballgame. Losing Garrett Whitlock, who surrendered the bomb, might've been the Yankees' most prudent Rule 5 Draft move in franchise history. It's called the long game.
For those keeping track at home, the 2026 Red Sox rode a 32-5 midsummer stretch to the postseason, reached within a half-game of the Yankees and got high on their own supply. From that point forward, they were much closer to .500, losing impact role players and stars alike by the bowlful. Sox fans were undeterred. They continued to crow. They loved to laugh at Aaron Judge's injury troubles. They purported to be inside Cam Schlittler's head. If they truly were in there, they might've been able to pick up some knowledge on what it takes for a pitcher to go deep into games in the postseason and dominate.
And so, for the second season in a row, the Yankees have flushed the Sox out of the postseason - Boston actually doesn't even reach October this year, which begins tomorrow. Last year, it was Schlittler, the Massachusetts native, growing up on the big stage. He helped this year, too.
But this time around, it ended with Tracy hooking Gray for no apparent reason and Bellinger, a son of pinstripes, delivering the crushing blow. Maybe, just maybe, order has returned to the universe and karma has begun to punish the brashness of Bostonians in new and unique ways. Whitlock gagging, Garrett Crochet disintegrating after an Adley Rutschman slow play (the trade target the Sox outbid the Yankees for, by the way), and Caleb Durbin making the final out ... in a game Gray should've owned ... was a pretty clever way to get it done.
Thanks, Belli.

item.title: [MLB.com] After dad's first pitch, Bellinger lights up Bronx with huge night
item.dc:creator: Bryan Hoch
item.description: NEW YORK -- It was the middle of July, and Cody Bellinger was seated in a windowless press conference room deep inside Philadelphia’s Citizens Bank Park, having been announced as the MVP of the All-Star Game. Still dressed in his road gray Yankees uniform, Bellinger fielded questions from dozens of reporters, one daughter by his side and another snuggled in a fifth-row seat with her mother, Chase. “You always hope,” Clay said that night, “for your kids to do well -- whether that’s playing baseba
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK -- It was the middle of July, and Cody Bellinger was seated in a windowless press conference room deep inside Philadelphia’s Citizens Bank Park, having been announced as the MVP of the All-Star Game.
Still dressed in his road gray Yankees uniform, Bellinger fielded questions from dozens of reporters, one daughter by his side and another snuggled in a fifth-row seat with her mother, Chase.
“You always hope,” Clay said that night, “for your kids to do well -- whether that’s playing baseball or doing whatever they like to do. He’s been pretty good at it for quite a long time, so yeah, it’s fun.”
Pinstripes are an outsized piece of the family business now, with the younger Bellinger wearing the same No. 35 that his dad -- now a firefighter in Gilbert, Ariz. -- sported in a supporting role during the franchise’s most recent World Series dynasty.
“I definitely appreciate it. I'm able to appreciate it in the moment,” Bellinger said. “That was a cool moment -- just a great game. I’m happy I was able to contribute, and we've got a lot more work to do.”
The evening began with Clay toeing the rubber, tossing a ceremonial first pitch. Bellinger said he was told on Tuesday about the arrangement; squatting behind the plate, he later said: “I knew he was going to throw a strike.”
Dad delivered, popping the glove with a firm toss.
“He didn’t even warm up,” Bellinger said, with a grin.
Red Sox manager Chad Tracy pointed to the bullpen in the fifth inning, lifting starter Sonny Gray in favor of left-hander Erik Miller, who’d served up Ben Rice’s first homer in Game 1. The move again backfired; one of the league’s better left-on-left batters, Bellinger laced an RBI single that put the Yanks up by two runs.
“There’s no secret sauce,” Bellinger said. “For me, just take it as another at-bat. It felt like when I was playing baseball coming up, you didn't hear too much about the matchups. I was just playing baseball.”
The decision-making grew even more curious in the sixth, with three Yankees runs already in during that frame. Boston issued an intentional walk so Garrett Whitlock could face Bellinger. Tossing his bat aside, Rice wasn’t sure why.
“I was very surprised they were willing to face Cody Bellinger, a guy who absolutely thrives with runners in scoring position and has done it his whole career,” Rice said. “Interesting decision.”
Bellinger said he understood Boston’s thinking, noting Rice’s presence.
“He’s been red-hot, and it was in the back of my mind,” Bellinger said. “You never really know.”
The next swing set off bedlam in the Bronx, with Bellinger launching a Whitlock changeup over the right-field wall for a three-run homer that sent popcorn and various liquids flying throughout the bleachers.
Bellinger made sure to savor his trot around the bases, soaking up the moment.
“Man, it's a good feeling,” Bellinger said. “I think that you enjoy it, but I feel like there's just so much more to do. So you obviously enjoy the moment, understand how cool it is, but keep on going.”

item.title: [New York Post] Aaron Judge takes another step toward potential Yankees playoff return: ‘I want to be in there’
item.dc:creator: Greg Joyce
item.description: Not even the bubbly and suds that dripped down his 6-foot-7 frame late Wednesday emboldened Aaron Judge enough to make any proclamations about his chances of being on the Yankees ALDS roster. But his teammates are at least giving him a chance. Access the Yankees beat like never before Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees. On a day that began with Judge going to Somerset to get another round of li
item.content:encoded:
Not even the bubbly and suds that dripped down his 6-foot-7 frame late Wednesday emboldened Aaron Judge enough to make any proclamations about his chances of being on the Yankees ALDS roster.
But his teammates are at least giving him a chance.
Access the Yankees beat like never before
Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
On a day that began with Judge going to Somerset to get another round of live at-bats and continue his running progression as he rehabs a right calf strain, the Yankees finished off a sweep of the Red Sox with a 9-2 win in Game 2 of the AL wild-card series in The Bronx.
“Saturday’s a long ways away,” Judge said, referring to Game 1 of the ALDS against the Rays. “But I’m doing everything I can, all morning, night, during the game, everything to prepare myself to be ready to go. Yeah, I want to be in there. But we’ll see what happens.”
Wednesday marked two weeks since Judge sustained the calf injury, and while he tried to defy the odds and make a late push to be on the roster for the wild-card series, the Yankees ultimately left him off because he was not ready.
Whether he can be ready to go by Saturday remains to be seen, especially with the complicating factor of having to play on the turf at Tropicana Field, which can be troublesome for players dealing with soft-tissue leg injuries.
“We just finished the wild-card [series]. We’ll get into that as we get closer,” Judge said amid the champagne celebration. “I got nothing for you on that yet, but my job is to continue to get ready. That’s what I’ve been doing every day.”
Judge’s around-the-clock treatment is apparently what kept him missing from Tuesday’s pregame player introductions ahead of Game 1. He arrived in the dugout by first pitch, and then Wednesday, pulled up a seat around the sixth inning to watch his teammates finish the win.
The three-time AL MVP said he did not run the bases Wednesday afternoon in Somerset, which is a hurdle he will likely have to clear to prove he can be a right fielder for the ALDS.
“I think it’s been encouraging that a couple nights ago [Monday] for the workout he was able to get out there for live BP,” manager Aaron Boone said before Game 2. “Again, that wasn’t just, he’s just going out for live BP. He had to check a lot of boxes for the trainers and the strength guys to say, ‘OK, you’re ready for that, you can go do that.’

Thank you
“So I feel like in the couple weeks since the injury, he’s made real strides and significant improvements. And hopefully we’re in a position to make another decision in a couple of days.”
It is possible the Yankees could carry Judge on their ALDS roster to serve as a DH, but even he has acknowledged that it would be best for the team if he can return as a right fielder because of the logjam at DH/first base involving Game 1 hero Ben Rice, Luis García Jr. and Paul Goldschmidt.

item.title: [wral.com] Fried, Bellinger and García lead Yankees over Red Sox 9-2 for 2-game Wild Card Series sweep
item.dc:creator: RONALD BLUM
item.description: NEW YORK (AP) — One year after rallying past the Red Sox to win an AL Wild Card Series, the New York Yankees battered Boston. Max Fried dominated the Red Sox in the playoffs for the second straight year, Cody Bellinger and Luis García Jr. homered, and the Yankees rolled to a 9-2 win Wednesday night that completed a two-game sweep. Other WRAL Top Stories “We enjoyed tonight. We got a lot more work to do,” Bellinger said. New York will face AL East champion Tampa Bay in an AL Division Series start
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK (AP) — One year after rallying past the Red Sox to win an AL Wild Card Series, the New York Yankees battered Boston.
Max Fried dominated the Red Sox in the playoffs for the second straight year, Cody Bellinger and Luis García Jr. homered, and the Yankees rolled to a 9-2 win Wednesday night that completed a two-game sweep.
Other WRAL Top Stories
“We enjoyed tonight. We got a lot more work to do,” Bellinger said.
New York will face AL East champion Tampa Bay in an AL Division Series starting Saturday.
“The fans were electric from the first pitch and the boys were hungry. We got a young, hungry team here," Yankees captain Aaron Judge said as teammates sprayed him with bubbly during the clubhouse celebration. “This makes me feel young every single time.”
Judge missed this series because of a calf injury and isn't sure whether he will play against the Rays, who beat New York 7-6 in the season series.
“Saturday’s a long ways away," he said.
Clinging to a 2-1 lead after Willson Contreras homered to end Boston's 26-inning postseason scoreless streak, the Yankees broke open the game with a six-run sixth after Spencer Jones reached on a wild pitch while striking out leading off — with the help of a video review.
García, acquired at the trade deadline, had three hits in his first postseason start, and Bellinger had four RBIs that included a three-run homer capping the sixth-inning burst that put New York ahead 8-1.
“Step one,” said Bellinger, who caught the ceremonial first pitch from his dad, Clay, a 2000 Yankees World Series champion. “Now we got to go into Tampa and play against a tough team."
Boston, which reached the playoffs after rebounding from a 32-46 start, lost last year's wild-card matchup after defeating the Yankees in the opener.
“Regardless of all the special things that happened this summer, and there was quite a few, the goal is to win the World Series and that ended for us tonight, so it’s frustrating,” Red Sox manager Chad Tracy said. “There’s a lot of things you can say, but in the moment right now, I think the guys only care that we lost. And it’s going to take some time to get over that.”
Boston, which also got a seventh-inning homer from Nick Sogard off Will Warren, was missing leadoff hitter Roman Anthony because of a hand injury. The Red Sox were held to a .117 average in the series (7 for 60) with 18 strikeouts and outscored 18-2.
New York hit .382 in the series. Boston's bullpen had a 20.25 ERA.
“We played great baseball in a lot of ways here, obviously anchored by our two great starters," Yankees manager Aaron Boone said.
Yankees batters hit .450 (9 for 20) with runners in scoring position after finishing 19th among the 30 teams with a .246 RISP during the regular season.
“I feel like it’s a whole new level from regular season to these last two days,” Austin Wells said.
A day after Cam Schlittler led New York to a 9-0 win, Fried pitched three-hit ball over six innings to win a postseason game for the first time since the 2021 World Series clincher with Atlanta.
New York started eight left-handed hitters against Sonny Gray, back on the mound where his career derailed during a dismal Yankees stretch in 2017 and ’18.
García's fourth-inning homer put the Yankees ahead and Bellinger, one of the top lefty-on-lefty hitters in the major leagues, added a fifth-inning RBI single against left-handed Erik Miller, who had just relieved.
Gray was disappointed he wasn't allowed to face Bellinger.
“I think I’m the best pitcher in the American League going through the order a third time. I think that’s a fact,” Gray said. "I would’ve liked to live or die with me in that moment, but that's the competitor I am. And, yeah, I think you can probably ask the guys and they felt the same way. So I felt strong. I felt confident. I felt convicted.”
Jones struck out both to start and end the bottom of the sixth, a weird half-inning that included a wild pitch, throwing error, stolen base, bunt single and intentional walk to Ben Rice that preceded Bellinger's homer.
"I can’t believe they were willing to face a guy like Belli with men on base there," Rice said.
Garrett Crochet, who beat the Yankees in last year's Wild Card Series opener, hadn't pitched since April 25 because of left shoulder inflammation when he bounced a sweeper off Adley Rutschman's chest. The catcher picked up the ball and threw to first, where umpire John Libka signaled that Jones was out. The Yankees appealed and the call was reversed by the video umpire at the commissioner's office.
“I couldn’t believe he was there,” Boone said. "I saw the ball squirt away a little bit. I didn’t think that much of it, and looked up and I was, like, 'Oh, he’s safe.'''
Jones swiped second and kept going to third when Rutschman’s throw skipped into center. Rookie George Lombard Jr. singled for his first postseason RBI, Jazz Chisholm Jr. singled and Trent Grisham loaded the bases with a bunt single.
Wells' sacrifice fly against Garrett Whitlock increased the lead to 4-1, Ryan McMahon hit an RBI groundout and Rice, who had four hits and six RBIs in the opener, was intentionally walked. Bellinger reached down and pulled a changeup into the right-center field seats.
Fried struck out six and walked one. He has allowed one run over 12 1/3 innings in the two Wild Card Series against the Red Sox.
“Definitely wasn’t sharp from the get-go but just wanted to challenge them, not try to give any free passes, especially in the first inning," Fried said.
After a night of celebration and a day off, the Yankees will head to Florida on Friday.
“There’s just so much more to do,” Bellinger said after the big night with his father on hand. “So obviously enjoy the moment, understand how cool it is, but keep on going.”
Up Next
New York RHP Gerrit Cole (10-9, 3.61), who would have started a third game against Boston, is likely to start Game 1 against the Rays.
___

item.title: [sports.yahoo.com] Once an imperfect fit, Luis Garcia Jr. becoming crucial to Yankees' World Series aspirations
item.dc:creator: Chelsea Janes
item.description: Luis Garcia Jr. was not a perfect fit for the Yankees when they traded for him. They needed an offensive catcher and relievers, and maybe a guy who could hit more than the people they had playing third, depending on one's perspective. But a lefty-hitting first baseman with defensive limitations? They already had a few of those. And yet, with a Division Series bid at stake against their most ancient rivals, Garcia delivered a resounding fourth-inning homer that broke a scoreless tie -- exactly wh
item.content:encoded:
Luis Garcia Jr. was not a perfect fit for the Yankees when they traded for him.
They needed an offensive catcher and relievers, and maybe a guy who could hit more than the people they had playing third, depending on one's perspective. But a lefty-hitting first baseman with defensive limitations? They already had a few of those.
And yet, with a Division Series bid at stake against their most ancient rivals, Garcia delivered a resounding fourth-inning homer that broke a scoreless tie -- exactly what the Yankees needed. He finished with a three-hit night.
"My mom has a good saying. She's always telling me never stop dreaming," Garcia said through an interpreter before the game. "…Having this opportunity to be here, being able to go out there and be part of the playoffs, go out and represent the Yankees, it feels great. And just hoping that I'm able to go out there and do the little things that can help us keep winning."
When the Yankees weighed options at the deadline, they had a perfectly functional first base situation that centered around Ben Rice and made room for Paul Goldschmidt against tough lefties. With Giancarlo Stanton on the way back from injury, they did not plan to have at-bats to spare at designated hitter, so they looked ill-equipped to navigate a logjam.
But Garcia was the best bat available -- at least of those players who were actually traded -- so they added him to a lineup that sometimes resembled a revolving door, but sometimes would need to revolve around him.
Garcia seemed to adjust to New York quickly. He was born here and grew up a Yankees fan, so playing at Yankee Stadium was aspirational, not intimidating. The 26-year-old isn't the type to stress much anyway. His demeanor is as easy as his swing and just as level. He hit .290 with an .842 OPS in August. He did not look overwhelmed.
Then, just as the Yankees began their final push for the postseason, Garcia stumbled into a vexing slump. He hit .105 with a .255 OPS and no extra-base hits in their last 10 games. The contact savant struck out 11 times in 38 at-bats. He pinch-hit in Game 1, his first career postseason at-bat, and grounded into a double play.
Aaron Boone chose to hit him third in Game 2 of his first ever playoff start anyway. And with the game still scoreless in the fourth, he clicked. He pulled a homer to right center that gave the Yankees the lead before singling twice more – once to left, once to right, a perfect display of the evolution that has turned him into a crucial piece of a World Series contender.
In the early years after the Nationals signed him, Garcia earned comparisons to Juan Soto, not necessarily because of his style, but because of his talent. Then, as now, Garcia had incredible bat-to-ball ability -- a smooth flick of the wrists he designed to mirror Robinson Cano and succeeded.
But through parts of six major league seasons, some of which Nationals officials later admitted probably came before he was ready, as they filled needs instead of prioritizing development, Garcia never quite emerged as the star he seemed capable of being. He hit for a high average as a Nationals regular over the last three seasons, but he settled for hitting pitches because he could get his bat on them instead of prioritizing clobbering.
That changed this year when an overhauled Nationals coaching staff and front office encouraged him to choose more pitches he could drive while also helping him use his lower half to move the bat instead of just relying on his hands.
"I think the biggest difference has to be using my back leg in a better way to help me generate more bat speed. Previously, since I think I was able to use my hands, the quickness of my hands and rely on that more," Garcia said through an interpreter. "But I worked really hard on incorporating my lower part of the body, especially my back leg, and I think that's what helped me get to where I am today."
Garcia's average bat speed jumped dramatically, from 72.4 miles per hour in 2025 to 74.3 miles per hour in 2026 – a jump that moved him from the 98th fastest in baseball into the top 50. He started pulling the ball in the air far more than he ever had before, and damage followed: Garcia's .831 OPS was the highest of his career by more than 50 points.
"Part of his success this year is he's a more mature player today," said Amed Rosario, who played with Garcia in Washington in 2025. "He's made adjustments over the years, and it's showing. The talent is there, but I think that's why he's having such a great season."
Rosario said he tried to help ease Garcia's transition to the Yankees -- one Garcia admitted he was anxious about in the hours after being traded.
"All the teammates that you're leaving behind, all the relationships you've built over the years, you're leaving behind and you're starting from zero," he said. So coming in, you feel a little afraid, if you will, that you have to do that over again. But I can tell you that from the moment that I walked into the clubhouse, that went away, that fear went away very quickly because the guys make me feel as part of this team immediately."
Now, Garcia looks at home in New York, where he is surrounded by family so much that he said recently it reminds him of being in the Dominican Republic.
"The energy we have in this team, the fans, the clubhouse, everything that is part of this team, it's a great spot to be here at this moment," Garcia Jr. said after the game.
As his interpreter shared his answer, Rosario and a handful of teammates interrupted. It was time to shower the newest Yankees hero in Budweiser and champagne.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are hoping to advance to the ALDS (obviously) and return the services of star outfielder Aaron Judge.
Judge was left off the Yankees' Wild Card roster against the Red Sox as he continues to battle a calf injury.
If the Yankees are to advance, it's possible that Aaron Judge will return to the roster, but how long will he last?
In a recent bold prediction, FanSided.com believes that if Judge is activated to the Yankees playoff roster, it will be a short-lived move.
More MLB on Heavy: Los Angeles Dodgers Announce 3 Sudden Roster Moves Amid MLB Playoffs
Aaron Judge Handed Cryptic Prediction
In a recent piece for FanSided.com, the contributors came up with 30 bold predictions, and one of them involved Aaron Judge, per Chris Landers:
Here is the headline for the cryptic prediction:
"Aaron Judge forces his way onto the Yankees roster — but doesn't last more than a game"
"This just has disaster written all over it. Judge suffered a Grade 2 calf strain on Sept. 16; less than two weeks later, he's publicly turning up the heat on his own team to let him on the Wild Card roster anyway. I doubt New York says no to its foundational star. I also doubt Judge is ready to be an impactful player."
Landers does have a point: if Judge does return, and he even swings the wrong way, his status could be in jeopardy.
It certainly would be something if the Yankees are able to advance to the Fall Classic without their megastar in Judge, which at this particular junction, feels entirely possible.

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK — For about 10 minutes, there was a ballgame.
The window opened around 9:56 p.m. ET on Wednesday. Boston first baseman Willson Contreras sliced a Max Fried fastball through the crisp Bronx air into the first row in right for a solo home run. That cut New York's lead in half. For the first time in this best-of-three wild-card series between longtime rivals, a Red Sox hitter touched home plate. And so, a glimmer of hope flickered in the visiting dugout as Game 2 flipped to the bottom of the sixth.
By 10:06 p.m., when rookie George Lombard Jr. laced an RBI single over the second baseman's head, that flame had already begun to falter. By the end of the inning, it was thoroughly extinguished.
Ten Yankees hitters came to the plate in the bottom of the sixth; six scored. Last year's AL Cy Young runner-up Garrett Crochet, injured for nearly the entire regular season, entered as a reliever and did not record an out (though he did strike out a batter). Boston's most trusted setup man, Garrett Whitlock, then entered the ballgame to serve up the final blow: a moon-scraping, three-run homer via Cody Bellinger that pushed New York's lead to seven.
Yankee Stadium rumbled as Bellinger's ball returned to Earth. Libations sprung into the sky like a Bellagio fountain of booze. Popcorn rained from the heavens. Bellinger rounded the sacks and entered the dugout to a tunnel of high-fives and atta-boys. The rest of this lopsided laugher was merely epilogue. By the ninth inning, Yankee fans were serenading the defeated Sox with "na, na, na, na, hey, hey, hey, goodbye." A few minutes later, they were hollering Sinatra's "New York, New York" as the Yankees strolled onto the diamond in a casual celebration.
No doubt — not a crumb — was left as to which is the better team.
"Total domination," a Yankees employee could be heard saying to a colleague in the champagne-soaked afterparty.
Predictably, New York skipper Aaron Boone offered Boston its flowers, but it was incredibly telling that the first question asked to him at his postgame media conference was: "Were you surprised by the margins of victory?"
"Yes," Boone, ever the politician, replied. "As I said, kind of all year, but even going into this series, that was a scary team to us, especially as well as they pitch. So for us to have the offensive outbreaks that we had here these last two nights and late, credit to those guys."
No more than 30 minutes later, Boone could be seen stampeding past the Yankees' clubhouse with neither a shirt nor a worry in the world. Nothing about this wild-card matchup provided any reason for him or any other Yankees employee to view the Red Sox as a scary team. No, this was a drubbing.
The Yankees outscored the Red Sox 18-2 across the two games. Boston mustered seven total hits, the fewest ever in a wild-card series (this format was implemented in 2022). It was a damning, telling offensive performance by a lineup that lacked both the impact and the depth of a legitimate championship contender. And while the Sox certainly felt the absence of Roman Anthony — the young slugger was scratched from the roster after suffering a wrist injury in Game 1 — not even a resuscitated, cryogenically unfrozen Ted Williams could've helped this Boston ballclub.
"You're thinking we're going to play closer games," Red Sox manager Chad Tracy admitted postgame. "They swung the bats extremely well. You've got to give them credit. It was frustrating."
Also frustrating, for Tracy, must have been the noticeable chasm in talent between the two clubs. The Red Sox drew deserved plaudits ahead of the series for their run-prevention prowess. And yet, on paper, the Yankees' rotation looked far more dangerous. And that's how it played out, with soon-to-be Cy Young winner Cam Schlittler dicing in Game 1 and Fried cruising in Game 2.
New York's decision to roster just 10 pitchers for this series was also an indication of the organization's immense level of confidence in its staff, particularly its starters. Why enter the battle with an army when a small special-ops unit can do the job?
"That's been the biggest strength for us throughout the year," Boone said of his team's rotation. "It sustained us. It got us through some difficult times. And I feel like they're all in a good place right now."
The Yankees' lineup is also clearly in a very good place. With captain Aaron Judge off the roster and watching from the dugout in a hoodie, New York's offense impressed. In both games, the Bombers needed a few innings to get revved up but eventually bludgeoned Boston's bullpen into submission. They tallied 26 total hits, the most by the Yanks in a two-game playoff span since 2004.
Judge's status for the ALDS against Tampa Bay remains a mystery. Fellow injured large man Giancarlo Stanton was on the roster for the wild-card round but wasn't called upon for a plate appearance. The Rays will likely present a stiffer challenge than whatever this was, but New York's lineup is humming at the perfect time.
Boston, meanwhile, didn't even get to play October baseball. When closer David Bednar punched out Caleb Durbin to conclude the proceedings, the clock read 11:14 p.m. ET.
September lived on. The Red Sox did not.

item.title: [nydailynews.com] Yankees set sights on tougher Rays team after embarrassing Red Sox with Wild Card sweep
item.dc:creator: Gary Phillips

He talked about it with his new teammates, many of whom spoke from experience that he did not have. The New York native got his first taste on Tuesday, going 0-for-1 off the bench in the Yankees’ easy 9-0 win over the Red Sox in Game 1 of the Wild Card Series. item.content:encoded:
Ever since the Yankees acquired Luis García Jr. on Aug. 3, the former National pictured what postseason baseball would look and feel like. He talked about it with his new teammates, many of whom spoke from experience that he did not have.
The New York native got his first taste on Tuesday, going 0-for-1 off the bench in the Yankees’ easy 9-0 win over the Red Sox in Game 1 of the Wild Card Series. But on Wednesday, he made his mark in his first postseason start, hammering a Sonny Gray sweeper in the fourth inning of Game 2.
The solo shot jumpstarted an offense that ensured there would not be a Game 3, as the Yankees cruised to a 9-2 victory after García got them on the board. Complete with an animated bat flip, he sparked the dugout’s first celebration of the night.
“It’s unforgettable to be in the middle of all that,” said García, draped in a towel. “I’m sure it’s something I’m not gonna forget.”
With Cody Bellinger adding a three-run homer in the sixth and Max Fried holding Boston to one earned run over six innings, the party eventually moved to the mound and then the home clubhouse at Yankee Stadium. There, the boozy Bombers celebrated a rather smooth sweep of their embarrassed archrivals with bubbly and beers.
“That was a scary team to us, especially as well as they pitch. So for us to have the offensive outbreaks that we had here these last two nights and late, credit to those guys,” Aaron Boone said. “That was very satisfying to play that well in these two games.”
Now another division foe awaits in the ALDS, and a tougher one at that.
The Yankees already know how formidable the Rays, their next playoff opponent, are, as the pinstripers failed to win the American League East for the second straight season because of Tampa Bay. Despite a luxury tax payroll that fell $228.9 million short of the Yankees’, the Rays finished the season with the AL’s best record at 98-64 and earned a first-round bye in the postseason.
The Yankees’ meanwhile, ended up 93-68, settling for the top Wild Card spot and a rematch with the overmatched Red Sox.
Cam Schlittler, who shoved in Game 1 of the Wild Card Series, said it was “frustrating” to lose the AL East to the Rays, but he tipped his hat to them, too.
“They’ve been great all year,” said Schlittler, who is expected to start Game 2 of the ALDS. “We had opportunities to take the [division] lead, and we couldn’t get that done.”
But, he said, “We’re on a roll at the right time.”
While the Yankees are hot after beating up on Boston, the rested Rays, who celebrated their division crown in the Bronx on Sept. 22, have home field advantage in the best-of-five ALDS. Carried by its quickness, pitching staff and Junior Caminero’s rising star, Tampa also has the comfort of knowing that it won the season series against the Yankees, 7-6.
“They bring speed to the game,” said Carlos Rodón, a candidate to start Game 1 of the ALDS alongside Gerrit Cole. “They have some good pitching. They play good defense. They’ll take the extra bag. They’re gonna be running. They’re gonna be bunting. You don’t see that in the game much anymore, but it’s worked for them. They’re a solid club. They play well, so it should be a good series.”
“It’s going to be a tough series,” Bellinger added.
If the Yankees are lucky, a reinforcement or two will join them in Florida for the showdown. Ryan Weathers, working his way back from a flexor strain as a reliever, could be one of them.
Getting Aaron Judge back would be a much bigger deal, however, after the back-to-back MVP watched the Wild Card Series from the bench in a jacket and a hoodie.
The Yankees managed to take Boston down without the captain after a right calf strain kept Judge off their Wild Card roster. On Wednesday, Boone said it’s “too early to tell” if Judge will be available for Game 1 of the ALDS, which begins on Saturday.
The manager added that Tampa Bay’s turfed Tropicana Field “could” factor into the Yankees’ decision with Judge having yet to run the bases. That call, however, is still a few days away from being made after the Yankees bought themselves some time with a quick Wild Card Series.
Judge, who lobbied to be on the Wild Card roster, declined to talk about his potential availability for the ALDS. But the slugger, who also missed 99 days with a fractured rib this season, did take a moment to praise what his peers have accomplished thus far.
“I’ve been so proud of these guys,” Judge said as he dodged champagne spritzes. “I’ve been out for quite a long time this season, and they never wavered. They never took a step back. They just kept going forward.”
“When the Yankees win, we all win. So it doesn’t matter if you played, didn’t play, hit the game-winning hit, pitched a shutout. We’re all wearing ‘NY’ in this room. That’s why we’re all celebrating together.”

item.title: [nydailynews.com] Luis Garcia Jr. has first Yankees moment in series-clinching win vs. Red Sox
item.dc:creator: James O'Connell

Never thought I was going to be part of [the Red Sox-Yankees rivalry in the postseason],” Garcia said before Game 2. “But my mom has a
item.content:encoded:
If you would’ve told Luis Garcia Jr. before this season what he’d be doing on Sept. 30, he probably wouldn’t believe you.
That’s because the 26-year-old was slated to bat in the middle of the order for the lowly Washington Nationals, who had virtually no aspirations of competing, with October as a good target month for a postseason vacation.
“No, no, not at all. Never thought I was going to be part of [the Red Sox-Yankees rivalry in the postseason],” Garcia said before Game 2. “But my mom has a good saying, and she’s always telling me never stop dreaming.”
Garcia delivered one of the biggest swings of the night for the Yankees in their Game 2 victory on Wednesday to eliminate the Boston Red Sox and advance from the Wild Card series to the ALDS to take on the Tampa Bay Rays.
The slugger launched a solo shot in the bottom of the fourth off of Red Sox starter Sonny Gray — who was cruising early — to jumpstart the Bombers offense that delivered another strong performance in their 9-2 victory, and hand them a much-needed early lead against an opponent that was on the ropes.
Garcia tossed his bat into the air and celebrated his first postseason moonshot.
“Not a lot is going through my mind in that moment. It’s just a reaction,” said Garcia. “But I could tell you what’s going through my body is just pure happiness. Being able to come through for the team, being able to put this team ahead in that moment, you’re just feeling joy as you’re running.”
It was Garcia’s first career homer in his first postseason start. He did get a taste of the playoffs during Tuesday’s victory, however, he was limited to just one pinch hit appearance.
On Wednesday, Garcia was one of the main reasons for the fans excitement in the Bronx. The left-handed hitter went 3-for-5 with a homer and two singles.
“It’s unforgettable, to be in the middle of all of that,” Garcia said. “Like I mentioned before the game, fans are standing from the first pitch until the last. Being in the middle of it and just taking it all in, I’m sure it’s something I’m not going to forget.”
The first baseman entered the postseason struggling mightily as he slashed .229/.250/.343 in 19 games during September. However, it was largely a solid run for Garcia during his first stint with the Yankees as he posted a .736 OPS in 43 games with the team.
Garcia is expected to pick up a bulk of the offensive load left behind by the injured Aaron Judge, who’s status remains uncertain heading into the upcoming series against the Rays.
Aaron Boone will almost certainly continue to pencil Garcia’s name into the third spot in the order, especially against right-handed pitching, for as long as this postseason run continues for the Yankees.

item.title: [sports.yahoo.com] Yankees undecided on ALDS Game 1 starter, but Gerrit Cole looking forward to his next turn

However, the team isn't going to divulge that information just yet. "We'll talk about that," Ya
item.content:encoded:
Now that the Yankees are heading to the American League Division Series to take on the Tampa Bay Rays, the next question is: who will start Game 1?
Cam Schlittler took the mound in Game 1 of the Wild Card Series and is expected to be called upon to start Game 2 against their AL East rivals, so it makes sense for Gerrit Cole -- who was going to start WC Game 3, if it went that far -- to be the starter. However, the team isn't going to divulge that information just yet.
"We'll talk about that," Yankees manager Aaron Boone said of the Game 1 starter. "Obviously, Gerrit's lined up for that. Carlos [Rodon] is very much in play for that. We have a ton of confidence in both guys. I think they're both throwing the ball really well. That will be what we do here these next couple of days as we get ready It's possible. It's definitely possible. Again, it's a long ways away."
Yankees pitching coach Matt Blake told the media, including The Athletic's Chris Kirschner, after Game 2's win that a decision on the Game 1 starter has yet to be made and reiterated what Boone said -- it'll either be Cole or Rodon.
The ALDS starts this Saturday, so a decision will be made really soon. But who is better suited to start the pivotal first game of the series?
Cole's last start came against the Rays back on Sept. 23, a week after the Yankees' Wild Card Series clinching win. In that start, he struck out eight batters and allowed two runs on three hits and three walks across 5.2 innings.
His last postseason start came in the now-infamous Game 5 of the 2024 World Series against the Dodgers. He pitched 6.2 innings, but allowed five unearned runs. His career postseason ERA sits at 2.77 across 22 starts.
"[Expecting] some good baseball. Just excited," Cole told SNY's Nikki Lattarulo of what he expects from the next series after Game 2. "I haven't pitched in a while. Looking forward to getting back out there."
Despite being down for about 10 days before his potential Game 1 start, Cole didn't say whether it's difficult being down that long, but is looking forward to when he pitches.
"It's the postseason, man. There's no expectations," he said. "You play when you're told to play and that's a beautiful thing."
Whether it's Cole or Rodon, the Yankees are confident in whoever toes the slab for them. It's been that way all season as they led all of MLB with a 3.24 team ERA.
"There's no question I feel great about those guys, obviously. That's been the biggest strength for us throughout the year," Boone said of his rotation. "It sustained us. It got us through some difficult times. And I feel like they're all in a good place right now. That's one of the ways we're going to have to do it, obviously leaning on the strength of those guys. But I like where they're at."
"Stick to our evaluation process and what we do, and our preparation," Cole said of how the team can keep their momentum. "We played well, but we'll look back, see what we could have done better and get ready for the next series."
The best-of-five series with the Rays begins Saturday at Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, Fla.

item.content:encoded:
On Wednesday, the New York Yankees will continue their series with the Boston Red Sox in the Bronx.
They won the first game (on Tuesday) by a score of 9-0.
A victory (on Wednesday) would send the Yankees to the ALDS for a series with the Tampa Bay Rays.
UPDATE: The Yankees won 9-2.
Kay Makes Statement On Volpe’s Future
Anthony Volpe got the start at second base on Tuesday.
He finished with one hit in three at-bats.
Ahead of the game, legendary Yankees broadcaster Michael Kay spoke about Volpe (via ESPN New York).
Kay: “I’ve been saying it since they brought up Lombard. Lombard impressed right away, and people said, “Well, that’s the last we’ll see of Anthony Volpe,” and it seemed like for some reason Yankee fans really turned against this guy. Now, he wasn’t what everybody expected him to be, but he did play shortstop for a team that went to the World Series, hit a grand slam in the World Series as well. Maybe he’s better suited at second. I have always felt, Dan, that he is going to be the second baseman next year.”
Looking At Volpe
Volpe finished the 2026 regular season batting .245 with 54 hits, two home runs, 28 RBIs, 24 runs and 12 stolen bases in 70 games.
He is in the middle of his fourth season in the MLB.
That said, Volpe also spent time in Triple-A this season.
Volpe was initially picked in the 1st round of the 2019 MLB Draft out of high school.
He has spent his entire career with New York.
Looking At The Yankees
The Yankees finished the year as the second-place team in the American League East with a 93-68 record in 161 games.
They are looking to win their first World Series title since 2009.

item.dc:creator: Dan Martin

item.content:encoded:
The Yankees have always insisted Spencer Jones was more than just a power hitter.
They also praised his quickness and athleticism.




Access the Yankees beat like never before


Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
It was that latter part that was on display in Wednesday’s Game 2 wild-card-clinching 9-2 win in The Bronx.
With the Yankees clinging to a two-run lead, Jones led off the bottom of the sixth against Garrett Crochet, one of the game’s premier lefty pitchers, just coming back from a five-month absence because of a shoulder injury.
Jones whiffed, but Crochet badly bounced the third strike, and it got away from Adley Rutschman.
Jones hustled down the line, and after initially being ruled out, reached first when the call was overturned.
“When he gets it going, he can really go,’’ Aaron Boone said.
The 6-foot-7 Jones then attempted to steal second, and Rutschman’s throw went into center, allowing Jones to get to third.
With the infield in, fellow rookie George Lombard Jr. drove in Jones with a single to spark a six-run inning.
“Speed is something I’ve always had,’’ Jones said. “I’m glad it worked out. It was a fun night.”
There have been a few of those lately for the 25-year-old, who has contributed in numerous ways down the stretch after getting off to a 4-for-24 start with 12 strikeouts in his first 10 games in the majors.
When Jones returned to The Bronx later in the season, he had improved his approach at the plate and showed he could hit in the majors.
Jim Hendry, special assistant to GM Brian Cashman — who was among the Yankee scouts who evaluated Jones while he was at Vanderbilt — said the fast development shouldn’t come as much of a surprise.
“Big guys like that, it takes them longer to adjust,’’ Hendry said prior to the game. “Sure, they’re gonna strike out a lot. They’ve got more holes to figure out how to fix. But you know when they do, they can be special.”
As Hendry noted, the Yankees “have always liked big players.”
Still, there aren’t many examples of players Jones’ size hitting well, with Aaron Judge and Giancarlo Stanton being two exceptions.
Jones is trying to become another, and the Yankees have seen some promising signs in the second half of the season.
As they’ve dealt with the lengthy absence of Judge because of rib and calf injuries, multiple injuries to Trent Grisham, as well as another disappointing season from Jasson Domínguez, Jones has been thrust into an important role.
In Game 1, the Yankees went with the lefty-swinging Jones against left-hander Payton Tolle.
Shop Yankees Merch
He had a pair of solid at-bats against Tolle, and Aaron Boone said Wednesday that he considered having Giancarlo Stanton pinch hit for Jones to lead off the bottom of the seventh against another southpaw, Alec Gamboa.
Instead, Boone stayed with Jones, who singled.
Among the reasons Boone stuck with Jones was the success he’d had versus lefties in the majors — just part of what’s developing into a well-rounded game for the former first-round pick.
“It’s hard in the modern game to hit when you’re 6-foot-7,’’ Hendry said. “But when you do it well, you don’t have to worry about launch and other things. When you’re that big, the ball lifts itself. He’s still got a lot of work to do, but he’s becoming a good player already.”

It's the second straight season Fried shut down Boston in the wild-card round, as he f
item.content:encoded:
Fried earned the win in Game 2 of the AL Wild Card Series against the Red Sox on Wednesday. He struck out six and allowed one run on three hits and one walk over six innings.
The veteran left-hander was working on a shutout until Willson Contreras launched a two-out, solo homer during the top of the sixth inning, which spelled an end to his day after the Yankees erupted for six runs in the bottom of the frame. It's the second straight season Fried shut down Boston in the wild-card round, as he fired 6.1 scoreless frames in Game 1 of that series last year. He missed time in 2026 due to elbow issues but still made 20 regular-season starts and had a 2.80 ERA, 0.99 WHIP and 104:33 K:BB across 112.2 innings.

item.title: [New York Post] Cody Bellinger makes Red Sox pay with game-changing homer to help seal Yankees’ wild-card series win
item.dc:creator: Mark W Sanchez
item.description:
There were reasons for Cody Bellinger to feel disrespected, even if he publicly shrugged off both. The Red Sox wanted to pitch to a slugging outfielder who had been signed to a $162.5 million contract this winter. With two outs in the sixth inning and Trent Grisham on second base, Boston intentionally walked Ben Rice to take its chances with Bellinger.
Access the Yankees beat like never before
Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time
item.content:encoded:
There were reasons for Cody Bellinger to feel disrespected, even if he publicly shrugged off both.
The Red Sox wanted to pitch to a slugging outfielder who had been signed to a $162.5 million contract this winter. With two outs in the sixth inning and Trent Grisham on second base, Boston intentionally walked Ben Rice to take its chances with Bellinger.




Access the Yankees beat like never before


Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
And after Bellinger reached out and got just enough juice behind a Garrett Whitlock changeup for a three-run home run, he slowly trotted around the bases in a fashion that hinted he may have noticed Boston’s Willson Contreras had done the same in the top of the inning.
Regardless of the motivations, Bellinger’s execution was flawless in turning a close game lopsided, his blast the last that mattered in what became a 9-2 smacking of the Red Sox to clinch the wild-card series Wednesday in The Bronx and earn a date with the Rays in the ALDS.
Chad Tracy and the Red Sox had reason to prefer facing Bellinger in what was then a game they trailed, 5-1, simply because Bellinger was not Rice. A night earlier, the Yankees first baseman/DH was unstoppable in going 4-for-5 with a pair of home runs and six RBIs. And in his previous at-bat Wednesday, Rice had stroked a single through the right side.
And so it was Bellinger whom the Red Sox chose, though the veteran said he did not take the decision personally.
“I had a feeling that they might do that,” Bellinger said in a clubhouse filled with puddles of beer. “I think when you hit behind [Aaron] Judge so often, you just get used to it.”
Shop Yankees Merch
If he were not especially inspired, he instead was just himself: a good hitter who got under the Whitlock changeup, lifting it high enough that there was no doubt it would be a home run or an out at the wall. He did not know if he got enough.
He did, with an assist to Yankee Stadium, the only ballpark in which that ball would leave the yard.
“I enjoyed it. That was a cool moment,” said Bellinger, who enjoyed an unusually slow trot around the bases.
He walked, then slow-jogged to first, saw it land in the stands 360 feet away just beyond the reach of Wilyer Abreu, and then saw no reason to speed up.
Just a few minutes earlier, Contreras had popped a home run for the Red Sox’s first run of the series and ran as if he wanted Boston to savor every moment of the drought-stopper. The trot was officially clocked at 30.09 seconds.
“I didn’t even see [Contreras’ trot],” said Bellinger, sidestepping any notion of pettiness.
Regardless, in a series in which the Yankees beat the Red Sox in every way imaginable, this possible battle of pettiness went to the Yankees too: Bellinger slogged around the bases absorbing the cheers just a bit longer at 31.29 seconds.

item.title: [bostonherald.com] Yankees humiliate, eliminate Red Sox in Wild Card for second straight year
item.dc:creator: Gabrielle Starr
item.description: NEW YORK – As the Red Sox were outscored 18-2 and eliminated in a two-game Wild Card sweep by the Yankees on Tuesday (9-0) and Wednesday night (9-2) at Yankee Stadium, the aura of ‘Fool me once, shame on you; fool me twice, shame on me’ was brutal and undeniable. A week after the 2025 Red Sox fell to their eternal rivals in the Wild Card round in the Bronx, including a shutout in the deciding Game 3, chief baseball officer Craig Breslow sat in the Fenway Park interview room, flanked by manager A
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK – As the Red Sox were outscored 18-2 and eliminated in a two-game Wild Card sweep by the Yankees on Tuesday (9-0) and Wednesday night (9-2) at Yankee Stadium, the aura of ‘Fool me once, shame on you; fool me twice, shame on me’ was brutal and undeniable.
A week after the 2025 Red Sox fell to their eternal rivals in the Wild Card round in the Bronx, including a shutout in the deciding Game 3, chief baseball officer Craig Breslow sat in the Fenway Park interview room, flanked by manager Alex Cora and team president Sam Kennedy, and declared that adding home-run power to the lineup would be a top priority for 2025-26 offseason.
Breslow reiterated as much throughout the ensuing months, while the front office failed to sign any of the top free-agent hitters, including Alex Bregman, who opted out of his Red Sox contract and went to the Chicago Cubs after the former refused to give him a no-trade clause.
The week after Bregman signed his five-year deal with the Cubs in mid-January, Breslow inked left-hander Ranger Suarez to a five-year contract. Breslow then proclaimed at Suarez’s introductory presser, “I don’t think there’s a question anymore that the identity of our team, the strength of our team, is going to be our pitching.”
And it was. So much so that when the Red Sox and Yankees met in the Wild Card round again this week, the Boston bats were silent as the grave.
“Uncompetitive. We got boat-raced,” veteran infielder Isiah Kiner-Falefa told reporters postgame. “To lose in the Wild Card is unacceptable.”
Hitting, or lack thereof, was far from the only problem. Chad Tracy’s inexperience was on display, particularly where pitching decisions were concerned. The new Red Sox skipper managed both contests, not like the must-win games they were, but like a Triple-A game, where there is endless runway because the priority is player development and any victories are simply a nice bonus.
Yankees batters did plenty of damage, and the Red Sox played non-urgent defense at times. But offense remained Boston’s most glaring issue, because it was the key offseason need left unmet.
Yankees southpaw Max Fried allowed one earned run on three hits, walked one and struck out six over six innings (98 pitches, 62 strikes).
Red Sox starter Sonny Gray was largely dominant in 4 2/3 innings. He allowed two earned runs on six hits, issued zero walks and struck out five.
But for the second straight game, Tracy pulled his starter with two outs in the fifth in favor of left-hander Erik Miller, who had allowed earned runs in four of his last five regular-season appearances, and immediately given up a home run to Ben Rice in Game 1.
Rice scored on Miller again in Game 2, in the form of a start-ending single off Gray and Cody Bellinger’s RBI single off the Sox southpaw.
But the true implosion came when Garrett Crochet took the mound in the bottom of the sixth, his first game at any level since April 25. All four Yankees batters reached before Tracy called upon righty Garrett Whitlock. An Austin Wells RBI sacrifice fly and Ryan McMahon RBI groundout increased the lead to 5-1. After an intentional walk to Rice, Bellinger took Whitlock deep to put a long-over game firmly in the ground.
New York out-hit Boston 14-4 on Wednesday night. The losing team managed two walks, struck out eight times, were 0 for 2 with runners in scoring position, and left four men on base.
The 2026 Red Sox took steps forward. Pitching was largely better, the postseason notwithstanding. Defense was markedly better, an irony that cannot be lost on Cora, who spent years lamenting his team’s poor defense, only to see them improve right before and after his late-April firing.
But the Red Sox also took steps backward this year; some baffling, some beyond their control, others by their own design.
They finished this regular season 87-75, two losses worse than last year.
The offense was markedly worse. The 2025 Red Sox collectively slashed .254/.324/.421 with 324 doubles, and 186 home runs in the regular season. They finished this regular season with a .245/.319/.397 line, 285 doubles, and 163 home runs. (Bregman finished the regular season with 28 home runs, more than any player on the Red Sox roster; he drove the point home, literally, by hitting the last two off Boston pitchers in Game 162 on Sunday.)
True, the Red Sox struck out significantly less this year – 1,326 down from 1,419 – but they also finished one walk shy of last year’s total (518).
Above all, they scored 689 runs this year, a whopping 97 fewer than last year.
The two things the 2025 Red Sox needed most in October, runs and homer power, were in even shorter supply on Wednesday night. As a result, their “October run” came to an end before the month even began.
The 2026 Red Sox were a horror show at both start and finish.
But in the immortal words of the movie “Grease,” “Oh! Those summer nights.”

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK — Cody Bellinger hit a three-run homer during a six-run sixth inning and finished with four RBIs as the New York Yankees pulled away for a 9-2 rout of the Boston Red Sox on Wednesday and a two-game sweep of an American League wild-card series.
The Yankees beat the Red Sox in the wild-card round for the second straight year and were significantly more prolific at the plate than last year, when they needed three games to advance.
Despite the absence of Aaron Judge, who has a strained right calf, New York scored 18 runs and totaled 26 hits in the series to advance to the AL Division Series against the top-seeded Tampa Bay Rays. The best-of-five ALDS begins Saturday in St. Petersburg, Fla.
Bellinger capped New York’s big inning by hitting a 1-0 changeup from Garrett Whitlock into the right-center-field seats after the Red Sox opted to intentionally walk Ben Rice. The blast pushed New York’s lead to 8-1.
In the fifth, Bellinger chopped an RBI single against left-hander Erik Miller over second baseman Nick Sogard’s head to give the Yankees a 2-0 lead.
New York’s Max Fried (1-0) followed Cam Schlittler’s dominance in the series opener by allowing one run on three hits in six innings on Wednesday. Fried struck out six and walked one.
Luis Garcia Jr. also homered for the Yankees, connecting against Sonny Gray’s 1-2 sweeper while leading off the fourth to open the scoring.
The Yankees sent 10 to the plate against Garrett Crochet and Whitlock in their big inning, getting things started with rookie Spencer Jones hustling around the bases.
Jones started things by reaching on a wild-pitch strikeout when he beat catcher Adley Rutschman’s throw by a step on a call that was overturned on replay after the Yankees challenged. Jones then stole second, advanced to third on Rutschman’s throwing error and scored on George Lombard Jr.’s single.
After singles by Jazz Chisholm Jr. and Trent Grisham loaded the bases, Whitlock replaced Crochet. Austin Wells lifted a sacrifice fly, and Ryan McMahon followed with a soft RBI groundout for a 5-1 lead.
Willson Contreras homered off Fried in the sixth, and Nick Sogard homered off Will Warren in the seventh.
Wells added an RBI single in the bottom of the seventh.
Gray (0-1) allowed two runs on six hits in 4 2/3 innings, with five strikeouts and no walks. Crochet made his first appearance since April 25, having recovered from a shoulder ailment, and was charged with four runs without recording an out.
The Red Sox finished with seven hits in the series and experienced a disappointing end to a season where they overcame firing their manager in April and having a 32-46 record in late June. Boston vaulted into playoff contention with a 32-5 surge that included a 15-game winning streak but struggled at the plate in the final month.

item.content:encoded:
It took seven seasons and 751 regular-season games for Luis García Jr. to get his first shot as a starter in a playoff game.
It then took all of two at-bats Wednesday for the slugger to make it count.




Access the Yankees beat like never before


Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
García, who had spent his career with the Nationals until the trade deadline and had never played a postseason game before pinch hitting Tuesday, earned the start a night later and immediately demonstrated why he always is in the lineup against opposing right-handers.
The ice-breaking swing of what would become a 9-2, going-away blowout of the Red Sox to clinch the wild-card series belonged to García, who made sure his first trip to October (or technically late September) would be memorable.
In a scoreless game in the fourth inning with former Yankee Sonny Gray dealing, García stepped to the plate and stepped up. He got a 1-2 sweeper that was not poorly located — right at the bottom of the strike zone — but showed off a violent swing and rare power, clubbing the pitch 387 feet into the bleachers in right-center to begin another strong night for the Yankees offense.
When the Yankees traded for García, the fit did not look natural. He was another first baseman on a team that had two (Ben Rice and Paul Goldschmidt) or maybe a DH on a team that was awaiting a return from its DH (Giancarlo Stanton).
But a swing like García’s, which produced 30 total homers this season and seven after the trade, will be shoehorned into lineups regardless. And further injuries, such as another calf strain to Stanton, ensured García would be a factor either way.
While sitting against lefty Payton Tolle on Tuesday, García looked around and breathed in an atmosphere he had never experienced before.
“The experience is very different, actually — just seeing the atmosphere around the ballpark, the fans standing from pitch one all the way to the end, very different,” García said Wednesday afternoon through interpreter Marlon Abreu. “At the same time, very exciting. You can feel the excitement in the air.”
Also in the air was a home run and a pair of singles in the fifth and sixth innings, including a rare left-on-left knock against Erik Miller on a play that ended with Ben Rice gunned down at the plate.
Given a chance — a first in the series and a first in his career — García did some of everything to ensure he would have more playoff chances this weekend.
